## Khuddaka Nikāya
## Therīgāthā-Aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Ekakanipāta
## 1. Aññatarātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

Now the opportunity has arrived to explain the meaning of the Therīgāthā. Among these verses of the elder nuns, if the explanation is made by first showing how they obtained the state of a nun and higher ordination (upasampadā), the origin of the circumstances (aṭṭhuppatti) for those various verses will be easy to distinguish and very clear. Therefore, in order to show that matter, I shall briefly state this sequential account starting from the beginning:

This Lord of the World, the Buddha, having fulfilled the eight factors such as "being human, being of the male sex," etc., made the great aspiration (mahābhinīhāra) at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara. While fulfilling the thirty perfections (pāramīs), he received the prophecy in the presence of twenty-four Buddhas and fulfilled the perfections in due order. Having reached the pinnacle of the three modes of conduct—conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and conduct for the attainment of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā)—he was reborn in the Tusita heaven and stayed there for the full lifespan. At that time, the deities and Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems requested him to become a Buddha:

"O Great Hero, it is time for you to take conception in your mother's womb.
Saving the world together with its devas,
May you realize the deathless state of Nibbāna."
2:
Having accepted the request of the deities and Brahmas and having made the five great observations, he descended into his mother's womb with mindfulness and clear comprehension in the palace of the Great King Suddhodana of the Sakyan clan. He stayed in that womb for ten months with mindfulness and clear comprehension, and with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he emerged from that womb. Born in the delightful Lumbinī grove of Sal trees, he was well-cared for by a great retinue, including various nurses, and grew up in due order. While enjoying pleasures like a son of the devas, surrounded by various dancers in three palaces, he experienced spiritual urgency (saṃvega) upon seeing old age, sickness, and death. As his wisdom reached maturity, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation (nekkhamma).

On the day Prince Rāhula was born, riding the horse Kanthaka with the courtier Channa, he made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) at midnight through the gate opened by the deities. Within the remainder of that very night, he crossed three kingdoms, reached the bank of the Anomā River, and went forth as a monk, accepting the requisites of an Arahant (arahattaddhaja) brought by the Great Brahma Ghaṭīkāra. At that very moment, endowed with the appearance of an elder of sixty years' standing, he reached the city of Rājagaha in due order with an inspiring deportment. While wandering for alms in that city and partaking of the alms-food at the foot of Mount Paṇḍava, he was invited by the King of Magadha with the offer of the kingdom, but he refused it. Having gone to the hermitage of the sage Bhaggava and studied his doctrine, he then studied the doctrines of Āḷāra and Uddaka. Realizing all those doctrines were without essence, he proceeded in due order to the Uruvelā forest and there practiced austerities (dukkaracariyā) for six years.

Realizing that the Noble Dhamma could not be penetrated through such practices, thinking "This is not the path to enlightenment," he took solid food and regained his strength within a few days. On the full moon day of Visākhā, he partook of the excellent milk-rice offered by Sujātā and floated the golden bowl upstream in the river. Having made the resolution, "Today I shall become a Buddha," in the evening, receiving the praises of the Naga King Kāla, he ascended the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimanda). Facing the eastern world-sphere in an unshakeable place, he sat upon the Unconquered Throne (Aparājita-pallaṅka) and resolved upon the fourfold effort. Even before the sun set, he defeated the army of Māra, and in the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), and in the last watch, he applied his knowledge to dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). Contemplating the chain of causes in forward and reverse order, and developing insight (vipassanā), he attained the Supreme Self-Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi) which is unique and attained by all Buddhas. With the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) having Nibbāna as its object, right there...
3:
Having spent seven days [at the foot of the Bodhi tree], and in the same manner having spent other seven-day periods at the Bodhimaṇḍa, He partook of the Madhupiṇḍika food at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Again, while staying at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, He reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma as is its nature. As His mind inclined towards inaction [due to the difficulty for beings to understand], He was entreated by Mahābrahmā. Surveying the world with the Buddha-eye, He saw beings with varying degrees of faculties, such as those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties, and He gave His word to Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma.

Reflecting, 'To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?', He realized that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away. He then thought, 'The five monks (Pañcavaggiya) who attended to me while I was striving in my ascetic practices were of great help to me. It would be well if I first taught the Dhamma to the five monks.' On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, He set out from the Great Bodhi tree towards the city of Bārāṇasī, a journey of eighteen yojanas. On the way, He conversed with Upaka the Ājīvaka and eventually reached Isipatana Migadāya. There, making the five monks understand, He delivered the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, beginning with 'Monks, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth.' He thus offered the nectar of the Dhamma to eighteen crores of Brahmas, led by Aññāsikoṇḍañña.

On the first day of the waning moon, He established Venerable Bhaddiya in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala); on the second day, Venerable Vappa; on the third day, Venerable Mahānāma; and on the fourth day, Venerable Assaji. On the fifth day, through the discourse of the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, He established all of them [the five monks] in the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). Furthermore, He led many people into the Noble Plane (Ariyabhūmi), including the fifty-five men led by the merchant's son Yasa, the thirty Bhaddavaggiya youths in the Kappāsika grove, and the thousand former matted-hair ascetics on the Gayāsīsa stone slab. He established eleven nahutas (110,000) of people led by King Bimbisāra in the fruit of Stream-entry, and one nahuta (10,000) in the three refuges. Having accepted the donation of the Veḷuvana monastery, He resided there.

Sāriputta, who had attained the first path because of Venerable Assaji, took leave of Sañjaya the wanderer and, together with his followers, approached the Buddha. The Buddha enabled Sāriputta and Moggallāna to realize the highest fruit, and when they reached the pinnacle of the perfection of a disciple (sāvaka-pāramī), He appointed them to the positions of Chief Disciples. At the request of Venerable Kāḷudāyī, He went to the city of Kapilavatthu. He subdued His proud relatives with the Twin Miracle (Yamakapāṭihāriya) and established His father in the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala) and Mahāpajāpatī in the fruit of Stream-entry.
4:
Having established the Dispensation and ordained Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula, the Teacher returned once more to the city of Rājagaha.

At another time, while the Teacher was staying at the Kūṭāgārasālā in Vesālī, King Suddhodana realized the fruit of Arahantship even while under the white royal umbrella and attained Parinibbāna. At that time, the desire to ordain arose in Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Then, five hundred princesses, who had been attending to the five hundred princes who had left the world and ordained at the end of the Kalahavivāda Sutta discourse on the banks of the Rohiṇī River, shared the same desire. They approached Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and, making her their leader, all the princesses wished to go to the Teacher to ordain, saying, 'We shall ordain in the presence of the Teacher.' This Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī had previously requested ordination from the Teacher once but did not receive it. Therefore, she summoned a barber, had her hair cut, put on saffron-colored robes, and taking all those Sākiyan princesses, went to Vesālī. Through Venerable Ānanda, she entreated the Buddha, the Possessor of Ten Powers, and by accepting the eight heavy rules (Garudhamma), she obtained ordination and the act of Upasampadā. All the other princesses also received ordination at the same time. This is a brief summary here; the detailed account of this story appears in various Pali texts (Cūḷavagga, 402).

Having thus attained ordination, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. Taking a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher, she attained the fruit of Arahantship. The remaining five hundred bhikkhunīs also attained the fruit of Arahantship at the end of the Nandakovāda Sutta discourse. In this way, when the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha was well-established and grew in number, noble women, noble daughters-in-law, and noble maidens in various villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals heard of the Buddha's perfect enlightenment, the excellence of the Dhamma, and the good conduct of the Saṅgha. Being greatly inspired by the Dispensation and feeling spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding saṃsāra, they obtained permission from their husbands, parents, and relatives. Dedicating themselves to the Dispensation, they ordained. After ordaining, being endowed with virtue and proper conduct, they received instructions from the Teacher and various elders. Through their diligent efforts, they soon realized the fruit of Arahantship. Those bhikkhunīs, by the power of their inspired utterances (udāna) and such, in various...
5:
Later, the Elders who were the Reciters (Saṅgītikārakas) compiled the verses that had been spoken, organizing them into sections such as the Book of Ones (Ekanipāta), and conducted the rehearsal, saying, "These are called the Therīgāthā." The classification of these verses into sections (Nipātas) and so forth has already been mentioned below. Among those sections, the Book of Ones is the first. In that Book of Ones—

"Sleep happily, Therikā, clad in a robe made of rags;
For your lust is stilled and dried up,
Like dried vegetables in a pot."

This verse is the first. What is the origin of this verse? In the past, during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, a certain daughter of a good family, having great faith in the Dispensation, invited the Teacher. On the second day, she had a pavilion of branches constructed, spread sand, hung a canopy above, and after making offerings of scents, flowers, and so forth, informed the Teacher that it was time for the meal. The Teacher went there and sat on the prepared seat. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and served Him with choice food and edibles, she presented the Blessed One—who had finished His meal and removed His hand from the bowl—with a set of three robes (ticīvara). The Blessed One gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) to her and departed.

Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she was reborn in the celestial realm at the end of her life. Wandering only through the happy destinies (sugati) for an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara), she was reborn in a householder’s family during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa. Upon reaching maturity, she felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the round of rebirths, ordained in the Dispensation, and after receiving higher ordination, fulfilled the precepts of a bhikkhunī for twenty thousand years. Passing away while still a worldling (puthujjana), she was reborn in the celestial realm. After enjoying celestial bliss for an entire interval between Buddhas, she was reborn in this Buddha’s era in Vesālī, in a family of wealthy nobles (khattiyamahāsāla). Because she had a firm and calm body, they called her "Therikā."

When she reached maturity, her parents gave her in marriage to a young noble of equal status. While living as a devoted wife who revered her husband like a deity, she gained faith in the Dispensation when the Teacher came to Vesālī and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, after hearing the Dhamma from the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatigotamī, a desire to ordain arose in her, and she asked her husband for permission, saying, "I wish to ordain." Her husband did not grant permission. However, because she had performed requisite merits (adhikāra) in the past, she reflected on the Dhamma she had heard, discerned the phenomena of mind and matter (rūpa-arūpa), and lived devoted to insight meditation (vipassanā).

Then one day, while a curry was being cooked in the kitchen, a great flame arose. That flame burned the entire pot, making a crackling "tata-tata" sound. Seeing that fire...
6:
Taking that very object, she contemplated it, making the nature of impermanence (aniccatā) very clear. Beyond that, she applied the characteristics of suffering, impermanence, and non-self (dukkha, anicca, anatta) to that object, developed insight, and by gradually striving through the sequence of the paths, she was established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). From then on, that woman no longer wore jewelry or ornaments. When asked by her husband, "Dear, why do you no longer wear jewelry or ornaments as you did before?", she informed him of her inability to enjoy the lay life and obtained his permission to ordain. Like the lay follower Visākha for Dhammadinnā, her husband took her to Mahāpajāpatigotamī with a great retinue and said, "Noble Lady, please ordain this person." Then Mahāpajāpatigotamī ordained her, granted her higher ordination, and taking her to the monastery, presented her to the Teacher. The Teacher, clarifying the very object she had naturally seen, spoke the verse beginning with "Sukhaṃ supāhi."

In that verse, "sukhaṃ" is an adverbial designation (bhāvanapuṃsakaniddesa). "Supāhi" is a word of command (āṇattivacana). "Therike" is a word of address (āmantanavacana). "Katvā coḷena pārutā" is an exhortation toward fewness of wishes (appicchatā). "Upasanto hi te rāgo" is a praise of her practice. "Sukkhaḍākaṃvā" shows the essence-less nature of the defilements that are to be stilled. "Kumbhiyaṃ" shows the nature of impermanence, emptiness, and so forth of the body, which is the support for those defilements.

"Sukhaṃ" is a designation for what is desired. It means "happily, being free from suffering." Although "supāhi" indicates lying down, it refers to all four postures. Therefore, it means "spend your time happily in all four postures; live happily." Although "Therike" is her name, because it is generally a significant name (anvatthasaññā), it means "one who has reached a state of firmness in the firm Dispensation, one who is endowed with firm qualities such as virtue (sīla)." "Katvā coḷena pārutā" means having the body covered by making a robe out of rag-cloth (paṃsukūla), being both dressed in and covered by that robe. In "upasanto hi te rāgo," the word "hi" has a causal meaning (hetvattha). It means: because the sensual lust (kāmarāga) that tends to arise in your continuity has been stilled, being burned by the fire of the knowledge of the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga), now burn the remaining lust with the fire of the knowledge of the Highest Path (arahattamagga) and live happily. "Sukkhaḍākaṃva kumbhiyaṃ" means "like dried vegetables in a pot." For example, when a small amount of vegetable curry in a cooked pot is cooked with a great flame, it burns, dries up, and is stilled. Or, when vegetable curry mixed with water is placed on a stove and cooked, as long as there is water, it makes the sound "cicciṭāyati ciṭiciṭāyati"...
7:
Just as when water is cut off, it becomes still, so too has sensual desire (kāmarāga) become still in your continuity. Having stilled the remaining defilements as well, sleep peacefully. Because that Therī had reached the maturity of her faculties and through the Buddha's manner of teaching, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) at the conclusion of the verse. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna: 

“I had a pavilion built for the Buddha Koṇāgamana. I constantly offered the three robes to the Buddha, the kinsman of the world. To whichever province, town, or royal capital I go, I am honored in every place; this is the fruit of my meritorious deed. My defilements (kilesas) have been burnt away; all existences have been uprooted. Like a female elephant having broken her bonds, I live without taints (anāsava). My coming into the presence of the Best of Buddhas was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) have been attained; the Buddha’s bidding has been done. The four analytical insights, the eight liberations (vimokkha), and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) have been realized; the Buddha’s bidding has been done.”

Upon reaching Arahantship, while uttering an inspired utterance (udāna), the Therī recited that very verse; therefore, this verse became the verse of that Therī. In that verse, the “stilling” spoken of by the Therī refers to the total eradication of greed (rāga) by the Path of Arahantship (aggamagga). It should be understood that by the stilling of greed alone, the stilling of all defilements is meant, because all defilements are stilled by the accomplishment of the stilling of greed, as they share the same purpose. Thus it is said:

“That delusion (moha) which is known to be co-nascent with restlessness (uddhacca) and doubt (vicikiccha) is abandoned along with greed, because they share the same state in the matter of abandonment.”

Just as the stilling of all defilements is spoken of here, it should be understood that their stilling is spoken of in all contexts. This is because the accomplishment of stilling occurs in the preliminary stage by substitution (tadaṅga), at the moment of serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā) by suppression (vikkhambhana), at the moment of the Path by eradication (samuccheda), and at the moment of the Fruit by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi). In this way, the four kinds of abandonment are accomplished.
8:
It should be understood. In that context, the fulfillment of the perfection of virtue (sīlasampadā) is shown through abandonment by substitution (tadaṅgapahāna), the fulfillment of the perfection of concentration (samādhisampadā) through abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna), and the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (paññāsampadā) through the remaining types of abandonment, because of the accomplishment of the breakthrough by abandonment (pahānābhisamaya). Just as the breakthrough by development (bhāvanābhisamaya) is achieved—since without it, those (virtue, concentration, wisdom) cannot exist—so too are the breakthrough by realization (sacchikiriyābhisamaya) and the breakthrough by full understanding (pariññābhisamaya) achieved. It should be understood that through the accomplishment of the four breakthroughs by this verse, the three trainings (sikkhā), the threefold excellence of the practice (paṭipatti), and the seven purifications (visuddhi) are fulfilled. The meaning is that a certain Therī, whose name and clan were not well-known but who was endowed with the marks, recited this verse.

## Commentary on the Verse of the Unknown Therī is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verse of Muttā Therī

“Muttā, be free from the bonds (yogas), like the moon from the grasp of Rāhu;
With a mind fully liberated, being debtless, eat the alms-food.”

This is the verse of a probationer (sikkhamānā) named Muttā. She too, having performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, was born into a respectable family during the time of the Buddha Vipassī. When she came of age, one day she saw the Teacher walking on the road and, with a devoted heart, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration and, moved by a surge of joy, lay prostrate at the Teacher's feet. Due to that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the deva world and wandered only through happy destinies (sugati). In this Buddha's era, she was born in Sāvatthī into a wealthy Brahmin family and was named Muttātissā. Being endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), at the age of twenty, she went forth into the Buddha's Dispensation under Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. While still a probationer, she requested a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and applied herself to the work of insight (vipassanā). One day, after finishing her meal and returning from the alms-round, she performed her duties toward the elder nuns and went to her daytime resting place. Sitting in seclusion, she began to apply her mind to insight. The Teacher, while staying in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), emitted a radiance and, appearing as if sitting before her, spoke this verse: “Muttā, be free from the bonds.”
9:
In that verse, 'Muttā' is an address to her. 'Be free from the bonds' means to be liberated from the four bonds such as the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga) through the sequence of the Path; become one whose mind is liberated from those bonds. In what way? 'Like the moon from the grasp of Rāhu' means to be free from the defilements (upakkilesa) like the moon from the grasp known as Rāhu. 'With a mind fully liberated' (vippamuttena cittena) means with a mind well-liberated through the Noble Path by way of liberation through eradication (samucchedavimutti); here, the instrumental case denotes the characteristic of a state. 'Being debtless, eat the alms-food' means having abandoned the debt of defilements, being debtless, you should eat the alms-food of the country. For one who consumes the requisites permitted by the Teacher without abandoning defilements is said to eat as a debtor. As the Venerable Bākula said: 'Friends, for only seven days did I eat the alms-food of the country as a debtor.' Therefore, one who has gone forth in the Dispensation should consume the gifts of faith being debtless, in order to abandon the debt of sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth. 'Alms-food' (piṇḍakaṃ) is merely the head of the teaching; the meaning is all four requisites. 'He exhorted her repeatedly' means that by her reaching the Noble Path, He gave many exhortations while purifying the defilements.

That Therī Muttā, established in that exhortation, attained Arahantship before long. Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna: 'When the Buddha Vipassī... was walking on the road... I came out from my house and prostrated in worship... The Buddha stepped upon my head... With that devoted heart, I went to the Tusita heaven... My defilements have been burnt... the Buddha's bidding has been done.' Upon reaching Arahantship, she uttered that very verse as an inspired utterance. Having fulfilled the training and reached the status of a fully ordained nun, she also recited that same verse later at the time of her final passing (parinibbāna).

## Commentary on the Verse of Muttā Therī is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇā

The verse beginning with "Puṇṇe pūrassu dhammehi" is the verse of a probationer (sikkhamānā) named Puṇṇā. This Elder Puṇṇā also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and, while accumulating the merit of being a powerful support for Nibbāna (vivaṭṭūpanissaya-kusala) in various lives, she was born as a Kinnarī on the banks of the Candabhāgā River in a world empty of Buddhas. One day, seeing a certain Paccekabuddha there, with a devoted mind, she worshipped that Paccekabuddha with a garland of reeds and stood with joined palms.

Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered only in the happy realms of devas and was born in this Buddha's era into a wealthy merchant family in Sāvatthī. Her name was Puṇṇātissā. Being endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya), at the age of twenty, she heard the Dhamma from Mahāpajāpatigotamī, gained faith, and ordained in the Buddha's Dispensation. As a sikkhamānā, she began the practice of insight (vipassanā). The Blessed One, while staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), emitted a radiance and spoke this verse:

"Puṇṇā, be full of good qualities, like the moon on the fifteenth day of the full moon.
With perfected wisdom, shatter the mass of darkness."

In that verse, "Puṇṇe" is an address to her. "Pūrassu dhammehi" means may you be full of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma). In "cando pannaraseriva", the 'ra' is merely a euphonic connector (padasandhi). It means like the moon that is full in all its parts on the fifteenth day of the full moon. "Paripuṇṇāya paññāya" means with the wisdom of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-paññā) which is perfected by the completion of the sixteen tasks. "Tamokhandhaṃ padālaya" means shatter the mass of delusion (moha) completely; destroy it at the root. Along with the shattering of the mass of delusion, all defilements (kilesa) are also shattered.

Having heard that verse and developing insight, she attained Arahatship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"On the bank of the Candabhāgā River, I was then a Kinnarī.
I saw the stainless Buddha, the Self-Become, the Unconquered.
With a devoted mind and joyful heart, with joined palms,
Taking a garland of reeds, I worshipped the Self-Become."
11:
Through that well-performed deed, intention, and aspiration, abandoning the Kinnarī body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa realm.

I was the chief queen of thirty-six celestial kings, and I was the chief queen of ten universal monarchs. Having brought spiritual urgency (saṃvega) to my heart, I renounced the home life and ordained.

My defilements are burnt away; all births are uprooted. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

Ninety-four aeons ago, I worshipped with a flower; because of that flower offering, I have not known a bad rebirth.

My defilements are burnt away... I have carried out the Buddha's Dispensation."

Upon attaining Arahatship, that Elder spoke that very verse as an exclamation (udāna). This was her declaration of enlightenment (aññābyākaraṇa).

## End of the Commentary on the Verses of Elder Puṇṇā.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tissā

The verse beginning with "Tissā, train in the three trainings" was spoken to Elder Tissā while she was a sikkhamānā. This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated the merit of being a powerful support for Nibbāna (vivaṭṭūpanissaya-kusala) throughout her lives. By the power of that accumulated merit, she was born in this Buddha's era into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. When she reached of age, she became a consort of the Bodhisatta. Later, she renounced the world together with Mahāpajāpatigotamī, ordained, and practiced the work of insight (vipassanā). To her, the Blessed One, as mentioned before, emitted a radiance and spoke the verse:

"Tissā, train in the three trainings. Let not the opportunities (yogas) pass you by.
Free from all bonds, wander the world without taints."

In that verse, "Tisse" is an address to that Elder. "Sikkhassu sikkhāya" means train in the three trainings, starting with the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā). The three trainings associated with the Path...
12:
...means fulfill the three trainings. Now, to show the reason for fulfilling them, He said: "Mā taṃ yogā upaccaguṃ" (Let not the opportunities pass you by). The rare moments (yogas) such as human birth, the completeness of the senses, the appearance of a Buddha, and the gaining of faith—let them not pass you by. Or, let not the four bonds, such as the bond of sensual desire (kāmayoga), overwhelm you.

"Sabbayogavisaṃyuttā" means being liberated from all bonds like the bond of sensual desire, and thus being without taints (anāsava), wander the world; live in the bliss of the present life (diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra).

It should be understood that after hearing that verse, she developed insight and attained Arahatship, as described previously.

## End of the Commentary on the Verses of Elder Tissā.

## 5-10. Commentary on the Verses of Tissā and Other Elders

"Tisse yuñjassu dhammehi" is the verse of Elder Tissā. Her story is similar to the story of Tissā the sikkhamānā. However, this Elder attained Arahatship after becoming an Elder (Therī). Just like this Elder, the stories of the five Elders who follow—Dhīrā, Vīrā, Mittā, Bhadrā, and Upasamā—are exactly the same. All of them were residents of Kapilavatthu, were consorts of the Bodhisatta, and renounced the world with Mahāpajāpatigotamī. Except for the seventh one, all attained Arahatship through the verse spoken with the emission of radiance (obhāsa-gāthā).

That seventh Elder, however, without the obhāsa-gāthā, relied on the advice received earlier from the Teacher, applied herself to insight, attained Arahatship, and then spoke the verse "Vīrā vīrehi" as an exclamation (udāna). The other Elders also attained Arahatship and said:

"Tissā, apply yourself to the good qualities. Let not the right moment (khaṇa) pass you by.
For those who have missed the moment grieve when they are consigned to hell.

Dhīrā, touch the cessation (nirodha), the bliss of the stilling of perception (saññā).
Attain Nibbāna, the unsurpassed security from bonds (yogakkhema)."
13:
“That courageous bhikkhunī, endowed with courageous (noble path) qualities, with developed faculties, having conquered Māra and his army, bears her final body.

Having gone forth with faith, be one who delights in friends (noble friends). Cultivate wholesome qualities for the attainment of the end of bonds (Nibbāna).

Having gone forth with faith, O Bhadrā, be one who delights in the auspicious (Nibbāna). Cultivate wholesome qualities for the unsurpassed end of bonds (Nibbāna).

Established in peace, cross over the flood of saṃsāra, the realm of Death, so difficult to cross. Having conquered Māra and his army, bear your final body.” — Thus they spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘engage with the Dhamma’ means to make an effort in tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), the Noble Path, and the qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma). ‘Let not the opportunity pass you by’ means that for a person who does not practice meditation in this way, all these opportunities—being born in a suitable place, having the six sense bases complete, encountering the time of a Buddha’s arising, and gaining faith—tend to pass away. Let not that opportunity pass you by. ‘Those who have missed the opportunity’ means those who have let the opportunity pass fall into hell and grieve; it means they are reborn there and experience intense suffering.

‘Touch the cessation’ means to attain the cessation of defilements. ‘Attain Nibbāna, the bliss of the calming of perceptions’ means to attain Nibbāna, the ultimate bliss which is the cause for the calming of unwholesome perceptions such as sensual perceptions.

‘The courageous bhikkhunī with courageous qualities’ means the courageous bhikkhunī who has developed the faculties such as faith through the courageous and powerful Noble Path qualities based on energy (vīriya), having conquered the Māra of defilements along with the Māra of the objects of sensuality, bears her final body because there will be no future rebirth. Thus, the Elder nun presents herself as if she were another person.

‘Friend’ is an address to that person. ‘One who delights in friends’ means one who greatly delights in noble friends (kalyāṇamitta). Be one who shows respect and honor to those friends. ‘Cultivate wholesome qualities’ means to develop the Noble Path qualities. ‘For the end of bonds’ means for the arrival at and attainment of Arahatship and Nibbāna.
14:
“Bhadrā” is an address to that Elder nun. “Delighting in the auspicious” means be one who delights, who greatly delights, in auspicious qualities such as virtue. “The unsurpassed end of bonds” refers to the unsurpassed Nibbāna, which is safe and free from the four bonds. It means cultivate the wholesome qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) for the attainment of that Nibbāna.

“Upasamā” is an address to that Elder nun. In the phrase “cross over the flood, the realm of Death, so difficult to cross,” it is called “the realm of Death” (maccudheyya) because Death resides in this saṃsāra. It is called “difficult to cross” (suduttaraṃ) because it is very hard to cross for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit. Cross over that great flood of saṃsāra with the boat of the Noble Path. “Bear your final body” means by crossing that flood, become one who bears the final body.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nuns beginning with Tissā is finished.

## The Commentary on the First Chapter is finished.

## 11. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Muttā

The verse beginning with “Sumuttā sādhumuttāmhi” is the verse of the Elder nun Muttā. This Elder nun also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated merit in various lives, was reborn in this Buddha’s era in the Kosala country as the daughter of a poor brahmin named Oghātaka. When she reached of age, her parents gave her in marriage to a hunchbacked brahmin. Not delighting in domestic life with that brahmin, she asked his permission and went forth. She then practiced the work of insight (vipassanā). As her mind wandered toward external objects, she restrained that mind and, while reciting the verse “Sumuttā sādhumuttāmhi,” she strove in insight and reached the fruit of Arahatship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

“The Victor named Padumuttara, who has vision in all things,
Showing favor to all beings, entered the city for alms.

To that Teacher and Master who was arriving, all the city-dwellers,
Assembling with joy and delight, scattered sand.

Having swept the streets, and erecting banners and pots filled with banana trees,
They performed honor and offerings to the Teacher with incense, powder, and flowers.”
15:
“Having prepared a pavilion and invited the Leader, having given a great gift, I aspired for Supreme Enlightenment. Padumuttara, the Great Hero, the Remover of all beings' [suffering], the Supreme Person, having given thanks, made the prophecy: ‘After a hundred thousand aeons, there will be an auspicious aeon (Bhadda Kappa). Having obtained happiness in various lives, you will reach enlightenment. Those men and women who performed manual labor [for you] will all appear before you in the future. By the result of that deed and by the resolution of will, they will be your attendants in the celestial mansion that arises. They will experience immeasurable divine and human happiness for a long time, wandering through various lives in Saṃsāra.’ The deed I did a hundred thousand aeons ago made me delicate among humans and in the celestial city. Beauty, wealth, retinue, longevity, fame, happiness, and being loved—I constantly receive all these perfections of well-performed deeds. In my final birth, I was born in a Brahmin family in a delightful house, with delicate hands and feet. At all times, I never see the ground unadorned; I never see muddy or impure ground. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.” Thus she spoke. Upon reaching Arahatship, she uttered this paean of joy: “I am well-freed, happily freed from three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, and my hunchbacked husband. I am freed from birth and death; the craving that leads to becoming is uprooted.” Thus she spoke this verse.

At the end of the exhortation by the monk Nandaka, the nuns reached Arahatship. When the community of nuns was well-established and increased, noble daughters, noble daughters-in-law, and young noble maidens in various villages, market towns, districts, and royal cities heard of the Buddha's true Buddhahood, the Dhamma's true nature, and the Saṅgha's good conduct. With great faith in the Dispensation and a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding Saṃsāra, they asked permission from their husbands, parents, and relatives, and entered the Order, striving with their whole hearts. After ordaining, being endowed with virtue and receiving instructions from the Buddha and the elders, they soon realized Arahatship. The elders who compiled the scriptures later collected the verses spoken by these nuns as paeans of joy in various places and categorized them into sections like the ‘Book of Ones’ (Ekakanipāta), naming them ‘Therīgāthā’. The division of these Therīgāthā into sections has been mentioned before.

## 1. Commentary on the Verses of an Unknown Elder Nun (Aññatarā Therī Gāthā Vaṇṇanā)

Among those sections, the Ekakanipāta is the first. In that Ekakanipāta, the verse ‘Sukhaṃ supāhi... kummiyaṃ’ is the beginning. It means: ‘Dear daughter Therikā, just as the dried vegetables in a pot, the lust in your [continuity] has been extinguished by the Path of Non-returning. Therefore, wearing the rag-robe, sleep (live) in peace.’ What is the origin of this verse? In the past, an unknown noble daughter had great faith in the Dispensation during the time of Buddha Koṇāgamana. She invited the Buddha, and the next day, she had a pavilion of branches built, spread sand, hung a canopy, and made offerings of fragrant flowers. She informed the Buddha that it was time. The Buddha went to the pavilion and sat on the prepared seat. The woman paid homage, served him with excellent food, and after the meal, offered three robes to the Buddha.

The Buddha gave thanks and departed. The woman performed meritorious deeds throughout her life and was reborn in heaven. For the interval between two Buddhas, she wandered only in happy realms. In the time of Buddha Kassapa, she was born into a wealthy family. Reaching maturity, she felt spiritual urgency, ordained in the Dispensation, and fulfilled the precepts of a nun for twenty thousand years. She died as a worldling (puthujjana) and was reborn in heaven. After enjoying celestial bliss for the interval between two Buddhas, she was born into a royal family in Vesālī during the time of this Buddha Gotama. Because she had a firm and calm body, she was called ‘Therikā’. When she reached maturity, her parents married her to a prince of the same caste, and she served her husband like a household deity.

When the Buddha came to Vesālī, she became a lay follower (upāsikā) with faith. Later, after hearing the Dhamma from the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, she desired to ordain and told her husband, ‘I will become a nun.’

Although her husband did not permit it, Princess Therikā, due to her extraordinary past perfections (pāramī), contemplated the Dhamma she had heard, discerned mind and matter, and practiced insight meditation (vipassanā). One day, while cooking curry in the kitchen, a great flame flared up and burnt the whole pot with a crackling sound. Seeing this, she took it as an object of meditation, clearly noting the nature of impermanence. Applying the characteristics of suffering, impermanence, and non-self, she practiced insight meditation and gradually attained the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmiphala). From that day on, she no longer wore ornaments such as beads, earrings, flowers, or perfumes. When her husband asked, ‘Sister Therikā, why do you not wear ornaments as before?’, she told him she no longer delighted in the household life and asked permission to ordain. (Just as Visākha Upāsaka with Dhammadinnā and many attendants...)
16: In this verse, 'sumuttā' means well-freed. 'Sādhumuttāmhi' means 'I am well and truly freed.' Why is she well-freed? Because of being freed from three crooked things, as stated in 'tīhi khujjehi muttiyā.' The 'three crooked things' refers to being freed from three types of bends (vaṅkaka). Now, wishing to show these specifically, she said: 'udukkhalena musalena, patinā khujjakena ca' (by the mortar, the pestle, and my hunchbacked husband). For when one puts grain into a mortar and pounds it with a pestle, turning it, the back must be bent; thus, because they cause hunching, both the mortar and pestle are called 'crooked' (khujja). Her husband was indeed a hunchback. Now, illustrating that liberation, she said 'muttāmhi jātimaraṇā' (I am freed from birth and death), showing her release from rebirth and dying. The reason for this liberation is 'bhavanetti samūhatā' (the craving for existence is uprooted), meaning that the craving (taṇhā) which leads to existence has been totally uprooted by the Path of Arahantship. The meaning is: 'I am not only freed from those three crooked things, but also from all birth and death, because the craving that leads to all forms of existence has been uprooted by me through the Highest Path.' ## The Commentary on the Verses of Therī Muttā is finished. ## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Therī Dhammadinnā. The verse beginning with 'Chandajātā avasāyī' is that of Therī Dhammadinnā. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she lived in the city of Haṃsāvatī as a servant dependent on others. Having offered a gift preceded by honor and respect to the Chief Disciple who had emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodha), she was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from there and wandering through the rounds of rebirth among devas and humans, during the time of Phussa Buddha, she lived in the house of a worker for the Buddha's half-brothers. When her husband said, 'Give one,' she gave two, performing many meritorious deeds. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was reborn in the house of Kiki, the King of Kāsī, as one of the seven sisters. She practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) for twenty thousand years. After wandering among devas and humans for one Buddha-interval, in this Buddha-dispensation, she was reborn into a noble family in Rājagaha. Upon reaching maturity, she went to the house of the merchant Visākha. Then one day, the merchant Visākha, having heard the Dhamma from the Teacher and becoming a Non-returner (anāgāmī), returned home. While ascending the mansion, he did not take the hand extended by Dhammadinnā, who was standing at the top of the stairs, but ascended the mansion alone.
17: Even while eating, he ate only in silence. Dhammadinnā, reflecting on this behavior, asked, "My lord, why did you not take my hand today? While eating, you did not say anything at all. Is there some fault in me?" Visākha said, "Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you. However, from today onwards, I am no longer fit to touch a woman's body or to indulge in the craving for food. I have realized such a Dhamma. If you wish, stay in this very house. If you do not wish, take as much wealth as you need and go to your family home." She replied, "My lord, I do not wish to swallow again the vomit you have spat out. Please allow me to ordain." Visākha said, "Very well, Dhammadinnā," and sent her to the nunnery in a golden palanquin. After ordaining and taking a meditation subject, she stayed there for a few days. Desiring to live in solitude, she approached her teachers and preceptors and said, "Noble ladies, my mind does not delight in a crowded place; let me go to a village dwelling." The nuns took her to a village dwelling. While staying there, because she had mastered the formations (saṅkhāra) in the past, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "The Conqueror named Padumuttara, who reached the far shore of all phenomena, the Leader, arose one hundred thousand eons from now. At that time, I was in a certain family in Haṃsāvatī; I was a worker for others, wise and restrained by virtue. Sujāta, the Chief Disciple of Padumuttara Buddha, came out from the monastery and was walking for alms. At that time, while going to fetch water carrying a jar, I saw him and, with a confident heart, offered a cake with my own hands. Having accepted it, he sat right there and consumed it. Then, I led him to my house and offered him a meal. Then my grandfather was pleased and made me his daughter-in-law. Going together with my mother-in-law, I paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One."
18: At that time, that Blessed One praised a certain bhikkhunī who was a Dhamma preacher and placed her in the foremost rank. Having heard those words, I was filled with joy. Having invited the Buddha, the Protector of the World, along with the Saṅgha, and having given a great gift, I made an aspiration for that foremost rank. Then the Buddha, whose voice was deep and sweet like the sound of thunder, spoke to me—who delighted in serving him, who attended to the Saṅgha, who was devoted to hearing the True Dhamma, and whose mind was increased in virtue: 'Dear daughter, be joyful; you will receive the fruit of your aspiration. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka race, will arise in the world. You will be an heir to his Dhamma, a breast-born daughter, created by the Dhamma, a female disciple named Dhammadinnā.' Having heard those words, I was joyful and, with a heart of loving-kindness, served the Great Sage, the Leader, with the four requisites for the rest of my life. Through that well-performed deed, intention, and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda-kappa), the famous Kassapa of the Brahmabandhu clan, the best of speakers, arose. At that time, the attendant of that Great Seer was a king of men, King Kikī of Kāsi, in the noble city of Bārāṇasī. I was the sixth daughter of that king, known as Sudhammā. Having heard the Dhamma of the Great Victor, I delighted in renunciation. Our father did not grant us permission, so at that time we lived in the home for twenty thousand years, practicing diligently without laziness. Though we princesses grew up in comfort, we were seven daughters who delighted in service to the Buddha and joyfully practiced the holy life as virgins.
19: They were Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh was Saṅghadāyikā. Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, Kuṇḍalā, Gotamī, I (Dhammadinnā), and Visākhā was the seventh. Through those well-performed deeds, intentions, and aspirations, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In this final birth, I was born in the noble city of Giribbaja (Rājagaha) in a wealthy merchant's family, endowed with all sensual pleasures. Endowed with beauty and reaching the first stage of youth, I went to another family and lived in happiness. Having approached the Buddha, the refuge of the world, and having heard the Dhamma teaching, my husband (Visākha) was a wise man and attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). Then, having asked permission, I went forth from home to homelessness, and in a short time, I attained Arahantship. Then that lay follower approached me and asked profound and subtle questions, all of which I answered. The Victorious Buddha, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost rank (etadagga) among the bhikkhunīs who are Dhamma preachers; he saw no other like me. 'Monks, just as Dhammadinnā is wise, so should you remember her,' he said. Thus, I was a wise one who received the favor of the Leader. I have served the Teacher, fulfilled the Buddha's teaching, laid down the heavy burden, and uprooted the bond of existence (craving). The purpose for which I went forth from home to homelessness—the destruction of all fetters, the fruit of Arahantship—has been attained. I am a master of psychic powers, I possess the divine ear element (dibba-sota), I know the minds of others, and I am a doer of the Teacher's instruction.
20:
“I know my former lives; the divine eye has been purified. Having exhausted all taints, I have become pure and stainless.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.” (As found in Apadāna, Therī 2.3.95-130).

Having attained Arahatship, she thought: “My mind has reached the summit. What is the use of staying here now? I will go to Rājagaha to pay homage to the Teacher, and my relatives will also perform meritorious deeds.” Thus, she returned to Rājagaha with other bhikkhunīs. When the merchant Visākha heard of her arrival, wishing to test her attainment, he asked questions regarding the five aggregates and so forth. Dhammadinnā Therī answered every question asked, like one cutting a lotus stalk with a sharp sword. Visākha reported the entire method of questioning and answering to the Teacher. The Teacher praised her, saying, “Visākha, the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā is wise,” and so forth. Comparing her answers with His own omniscience, He declared her explanation to be correct. Making that very Cūḷavedalla Sutta (MN 44) the occasion, He placed Dhammadinnā Therī in the foremost position (etadagga) among the bhikkhunīs who are speakers of Dhamma (dhammakathikā). While she was staying in that village dwelling, having attained the three lower paths and undertaking insight (vipassanā) for the sake of the highest path (Arahatship), she uttered this verse:

“One who has a desire for the goal, who is determined, and whose mind is permeated [with the fruit], whose heart is not bound to sensual pleasures, is called ‘one who flows upstream’ (uddhaṃsoto).”

In that verse, “chanda-jātā” means having a desire for the sake of the highest fruit (Arahatship). “Avasāyī” refers to the end or completion. Since her mind is not bound to sensual pleasures and she will be called “uddhaṃsoto,” this should be understood as the completion of the recluse's task. This does not refer to just any person; therefore, by these two words, it means one who, though not yet having reached the path and fruit, aspires for the unsurpassed security from bondage (Nibbāna). “Manasā ca phuṭā siyā” means Nibbāna should be touched or realized by the three lower path-minds. “Kāmesu appaṭibaddhacittā” means one whose mind is not bound to sensual pleasures by the power of the path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). “Uddhaṃsotā” means her stream of the path and stream of saṃsāra flow only upwards. For Non-returners, just as the highest path arises and no other [lower path], so too, having been reborn in the Aviha realm and so forth, they only arise upwards until the Akaniṭṭha realm.

## The Explanation of the Verses of Dhammadinnā Therī is finished.

## 13. Explanation of the Verses of Visākhā Therī

The verse beginning with “Karotha buddhasāsanaṃ” is that of Visākhā Therī. Her story is similar to that of Dhīrā Therī. Having attained Arahatship and spending her time in the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha)—

“Carry out the Buddha's teaching; having done so, one does not regret it. Quickly wash your feet and sit down to one side.”

With this verse, she declared her attainment of Arahatship (aññābyākaraṇa).

In that verse, “Karotha buddhasāsanaṃ” means follow the advice and instruction of the Buddha's teaching; practice according to what has been taught. “Yaṃ katvā nānutappati” means one does not regret because of the act of following the instruction, for the desires of such a practitioner are perfectly fulfilled. “Khippaṃ pādāni dhovitvā, ekamante nisīdatha” was said because she herself, after returning from the alms round and finishing her meal, performed the duties for her teachers and preceptors, then washed her feet in her day-quarters and, sitting in seclusion, brought her task (Arahatship) to its summit. Thus, she spoke this to encourage others as well.

## The Explanation of the Verses of Visākhā Therī is finished.

## 14. Explanation of the Verses of Sumanā Therī

The verse beginning with “Dhātuyo dukkhato disvā” is that of Sumanā Therī. Her story is similar to that of Tissā Therī. To her also, the Teacher emitted a radiance and, appearing as if sitting before her, spoke this verse:

“Having seen the elements as suffering, do not come back to birth again. Having dispelled desire for existence, you shall live at peace.”

At the end of the verse, she attained Arahatship.

In that verse, “Dhātuyo dukkhato disvā” means having seen with the eye of wisdom that the elements such as the eye, which are included in one's own continuity, as well as other elements, are “suffering” because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. “Mā jātiṃ punarāgami” means do not [come] to a new birth again in the future, a new birth in the time to come...
22:
Approached the Noble One. "Bhave chandaṃ virājetvā" means having abandoned the desire and craving for all forms of existence, such as the sensual realm, through the Path known as dispassion (virāga). "Upasantā carissasi" means you will live in a state of peace because all defilements have been completely eradicated.

In this verse, by the phrase "dhātuyo dukkhato disvā" (seeing the elements as suffering), insight (vipassanā) is shown through the method of contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā). By the phrase "bhave chandaṃ virājetvā," the Path (magga) is shown. By the phrase "upasantā carissasi," the Nibbāna element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) is shown. By the phrase "mā jātiṃ punarāgamī" (do not come to birth again), the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) is shown.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Therī is Finished.

## 15. Commentary on the Verses of Uttarā Therī

"Kāyena saṃvutā āsiṃ" and so on is the verse of the Elder Uttarā. Her story is similar to that of Tissā Therī. She was born into the Sakyan clan and was a consort of the Bodhisatta. She went forth with Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and attained Arahantship through a verse spoken by the Buddha while emitting rays of light. Then, she spoke this same verse as an inspired utterance (udāna):

"I was restrained in body, and also in speech and mind.
Having uprooted craving with its root, I have become cool and attained Nibbāna."

In that verse, "kāyena saṃvutā āsiṃ" means I was restrained by bodily restraint. "Vācāya" (in speech) should be connected as "I was restrained by verbal restraint." By these two terms, restraint by virtue (sīla-saṃvara) is shown. "Uda" means "and." "Cetasā" (by mind) means by the mind of concentration (samādhi-citta). By this term, the development of insight (vipassanā-bhāvanā) is shown. "Samūlaṃ taṇhamabbuyha" (having uprooted craving with its root) means having pulled out craving along with its latent tendencies (anusaya) or along with ignorance (avijjā). Because ignorance conceals the faults, craving arises in the three realms of existence.

Another way: "Kāyena saṃvutā" means having restrained the body by the restraint of the Path (magga-saṃvara) through the total abandonment of wrong action (micchā-kammanta) by Right Action (sammā-kammanta). "Vācāya" means having restrained the speech by the restraint of the Path through the total abandonment of wrong speech (micchā-vācā) by Right Speech (sammā-vācā). "Cetasā" means by concentration (samādhi).
23:
In this context, Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi) is spoken of by making the mind the chief. By taking Right Concentration, the other Path factors (magga-dhamma) such as Right View, which have the same characteristic as the Path, are also included. This shows the complete abandonment of non-restraint, such as covetousness (abhijjhā), through the restraint of the Path (magga-saṃvara). Therefore, it is said, "Having uprooted craving with its root." "I have become cool and attained Nibbāna" means having reached the state of coolness due to the absence of all heat of defilements, I have attained Nibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Uttarā Therī is Finished.

## 16. Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Therī Who Ordained Late

"Sleep happily, old woman" is the verse of Sumana Therī who ordained in her old age. She also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit in various lives. In this Buddha's era, she was born in Sāvatthī as the sister of King Mahākosala. Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher to King Pasenadi of Kosala, such as "Great King, there are four things that should not be despised because they are young," she gained faith and established herself in the Refuges and the Precepts. Although she wished to ordain, she spent a long time thinking, "I will look after my grandmother." Later, when her grandmother passed away, she took expensive rugs and blankets with the King, went to the monastery, and offered them to the Saṅgha. After hearing the Dhamma from the Teacher, she was established in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) and requested ordination. The Teacher, seeing the maturity of her knowledge, spoke this verse:

"Sleep happily, old woman, wrapped in a coarse cloth,
For your passion is stilled,
You have become cool and attained Nibbāna."

At the end of the verse, she attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and spoke that same verse as an inspired utterance. This was her declaration of final knowledge (aññā-byākaraṇa). She ordained at that very moment. In the verse, "vuḍḍhike" means an elderly person, one advanced in age. This Elder was also great in qualities such as virtue (sīla). In the fourth line of the verse spoken by the Elder, it should be connected as "you have become cool and attained Nibbāna." The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sumana Therī Who Ordained Late is Finished.

## 17. Dhammātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Piṇḍapātaṃ caritvāna' is that of the Elder Nun Dhammā. This elder nun also had performed meritorious service under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a strong support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (Nibbāna) in various existences. Having gathered the requisites of merit, she was reborn in a respectable family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, she went to the home of a suitable husband. Although she gained faith in the Dispensation and wished to ordain, her husband did not grant permission. Later, when her husband passed away, she ordained and practiced insight meditation (Vipassanā). One day, while returning to the monastery after wandering for alms, she fell down. Taking that very fall as her object of meditation, she developed insight and attained Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). She then uttered this verse as an inspired utterance:

'Having wandered for alms, leaning on a staff, being weak,
With trembling limbs, I fell right there on the ground.
Having seen the danger in the body, then my mind was liberated.'

In that verse, 'piṇḍapātaṃ caritvāna daṇဍ္ဍmောလုဗ္ဘ' (piṇḍapātaṃ caritvāna daṇḍamolubbha) means after wandering for alms in the city, supporting oneself with a staff for the sake of almsfood. 'Chamā' means on the ground; it refers to falling on the ground due to the weakness of the feet. 'Disvā ādīnavaṃ kāye' means seeing the faults of the body with the eye of wisdom through various methods such as foulness, impermanence, suffering, and non-self. 'Atha cittaṃ vimucci me' means that through the contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā) and others that arise after the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā), my mind was first liberated from the defilements by way of suppression (vikkhambhanavasena), and then completely liberated through the Paths and Fruits in successive order by way of eradication (samucchedavasena) and by way of tranquillization (paṭippassaddhivasena). It means there is now nothing further to be done for the liberation of that mind. This indeed was her declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dhammā ends.

## 18. Saṅghātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with 'Hitvā ghare pabbajitvā' is that of the Elder Nun Saṅghā. Her story is similar to that of the Elder Nun Dhīrā. The verse, however, is:
25:
'Having left home and ordained, having left son, cattle, and dear ones,
Having left lust and hatred, and having dispelled ignorance,
Having uprooted craving along with its root, I am quenched and liberated.'

In that verse, 'hitvā' means having abandoned. 'Ghare' refers to the home. The word 'ghara', although having a single meaning, is sometimes used in the sense of many meanings through usage (rūḷhī), like the word 'seed'. 'Hitvā puttaṃ pasuṃ piyaṃ' means having abandoned dear sons and cattle such as cows and buffaloes by abandoning the desire and lust (chandarāga) attached to them. 'Hitvā rāgañca dosañca' means having completely cut off lust, which has the nature of attachment, and hatred, which has the nature of corruption, by means of the Noble Path. 'Avijjañca virājiya' means having dispelled delusion (moha), which is the precursor to all unwholesome states, and having uprooted it by means of the Path. The meaning of the remaining words is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Saṅghā ends.

## The Commentary on the Book of Ones ends.
26:
## 2. Dukanipāta

## 1. Abhirūpanandātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Book of Twos, the verse beginning with 'Āturaṃ asuciṃ pūtiṃ' is that of the probationer (sikkhamānā) Abhirūpanandā. It is said that during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, she was the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the city of Bandhumatī. Having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she established herself in the three refuges and the precepts. When the Teacher attained Parinibbāna, she made an offering to the relic stupa with a golden parasol adorned with jewels. After passing away, she was reborn in the celestial realm. Thereafter, wandering only in happy destinations (sugati), she was conceived in the womb of the chief queen of Khemaka the Sakyan in the city of Kapilavatthu during the time of this Buddha.

Her name was Nandā. Because she attained extreme beauty of form, she was famously known as 'Abhirūpanandā'. On the very day of her marriage when she reached maturity, the Sakyan prince who was her intended groom passed away. Then, her parents made her ordain as a nun against her will.

Even after ordaining, she possessed pride born of her beauty. Thinking, 'The Teacher disparages beauty and shows the danger of form through many methods,' she did not go to pay respects to the Buddha. The Blessed One, knowing the maturity of her knowledge, commanded Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, 'Let all the bhikkhunīs come for instruction in order.' When her turn arrived, she sent someone else. The Blessed One said, 'When one's turn arrives, one must come oneself; another should not be sent.' Being unable to disobey the Buddha's command, she went to pay respects to the Buddha along with the other bhikkhunīs. The Blessed One, by means of psychic power, created a very beautiful female form and then showed it as aged and decrepit, thereby causing spiritual urgency (saṃvega) to arise, and said:

'Behold, Nandā, this assembly (of the body), which is diseased, impure, and putrid.
Develop the mind to be one-pointed and well-concentrated on the foul (asubha).

Develop the signless (animitta) meditation and abandon the underlying tendency to pride (mānānusaya).
Then, through the full understanding and abandonment of pride, you shall live as one who is quenched.'
27:
She spoke these two verses. The meaning of those verses is just as explained below. At the conclusion of the verses, Therī Abhirūpanandā attained Arahantship. This is stated in the Apadāna:

'In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a king named Bandhumā. I was the queen of that king and we lived together.

While sitting in a secluded place alone, I then thought: I have not performed any merit that can be taken along (to the next life).

I will surely go to hell, which is very hot, bitter, terrifying, and extremely cruel; of this, I have no doubt.

Having thought thus, and gladdening my mind, I approached the king and spoke these words:

"O King, we women are always followers of men. Please give me a monk, O Noble One, and I will offer food to him."

The Great King gave me a monk who had developed his faculties. Taking his bowl, I filled it with excellent food.

Having filled it with excellent food worth a thousand, and covering it with a pair of cloths, I offered it with a joyful heart.

Due to that well-performed deed, the intention, and the aspiration, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

I became the chief queen of a thousand celestial kings. I also became the chief queen of a thousand wheel-turning monarchs.

I also attained the extensive position of queen to regional kings; due to the fruit of that deed, I obtained various immeasurable merits.

My complexion is like a blue lotus, very beautiful and lovely to behold. I am a woman endowed with all limbs, born into a noble family, and possessing a radiant complexion.'
28:
'In my final birth, I was born in the Sakyan clan. I was the leader of a thousand women and the sister of King Suddhodana's son (the Buddha).

Weary of the household life, I entered the homeless life. On the seventh night after ordaining, I realized the Four Noble Truths.

The benefits of the four requisites—robes, alms-food, medicine, and lodging—cannot be measured. This is the fruit of the offering of alms-food.

O Sage, O Great Hero, for your sake, I have cultivated much former merit.

Thirty-one aeons ago from this world, because of the gift I gave then, I have never known a miserable state. This is the fruit of the offering of alms-food.

I have known only two destinations: the celestial state and the human state; I have known no other destination. This is the fruit of the offering of alms-food.

I have known only high birth, in the three great wealthy clans; I have known no other clan. This is the fruit of the offering of alms-food.

Wandering through various lives, urged by the root of merit, I have seen nothing unpleasant and have only received the fruit of joy.

O Great Sage, I am a master of psychic powers, the divine ear element, and the knowledge of others' minds.

I know my past lives, my divine eye is purified, all taints are exhausted, and now there is no more rebirth.

O Great Hero, in your presence, the analytical knowledges of meaning, doctrine, language, and eloquence have arisen in me.

My defilements are burned away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.'

After reaching Arahantship, she herself spoke those very verses as an inspired utterance, and this was her declaration of final knowledge.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Therī Abhirūpanandā is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Therī Dhammadinnā

The verse beginning with 'Chandajātā avasāyī' is the verse of Therī Dhammadinnā. To speak in detail, in the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was a servant girl in Haṃsavatī who lived depending on others. While living thus, she made an offering to the Chief Disciple Sujāta, who had just emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and was reborn in heaven. Passing away from there, she wandered through celestial and human realms. In the time of Phussa Buddha, while living in the house of the treasurer of the royal brothers born to the Buddha's stepmother, she gave two gifts when her husband said 'give one', performing much merit. In the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was conceived in the palace of King Kikī of Kāsi and was one of the seven sisters. After practicing the holy life for twenty thousand years, she wandered among gods and humans during the interval between two Buddhas.

When this Gautama Buddha appeared, she was born into a noble family in Rājagaha and, upon reaching age, went to the house of the merchant Visākha. One day, Visākha heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, became an Anāgāmī (Non-returner), and returned home. When climbing the palace, he did not take Dhammadinnā's hand which she offered at the top of the stairs. When eating, he ate in silence. Dhammadinnā reflected on this and asked: "My lord, why did you not take my hand today? Why did you not say a single word while eating? Is there some fault in me?" Visākha replied: "Sister Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you. However, from today, it is no longer proper for me to touch a woman's body or to crave food. I have realized such Four Noble Truths. If you wish to stay in this house, stay. If not, take as much wealth as you desire and return to your parents' house."

Dhammadinnā said: "My lord, I do not wish to swallow again the vomit you have spat out. Please allow me to ordain." Visākha said: "Very well," and sent her to the nunnery in a golden palanquin. Dhammadinnā ordained, took a meditation subject, and after staying in Rājagaha for two or three days, wishing for seclusion, she went to her teachers and preceptors and said: "Ladies, my mind does not delight here, mixed with the five sense objects. I wish to go to a village monastery." The nuns sent Therī Dhammadinnā to a village monastery. While living there, because she had practiced contemplating formations (saṅkhāra) in many past lives, she soon reached Arahantship along with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna: "The Victor named Padumuttara... the Buddha's teaching has been done." One hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, the one named Padumuttara, who reached the far shore of all dhammas...
29:
## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jentā

These verses beginning with 'Ye ime satta bojjhaṅgā' are the verses of Elder Jentā. The stories of this Elder Jentā's past and present are similar to those of Elder Abhirūpanandā. However, the only difference is that this Elder Jentā was born into the Licchavi royal family in the city of Vesālī. Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, she attained the fruit of Arahatship at the end of the discourse. Reflecting on the special attainment she had achieved, she uttered these two verses through the power of joyful inspiration:

"These seven factors of enlightenment, which are the path to the attainment of Nibbāna, have all been developed by me, just as they were taught by the Buddha.

I have indeed seen that Blessed One (through the Dhamma-body); this physical form is my last; the cycle of birth and death is exhausted; now there is no more rebirth."

In those verses, 'Ye ime satta bojjhaṅgā' refers to these seven factors named 'Bojjhaṅga' because they are parts of the knowledge of enlightenment (bodhi-ñāṇa), which is the aforementioned collection of states known as mindfulness (sati), investigation of states (dhammavicaya), energy (viriya), joy (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā); or because they are the constituent parts of the person who awakens to the Four Noble Truths. 'Maggā nibbānapattiyā' means they are the means for the attainment of Nibbāna. 'Bhāvitā te mayā sabbe, yathā buddhena desitā' means that I have brought into being and developed all those thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) exactly as they were taught by the Blessed One.

In the phrase 'Diṭṭho hi me so bhagavā', the word 'hi' has a causal meaning. Because that Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One who is the Dhamma-body, has been seen through the vision of the Noble Dhamma attained by oneself, it is thus connected to the phrase 'this physical form is my last'. Indeed, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and other Noble Ones (ariyas) are said to be 'seen' only through the vision of the Noble Dhamma, not merely by seeing the physical body (rūpakāya). Therefore, it was said: "Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me," and "Monks, the learned noble disciple is one who sees the Noble Ones," and so forth. The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Jentā is finished.
30:
## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sumangalamātā

The verse beginning with "Sumuttikā" is the verse of Elder Sumangalamātā. This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, having accumulated merit in various lives, was born into a poor family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. When she came of age, she was given in marriage to a certain reed-worker and, in her very first pregnancy, she obtained a son who was in his final existence. The name of that son was Sumangala. From then on, that woman was known as Sumangalamātā (Sumangala's mother). Because the name and clan of this Elder were not well-known, she is referred to in the Pali text as "a certain unknown Elder nun."

Her son also, upon reaching maturity, ordained and attained Arahatship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), becoming famous as Elder Sumangala. His mother also ordained among the nuns and, while striving in the work of insight meditation (vipassanā), one day reflected on the suffering she had experienced during her lay life. Stirred by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she developed her insight and attained Arahatship along with the analytical insights. She then uttered this inspired exclamation:

"I am well-freed, I am well-freed, I am well-freed from the pestle.
My shameless husband, my parasol-making, and my pots and water-snake-like impurities (are also freed from).
I destroy lust and hatred with a 'cicciṭi cicciṭi' sound (as they burn).
That 'I' having approached the foot of a tree, meditate happily, thinking 'Oh, what bliss!'"

In those verses, "Sumuttikā" means well-freed. The letter "ka" is merely a syllable to complete the verse, and the meaning is "Indeed, I am truly well-freed." That Elder, seeing the success (sampatti) she had attained in the Dispensation, addressed herself out of devotion or out of praise for that success. Wishing to show her liberation from what was particularly loathsome in her lay life, she said "Sādhumuttikāmhi" and so on. There, "Sādhumuttikāmhi" means "Indeed, I am perfectly freed." "Musalassa" means from the pestle. It is said that because of her poverty during her lay life, she had to do the work of pounding with a pestle herself; therefore, she spoke thus. "Ahiriko me" means "My husband is shameless, devoid of shame; I do not like him"—this is the remaining sense to be filled in. Being naturally weary of sensual pleasures, she spoke thus out of disgust for the behavior of those devoted to sensual pleasures. "Chattakaṃ vāpi" means "I do not like even the parasol-making work done for the sake of livelihood." The word "vā" has the sense of aggregating things not yet mentioned.
32:
...she was known as Aḍḍhakāsī. Her going forth and her higher ordination by messenger (dūtena upasampadā) are recorded in the Khandhaka. Indeed, it was said:

At that time, the prostitute Aḍḍhakāsī had gone forth among the bhikkhunīs. She wished to go to Sāvatthī, thinking, "I will receive higher ordination in the presence of the Blessed One." Rogues (dhutta) heard, "The prostitute Aḍḍhakāsī, it is said, wishes to go to Sāvatthī." They waylaid her on the road. Aḍḍhakāsī the prostitute heard, "Rogues, it is said, are waylaying the road." She sent a messenger to the Blessed One, saying, "I wish to receive higher ordination; how should I proceed?" Then the Blessed One, on that occasion and in that connection, gave a Dhamma talk and addressed the monks: "Monks, I allow higher ordination to be given even by messenger." (Cūḷavagga, 430).

Having thus obtained higher ordination, while performing the work of insight (vipassanā), she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In this auspicious aeon (bhadda-kappa), a Buddha of great fame and noble lineage,
Kassapa by clan name, the best of speakers, arose.

Then, having gone forth in the teaching of that Buddha,
I was restrained in the Pātimokkha and in the five faculties.

Knowing moderation in eating and devoted to wakefulness,
I, possessing applied effort, lived depending on a bhikkhunī who was free from taints (khīṇāsava).

At that time, with a corrupt mind, I insulted her, saying 'Prostitute!';
Because of that evil deed, I was boiled in hell.

By the remainder of that karma, I was born into the class of prostitutes in many births,
being dependent on others; and so too in my final birth.

Born into a merchant family in Kāsī, by the power of my former holy life,
I was endowed with beauty like a celestial nymph among the gods.

Seeing me, who was lovely to behold, in the supreme city of Giribbaja,
they placed me in the position of a prostitute by the power of my [past] insult."
33:
“Having heard the True Dhamma taught by the noblest Buddha, and being endowed with the predispositions from previous lives, I went forth from the home life into homelessness.

While traveling to the presence of the Victorious Buddha to receive that higher ordination, I heard that rogues were waiting on the path; thus, I received ordination by messenger.

All kamma has been exhausted, as have both merit and demerit. I have escaped from the entire cycle of rebirth, and the state of being a courtesan has been ended.

O Great Sage, I have mastery over the psychic powers, the divine ear element, and the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others.

I know my past lives, and the divine eye has been purified. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

O Great Hero, in your presence, knowledge has arisen in me regarding the analytical insights of meaning, dhamma, language, and perspicuity.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.” (Ap. Therī 2.4.168-183).

Upon reaching Arahantship, she uttered these verses as an inspired utterance:

'As much as the tax of the Kāsī region was, so much was my price. Having set that price, the townspeople fixed my value and kept me at half that price.

Then I became weary of form; through weariness, I became dispassionate. May I never again run through the cycle of birth and death repeatedly. The three knowledges have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'

In those verses, 'As much as the tax of the Kāsī region was, so much was my price' means: the tax arising in the Kāsī districts is called 'Kāsijanapada'; however much that tax was, that much was my fee (price). How much was that? It was about a thousand kahāpaṇas. It is said that at that time in the Kāsī kingdom, the daily revenue arising for the King by way of tax was about a thousand; the wealth this woman received from the hands of men in one day was also that much. Therefore, it is said, 'As much as the tax of the Kāsī region...'
34:
"...so much was my price." She received the name "Kāsī" because her fee was equal to the Kāsī tax. At that time, since most people were unable to give a thousand, they would pay half of that and depart after enjoying themselves for only a part of the day. Because of those people, she became known as "Aḍḍhakāsī" (Half-Kāsī). Therefore, it is said, "The merchants fixed my value and kept me at half that price." The meaning is: the merchants living in the market town, having set the price at five hundred, although she was priceless as a 'jewel of a woman', they designated her at half the price by the name "Aḍḍhakāsī" and addressed her as such.
