Then, "I became weary of form"—thus she had remained living by means of her form. Later, depending on the Dispensation, she saw, "Thus form is impermanent; thus this form is suffering and foul," and while observing this, she became weary of form and disgusted with it. "Through weariness, I became dispassionate" means that being weary, she thereafter attained dispassion. Here, by the mention of "weariness" (nibbidā), tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) is shown; by the mention of "dispassion" (virāga), strong insight (balava-vipassanā) is shown. For has it not been said, "One who is weary becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated"? By the words "May I never again run through the cycle of birth and death repeatedly," she shows the manner of weariness and dispassion. By the words "the three knowledges," etc., she shows the attainment of their peak; this is in the same manner as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Aḍḍhakāsī Therī Ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Cittā Therī

The verse beginning with "Though I am thin" is the verse of Cittā Therī. She also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and was accumulating wholesome roots that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭa) in various lives. Ninety-four aeons ago, she was reborn in the Kinnarī species on the banks of the Candabhāgā River. One day, seeing a Paccekabuddha sitting at the foot of a tree, she felt clear faith in her heart, worshipped him with reed-flowers, paid homage, raised her hands in salutation, circumambulated him, and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha-era, she was reborn in a family of a wealthy householder in Rājagaha. Upon reaching the age of discretion, she gained faith when the Teacher entered Rājagaha, and later went forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. In her old age, she climbed Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) mountain, performed the duties of a recluse, developed insight, and attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:
35:
At that time, I was a Kinnarī by the banks of the Candabhāgā River. I saw the Buddha, the Self-Awakened One, the Unconquered, who was free from the dust of defilements. With a clear mind and joyful heart, I paid homage with joined palms, took a garland of reeds, and specially honored the Self-Awakened One. Through that well-performed deed, and through my intention and aspiration, I abandoned the body of a Kinnarī and reached the destination of the Thirty-Three (Tāvatiṃsa) heaven. I became the chief queen of thirty-six kings of gods. I also became the chief queen of ten wheel-turning monarchs. Having stirred my mind with urgency, I left the household life and went forth. My defilements have been burned away; all existences have been uprooted; all taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth. In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, I specially honored [the Buddha] with flowers. Due to the merit of that flower offering, I have not known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of offering flowers. My defilements have been burned away ... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha. (Thus she spoke).

Having attained Arahantship and reviewing her own practice, she uttered these two verses:
'Even though I am thin, sick, and very weak, I climb the mountain leaning on a staff. Having laid down my outer robe and turned my bowl upside down, I steadied myself against the rock and broke through the mass of darkness (ignorance).'

In those verses, 'kiñcāpi khomhi kisikā' means: although I have a thin body because I am worn out by old age and have little flesh and blood. 'gilānā bāḷhadubbalā' means: sick due to the disturbance of the elements, and extremely weak because of that very sickness. 'daṇḍamolubbha gacchāmi' means: wherever I go, I go only by leaning on a walking staff. 'pabbataṃ abhirūhiya' means: even in such a state, desiring seclusion, I climbed up the Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa) mountain.
36:
'saṅghāṭiṃ nikkhipitvāna' means: wearing only the inner and upper robes, and placing the Saṅghāṭi (outer robe), which was folded and kept on the shoulder, within arm's reach. 'pattakañca nikujjiya' means: turning the clay bowl I used upside down and placing it to one side. 'sele khambhesimattānaṃ, tamokhandhaṃ padāliya' means: while sitting on the mountain, I broke through the mass of delusion (moha) which had never been broken through during this long saṃsāra; and by that very breaking of the mass of delusion, I steadied myself, my own being; the meaning is that I removed the defilements through the abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna) by bringing about the nature of not being reborn in my continuity in the future.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Cittä Therī is finished.

## 6. The Commentary on the Verses of Mettikā Therī

The verse beginning with 'kiñcāpi khomhi dukkhitā' is that of Mettikā Therī. This Elder Nun also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that was a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. In the time of Buddha Siddhattha, she was born into a wealthy family, and upon reaching maturity, she offered a jeweled belt (mekhalā) to the Buddha's stupa. Through that meritorious deed, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was born into a wealthy Brahmin family in Rājagaha. The rest is similar to what was said for the previous Elder Nun. However, this Elder Nun climbed the Paṭibhāgakūṭa peak, practiced the Dhamma of a recluse, developed insight, and attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Thus it is said in the Apadāna:

'I was a repairer of the stupa of the Blessed One Siddhattha;
I gave a belt (mekhalā) for the new work of the Teacher's [stupa].

When the great stupa was completed, I again gave a belt to the Sage, the Lord of the World, with a clear mind and with my own hands.

In the ninety-fourth aeon from now, when I gave that belt, I have not known a miserable rebirth since then; this is the fruit of honoring the stupa.

My defilements have been burned away ... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha.'
37:
After attaining the fruit of Arahantship, she reviewed her own practice and uttered these two verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

'Even though I am suffering, oppressed by disease, weak, and past my youth,
I go climbing the mountain leaning on a staff.
Having laid down my outer robe and turned my bowl upside down,
While sitting on the rock, my mind was liberated (from defilements).
I have attained the three true knowledges; the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.'

In those verses, 'dukkhitā' means suffering because of being overcome by disease, having pain arisen, or having reached suffering. 'dubbalā' means being devoid of strength because of that reaching of suffering and because of being worn out by old age. Therefore, she said 'gatayobbanā', which means one who is advanced in age.

'atha cittaṃ vimucci me' means: while sitting on the rock, at that very moment, because of having practiced rightly with balanced energy, my mind was liberated from all taints (āsavas) through the sequence of the paths. The remaining words are just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mettikā Therī is finished.

## 7. The Commentary on the Verses of Mittā Therī

The verse beginning with 'cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ' is that of another Elder Nun named Mittā. This Elder Nun also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and was one who accumulated vivaṭṭūpanissaya merit, which is a strong support for Nibbāna, throughout successive lives. In the time of Buddha Vipassī, she was born into a Khattiya (warrior-noble) family, and upon reaching maturity, she became a lady of King Bandhuma's court. Seeing an Arahant nun who was a disciple of Buddha Vipassī, she became clear in mind, took the bowl from the nun's hand, filled it with excellent food, and offered it together with a pair of costly garments. Through that meritorious deed, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was born into the Sakyan royal family in Kapilavatthu. Upon reaching maturity, she heard the Dhamma from the Buddha, gained faith, and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī...
38:
Having ordained and performed the preliminary duties, while striving in the work of insight (vipassanā), she attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Referring to that, it was stated in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a king named Bandhumā. I was the queen of that king, and we traveled together.

"Sitting in a secluded place, I then thought: 'I have performed no merit that is worthy of being carried to the next life.'

"'I shall surely go to hell, which is intensely burning, bitter, terrifying, and very cruel. In this, I have no doubt.'

"Approaching the king, I spoke these words: 'O King, give me a monk; I shall offer him food.'

"The Great King gave me a monk who had developed his faculties. Taking his bowl, I filled it with excellent alms-food.

"Having filled it with excellent food, I made an offering by anointing it with soft perfumes. I covered it with a net and shrouded it with a pair of robes.

"I remembered that merit as my object of reflection for the rest of my life. With a clear mind in that merit, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

"I attained the status of chief queen to thirty celestial kings. Whatever I desired in my mind was fulfilled according to my wish.

"I also attained the status of chief queen to twenty Universal Monarchs. I was one who had accumulated merit throughout my wandering in existences.

"Now I am freed from all fetters; my clingings (upādāna) have disappeared. All taints (āsavas) are exhausted; now there is no further rebirth.

"Because of the gift I gave ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of the offering of alms-food.

"My defilements are burnt up... (and so forth) ... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha."
39:
After reaching the fruit of Arahantship, reflecting on her own practice and being filled with joy and happiness, she uttered these two verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

“On the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight, and on the special period of the Uposatha (pāṭihāriyapakkha) well-endowed with the eight factors,

Delighting in the heavenly realm, I used to observe the Uposatha. But today, eating only one meal, with shaven head and wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), I have removed the fever (defilements) in my heart and no longer long for the heavenly realm.”

In those verses, ‘cātuddasiṃ pañcadasiṃ’ means the fourteenth day and the fifteenth day. It is connected with ‘pakkhassa’ (of the fortnight). Here, the accusative case is used to denote a period of time. ‘Yā ca pakkhassa aṭṭhamī’ means also the eighth day of the month. ‘Pāṭihāriyapakkhañစာ’ refers to the observance of the Uposatha on the days preceding and following the 14th, 15th, and 8th days—namely the 13th, 1st, 7th, and 9th days. ‘Aṭṭhaṅgasusamāgataṃ’ means being well-endowed with the eight factors, such as abstaining from taking life. ‘Uposathaṃ upāgacchiံ’ means I entered upon the fast, I observed the Uposatha.

Regarding that Uposatha:
“One should not kill living beings, nor take what is not given, nor speak lies, nor be a drinker of intoxicants. One should abstain from unchaste conduct, from sexual intercourse. One should not eat at night, at the wrong time (vikālabhojana).

One should not wear garlands or use perfumes. One should sleep on a mat spread on the ground or on a low couch. The Buddha, who has reached the end of suffering, proclaimed this eightfold Uposatha.” (as stated in the Sutta Nipāta).

‘Devakāyābhinandinī’ means observing the Uposatha while longing for the heavenly realm, such as the Cātumahārājika heaven, with the desire to be reborn there.
40:
"Ekena bhattena" means "by a single mealtime on this very day." "Muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā" means having shaven hair and having the body clad in the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), thus having gone forth. "Devakāyaṃ na patthehaṃ" means that because the highest path (Arahatta-magga) has been attained, I do not long for any group of devas. For that very reason, it was said, "Vineyya hadaye daraṃ," which means having removed the fever of defilements in the heart by way of eradication. This was her declaration of final knowledge (aññābyākaraṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Mittā Therī is finished.

## 8. The Commentary on the Verses of Abhayamatā Therī

The verse beginning with "Uddhaṃ pādatalā" is that of the Elder Abhayamatā. This Elder also had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit in various lives, was born into a good family during the time of Tissa Buddha. When she reached the age of discretion, one day, seeing the Teacher wandering for alms, she, with a heart full of faith, took his bowl and offered a spoonful of alms-food. Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, as a result of that karma, she became a courtesan named Padumavatī in the city of Ujjeni. King Bimbisāra, hearing of her beauty and other qualities, said to his chaplain, "I hear there is a courtesan named Padumavatī in Ujjeni; I wish to see her." The chaplain replied, "Very well, O King," and by the power of a mantra, he summoned a yakkha named Kumbhīra. By the power of the yakkha, he immediately transported the King to the city of Ujjeni. The King spent one night with her, and she conceived. She informed the King, "A child has been conceived in my womb." Hearing this, the King said, "If it is a son, send him to me when he grows up," and giving her a signet ring, he departed. After ten months, she gave birth to a son and named him Abhaya on the naming day. When the son reached seven years of age, she sent him to the King, saying, "Your father is the Great King Bimbisāra." When the King saw the son, he felt fatherly love and raised him with the honors of a prince. The attainment of faith, going forth, and attainment of distinction of that Prince Abhaya have already been mentioned below. Later, his mother, hearing the Dhamma from her son, the Elder Abhaya, gained faith and went forth among the bhikkhunīs...
41:
...while practicing insight (Vipassanā), she attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. In reference to this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"While the Teacher named Tissa was wandering for alms, I raised and offered a spoonful of alms-food to that most excellent Buddha.

Having accepted it, the Buddha Tissa, the supreme leader of the world, standing in the street, gave me a blessing (anumodanā):

'By offering this spoonful of alms-food, you will go to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; you will be the chief queen of thirty-seven kings of devas.

You will also be the chief queen of fifty wheel-turning monarchs; you will always obtain everything you desire in your mind.

After enjoying these riches, you will go forth without any attachments; having fully understood all taints (āsavas), you will attain Nibbāna, free from taints.'

Having said this, the Buddha Tissa, the supreme leader of the world, the hero, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air.

My noble gift was well-given; the perfection of the gruel-offering was well-sacrificed; by offering a spoonful of alms-food, I have reached the immovable state (Nibbāna).

Ninety-two aeons ago from now, I gave that gift; because of that gift of alms-food, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati).

My defilements are burnt up... (pe)... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

After attaining Arahatship, she herself repeated, as an utterance of joy (udāna), the verses that her son, the Elder Abhaya, had spoken as an exhortation while preaching the Dhamma:

"Mother, contemplate this body from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, as impure and foul-smelling.

Living thus, all lust has been uprooted in me; the fever (of defilements) has been cut off; I am cooled and extinguished (nibbutā)," she said.
42:
Among those verses, the summary of the meaning of the first verse is: Dear daughter Padumavatī, upwards from the soles of the feet and downwards from the tips of the hair, this body is filled with various kinds of impurities; it is always impure and foul-smelling because it emits a putrid odor. Contemplate this body, which is an accumulation of loathsome things, with the eye of wisdom. This verse was spoken by her son as a word of advice.

Having heard those words and attained the fruit of Arahantship, she wished to utter an exclamation of joy. Out of reverence for her teacher, she first recited that very verse, and then, wishing to describe her own practice, she spoke the second verse beginning with, "To me who lives thus."

In that verse, "To me who lives thus" means: abiding in the advice given by my son, the Elder Abhaya, beginning with the words "upwards from the soles of the feet," I viewed the entire body as foul (asubha). With a concentrated mind, I discerned the material phenomena (rūpa-dhamma) consisting of the primary elements and derived materiality, as well as the mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma) such as feeling (vedanā) connected with that materiality. Then, applying the three characteristics to those phenomena, I lived practicing insight such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā). "All lust has been uprooted" means that through the sequence of the path associated with insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā), and specifically by the highest path (the path of Arahantship), all lust has been uprooted and destroyed by me. "The fever of defilements has been extinguished" means that by that very path, all the fever of defilements has been completely cut off. Because they have been cut off, I have become one who is cooled and extinguished by the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (saupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhayāmātā is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Abhayā

The verse beginning with "Abhaya, the body is fragile" is the verse of the Elder Abhayā. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation from the round of rebirths (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhi, she was reborn in a noble wealthy family (khattiyamahāsāla). Upon reaching maturity, she became the chief queen of King Aruṇa. One day, the king gave her seven fragrant lotuses. She took them and thought, "What is the use of me wearing these flowers? What if I were to offer these to the Blessed One?" and she sat down. The Blessed One, at the time of seeking alms, [entered] the king's palace...
43:
She entered (the monastery). Seeing the Blessed One, she was filled with a devout mind, went out to meet Him, offered those flowers, and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was reborn in a good family in the city of Ujjeni. Upon reaching maturity, she became a friend of Abhayāmātā. When Abhayāmātā ordained, she herself ordained out of affection for her. While living in Rājagaha with her, she went to the Sītavana cemetery one day to contemplate foulness (asubha). The Teacher, while staying in the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), placed before her an object she had experienced before and manifested a bloated corpse and so forth in her presence. Seeing that corpse, she stood there with a mind full of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). The Teacher, emitting a radiance and manifesting Himself as if sitting right in front of her, spoke these verses:

"Abhaya, the body is fragile, wherein ordinary worldlings are attached. I shall lay down this body, being clearly comprehending and mindful."

"Though oppressed by many painful states, I, delighting in diligence, have reached the destruction of craving; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

At the conclusion of the verses, she attained the fruit of Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Aruṇavatī, there was a king named Aruṇa. I was the wife of that king, and I restrained what was to be restrained."

"Taking seven lotuses with divine fragrance, while sitting on the noble palace, I then thought thus:"

"What is the use of these flowers placed upon my head? It is better for me to offer them to the wisdom of the most excellent Buddha."

"Waiting for the Fully Enlightened One, I sat near the door, thinking: 'When the Fully Enlightened One comes, I will worship the Great Sage (Mahāmuni).'"

"Like a majestic bull, like a maned lion, the Conqueror (Jina) came along the street together with the community of monks."

"Seeing the radiance of the Buddha, with a heart joyful and stirred, I opened the door and worshipped the most excellent Buddha."
44: Seven lotus flowers were scattered in the sky. Those lotus flowers, forming a canopy above the Buddha, remained over His head. With a joyful and delighted mind, experiencing rapture and with hands joined in reverence, I gained confidence in that Buddha and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. A great canopy of blue lotuses remains over my head. I emit a divine fragrance; this is the fruit of offering seven lotuses. Once, when I was being led by a group of relatives, as long as my retinue existed, the canopy of blue lotuses remained. I became the chief queen of seventy celestial kings. Being a ruler in all places, I wandered through various existences. I became the chief queen of sixty-three universal monarchs. All people followed my will. I was one whose words were accepted by others. My complexion is like that of a lotus, and a fragrance wafts from me. I have never known ugliness; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha. Being skilled in the four bases of power (iddhipāda), delighting in the development of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and reaching the pinnacle of direct knowledges (abhiññā) is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha. Being skilled in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), having concentration (samādhi) and meditative absorption (jhāna) as my domain, and being devoted to the right efforts (sammappadhāna) is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha. My energy is like a draft ox that carries the burden to the security from bondage (yogakkhema). All taints (āsavas) are exhausted. Now there is no more rebirth. In the thirty-first aeon from this one, I worshipped with that flower. Due to the merit of worshipping the Buddha, I have not known a miserable rebirth. My defilements have been burnt away... I have followed the teaching of the Buddha. (Apadāna, Therī, 2.1.71-90). Having reached the fruit of Arahantship, that Elder Nun recited those very verses with modifications as an inspired utterance (udāna). In that verse, 'Abhaya' refers to addressing herself. 'Bhiduro' means having the nature of breaking, meaning impermanent (anicca). 'Yattha sattā puthujjanā' means in that (body) which has the nature of breaking in an instant...
45:
In this body, which is impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive, these blind worldlings (puthujjana) are attached. 'I shall discard this body' means I will discard and abandon this foul body without taking it up again through grasping (upādāna) and without longing. He stated the reason for being able to discard it as 'being clearly comprehending and mindful.'

'By many painful things' means being touched and oppressed by many painful things such as birth, old age, and so on. 'Because of delighting in diligence (appamāda)' means because of delighting in diligence, which is called the non-absence of mindfulness, having gained spiritual urgency (saṃvega) from seeing the way to escape from that suffering. The remaining words are as previously explained. Here, according to the method taught by the Teacher:

'You who delight in diligence, discard this body;
Strive to reach the destruction of craving (Nibbāna);
Follow the teaching of the Buddha.'

This is the text, as it was recorded in the Council according to the method spoken by the Elder Nun. 'Appamādaratāya te' means you must be one who delights in diligence.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Abhayā Therī is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Sāmā Therī

The verse beginning with 'Four times, five times' is the verse of the Elder Nun Sāmā. This Elder Nun also, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various lives, wandered only in happy realms. In the time of this Buddha, she was born into a wealthy merchant family in the city of Kosambī and was named Sāmā. When she reached maturity, she became a dear friend of the laywoman Sāmāvatī. When Sāmāvatī passed away, she gained spiritual urgency and ordained as a nun. After ordaining, she was unable to dispel the grief that arose on account of Sāmāvatī and was thus unable to attain the Noble Path. Later, hearing the instruction of the Elder Ānanda who was sitting in the refectory, she developed insight (vipassanā) and on the seventh day, reached Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
46:
Having reached Arahantship and reflecting on her own practice, wishing to make that practice manifest:

'I went out from the monastery four times, five times,
Not having obtained peace of mind, and unable to bring the mind under control.
On the eighth night for me, craving was completely uprooted.

Though oppressed by many painful things, for me who delights in diligence (appamāda),
The destruction of craving (Arahantship) has been reached; the teaching of the Buddha has been followed.'

She recited these two verses as an inspired utterance (udāna).

In those verses, 'I went out from the monastery four times, five times' means: 'Though I sat practicing insight meditation in the monastery where I resided, I was unable to bring the monk's task to its pinnacle. Thinking, "Is it because of the lack of suitable weather (utu-sappāya) that my insight does not strike the Path?" I went out from the monastery nine times in total—four and five.' Therefore, she said, 'Not having obtained peace of mind, and unable to bring the mind under control.' There, 'peace of mind' refers to the concentration of the Noble Path (ariyamagga-samādhi). 'Unable to bring the mind under control' means my meditation mind did not follow my will because of the lack of balance in energy (vīriya). It is said that this Elder Nun was one who exerted excessive energy. 'On the eighth night for me' means from the time she received the instruction from the Elder Ānanda, she practiced insight meditation day and night without laziness. Although she went out from the monastery four or five times during the night to meditate but did not gain any distinction, on the eighth night, she gained balance of energy and exhausted the defilements through the sequence of the Path. Therefore, she said, 'On the eighth night for me, craving was completely uprooted.' The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sāmā Therī is finished.

## The Commentary on the Two-Verse Section (Dukanipāta) is finished.
47:
## 3. Tikanipāta
## 1. Aparāsāmātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Tikanipāta (The Book of the Threes), the verse beginning with 'Paṇṇavīsativassāni' is the verse of the Elder Nun Aparāsāmā. This elder nun had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, while accumulating merit as a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences, she was reborn as a Kinnarī on the banks of the Candabhāgā River during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. There, she wandered about, devoted to playing with other Kinnaras. Then one day, the Teacher, in order to plant the seed of merit for that Kinnarī, went to that place and walked in meditation on the riverbank. Seeing the Blessed One, the Kinnarī was filled with joy and delight; she took salala flowers, approached the Teacher, paid homage, and worshipped the Blessed One with those flowers.

Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered through the realms of devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was reborn into a noble family in the city of Kosambī. When she reached of age, she became a companion of Queen Sāmāvatī. When Queen Sāmāvatī passed away, she was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and entered the Order. For twenty-five years, she did not attain composure of mind. However, in her old age, she received the instruction of the Sugata, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). This account is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

'At that time, I was a Kinnarī on the bank of the Candabhāgā River. I saw the God of gods, the Bull among men, walking in meditation.

Having picked salala flowers, I gave them to the most excellent Buddha. The Great Hero smelled the salala flowers, which had a divine fragrance.

The Fully Enlightened One Vipassī, the Leader of the World, the Great Hero, accepted and smelled them while I was watching him.

Raising my hands in reverential salutation and paying homage to the Best of bipeds, I gladdened my own mind and then climbed the mountain.

In the ninety-first aeon from this, because I gave that flower then, I have not known a miserable rebirth; this is the fruit of worshipping the Buddha.

My defilements are burnt... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.'
48:
Having attained Arahantship and reflecting on her own practice, she uttered these verses by the power of an inspired utterance (udāna):

"For twenty-five years since I went forth, I do not recall having attained peace of mind even once.

Not having attained peace of heart, I could not bring my mind under control. Therefore, remembering the Victor's teaching, I felt spiritual urgency.

Being devoted to diligence, through many painful states, I have reached the destruction of craving; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Today is the seventh night since my craving was dried up."

In those verses, "cittassa samaṃ" means the calming of the mind, the concentration of the path and fruit of mental tranquility (cetosamatha-magga-phala-samādhi). "Tato" means because of that inability to bring the mind under control. "Saṃvegamāpādiṃ" means that while the Teacher was still present, she was unable to bring the recluse's task to its peak, and thinking, "How shall I reach it later?", she arrived at the terror of knowledge (ñāṇutrāsa) through spiritual urgency. "Saritvā jinasāsanaṃ" means having repeatedly reflected on the Teacher's advice, such as the simile of the blind turtle (kāṇakacchapa). The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Aparāsāmā is finished.

## 2. Uttamātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Catukkhattuṃ pañcakkhattuṃ" is the verse of the Elder Nun Uttamā. This elder nun had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit as a powerful support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, she was reborn as a domestic slave in the house of a certain householder in the city of Bandhumatī. When she reached of age, she lived by performing the service (veyyāvacca) of her masters. At that time, King Bandhumā was one who observed the Uposatha on full-moon days; he would perform acts of merit such as giving (dāna) in the morning and go to listen to the Dhamma in the afternoon. Then, just as the King practiced, all the people also...
49:
On the full-moon day, [the people together with the King] observed the factors of the Uposatha. Then, that slave girl had this thought: "Now the Great King and the people are living having undertaken the factors of the Uposatha; what if I too were to live having undertaken the Uposatha virtue on Uposatha days?" She did so, and by guarding the Uposatha virtue very purely, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wandering only in happy realms thereafter, in this Buddha's era, she was born into a treasurer's family in the city of Sāvatthī. When she reached the age of discretion, she heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā and went forth in the Buddha's dispensation. Although she developed insight (vipassanā), she was unable to bring it to its peak. The Elder Nun Paṭācārā, knowing the movement of her mind, gave her instruction. Abiding by that instruction, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). This account is stated in the Apadāna as follows:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, there was a kshatriya named Bandhumā. On the full-moon day, he observed the Uposatha.

At that time, I was a water-carrying slave there. Seeing the King together with his army, I then thought thus:

'Even the King, abandoning his kingship, observes the Uposatha. The people are delighted; surely that deed is fruitful.'

Reflecting wisely on my own state of misery and poverty, and gladdening my mind, I observed the Uposatha.

Having observed the Uposatha in the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One, by that well-performed deed, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In that heaven, I had a well-made mansion, two leagues high. It was beautiful in the form of a gabled palace and well-adorned with excellent seats.

A hundred thousand nymphs always attended me. Surpassing other deities, I always shone very brightly.

I was made the chief queen of sixty-four kings of gods. I was also made the chief queen of sixty-three wheel-turning monarchs.

Having a complexion like the color of gold, I wandered through existences. I was excellent in all places; this is the fruit of observing the Uposatha."
50:
"I obtain elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and palanquins. All this is the fruit of observing the Uposatha.

I obtain everything made of gold, made of silver, as well as those made of crystal and red ruby.

I obtain all precious garments: silk, wool, linen, and cotton fabrics.

I obtain all alms-food, snacks, drinks, clothing, and monastery lodgings. This is the fruit of observing the Uposatha.

I obtain all excellent perfumes, flowers, scented powders, and ointments. This is the fruit of observing the Uposatha.

I obtain all storied houses, palaces, pavilions, pinnacled houses, and cave-dwellings. This is the fruit of observing the Uposatha.

At the age of seven, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. Before even half a month had passed, I attained the fruit of Arahantship.

My defilements are burned away; all forms of existence are uprooted. All taints are exhausted; there is now no more renewed existence.

Because of the deed I performed ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of observing the Uposatha.

My defilements are burned away... (and so forth) ...the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

After attaining Arahantship, reflecting on her own practice, she spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna):

'Four or five times I went out from the monastery, having failed to find peace of mind, my mind being uncontrolled.

I approached a bhikkhunī whom I trusted. She taught me the Dhamma concerning the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.'
51:
'Having heard the Dhamma of that Therī, just as she instructed me, I sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, endowed with rapture and happiness. On the eighth day, having shattered the mass of darkness, I stretched out my legs.' — Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, "I approached that bhikkhunī who was trustworthy to me" means I approached with faith that Paṭācārā Therī, whose words were worthy of belief. There is also a variant reading: "That bhikkhunī approached me, she who was my benefactor." The meaning is that Paṭācārā Bhikkhunī approached me out of compassion, she who accomplished my welfare. "She taught me the Dhamma, the aggregates, sense bases, and elements" means that Paṭācārā Therī taught me the Dhamma by analyzing and showing, "These are the five aggregates, these are the twelve sense bases, these are the eighteen elements."

"Having heard the Dhamma of that Therī" means having heard the subtle and profound Dhamma of insight (vipassanā) which leads to the Noble Path, preceded by the analysis of aggregates and so forth, in the presence of that Therī who had attained the analytical insights. "Just as she instructed me" means that as the Therī instructed and exhorted me, so I practiced, and bringing the practice to its culmination, I sat for seven days in a single cross-legged posture. How? "Endowed with rapture and happiness" means being possessed of rapture and happiness born of meditative absorption (jhāna). "On the eighth day, having shattered the mass of darkness, I stretched out my legs" means that having shattered the entire mass of delusion with the Path of Arahantship, on the eighth day, breaking the cross-legged posture, I stretched out my legs. This itself was her declaration of final knowledge (aññā).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Uttamā Therī is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Verses of the Other Uttamā Therī

"Those seven factors of enlightenment..." and so forth are the verses of another Uttamā Therī. She too had performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a support for the ending of the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In the time of Vipassī Buddha, she was reborn as a household slave in the city of Bandhumatī. One day, seeing an Arahant Elder, a disciple of the Teacher, walking for alms, she gave him three cakes (modaka) with a clear and confident mind.
52:
Due to that meritorious deed, she wandered among devas and humans. In this Buddha-dispensation, she was reborn in a wealthy Brahmin family in the Kosala country. When she reached the age of wisdom, she heard the Dhamma from the Teacher who was wandering through the countryside. Having gained faith, she went forth as a nun and before long attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights. Concerning this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Bandhumatī, I was a water-carrier slave. I went to fetch water, taking my own portion. Seeing a monk on the path, peaceful in mind and composed, with a clear mind and joyful heart, I gave him three cakes. By that well-performed deed and by my intentions and aspirations, I did not go to a miserable rebirth for ninety-one aeons. Having experienced all forms of prosperity, because I gave those three cakes, I have now reached the unshakable state. My defilements are burned away... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having attained Arahantship and reflecting on her own practice, she spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance:

"These seven factors of enlightenment, which are the paths for the attainment of Nibbāna, have all been developed by me just as they were taught by the Buddha. I am one who attains at will the void and the signless meditations. A true daughter of the Buddha, I always delight in Nibbāna. All sensual desires, whether divine or human, have been completely cut off. The wandering in the cycle of births is exhausted; there is now no more renewed existence."

In those verses, "I am one who attains at will the void and the signless" means I am one who obtains at will both the void attainment (suññata-samāpatti) and the signless attainment (animitta-samāpatti). Among those attainments, whatever attainment I wish to enter, in whatever place and at whatever time, I can enter that very attainment in that very place at that very time.
53:
It means 'dwells having entered the attainment.' Indeed, although the three kinds of fruition—emptiness and so forth—of any path named 'emptiness' (suññata), 'desireless' (appaṇihita), and so forth can occur, this elder nun enters only the emptiness attainment (suññata-samāpatti) and the signless attainment (animitta-samāpatti). Therefore, she said: 'I am one who obtains the emptiness and signless attainments as I wish.' Or, this is said because it occurs frequently. Others say this is just an example.

'Those divine and those human' refers to the objects of sensual pleasure (vatthukāma) included in the deva world and the human world. All those objects of sensual pleasure have been well-severed by me through the abandoning of the lustful desire (chandarāga) associated with them; they have been made unworthy of enjoyment. For has it not been said: 'Friend, a monk whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is incapable of enjoying sensual pleasures as he did before when he was a householder'? The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Other Uttamā Therī is Finished.

## 4. The Commentary on the Verses of Dantikā Therī

The verse beginning with 'Divāvihārā nikkhamma' is that of the Elder Nun Dantikā. She, too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots that are a strong support for Nibbāna in various lives, was reborn in the species of Kinnarī on the bank of the Candabhāgā River during a period when the world was empty of Buddhas. One day, while wandering and playing with other Kinnaras, she saw a Paccekabuddha sitting for his day-abiding at the foot of a certain tree. Seeing him, with a heart full of faith, she approached, made an offering of Sāla flowers, paid homage, and departed.

Through that meritorious deed, she wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was reborn in Sāvatthī in the house of the chaplain brahmin of King Kosala. When she reached the age of discretion, she gained faith during the acceptance of the Jetavana monastery and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, she went forth as a nun under Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. While living in Rājagaha, one day after her meal, she climbed the Gijjhakūṭa Hill and sat for her day-abiding. Seeing an elephant stretching out its leg for the mahout to mount, she took that very object as her basis, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

'The Blessed One, having accepted the alms-food and standing on the road, gave me a blessing (anumodanā).
"Because of giving a single spoonful of alms-food, you shall go to the Tāvatiṃsa realm; you shall be the chief queen of thirty-six king of gods.
You shall be the chief queen of fifty universal monarchs (cakkavatti); you shall obtain everything desired by the mind at all times.
Having enjoyed wealth and being free from anxiety, you shall go forth as a nun; having fully understood all taints and being free from taints, you shall attain Parinibbāna," (so he said).
The Blessed One Tissa, the foremost leader in the world, having spoken these words of prophecy, ascended into the sky like a king of hamsas flying up.
This noble gift was well-given by me; the perfect worship was well-performed; because of giving a single spoonful of alms-food, I have reached the unshakable Nibbāna.
Ninety-two aeons ago from this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), I gave that gift of a spoonful of alms-food; since then, I have not known a woeful rebirth. This is the fruit of giving alms-food.
My defilements are burnt away... (etc.)... I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching.'
54:
At that time, I was a Kinnarī by the bank of the Candabhāgā River. I saw the Buddha, the stainless one, the unconquered (aparājita), the self-become (sayambhū).

With a heart of faith and full of joy, I paid homage with joined palms, took a cluster of Sāla flowers, and specially worshipped the Self-become One.

Through that well-performed deed, and through my volition and aspiration, I left the Kinnarī body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

I obtained the position of chief queen to thirty-six kings of gods. Everything I desired in my mind was fulfilled according to my wish.

I also obtained the position of chief queen to ten universal monarchs. Because I had accumulated merits, I wandered through successive births.

Wholesome states exist in me; I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness. Today, in the teaching of the Son of the Sakyans (Sakyaputta), I have become one worthy of special offerings.

Today, with a purified mind, being free from the stains of the mind, all my taints (āsava) are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

Because I worshipped the Buddha ninety-four aeons ago, I have not gone to a woeful state since then. This is the fruit of offering a cluster of Sāla flowers.

My defilements are burnt away... I have done what was to be done in the Buddha's teaching.

Upon attaining Arahantship, reflecting on her own practice, she was filled with joy and inspiration, and uttered these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

'Coming out from my day-abiding on the Gijjhakūṭa Hill, I saw a great elephant on the riverbank that had emerged from the water.

A man, taking a goad, requested: "Give me your leg." The great elephant stretched out its leg, and the man mounted the elephant.

Seeing the untamed being tamed and coming under the control of humans, I then concentrated my mind and indeed went to the forest.'
55:
In that verse, 'nāgaṃ ogāhamuttiṇṇaṃ' means the noble elephant descended into the river and emerged from where it had descended. There is also a variant reading 'ogayha muttiṇṇaṃ'. The letter 'ma' is a euphonic junction (padasandhi). 'Nadītīramhi addasaṃ' means she saw it on the bank of the Candabhāgā River.

To show what that elephant was doing, the words beginning with 'puriso' were spoken. There, 'give the foot' (pādam dehi) means giving a signal to extend the foot in order to mount its back. Giving a signal that is already familiar is what is called 'requesting' here.

'Seeing the untamed tamed' (disvā adantaṃ damitaṃ) means seeing that which was previously untamed by nature, now brought to a state of being tamed through elephant-training by an elephant trainer. How was it tamed? It should be connected as: seeing it follow the will of humans and doing whatever humans command. Because of seeing that elephant and due to the elephant's behavior, she went to the forest and made her mind tranquil. The word 'khalu' is a particle used for emphasis (avadhāraṇa). How? 'Even this elephant, which is an animal, has reached a state of being tamed by following the will of an elephant trainer. Why should I, being a human, not reach a state of being tamed by following the will of the Teacher, the trainer of men?' Thus, having felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she developed insight (vipassanā) and, with the concentration of the Path of Arahantship, made her mind perfectly tranquil, completely exhausting all defilements.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Dantikā is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Ubbirī

The verse beginning with 'Amma jīva' is that of Elder Ubbirī. This elder nun had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī. When she reached the age of discretion, one day, while her parents had gone to another house to attend a festive ceremony, she remained at home alone. Near midday, seeing an Arahant elder, a disciple of the Blessed One, passing by the door of the house, she wished to offer alms. She invited him, saying, 'Venerable sir, please enter here.' When the elder entered the house, she paid homage to him with the five-point prostration, prepared a seat with rugs and so forth, and offered it. The elder sat down.
56:
On the prepared seat, that woman took the bowl, filled it with alms-food, and placed it in the elder's hand. The elder gave a blessing (anumodanā) and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where she enjoyed sublime divine bliss for the duration of her lifespan. Passing away from there, she wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). In this Buddha's era, she was born into a wealthy merchant family in Sāvatthī and was named Ubbirī. She was extremely beautiful, lovely, and pleasing to behold. When she reached marriageable age, King Kosala took her to his palace. After a few years, she gave birth to a daughter. They named the daughter Jīvantī. Seeing the daughter, the King was delighted and anointed Ubbirī as queen. However, that young daughter passed away at the age when she could run and play here and there. The mother went to the cemetery where the daughter's body was laid and wept every day. One day, she went to the Teacher, paid homage, sat for a while, and then left. Standing on the bank of the Aciravatī River, she wept again on account of her daughter. Seeing her, the Teacher, while remaining seated in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), manifested himself and asked, 'Why are you lamenting?' She replied, 'Blessed One, I am lamenting on account of my daughter.' The Teacher said, 'In this cemetery, about eighty-four thousand of your daughters have been cremated. For which of those daughters are you lamenting?' Showing her the various cremation sites of those daughters, he spoke this half-verse:

'Dear Ubbirī, you cry out "O Jīva" in the woods; come to know yourself. Eighty-four thousand daughters, all named "Jīva", have been burnt in this cremation ground. For which of them do you grieve?'

In that verse, 'Amma jīva' is addressing the daughter with the name used by a mother; this shows the manner of Ubbirī's lamentation. 'Vanamhi kandasi' means you weep in the middle of the woods. 'Attānaṃ adhigaccha Ubbirī' means, Ubbirī, first know your own self; know it as it really is. 'Cullāsītisahassāni' means eighty-four thousand. 'Sabbā jīvasanāmikā' means all those daughters had the same name, 'Jīvantī'. 'Etamhāḷāhane daḍḍhā' means they were cremated in this cemetery. 'Tāsaṃ kamanusocasi' means, among those eighty-four thousand daughters named 'Jīvantī', for which one do you grieve or fall into sorrow? Thus, when the Teacher taught the Dhamma, following the sequence of the teaching...
57:
Directing her knowledge and undertaking insight meditation (vipassanā), through the grace of the Teacher's teaching and the perfection of her own supporting conditions, she intensified her insight just as it stood. By the sequence of the paths, she became established in Arahantship, the highest fruit. Regarding this, it was said in the Apadāna:

“In the city of Haṃsāvatī, I was then a young girl. My mother and my father went to their place of work.

At midday, when the sun was high, I saw a Samana walking along the street, and I prepared a seat for him.

Having prepared my seat with rugs and woolen covers, with a clear and joyful mind, I spoke these words:

‘The ground is heated and boiling, the sun stands at midday, the winds do not blow; it is time to rest here.

This seat is prepared for your sake, O Great Sage (Mahāmuni); out of compassion for me, please sit upon my seat.’

The Samana, well-tamed and pure-minded, sat there. Taking his bowl, I offered whatever alms-food I had obtained.

Through that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations, I left the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

There, my well-constructed celestial mansion, created by the gift of the seat, was sixty yojanas in height and thirty yojanas in width.

My various thrones were made of gold, made of gems, made of crystal, and made of lohitaṅga stone.

My thrones were well-prepared with cushions of cotton, variegated coverings, and rugs with long hair on one side.

Whenever I desired to go, being devoted to joy and play, I would go to my desired place together with my noble throne.

I served as the chief queen of eighty celestial kings; I also served as the chief queen of seventy wheel-turning monarchs (cakkavatti).”
58:
“Wandering through various existences, I obtained great wealth. I had no lack of possessions; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

I wandered only in two existences: the celestial realm and the human realm. I do not know other existences; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

I was born only into two families: the Khattiya and the Brāhmaṇa. In all places, I was of high birth; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

I do not know the mental distress that burns the heart. I do not know physical deformity; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

Nurses, hunchbacks, and many maidservants who carry clothes attended to me. I went from lap to lap; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

Some bathed me, some fed me, some always entertained me, and some anointed me with perfumes; this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

Whether I was in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, knowing my thought, a throne would appear before me.

This is my last existence; my final birth is proceeding. Even today, having renounced the kingdom, I have gone forth from the home life into homelessness.

In the hundred thousandth aeon (kappa) ago, I gave that gift. Because of that gift, I do not know any miserable rebirth (duggati); this is the fruit of the gift of a single seat.

My defilements are burnt away... (as before) ...the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.”

Then, being established in Arahantship and wishing to manifest the special attainment she had reached, she spoke these two verses:

“O Sage, you have pulled out my dart, so hard to see, which was lodged in my heart. You have dispelled the sorrow for my daughter that overwhelmed me when I was possessed by grief.

Today, with the dart pulled out, I am without hunger (craving) and fully extinguished (nibbuta). I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha.”
59:
In those verses, “You have pulled out my dart, so hard to see, which was lodged in my heart” means: the sorrow and craving, which are called a “dart” because they are hard to see truly by those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit, because they reside in my mind, because they cause affliction, because they are difficult to extract, and because they pierce within—these the Buddha has indeed pulled out, indeed extracted. “Which was for me who was possessed by grief” means: because he dispelled without remainder the sorrow for my daughter that overwhelmed me, and extracted it without residue, therefore it is connected as “he has indeed pulled out my dart.”

“Today, with the dart pulled out, I am...” means: that I, today, having the dart of craving entirely uprooted, and for that very reason being without hunger (craving), am fully extinguished. “The Sage (Muni)” refers to the Omniscient Buddha; the ninefold supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma) consisting of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna taught by him; and the Saṅgha, which is the community of the eight noble persons established in that Dhamma. Because of being joined with these peerless Three Jewels and because they destroy all the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha), they are the refuge (saraṇa), the protection, the shelter, and the final resort. “I go to” means I approach, I realize, and I attend to them.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ubbirī Therī is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Sukkhā Therī

The verse beginning with “Kiṃ me katā Rājagahe” is that of Sukkhā Therī. She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating merit that is a strong support for liberation from the round of rebirth in various existences, was born in a family home in the city of Bandhumatī during the time of the Blessed One Vipassī. Having reached the age of discretion, she went to the monastery with other laywomen and, hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, gained faith and went forth. She became very learned (bahussuta), a bearer of the Dhamma, and possessed of eloquent wisdom. Having practiced the holy life there for many thousands of years, she passed away as a worldling (puthujjana) and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Similarly, during the times of the Blessed One Sikhī and the Blessed One Vessabhū—thus in the dispensations of three Fully Enlightened Buddhas—she guarded her virtue and was very learned and a bearer of the Dhamma. Likewise, in the dispensations of the Blessed Ones Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, she went forth and was of pure virtue, very learned, and a teacher of the Dhamma.

Thus, having accumulated much merit in those various lives and wandering only in the happy realms (sugati), she was born in this Buddha-era in the family of a great householder in the city of Rājagaha and was named Sukkhā. When she reached the age of discretion, at the time the Teacher entered the city of Rājagaha...
60:
(That woman) became a lay follower (upāsikā) who had gained faith. Later, upon hearing the Dhamma from the Theri Dhammadinnā, she was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and ordained under that very Theri. While practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), she attained the fruit of Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Regarding this, it is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Therī 2.4.111-142):

“Ninety-one aeons ago, the Leader named Vipassī, of beautiful appearance and a beholder of all phenomena, arose in the world.

At that time, I was born into a certain family in the city of Bandhumatī. Having heard the Dhamma of the Sage, I renounced the home life and ordained.

I was learned (bahussuta), a bearer of the Dhamma, possessed of ready wit, and likewise a speaker of variegated discourse, serving the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

Having given Dhamma talks then, I benefited many people. Passing away from that life, I, being illustrious, was reborn in the Tusita heaven.

Thirty-one aeons from now, the Conqueror Sikhī, like a crested flame, arose as the best of speakers, illuminating the world with his glory.

At that time also, having ordained and becoming expert in the Buddha’s Dispensation, I illuminated the words of the Conqueror and from there went to the celestial realm.

In that same thirty-first aeon, the Leader named Vessabhū, possessed of great wisdom, arose. At that time also, I was just the same.

Having ordained as a bearer of the Dhamma, I illuminated the Conqueror’s Dispensation. Having gone to the delightful city of the gods, I experienced great bliss.

In this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda-kappa), the supreme Conqueror Kakusandha, the refuge of men, arose. At that time also, I was just the same.

Having ordained in the Sage’s teaching and illuminating it for the duration of my life, I passed away from there and went to the celestial realm as if going to my own home.

In this very aeon, the Leader named Koṇāgamana, the refuge of the world, free from defilements and gone to the Deathless, arose.”
61:
“At that time also, having ordained in the Dispensation of such a virtuous Buddha, I was learned and a bearer of the Dhamma, illuminating the Dispensation of the Conqueror.

In this very aeon, the Buddha Kassapa, the refuge of the world, free from defilements, the ender of death, and supreme among sages, arose. In the Dispensation of that Hero among men, I also ordained, mastered the True Dhamma, and became confident in inquiry.

O Great Sage, I was virtuous and modest, expert in the three trainings (sikkhā), and I preached many Dhamma discourses throughout my life.

Through the result of that karma and through my volitional aspirations, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Now, in my final birth, I was born in the prosperous city of Giribbaja (Rājagaha) into a wealthy merchant family with a great accumulation of treasures.

When the Leader of the world, surrounded by a thousand monks and praised by the Thousand-eyed One (Sakka), arrived at Rājagaha—

The Blessed One, tamed along with the formerly tamed matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas), liberated along with the liberated ones, and having the complexion of pure gold, entered Rājagaha.

Seeing that Buddha-majesty and hearing the collection of his virtues, I gained faith in the Buddha and honored him according to my ability. At a later time, I departed from the household life and ordained under the Theri Dhammadinnā.

While my hair was being cut, I burnt away the defilements. Not long after ordaining, I mastered the entire Dispensation. Then I preached the Dhamma in a great assembly of people. While the Dhamma was being preached, the realization of the Dhamma occurred for many thousands of beings. Knowing that realization of the Dhamma and being greatly amazed, a Yakkha (deity) who was deeply devoted to me wandered through Giribbaja (proclaiming my virtues).”
62:
“What are the people in Rājagaha doing? They remain still as if they have drunk honey.
They do not attend to this pure Theri who is preaching the state of the Deathless (Nibbāna).

That Dhamma, which is irresistible, eternally delicious, and full of essence—
I think the wise drink it just as travelers drink water from a rain cloud.

O Great Sage, I am a master of psychic powers and the divine ear element. I am a master of the knowledge of encompassing others' minds.

I know my past lives, and my divine eye is purified. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

O Great Hero, in your presence, knowledge has arisen in me regarding the analytical insights of meaning, doctrine, language, and eloquence.

My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha’s Dispensation has been fulfilled.”

After reaching Arahatship, she became a great Dhamma preacher surrounded by five hundred bhikkhunīs. One day, after wandering for alms in Rājagaha and finishing her meal, she entered the bhikkhunīs' quarters and sat in the midst of a large assembly. She preached the Dhamma as if squeezing a honey-pot to feed them very sweet honey, or as if sprinkling them with the nectar of the Deathless. The assembly listened to her Dhamma talk attentively with undistracted minds. At that moment, a deity dwelling in a tree at the end of the Theri’s walkway (caṅkamana), being devoted to the Dhamma teaching, entered Rājagaha and wandered from street to street and crossroads to crossroads, making her virtues known:

“What are the people in Rājagaha doing? They remain still as if they have drunk honey.
They do not attend to this pure Theri who is preaching the Buddha’s Dispensation.

That Dhamma, which is irresistible, eternally delicious, and full of essence—
I think the wise drink it just as travelers drink water from a rain cloud.”

She uttered these two verses.

In those verses, 'Kiṃme katā rājagahe manussā' means: what are these people of Rājagaha doing, or in what business are they occupied? 'Madhūṃ pītāva acchare' means: like those who have taken and drunk honey from a jar, becoming unconscious and unable to lift their heads...
63:
(They) are unable; thus it means that these people, as if becoming devoid of perception through the perception of the Dhamma, are unable to raise their heads and are merely sitting there. "Ye sukkaṃ na upāsanti, desentiṃ buddhasāsanaṃ" means those who do not attend to or serve the Elder Sukkhā, who correctly preaches and reveals the Teaching of the Blessed Buddha. The connection is: what have these people in the city of Rājagaha done?

"Tañca appaṭivānīyaṃ" means that Dhamma brings about the state of not turning back and is leading out of suffering (niyyānika). Or, because of its excellence, it cannot be removed from the hearts of those who listen to it, being captivating. It is unmixed (asecanaka), requiring no other flavor to be poured in, having a great taste by its very nature, and therefore full of essence (ojavanta). There is also a Pali reading "osadhaṃ," meaning it is like a medicine for curing the disease of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha). "Pivanti maññe sappaññā, valāhakamivaddhagū" means that wise and learned people drink that Dhamma, or rather, they listen as if drinking it, just as travelers in a waterless desert drink water coming from the clouds.

Having heard that Dhamma, the people, with confident minds, approached the Elder and listened to the Dhamma respectfully. Later, at the time of the Elder's final passing (parinibbāna) at the end of her life, in order to manifest the liberating nature of the Sasana, she declared her own attainment of the Fruition of Arahatship:

"Sukkhā, through bright supramundane states, is free from lust and concentrated;
Having conquered Māra and his army, she bears her final body."

In that verse, "Sukkhā" means the Elder Sukkhā refers to herself as if she were another person. "Sukkehi dhammehi" means through the extremely pure supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). "Vītarāgā samāhitā" means being entirely free from lust through the Path of Arahatship and being concentrated through the Fruition of Arahatship (arahattaphala-samādhi). The rest of the sequence of words is just as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sukkhā Therī is finished.
64:
## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Selā Therī

The verse beginning with "Natthi nissaraṇaṃ loke" is that of the Elder Selā. This Elder had also performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a strong support for the cessation of the round of rebirths (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. She was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. When she reached maturity, her parents gave her in marriage to a young man of equal status. After living happily with that man for many hundreds of years, when he passed away, she herself had reached an advanced age. Filled with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and seeking what is wholesome, she wandered from park to park and monastery to monastery, thinking, "I will hear the Dhamma in the presence of recluses and brahmins."

One day, she approached the Bodhi tree of the Teacher and sat down, praying, "If the Blessed Buddha is peerless, equal to the peerless, and without a rival, let this Bodhi tree show me a miracle." Immediately upon that thought, the Bodhi tree blazed forth, branches made of gold appeared, and all directions became radiant. Seeing that miracle, with a confident mind and establishing deep respect, she sat right there for seven days and nights with her hands joined in reverence above her head. On the seventh day, she performed a grand offering and honor.

Through that meritorious deed, she wandered among devas and humans, and in this Buddha's era, she was born as the daughter of King Āḷavika in the kingdom of Āḷavī. Her name was Selā. Because she was the daughter of King Āḷavika, they also called her Āḷavikā. When she reached maturity, after the Teacher had tamed the ogre Āḷavaka and received the bowl and robes in his hands, she approached the Teacher as a young princess along with her father the King as he entered the city of Āḷavī. Having heard the Dhamma, she gained faith and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, having developed spiritual urgency, she ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Having performed the preliminary duties and established insight (vipassanā), she contemplated conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). Due to being endowed with the necessary support and having mature knowledge, she attained Arahatship before long. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

"In the city of Haṃsavatī, I was then a wanderer;
Seeking the wholesome, I wandered from park to park.

On a day of the dark fortnight, I saw the supreme Bodhi tree;
Having gained confidence in that Bodhi tree, I sat at its foot."
65:
Arousing a mind of reverence, with hands raised in salutation to my head, and expressing my joy, I thought thus at that moment:

"If the Buddha is of immeasurable virtue, if he is an incomparable person, let him show me a miracle; let this Bodhi tree shine with radiance."

As soon as I had thought this, at that very moment, the Bodhi tree blazed and shone; all directions became golden in hue and were radiant.

Sitting at the foot of that Bodhi tree for seven days and nights, when the seventh day arrived, I made an offering of lamps.

Surrounding the seat, five lamps blazed; until the sun rose, my lamps remained burning.

Due to that well-performed deed and the aspiration of my volition, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

There, my well-constructed mansion is called 'Pañcadīpa' (Five Lamps); it is sixty leagues in height and thirty leagues in width.

Incalculable lamps blazed surrounding me; the entire celestial mansion shone with the light of the lamps.

Even sitting with my back turned, if I wish to see, I see everything with my eye—above, below, and across.

As long as I desire to see the good destinations (sugati) and the bad destinations (duggati), there is no obstruction by trees or mountains.

I became the chief queen of eighty celestial kings; I became the chief queen of hundreds of universal monarchs.

In whatever birth I was born, whether as a deity or a human, a hundred thousand lamps blazed surrounding me.

Passing away from the deva world, I was conceived in my mother's womb; while in the mother's womb, my eyes did not close.

Being endowed with meritorious deeds, a hundred thousand lamps blazed in the birth-chamber; this is the fruit of the five lamps.
66:
Having reached the final birth, I have turned my mind away [from defilements]. I have touched and experienced Nibbāna, which is free from aging, free from death, and of a peaceful nature.

At the age of seven, I reached the fruit of Arahantship. The Buddha, born of the Gotama lineage, knowing my virtues, granted me ordination.

Whether living in a pavilion, at the foot of a tree, or in an empty house, at that time the lamp blazed; this is the fruit of the five lamps.

My divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) is purified; I am skilled in concentration (samādhi); I have reached the perfection of the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā); this is the fruit of the five lamps.

I have ended all the suffering of the round of rebirths, completed what was to be done, and am free from taints (āsava). O Great Hero, O One with Vision, [I who offered] five lamps pay homage to your feet.

One hundred thousand aeons ago, I gave that lamp; since then, I have not known a bad destination; this is the fruit of the five lamps.

My defilements are burnt away... I have carried out the Buddha's teaching.

Having reached Arahantship, the Therī lived in Sāvatthī. One day, after the meal, she left Sāvatthī and entered the Andhavana forest for the day's abiding and sat at the foot of a tree. Then Māra, wishing to disrupt her seclusion, approached her in a disguised form and said:

"There is no escape in the world; what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy the pleasures of sensual desire; do not be one who regrets later."

The meaning of that verse is: In this world, even when investigating at all times, there is no escape called Nibbāna; it is merely a term claimed by various recluses and brahmins according to their own wishes. Therefore, what will you do with seclusion? While staying in such a perfect first stage of life, what will you do with this physical seclusion (kāya-viveka)? Indeed, enjoy the pleasures of sensual desire based on the objects of desire (vatthu-kāma) and the defilements of desire (kilesa-kāma).

## 5. Ubbirītherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verses beginning with "Ahu jီvā" are the verses of the Therī named Ubbirī. This Ubbirī Therī also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, while accumulating merit which is a powerful cause for Nibbāna—the escape from the suffering of the round of rebirths—in various lives, she was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. When she reached the age of discretion, one day while her parents were away at another house to celebrate a festival, she remained home alone without a companion. As noon approached, seeing an Arahant elder, a disciple of the Buddha, passing near the house door, she wished to offer alms-food. She invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please enter this house." When the elder entered the house, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita), prepared a seat with a long-haired carpet and so on, and made the offering. The elder sat on the prepared seat. The woman took the bowl, filled it with alms-food, and placed it in the elder's hands. The elder gave a talk of appreciation and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, she was born in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and, after enjoying noble celestial bliss there until the end of her life, she passed away and wandered only in good destinations. In the time of this Buddha, she was born into a householder's family in Sāvatthī and received the name Ubbirī. She was extremely beautiful, charming, and inspiring. When Ubbirī reached of age, King Kosala took her to his palace. After a few years, she had a daughter. They named the daughter Jīvantī. The King, seeing the daughter of Queen Ubbirī...
67:
“Enjoy the delights and pleasures. Why? Lest you become one who is distressed and regretful in the future, thinking, ‘The Nibbāna for which I practiced the holy life does not exist; therefore, I have not attained it, and I have also missed out on sensual enjoyments. Alas, it is a loss for me!’” (Māra spoke with this intention).

Hearing these words, the Elder Nun thought, “This Māra is indeed a fool; he denies the Nibbāna that is manifest to me. He invites me to sensual pleasures, not knowing that I am one whose taints are exhausted (an Arahant). Come, I shall let him know and threaten him.” Having thought thus, she spoke these two verses:

“Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes; the aggregates are like a chopping block (upon which one is cut).
That which you call ‘delight in sensual pleasures’ is now no delight for me.

Delight (craving) is destroyed in every respect; the mass of darkness (ignorance) is shattered.
Know this, Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!”

In those verses, ‘sattisūlūpamā kāmā’ means: sensual pleasures should be seen as a sharp sword or a stake because they pierce the being who is obsessed by them. ‘Khandhā’ refers to the five aggregates of clinging. ‘Āsaṃ’ means being near those aggregates. ‘Adhikuṭṭanā’ means a chopping block which is the basis for cutting, meaning a place of extreme oppression. This is because beings, depending on the aggregates, come to be cut and destroyed due to sensual pleasures. ‘Yaṃ tvaṃ kāmaratiṃ brūsi, arati dāni sā mama’ means: O Evil One, that delight in sensual pleasures which you speak of as something to be enjoyed and cultivated, that delight is now for me like excrement, as I am devoid of such attachment; I have no need for any benefit from those sensual pleasures.

She stated the reason for this with the words beginning with ‘sabbattha vihatā nandī’. In that verse, ‘evaṃ jānāhi’ means: “Know me as one who has abandoned all craving and ignorance.” Because of such abandonment, she meant: “O Māra, you of low conduct, the Ender, because I have destroyed the powerful army of defilements and transcended your realm, you are defeated and obstructed by me; I am no longer one to be oppressed by you.”

When the Elder Nun had thus threatened Māra, he vanished right there. The Elder Nun, having spent the day in the Andhavana forest in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), returned to her dwelling place in the evening.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Selā Therī is finished.
68:
## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Somā Therī

The verse beginning with “Yaṃ taṃ isīhi pattabbaṃ” is that of Somā Therī. This Elder Nun had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that was a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. In the time of Sikhī Buddha, she was born into a wealthy Khattiya family and, upon reaching maturity, became the chief queen of King Aruṇa. All the stories of the past are similar to the story of Abhaya Therī.

As for the story of the present, this Elder Nun, wandering through the realms of gods and humans, was born in this Buddha’s era as the daughter of the chaplain (purohita) of King Bimbisāra in the city of Rājagaha. Her name was Somā. When she reached maturity, she gained faith when the Blessed One entered Rājagaha and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she was ordained among the bhikkhunīs and, performing the preliminary duties and practicing insight meditation, she soon attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“In the city of Aruṇavatī, there was a king named Aruṇa;
I was the wife of that king, and I restrained myself from forbidden evil.
As far as... (pe)... the teaching of the Buddha has been fulfilled.”

Everything is similar to the Apadāna of Abhaya Therī. After attaining Arahantship, while living in Sāvatthī in the bliss of liberation, she entered the Andhavana forest one day for the day-abiding and sat under a certain tree. Then Māra, wishing to disturb her seclusion, approached without showing his form and, standing in the air, spoke this verse:

“That state which is to be attained by sages (Buddhas and other wise ones), which is difficult to achieve,
Cannot be reached by a woman with her two-finger wisdom.”

The meaning of that verse is: That supreme place of peace known as Arahantship, which is to be attained by the Great Wise Ones such as the Buddhas—who are called ‘Isī’ (sages) because they seek the groups of virtue and so on—and which is difficult for others to achieve or accomplish, cannot be reached by a woman of inferior wisdom. For women, from the age of seven or eight, always cook rice, and when they put the rice into the boiling water...
70:
## 4. Catukkanipāta
## 1. Bhaddākāpilānītherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Catukkanipāta, the verse beginning with "Putto buddhassa dāyādo" is the verse of the Elder Bhaddā Kāpilānī. In the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, she was born into a respectable family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who can recollect past lives (pubbenivāsanussati). She performed an act of merit (adhikāra) and aspired for that same position herself. Having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, she passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans.

During a time when no Buddha had appeared, she was born into a respectable family in the city of Vārāṇasī. Having gone to her husband's house, one day she had a quarrel with her sister-in-law. Seeing her sister-in-law offering alms-food to a Paccekabuddha, she thought, "This woman will obtain great wealth by giving this gift." She took the bowl from the Paccekabuddha's hand, threw away the food, filled it with mud, and gave it back. The people rebuked her, saying, "O foolish woman, what wrong did the Paccekabuddha do to you?" Feeling deeply ashamed by the people's words, she took the bowl back, removed the mud, washed it, rubbed it with scented powder, and filled it with the four sweet foods (catumadhura).
