Placing the bowl, which shone with ghee the color of lotus pollen poured on top, into the hand of the Paccekabuddha, she made an aspiration: "Just as this alms-food is radiant, may my body also be radiant."

Passing away from there, she wandered only in the happy destinations (sugati). In the time of the Buddha Kassapa, she was born as the daughter of a wealthy merchant in Vārāṇasī. Due to her past kamma, she had a foul body odor and was loathed by people. Feeling spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she made a golden brick from her jewelry and enshrined it in the Buddha's stupa, making an offering with a handful of lotuses. Because of that merit, her body became fragrant and delightful in that very life. She became beloved and pleasing to her husband. Having performed merit throughout her life, she passed away and was reborn in the celestial realm. There too, she enjoyed divine bliss throughout her life. Passing away from there, she became the daughter of the King of Vārāṇasī, enjoying wealth similar to divine splendor. For a long time, she attended to and served Paccekabuddhas. When those Paccekabuddhas attained Parinibbāna, she felt spiritual urgency, ordained as a female ascetic, and lived in a grove developing jhānas. She was then reborn in the Brahma realm. Passing away from there, in the city of Sāgala...
71:
...she was born in the home of a Brahmin family of the Kosiya clan. Raised with great care, she reached maturity and was taken to the home of the youth Pipphali in the village of Mahātittha. When the youth Pipphali left to ordain, she also left for the sake of ordination, abandoning great wealth and a large circle of relatives. She entered and stayed in the grove of the titthiyas (non-Buddhist ascetics) for five years. Later, she received ordination and the higher ordination (upasampadā) in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she attained Arahantship before long. This is stated in the Apadāna:

“The Victor named Padumuttara, a master of all dhammas, the Leader, appeared one hundred thousand eons ago.”

“At that time, in Haṃsavatī, there was a merchant named Videha who possessed many jewels; I was his wife.”

“Once, he approached the Sun of Men (the Buddha) with his retinue and heard the Dhamma of the Buddha, which removes all suffering and fear.”

“The Leader praised a disciple who was foremost among those who practice the dhutangas. Having heard this, he gave a seven-day great offering to the Buddha, the Such-like One.”

“Prostrating with my head at the feet [of the Buddha], I aspired for that position. Then the Bull of Men (the Buddha), gladdening the assembly,”

“Spoke these verses out of compassion for the merchant: ‘You shall obtain the position you have prayed for; may you be one whose defilements are extinguished, dear daughter.’”

“One hundred thousand eons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will appear in the world.”

“His heir in the Dhamma, a spiritual son, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Kassapa by clan, will appear.”

“Hearing that, I was filled with joy. Throughout my life, I served that Victor, the Leader, with a heart of loving-kindness and the four requisites.”

“Having illumined the Dispensation, having crushed the false teachers, and having disciplined those who were to be disciplined, he, along with his disciples, attained Parinibbāna.”
72:
When that Buddha, the Supreme of the World, attained Parinibbāna, I gathered my relatives and friends to honor the Teacher and built a stupa together with them.

I built a stupa seven yojanas high, made of jewels, shining like the sun with a thousand rays, and as beautiful as a Sal tree in full bloom.

I had seven hundred thousand trays (or bowls) made for that stupa. Those trays were made only of the seven kinds of jewels and shone like a fire of reeds.

To honor the Great Sage, the Compassionate One who cares for all beings, I filled those trays with scented oil and lit lamps as an offering.

To honor the Great Sage, I also had seven hundred thousand water pots made, which were filled only with jewels.

In the middle of every eight pots, golden banners were erected. Those golden banners shone brilliantly with their color, like the sun in autumn.

Jeweled archways (toraṇa) stood beautifully at the four gates. Delightful planks (phalaka) made of jewels were also erected and looked beautiful.

Well-crafted wreaths and garlands surrounding the stupa shone brightly. The erected jeweled banners also radiated light.

The well-made, exquisite, and deep-red jeweled stupa shone intensely with its color, like the sun at sunset.

Of the three terraces (vedikā) of the stupa, I filled one with yellow orpiment (haritāla), one with red arsenic (manosilā), and one with black collyrium (añjana).

Having made such a delightful offering to the Buddha, the Speaker of Noble Words, I gave alms to the Sangha for the rest of my life according to my strength.

Together with that merchant (seṭṭhī), having performed those merits in every way throughout our lives, we both reached a happy destination (sugati).

After enjoying divine and human bliss, I wandered through Saṃsāra together with that merchant, like a shadow follows the body.
73:
Ninety-one aeons ago, the Leader named Vipassī, who was beautiful to behold and a seer of all phenomena (Dhamma), appeared in the world.

At that time, in the city of Bandhumatī, there was a Brahmin esteemed by the virtuous; though rich in qualities, he was very poor in wealth.

At that time, I was the wife of that Brahmin, being of one mind with him. Once, that noble Brahmin approached the Great Sage (Buddha).

Sitting in the midst of the crowd, hearing the Dhamma being preached about the state of the Deathless (Amata) by the Buddha, he was delighted and offered his single cloak (ekasāṭaka).

That Brahmin returned home with only one cloth and said to me, "Rejoice in this great merit of the cloak given to the Buddha."

Then, I was greatly pleased and, with folded hands, I rejoiced, saying, "Master, the cloak given to the Supreme Buddha, the Such-like One (Tādī), is well-given."

Due to that merit, wandering through various lives in Saṃsāra, he was endowed with happiness and adornments, and became a king, a lord of the earth, in the delightful city of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, I was his chief queen, the best among the group of women. I was the dearly beloved wife of that husband due to past affection.

Seeing eight Paccekabuddhas wandering for alms, we were greatly delighted and offered them highly valuable food.

Having invited them again and built a jeweled pavilion, we used golden bowls and golden trays made by goldsmiths.

Having brought all of them there, he, with a devoted heart, offered with his own hands to those noble ones who were seated on golden thrones.

I also gave that gift together with the King of Kāsi at that time. Later, I was reborn in a village of Kāsi within the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

In a wealthy householder (kuṭumbika) family, I lived happily with my brothers. I was the devoted wife of the elder brother, performing my duties well.
74:
Having seen a Paccekabuddha, I offered him the food portion of my husband, the younger brother, and when he returned, I told him about it.

That husband did not approve of that gift. Then I took the pot and gave that food into his hands, but he gave it back to me.

At that time, being angry, I threw away that food and filled the bowl of that Such-like Buddha (Paccekabuddha) with mud and offered it.

Seeing his face, which remained the same in mind whether giving, receiving, honoring, or being mistreated, I was then greatly terrified and shaken.

Taking the bowl back and washing it with scents, I, with a devoted heart, filled it with food together with ghee and sugar and offered it.

Because of that gift, I became beautiful in every birth where I was reborn. However, due to the offense against the Buddha, I had bad breath from my mouth.

Later, when the stupa of the Hero Kassapa was being built, I joyfully offered a noble golden brick.

Because I anointed that brick with four types of scents and offered it, I was freed from the defect of bad breath and became endowed with all limbs, large and small.

I had seven thousand trays made of the seven kinds of jewels, filled them with ghee, and made thousands of wicks.

To honor the Lord of the World, with a very clear mind, I placed those wicks, lit them, and offered seven rows of lamps.

At that time too, I was especially a sharer in that merit. Later, when I was born in the Kāsi region, I was known as Sumittā.

I was his beloved, adorned, and happy wife. At that time, I offered a thick cloak to a Paccekabuddha.

Having rejoiced in that supreme gift, I was a sharer of that merit. Again, I was born in the Koliya clan in the Kāsi kingdom.
75:
At that time, together with five hundred Koliyan princes, I attended upon five hundred Paccekabuddhas. For three months, I satisfied them and offered them sets of three robes. At that time, his wife was one who followed the path of meritorious deeds. Passing away from there, he became the famous king named Nanda. The queen of that king was also one whose every wish was fulfilled. At that time, when he was the great King Brahmadatta, he attended upon the Paccekabuddhas who were the sons of Padumavatī; at that time, he attended upon the five hundred Paccekabuddhas for as long as he lived. Having settled them in the royal garden, he also paid homage to them when they attained Parinibbāna.

Having built pagodas and both of us having renounced the world, we developed the Immeasurables (Appamaññā) and reached the Brahma realm. Passing away from there, he was born in the village of Mahātittha as Sujāta, named Pipphalāyana. His mother was Sumanadevī, and his father was a Brahmin of the Kosiya clan. I was the daughter of the Brahmin Kappila and the mother named Sucīmatī in the city of Sākala in the Madda kingdom. My father, having fashioned a statue of pure gold in my likeness, gave me to the wise Kassapa, who had already turned away from sensual pleasures.

Once, when that compassionate one went to inspect the work in the fields, he saw creatures being eaten by crows and other animals, and he was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega). I too, while drying sesame seeds at home, saw worms being eaten by crows and felt spiritual urgency at that time. Then that wise man renounced the world, and I followed him into renunciation. I lived for five years in the practice of a female wanderer (paribbājikā). When Gotamī, the foster mother of the Victorious Buddha, renounced the world, I approached her and received the instruction of the Blessed One.
76:
In no long time, I attained Arahantship. Oh, how wonderful is the good friendship of the glorious Elder Kassapa!

The son and heir of the Buddha, Kassapa, who is well-concentrated, knows his former lives and sees heaven and the states of deprivation.

Furthermore, having reached the end of birth, the sage who has mastered the higher knowledges is called a 'Threefold-Knowledge Brahmin' because of these three knowledges.

In the same way, Bhaddā Kāpilānī is one of threefold knowledge and has abandoned death. Having conquered Māra and his host, she bears her final body.

Seeing the danger in the world, we both renounced. We are those whose taints are exhausted, who are tamed, who have become cool, and are extinguished.

My taints are burnt away ... (extensively) ... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

After attaining Arahantship, she became proficient in the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa). Because of her extraordinary past merits in that knowledge, later, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the noble assembly at Jetavana Monastery, in appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions, he placed her in the foremost position (etadagga) among the bhikkhunīs who could recollect past lives. One day, that Theri, first praising the virtues of the Elder Mahākassapa and then manifesting her own achievement of the task, uttered this inspired utterance:

'The son and heir of the Buddha, Kassapa, who is well-concentrated, knows his former lives and sees heaven and the states of deprivation.

Furthermore, having reached the end of birth, the sage who has mastered the higher knowledges is called a "Threefold-Knowledge Brahmin" because of these three knowledges.

In the same way, Bhaddā Kāpilānī is one of threefold knowledge and has abandoned death. Having conquered Māra and his host, she bears her final body.

Seeing the danger in the world, we both renounced. We are those whose taints are exhausted, who are tamed, who have become cool, and are extinguished.'

Thus she spoke these verses.
77:
In those verses, "son and heir of the Buddha" means he is the well-born son (anujāta-putta) of the Perfectly Enlightened One because he followed and understood after the Buddha; he is an heir because he received the ninefold supramundane Dhamma which is the inheritance of that Buddha. Kassapa is "well-concentrated" (susumāhita) because his mind is well-established through mundane and supramundane concentration. "He who knows former lives" means that the Elder Mahākassapa made manifest, knew, and penetrated through the knowledge of recollecting past lives the continuity of the aggregates lived in the past by himself and others. "Sees heaven and the states of deprivation" means he sees with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) the heavens consisting of the twenty-six celestial realms and the four states of deprivation, like a myrobalan fruit on the palm of his hand.

Furthermore, "reached the end of birth" means he reached the fruit of Arahantship, which is the end of birth. "Mastered through higher knowledge" means having known through higher knowledge the things to be known, having fully understood the things to be fully understood, having abandoned the things to be abandoned, and having realized the things to be realized, he has reached the end, reached the goal, and completed the task. He is called a "sage" (muni) because he has reached the state of a sage (mona), which is the wisdom of the exhaustion of taints.

"In the same way, Bhaddā Kāpilānī" means just as Mahākassapa is one of threefold knowledge and one who has abandoned death through these three aforementioned knowledges, so too Bhaddā Kāpilānī is one of threefold knowledge and one who has abandoned death. Therefore, she shows herself as if she were another, saying, "she bears her final body, having conquered Māra and his host."

Now, wishing to show that "just as the Elder's practice is good in the beginning, middle, and end, so is mine," she spoke the concluding verse beginning with "Seeing the danger." In that verse, "We are those whose taints are exhausted and are tamed" means that we—the Elder Mahākassapa and I—are tamed with the highest taming and are entirely exhausted of taints. "We have become cool and are extinguished" means that because of the absence of the fever of defilements, we have become cool and are extinguished (nibbuta) through the Nibbāna element with residue remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbānadhātu).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Therī Bhaddā Kāpilānī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of the Fours is finished.
78:
## 5. Pañcakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of an Unknown Therī

In the Pañcakanipāta, the verse beginning with "Paṇṇavīsati vassāni" belongs to an unknown Therī. This Therī had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome merit that served as a strong support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In the time of this Buddha, she was born in the city of Devadaha and grew up as the wet-nurse of Mahāpajāpatigotamī. However, she was not known by name or clan. When Mahāpajāpatigotamī ordained, she herself also ordained. For twenty-five years, she was oppressed by sensual lust and did not obtain even a finger-snap's worth of mental concentration. With arms raised, she wept. After hearing the Dhamma in the presence of Dhammadinnā Therī, she turned her mind away from sensual pleasures, took up a meditation subject, and devoted herself to meditation. Before long, she became an Arahant with the six higher powers. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered these verses as an inspired utterance:

"For twenty-five years since I ordained,
I did not obtain peace of mind even for the duration of a finger-snap.

Without obtaining peace of mind, being soaked and oppressed by sensual lust,
With arms raised, weeping, I entered the monastery.

I approached that bhikkhunī in whom I had trust;
She taught me the Dhamma concerning the aggregates, bases, and elements.

Having heard her Dhamma, I sat down to one side;
I know my past lives, and the divine eye has been purified.

The knowledge of others' minds and the divine ear element have also been purified,
I have also realized supernormal powers, and I have reached the destruction of the taints,
The six higher powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled."

Thus she spoke these verses.
79:
In those verses, "even for the duration of a finger-snap" means for a moment as brief as a single snap of the fingers or a flick of a finger. "Did not reach the peace of mind" means she did not obtain the tranquility of mind which is one-pointedness of mind (concentration). "Soaked with sensual lust" refers to those whose minds are drenched with intense desire and lust due to being excessively attached to the objects of sensual pleasure known as the strands of sensual pleasure. "The bhikkhunī" refers to Dhammadinnā Therī. "The knowledge of others' minds" should be connected to mean that the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) has been purified and attained. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Unknown Therī is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Therī Vimalā

The verse beginning with "Intoxicated by my complexion, my beauty" belongs to Therī Vimalā. This Therī had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome merit that was a strong cause for liberation from the suffering of the cycle of rebirth in various existences. In the time of this Buddha, she was born in the city of Vesālī as the daughter of an unnamed woman who lived by her beauty (a courtesan). She was named Vimalā. When she came of age, she earned her living in the same manner. One day, seeing the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna walking for alms in Vesālī, she became infatuated and went to the Elder's dwelling place to attempt to seduce him. Some say she did so because she was incited by heretics. The Elder rebuked her by making clear the foulness (asubha) of the body and gave her an exhortation. That account has already appeared below in the Theragāthā. When the Elder gave that exhortation, she was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Establishing shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), she became a lay follower who gained faith in the Dispensation. Later, she ordained among the bhikkhunīs and, through her striving and effort, because of the perfection of her supporting conditions, she soon reached Arahantship. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:

"Intoxicated by my complexion, my beauty,
My fame, my large following,
And my youth, I was conceited;
I used to despise other women."
80:
## 
“Adorning this body, which is very variegated and deludes fools, I stood at the door of a brothel like a hunter setting a snare.

Displaying my ornaments and revealing many parts, both hidden and public, I practiced various deceits, laughing and mocking many people.

Today, having gone for alms, with shaven head and wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi), I sit at the foot of a tree, having attained the state of no-thought (absorption).

All bonds, both divine and human, have been completely cut off. Having exhausted all taints (āsavas), I am cooled and attained Nibbāna.” Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, ‘intoxicated by complexion and form’ (mattā vaṇṇena rūpena) means [intoxicated] by the quality of her complexion and the perfection of her physical form. ‘By beauty’ (sobhaggena) means by the state of being very beautiful. ‘By success’ (yasena) means by the perfection of her retinue. The meaning is that she became intoxicated through intoxication with complexion, intoxication with form, intoxication with beauty, and intoxication with retinue. ‘Stiff with the pride of youth’ (yobbanena cupatthaddhā) means having a mind that is repeatedly stiff with the intoxication of youth, a mind stiff with the egoism (ahaṅkāra) caused by youth, and a mind that is not at peace. ‘I despised others’ (aññāsamatimaññihaṃ) means that she surpassed other women in every way through her own qualities such as complexion and thought, ‘I alone am superior.’ Or, it means she thought of herself as surpassing the qualities of other women, such as their complexion, and thus showed contempt for them.

‘Adorning this body, very variegated, deluding fools’ (vibhūsitvā imaṃ kāyaṃ, sucittaṃ bālalāpanaṃ) means this body of mine, which is full of various impurities and is loathsome, is called ‘deluding fools’ (bālalāpana) because it entices fools as ‘mine.’ Having adorned this body with clothes and ornaments, making it well-decorated and attractive through skin-toning, hair-styling, and so on, to make it very variegated. ‘I stood at the door of a brothel like a hunter setting a snare’ (aṭṭhāsiṃ vesidvāramhi, luddo pāsamivoḍḍiya) means just as a hunter of deer sets a deer-snare made of sticks and cords to catch deer, I stood at the door of a prostitute's house, having spread out my aforementioned body, which is like a snare of Māra.

‘Displaying ornaments, many hidden and public parts’ (piḷandhanaṃ vidaṃsentī, guyhaṃ pakāsikaṃ bahuṃ) means displaying hidden parts such as the thighs, hips, and breasts, as well as public parts such as the feet, knees, and head; displaying various ornaments on both hidden and public parts. ‘I practiced various deceits, laughing...’ (akāsiṃ vividhaṃ māyaṃ, uzzhagghantī)...
81:
...laughing to deceive many foolish people who are intoxicated with the pride of youth, she practiced various deceptions through laughter, and by concealing the true nature of the body with scents, flowers, clothes, and ornaments, and through gestures like laughing and grace.

‘Sājja piṇḍaṃ caritvāna... avitakkassa lābhinī’: That ‘I’, who used to live in negligence, now, staying in the advice of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, having ordained in the Dispensation, with a shaven head and wearing the saṅghāṭi robe, having gone for alms and eaten, am now sitting at the foot of a tree in a secluded place. By attaining the highest fruit (arahatta-phala) based on the second jhāna, I have become one who has attained the state free from thought (avitakka). This is the connection of the meaning.

‘Sabba yogā’: This refers to all four yokes, such as the yoke of sensual desire (kāmayoga). ‘Samucchinnā’: This means they are well-uprooted and abandoned by the first path (sotāpatti-magga), etc., as appropriate. The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vimalā is finished.

## 3. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sīhā

The verse beginning with ‘Ayoniso manasikārā’ is the verse of the Elder Sīhā. This elder also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives. In this Buddha's era, she was born in the city of Vesālī as the daughter of General Sīha's sister. They named her Sīhā, saying, “Let us name her after her maternal uncle.” When she reached the age of discretion, one day she heard the Dhamma being preached by the Teacher to General Sīha. Having gained faith, she asked her parents for permission and ordained. After ordaining, although she began to practice insight (vipassanā), she was unable to restrain her mind, which was running towards various external objects. For seven years, she was oppressed by wrong thoughts and found no peace of mind. Thinking, “What is the use of this miserable life? I will die by hanging myself,” she took a rope, tied it to a tree branch, and while putting it around her neck, she directed her mind towards insight (vipassanā) as she had practiced before. Because she was in her final existence, while the noose was around her neck, her knowledge matured, and at that very moment, she developed insight...
82:
She attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). At the very moment she reached Arahantship, the noose tied around her neck was released and fell off. Established in Arahantship, she uttered these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna):

“Through unwise attention and being oppressed by sensual lust, formerly I was restless, my mind not under control.

Overcome by defilements, following the perception of beauty (subhasaññā), I did not obtain peace of mind, following the power of lustful thoughts.

For seven years I wandered, lean, pale, and discolored; being very miserable, I found no happiness by day or by night.

Then taking a rope, I entered the forest; better for me to hang myself here than to live again a low life (of defilements).

Having made a strong noose and tied it to a tree branch, I placed the noose around my neck; at that moment, my mind was liberated (from defilements).”

In those verses, 'ayoniso manasikārā' means through improper attention, or through the perverted view of perceiving beauty in the foul (asubha). 'Kāmarāgena aṭṭitā' means oppressed by the desire and lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Ahosiṃ uddhatā pubbe, citte avasavattinī' means that formerly, while my mind was not under my control, I was restless, with a mind distracted by various objects and not concentrated.

'Pariyuṭṭhitā klesehi, subhasaññānuvattinī' means being oppressed by defilements such as sensual lust that have arisen in a state of obsession, and having the nature of following the sensual perception that arises as 'beautiful' in forms and so on. 'Samaṃ cittassa na labhiṃ, rāgacittavasānugā' means that because I was following the power of the mind associated with sensual lust, I did not obtain even a slight degree of peace of mind, which is the tranquility of mind (cetosamatha) and one-pointedness of mind.

'Kisā paṇḍu vivaṇṇā ca' means being lean with veins standing out on the body due to such weariness, becoming very pale, and for that very reason, being discolored and losing the healthy complexion of the skin. 'Satta vassāni' means for seven years. 'Cārihaṃ' means I wandered. 'I found no happiness by day...'
83:
“...or by night, being very miserable” means thus for seven years, being afflicted by the suffering of defilements, I did not obtain even once, by day or by night, the happiness of a recluse (samaṇasukha).

“Then” means because of not obtaining the happiness of a recluse due to the obsession of defilements. “Taking a rope, I entered the forest” means taking a noose-rope, I entered the interior of the forest. For what purpose did she enter? She said: “Better for me to hang myself here than to live again a low life.” This means if I, being unable to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, were to live again the low life of a householder, then dying by hanging in this forest would be a hundred or a thousand times better for me. Then “my mind was liberated” means when she placed the noose tied to the tree branch around her neck, at that very moment, because of being joined with the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā), her mind was liberated from all taints (āsava) through the sequence of the paths (magga).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sīhā Therī is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Sundarīnandā Therī

The verse beginning with “Āturaṃ asuciṃ” is that of Sundarīnandā Therī. It is said that she too, in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī. When she came of age, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (etadagga) among those who practice jhāna. She performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that position. Accumulating merit, she wandered through the worlds of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, and in this Buddha's era, she was born into the Sakyan royal family.

They named her Nandā. Later, because she was endowed with beauty, she became known as Sundarīnandā and also as Janapadakalyāṇī. After our Blessed One attained omniscience and in due course went to Kapilavatthu, ordaining Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula before departing, and after King Suddhodana had passed away and Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the mother of Rāhula had also ordained, Sundarīnandā thought: “My elder brother has renounced the position of a Universal Monarch, ordained, and become the Buddha, the supreme person in the world. His son, Prince Rāhula, has also ordained. My husband-to-be, Prince Nanda, has also...”
84:
Mother Mahāpajāpatigotamī has ordained, and sister Rāhulamātā has also ordained. "What shall I do at home now? I too shall ordain," she thought. She went to the nunnery and ordained out of affection for her relatives, not out of faith. Therefore, even after ordaining, pride arose in her based on her physical beauty. Thinking, "The Blessed One disparages beauty, blames it, and shows the faults of physical form in many ways," she did not go to pay respects to the Blessed One. All this should be understood as stated in the story of Abhirūpanandā below.

The distinction in this story is: Seeing the form of a woman created by the Blessed One gradually overcome by old age, the Theri reflected on impermanence, suffering, and non-self, and her mind turned toward the meditation subject. Seeing this, the Blessed One, wishing to teach the Dhamma suitable for her, said:

"Nandā, look at this assembly of the body, afflicted by disease, impure, and putrid. Develop a mind that is firmly fixed and well-concentrated on the foulness of the body (asubha).

As this body is, so is that; as that is, so is this. Only fools greatly delight in that which is foul-smelling and putrid.

One who contemplates thus day and night without laziness will, through that contemplation, become weary (of defilements) through their own wisdom and see Nibbāna."

He spoke these three verses.

Following the teaching, she directed her insight and was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Wishing to teach the meditation subject for the higher paths, the Blessed One said, "Nandā, in this body there is not even a slight essence; it is merely a heap of bones, smeared with flesh and blood, the dwelling place of old age and death." To show this, he spoke this verse in the Dhammapada:

"A city is built of bones, smeared with flesh and blood, wherein old age, death, pride, and detraction are deposited." (Dhammapada 150).

At the end of the teaching, the Theri reached the Fruit of Arahantship. As stated in the Apadāna:

"The Victor named Padumuttara, the one who reached the far shore of all dhammas, the Leader, arose one hundred thousand aeons from now."
85:
"The Buddha, who is the admonisher, the one who makes (the truth) known, the one who crosses all beings over (the cycle of rebirth), and who is skilled in preaching the Dhamma, crossed many people over.

The Buddha, who is compassionate, merciful, and desirous of the welfare of all beings, established all the heretics who came to him in the five precepts.

Thus, (that Dispensation) was free from confusion and devoid of heretics. It was beautiful and adorned with Arahants who were endowed with the quality of 'tādi' and had attained mastery.

The Great Sage, fifty-eight cubits in height, with a complexion like a golden pillar and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, appeared (in the world).

At that time, the lifespan was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long, the Buddha crossed many people over.

At that time, I was born in a wealthy family in the city of Haṃsāvatī. I was endowed with great happiness, shining with the radiance of various jewels.

Approaching that Great Hero, I heard the Dhamma teaching, which is the Deathless, extremely pleasant, and makes known the ultimate truth.

Then, having invited the Leader of the World along with the Sangha, I offered a great gift to that Buddha with a devoted heart and my own hands.

Bowing my head to the Wise One, the Leader of the World, along with the Sangha, I aspired for the foremost position among the nuns who practice Jhana.

Then the Lord, the refuge of the three worlds, the tamer of the untamed, the leader of men, gave the prophecy: 'You shall obtain that well-requested wish.'

One hundred thousand aeons from this one, a Teacher named Gotama by lineage, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

You will be a female disciple of that Teacher, an heir to his Dhamma, like a daughter born of his breast, created by the Dhamma, named Nandā.

Hearing that prophecy, I was joyful. From then on, for the rest of my life, I served that Victorious Leader with a heart of loving-kindness and the four requisites."
86:
"Through that well-performed deed, intention, and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Passing away from there, I went to the Yāma heaven; from there, I went to Tusita; from there to Nimmānarati, and then to the city of Vasavatti.

Wherever I was reborn, by the power of that merit, I became the chief queen of kings in those respective lives.

Passing away from there and reaching the human realm, I became the chief queen of universal monarchs and regional kings.

Experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, being happy in all lives, I wandered through the cycle of rebirth for many aeons.

When the final birth arrived, I became the faultless daughter of King Suddhodana in the beautiful city of Kapilavatthu.

Seeing that I was endowed with a glorious physical form, that family was filled with joy. Therefore, my name was 'Nandā,' and that name was beautiful and excellent.

Among all the young maidens, I was famous as 'Kalyāṇī' (the beautiful one). In that pleasant city, excluding Yasodharā Devī, (I was known as the most beautiful).

The Buddha, the Supreme of the Three Worlds, is my elder brother. Likewise, the youngest (Prince Nanda) has also become an Arahant. I alone remained in the lay life, and my mother urged me:

'Born in the Sakyan clan, being the sister of the Buddha, and having been separated from Prince Nanda, why do you remain at home?' (my mother said).

Youth ends in old age. Physical form is regarded as impure. Health ends in disease. Life ends in death.

This beautiful form of yours is as pleasing as the moon. It can captivate the heart. It is like an ornament of ornaments. It is like a collection of glory.

It is as if the essence of the world is gathered together. It is like a medicine for the eyes. It causes the fame of meritorious deeds to arise. It brings joy to the Okkāka clan."
87:
“In no long time, old age will oppress you. Abandoning the pitiable home, practice the blameless Dhamma.”

“Having heard my mother's words, I went forth into homelessness. I went forth in body but not in mind, being infatuated with my beauty and youth.”

“Though my mother urged me with great effort to develop jhāna, I had no desire to strive for that jhāna.”

“Then the Great Compassionate One, the Buddha, seeing me infatuated with sensual pleasures, in order to cause disenchantment with the body, [created] before my eyes—”

“By his own psychic power, he created a beautiful woman, lovely to behold, even more beautiful than myself.”

“Seeing that woman with a most amazing body, I was astonished and thought, ‘My human eyes have found their fruit!’”

“I said to that woman, ‘O beautiful one, come! Tell me what you desire. Tell me your family, your name, and your clan if you please.’”

“That woman said, ‘O beautiful one, this is not the time for deception. Let me rest in your lap. My limbs feel as if they are sinking; let me sleep for a moment.’”

“Then that woman with beautiful eyes laid her head on my lap and slept. On her forehead, a most terrible and dreadful sore appeared.”

“As soon as that sore appeared, pustules broke out; they burst, and foul-smelling pus and blood flowed out.”

“Her face was ruined and smelled like a rotting corpse. Her whole body became swollen, dark blue, and filled with pus.”

“Trembling in all her limbs, sighing again and again, and experiencing her own suffering, she wept piteously.”

“‘I am afflicted with suffering; painful feelings oppress me. I am submerged in great misery. O friend, be my refuge!’”
88:
“Where is your mouth? Where is your prominent nose? Where has your face gone, with its lips red like the bimba fruit?”

“Where is your complexion like the moon? Where has your neck like a conch shell gone? Your ears, which were like swaying swings, have reached a state of disfigurement.”

“Your breasts, which were like jasmine buds, have burst and reached a state of foul-smelling decay like a rotting corpse.”

“Your beautiful hips, with a waist narrow like the middle of an altar, are now swollen, with impurities oozing out, and the middle is filled with worms. Oh, how impermanent is physical beauty!”

“Everything that has arisen in the whole body is foul-smelling, terrifying, and loathsome like a cemetery. Fools delight in such a body.”

Then the Great Compassionate One, the Leader of the World, my elder brother, seeing me with a terrified mind, spoke these verses:

“Nandā, look at this assembly of the body, which is diseased, a rotting corpse, and foul. Develop a mind that is concentrated, one-pointed, and well-composed on the meditation of foulness (asubha).”

“As this [body] is, so is that [corpse]; as that is, so is this. It gives off a foul, rotting smell; it is something greatly delighted in by fools.”

Reflecting thus day and night without indolence, I then, through my own wisdom, became disenchanted and saw the truth.

Then, being greatly terrified and having heard the well-spoken verses, standing right there, I became peaceful and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

Wherever I sit, I am always devoted to jhāna. The Victorious Buddha, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position (Etadagga).

My defilements are burnt up... I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching.

Having attained Arahantship and reviewing her own practice, through the power of inspired utterance, along with the three verses taught by the Teacher beginning with “Āturaṃ asuciṃ”—
89:
“I, being diligent and reflecting with proper attention (yoniso), have seen this body as it really is, both internally and externally.”

“Then I became disenchanted with the body, and passion faded away within. Diligent, detached, and peaceful, I am quenched (nibbāṇa).” — She spoke these two verses.

In those verses, “Reflecting thus... they shall see” means: reflecting and investigating with the eye of preliminary-stage knowledge (pubbabhāga-ñāṇa), preceded by attention, thinking “How shall I see? I shall see,” by piercing through and seeing truly the breaking up of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga) through one's own wisdom born of meditation (bhāvanāmaya-paññā) that has arisen within oneself based on that knowledge. This is done by setting aside the knowledge based on hearing (sutamaya-ñāṇa) received from others, and being without indolence at all times, day and night, in the manner described as “As this is, so is that,” regarding this body which has the nature of being diseased, etc.

Therefore, she said, “I, being diligent...” etc. The meaning is: I, being diligent through the non-lapse of mindfulness, and investigating with insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) by way of impermanence, etc., through proper means (yoniso), have seen this body—comprising the five aggregates—as it really is, both internally and externally, by distinguishing between one's own continuity and the continuity of others.

Then, after such seeing, through the path wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight wisdom, I became disenchanted with the body; I became disenchanted with this self-identity. Specifically, passion faded away (virāga) within my internal continuity. Having reached the summit of the practice of diligence according to reality, I am diligent; having completely cut off all fetters (saṃyojana), I am detached, peaceful, and quenched (nibbāṇa).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Therī Sundarīnandā is finished.

## 5. The Commentary on the Verses of Therī Nanduttarā

The verses beginning with “Aggiṃ candañca” are those of Therī Nanduttarā. She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots that are a support for liberation from the cycle of suffering (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives, was born into a brahmin family in the market town of Kammāsadhamma in the Kuru kingdom during the time of this Buddha...
90:
Having been reborn, and having learned some branches of knowledge and arts, she entered the Nigaṇṭha order. Devoted to debate, she held a rose-apple branch and wandered throughout Jambudīpa like Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā. Approaching the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, she asked him questions but was defeated. Abiding by the Elder's advice, she went forth in the Dispensation. While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, she attained Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered these five verses by way of inspiration (udāna):

"I used to worship the fire, the moon, the sun, and deities.
Having gone to the river banks, I would descend into the water.

Due to undertaking many vows, I shaved half of my head.
I made my bed on the ground and did not eat food at night.

Delighting in ornaments and decoration, and by means of bathing and anointing,
I pampered this body, afflicted as I was by sensual lust.

Then, having gained faith, I went forth into homelessness.
Seeing the body as it really is, sensual lust has been rooted out.

All existences have been completely cut off, as well as desires and longings.
Disjoined from all bonds, I have attained peace of mind."

She uttered these five verses.

In those verses, 'I used to worship the fire, the moon, the sun, and deities' means: to fulfill the desires of deities starting with fire, she offered oblations to the fire; to the moon on the second day of the waxing moon each month; to the sun every evening and morning; and to other external deities such as Hiranyagarbha, seeking the path of purity, she performed acts of worship. 'Having gone to the river banks, I would descend into the water' means: approaching the sacred bathing places of rivers like the Ganges, she descended into the water in the evening and morning, immersing herself and washing her limbs.

'Due to undertaking many vows' means: due to undertaking various vows such as the fivefold heat penance (pañcātapatappana). The word 'bahū' is lengthened for the sake of the verse's meter. 'I shaved half of my head' means: of my head...
91:
...I shaved only half. Some teachers say the meaning is: "Having tied half of the hair into a topknot, she let the other half hang down." 'I made my bed on the ground' means: being one who sleeps on the bare ground, she slept on the earth without any bedding. 'I did not eat food at night' means: being one who abstained from eating at night, she did not consume food during the night.

'Delighting in ornaments and decoration' means: having a body exhausted by the long-term practice of self-mortification, she thought, "There is no purification of wisdom through such exhaustion of the body. If, however, purification might occur by gratifying the senses and nourishing the body," she pampered this body, delighting in decorating it with clothes and ornaments, and in beautifying it with perfumes and garlands. 'And by means of bathing and anointing' means: having massages performed, she delighted in bathing and anointing. 'I pampered this body' means: I looked after and nourished this body of mine. 'Afflicted by sensual lust' means: being thus greatly devoted to making the body firm, she was afflicted and repeatedly harassed by sensual lust that arose due to improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra).

'Then, having gained faith' means: having broken those undertaken vows, being devoted to making the body firm and to debate, while wandering here and there, she later received advice and instruction in the presence of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and regained faith. 'Seeing the body as it really is' means: seeing this body of mine as it really is through the wisdom of the Path along with insight (vipassanā), sensual lust was entirely rooted out by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). Furthermore, all existences were completely cut off by the Highest Path (aggamagga). 'Desires and longings' should be connected as: "desire" (icchā), which is the longing for present objects, and "longing" (patthanā), which is the longing for future existence, and all existences have been completely cut off. 'I have attained peace of mind' means: she attained and reached the ultimate peace, the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Nanduttarā is finished.
92:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mittākāḷī

The verse beginning with “Saddhāya pabbajitvānā” is that of the Elder Mittākāḷī. This Elder had also performed meritorious deeds of service (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome roots in various existences, which served as a powerful support for Nibbāna, the escape from the round of rebirth. In the time of this Buddha, she was born into a Brahmin family in the market town of Kammāsadhamma in the Kuru country. Upon reaching maturity, she gained faith through the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and went forth as a nun among the bhikkhunīs. For seven years, being obsessed with gain and honor (lābhasakkāra), she wandered from place to place while practicing the recluse’s Dhamma. Later, having developed spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in a proper manner, she began the practice of insight (vipassanā) and soon attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Reviewing her own practice, she spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna):

“Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, I wandered from place to place, being eager for gain and honor.

Abandoning the highest goal, I pursued a low goal. Falling under the influence of defilements, I did not know the goal of monkhood.

While sitting in my small cell, spiritual urgency arose in me: I have entered the wrong path, having come under the power of craving.

My life is very short; old age and sickness oppress me. Before this body breaks apart, it is not the time for me to be negligent.

Contemplating the rise and fall of the aggregates as they really are, I have stood up with a mind liberated; the Buddha’s teaching has been completed.”

In those verses, “wandered from place to place, being eager for gain and honor” (vicariṃhaṃ tena tena, lābhasakkāra-ussukā) means that being devoted and committed to gain and honor, she wandered about using various means such as great learning and Dhamma talks as causes for the arising of gain.

“Abandoning the highest goal” (riñcitvā paramaṃ atthaṃ) means having discarded and abandoned the supreme goal such as jhāna, vipassanā, the Path, and the Fruit. “I pursued a low goal” (hīnamatthaṃ asevihaṃ) means that she pursued the low and inferior goal of material requisites (āmisa) through improper searching. “Falling under the influence of defilements” (kilesānaṃ vasaṃ gantvā) means that having come under the power of defilements such as conceit, intoxication, and craving, she said, “I did not know the goal of monkhood” (sāmaññatthaṃ), meaning the duties of a recluse.
93:
“While sitting in my small cell” (nisinnāya vihārake) means that spiritual urgency arose while she was sitting in the small room where she resided. How did it arise? She said, “I have entered the wrong path” (ummagga-paṭipannāmhi). In that phrase, “entered the wrong path” means that although she had gone forth in this Dispensation (Sāsana) which exists for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging, she was one who had entered the wrong path because she did not attend to the meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna). “Having come under the power of craving” (taṇhāya vasamāgatā) means having come under the influence of craving for the production of requisites.

“My life is very short” (appakaṃ jīvitaṃ mayhaṃ) means that because the time of death is not delimited and because there are many dangers, her life is small, brief, and fleeting. “Old age and sickness oppress me” (jarā byādhi ca maddati) means that like great mountains falling from all directions and crushing everything, old age and sickness oppress and grind her down. There is also a variant reading “maddare.” “Before this body breaks apart” (purāyaṃ bhijjati kāyo) means exactly before this body is destroyed. Since the breaking of this body is certain, “it is not the time for me to be negligent.” This time is the “ninth moment” (nava khana) which is free from the eight inopportune moments (akkhaṇa); connect the meaning that she felt spiritual urgency, thinking it is not proper to be negligent at such a time.

“Contemplating as they really are” (yathābhūtam-avekkhantī) means that she, having thus developed spiritual urgency, began insight and contemplated as they really are by attending to impermanence and so forth. What did she contemplate? She said, “the rise and fall of the aggregates” (khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ). By contemplating the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates of clinging, which have fifty modes of distinction such as “with the arising of ignorance, form arises,” through the knowledge of contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā-ñāṇa), she intensified her insight. Then, through the sequence of the Paths, she said, “I have stood up with a mind liberated” (vimuttacittā uṭṭhāsiṃ), meaning she became one who had emerged from the three worlds through the Path that is an emergence from both [defilements and existences]. The rest is just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Mittākāḷī is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sakulā

The verse beginning with “While living at home” (Agārasmiṃ vasantī) is that of the Elder Sakulā. It is said that in the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she was born in the city of Haṃsavatī as the daughter of King Ānanda. She was the half-sister of the Blessed One, named Nandā. When she reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those possessing the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Inspired by this, she performed meritorious deeds and, aspiring for that same position herself, she made a resolution. In that life, she...
94:
Having performed many noble meritorious deeds throughout her life, she was reborn in the celestial realm and wandered only through happy destinies (sugati). In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, she was born into a Brahmin family and, having gone forth as a female wanderer (paribbājikā), she lived as a solitary wanderer. One day, while wandering for alms of oil, she obtained some oil and with that oil, she performed an offering of lamps throughout the night at the shrine (cetiya) of the Teacher.

After passing away from that life, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, possessing an exceedingly pure divine eye. Having wandered only among the devas for the interval between two Buddhas, she was born into a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī at the time of the appearance of this Buddha. Her name was Sakulā. When she reached the age of discretion, she became a lay devotee (upāsikā) who gained faith during the Teacher's acceptance of the Jetavana monastery. Later, upon hearing the Dhamma from a certain Elder who had destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava), she was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), went forth as a nun, and while striving and exerting herself in the practice of insight (vipassanā), she attained Arahatship before long. Concerning this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"The Victor named Padumuttara, who reached the further shore of all dhammas, the Leader, arose one hundred thousand aeons from now.

For the welfare of all beings, for the happiness of the world including the devas, the Best of Speakers, the Noble Man, practiced for their benefit.

Having reached the pinnacle of fame, the Glorious One, the Victor endowed with renown, was worshipped by the whole world and was famous in all directions.

He had crossed over doubt, transcended uncertainty, and with his mental aspirations fulfilled, he attained supreme enlightenment (sambodhi).

He was the Best of Men who brought forth the Path that had not yet arisen. He declared the Dhamma that had not been declared and made known what was unknown.

He was the Knower of the Path, the Perceiver of the Path, the Proclaimer of the Path, the Bull among Men. The Teacher was skilled in the Path, the Supreme Charioteer of those to be tamed.

The Teacher, the Great Compassionate One, the Leader, taught the Dhamma. He rescued living beings who were submerged in the mire of sensual desire.

At that time, I was born in the city of Haṃsavatī as a daughter of the Khattiya clan, beautiful, wealthy, beloved, and glorious."
95:
"I was the daughter of the Great King Ānanda and the very beautiful half-sister of the one named Padumuttara. Accompanied by royal maidens and adorned with all ornaments, I approached the Great Hero and listened to the teaching of the Dhamma. At that time, the Teacher of the World, in the midst of the assembly, praised a certain nun who possessed the divine eye and placed her in the foremost position. Having heard that, I was delighted; I gave gifts to the Teacher, worshipped the Sambuddha, and aspired for the divine eye. Then the Teacher said to me, 'Nandā, you will obtain the wish you have yearned for; this is the certain fruit of the gifts of lamps and the Dhamma.'

One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will arise in the world. You will be a female disciple of that Teacher, an heir to his Dhamma, his spiritual daughter, created by the Dhamma, named Sakulā by name. Due to that well-performed deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In this very Bhadda-kappa, the Great Famous One, the Best of Speakers named Kassapa by clan, arose. At that time, I was a female wanderer (paribbājikinī) who lived as a solitary wanderer. Having wandered for alms, I obtained a measure of oil. Having lit a lamp with that oil, I attended upon the shrine of the Best of Bipeds throughout the night with a clear and confident mind. Due to that well-performed deed, and by my intentions and aspirations, I abandoned the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Wherever I am reborn, by the power of that deed, great lamps shine forth wherever I go."
96:
"Through walls and through rock mountains, I see whatever I wish to see, having transcended the mountain; this is the fruit of the gift of lamps. I have pure vision, I shine with fame, and I am endowed with faith and wisdom; this is the fruit of the gift of lamps. And now in my final birth, I was born in a Brahmin family, in a place of abundant wealth and grain, delightful and honored by kings. I was endowed with all limbs and adorned with all ornaments; when the Sugata was entering the city, I was standing at a lattice window. Seeing the one who was shining with fame, worshipped by devas and humans, endowed with the minor marks and adorned with the major marks of a Great Man,

With an uplifted and happy mind, I delighted in going forth. In no long time, I attained Arahatship. I am a master of the psychic powers (iddhis) and the divine ear element. I know the minds of others, being a doer of the Teacher's instruction. I know my former births, and my divine eye is purified. Having destroyed all taints (āsavas), I am pure and stainless. I have served the Teacher; the Buddha's instruction has been carried out. The heavy burden has been laid down, and the cord of existence (bhavanetti) has been uprooted. The purpose for which I went forth from the home life into homelessness, that purpose has been attained by me: the destruction of all fetters. Then the Great Compassionate One, the Best of Men, placed me in the foremost position, saying, 'Sakulā is the foremost among those with the divine eye.' My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's instruction has been carried out."

Having reached Arahatship, because of her past merits, she became a master of the knowledge of the divine eye. For that reason, the Teacher placed her in the foremost position among the nuns who possess the divine eye. Reviewing her own practice, she was filled with joy and satisfaction, and by the power of inspired utterance (udāna):
97:
“While living in the household, having heard the Dhamma of a monk, I saw the dustless Dhamma, Nibbāna, the deathless state.

Abandoning son and daughter, wealth and grain, and having my hair cut off, I went forth into homelessness.

As a trainee (sikkhamānā), being peaceful and developing the path, I abandoned lust and hatred, and the taints (āsavas) that reside together with them.

Having attained the higher ordination as a bhikkhunī, I recollected my former births; the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) was purified, stainless, and well-developed.

Seeing conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) as 'other' (not-self), arisen from causes and subject to decay, I abandoned all taints; I am cooled and extinguished (nibbūta).” She uttered these verses.

Among those verses, 'Living in the household, hearing the Dhamma of a monk' means: While I was living in the home in the past, I heard a discourse on the Four Noble Truths in the presence of a certain monk who had destroyed his defilements. 'I saw the dustless Dhamma, Nibbāna, the deathless state' means: It is called 'dustless' (viraja) because of the absence of the dust of lust and so on; 'Nibbāna' because of the exit from craving (vāna); 'deathless' (accuta) because there is no falling away (death) and because it is the cause of non-decay for those who have attained it; and 'state' (pada) refers to the unconditioned Dhamma (asaṅkhata-dhamma), which I saw with the Dhamma-eye (dhamma-cakkhu), known as vision, adorned with a thousand methods.

'Sāhaṃ' means: I, in the manner described, became a stream-enterer.

'As a trainee, being peaceful' means: While I was still a trainee (sikkhamānā), having gone forth but not yet completed the required years (for full ordination). 'Developing the path' means: Bringing forth the higher path, called 'the way' (aññasa) because it is the middle practice. 'And the taints associated with them' means: I completely cut off the taints that arise together with lust and hatred and are abandoned simultaneously with them by the third path (Anāgāmi-magga).

'Having attained the higher ordination as a bhikkhunī' means: Having attained higher ordination and becoming a bhikkhunī upon completing the required years. 'Stainless' (vimala) means: Free from stains because of being liberated from defilements such as ignorance. 'Well' (sādhu) means...
98:
...developed with respect and in the right way, or developed and produced by the Noble Ones such as the Buddha; this is the connection with 'the divine eye was purified.'

'Conditioned phenomena' (saṅkhāre) means the conditioned things of the three planes. 'As other' (parato) means as not-self (anatta). 'Arisen from causes' (hetujāte) means things produced by conditions. 'Subject to decay' (palokite) means seeing with the eye of wisdom those conditioned things that are of the nature of crumbling and breaking. 'I abandoned all taints' means: I abandoned and exhausted all remaining taints by the path of Arahantship (aggamagga). The rest of the phrasing is in the same manner as previously stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sakulā Therī is Finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Soṇā Therī

The verse beginning with "Having given birth to ten sons" is that of Soṇā Therī. She too was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Having reached the age of discretion, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those of great energy. Having performed meritorious deeds, she herself aspired to that position. After performing meritorious deeds throughout her life, she passed away and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In this Buddha's era, she was born into a good family in Sāvatthī. Upon reaching maturity, she went to her husband's home and, having had ten sons and daughters, became known as "Bahuputtikā" (One with many children).

When her husband went forth (as a monk), she settled her grown-up children in their households, divided all her wealth among them, and gave it away, keeping nothing for herself. Those sons and daughters cared for her for only a few days and then began to treat her with disrespect. She thought, "What is the use of me living in this house where they treat me with such disrespect?" and approaching the bhikkhunīs, she requested to go forth. The bhikkhunīs gave her the going forth.

After obtaining higher ordination, she thought, "Since I have gone forth in my old age, I must be diligent." While performing the major and minor duties for the bhikkhunīs, she resolved, "I will practice the recluse's Dhamma (samaṇa-dhamma) all night." She would hold a pillar with her hand on the ground floor of the mansion and, without letting go of that pillar, practice the recluse's Dhamma. Even when walking in meditation, she thought, "In a dark place, my head might hit a tree or something," so she would hold a tree with her hand and, without letting go of that tree, practice the recluse's Dhamma. From then on, she became famous for her great energy. The Teacher, [seeing] the maturity of her wisdom...
99:
Seeing (Therī Soṇā), the Blessed One, while staying in the Gandhakuṭi, emitted rays of light and manifested himself as if sitting in her presence, and spoke this verse:

“Better than living a hundred years without seeing the supreme Dhamma, is living a single day seeing the supreme Dhamma.” (Dhammapada 115).

At the end of the verse, Therī Soṇā attained the fruit of Arahantship. This matter is stated in the Apadāna:

“One hundred thousand aeons ago, the Conqueror named Padumuttara, who had reached the far shore of all dhammas and was a leader of the world, arose.

At that time, I was born in a merchant's family, wealthy, honored, and beloved. Approaching that noble Sage, I heard his sweet words.

The Conqueror praised a certain bhikkhuṇī as the foremost among those who put forth effort. Hearing that, I was delighted and made offerings to the Teacher.

Bowing to the Sambuddha, I then aspired for that position. The Great Hero expressed appreciation, saying, ‘May your wish be fulfilled.’

One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world.

You will be a disciple of that Teacher, an heir to his Dhamma, his spiritual daughter, created by the Dhamma, named Soṇā.

Hearing that, I was delighted and from then on, for the rest of my life, I served the Conqueror, the Leader, with a mind of loving-kindness and the four requisites.

Due to that well-performed deed, intention, and aspiration, I left the human body and went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Now, in my final birth, I was born in a merchant's family in the noble city of Sāvatthī, which is prosperous, flourishing, and of great wealth.

When I reached the age of maturity, I went to my husband's house and gave birth to ten sons who were particularly handsome.”
100:
“All those children grew up happily; they were pleasing enough to attract the eyes of all people; they were liked even by enemies, so what need is there to speak of me (their mother)?

After that, even though I did not wish it, my husband, surrounded by the ten sons, ordained in the Dispensation of the Buddha, the God of gods.

Then, left alone, I thought: ‘There is no benefit in living for me, who am abandoned by husband and children, very old, and pitiful.’

Thinking, ‘I too will go where my husband has gone (into the Dispensation),’ I left the household life and ordained.

Then the bhikkhuṇīs left me alone in the nunnery, gave me words of advice, and said, ‘Boil some water,’ and then they departed.

Then I fetched water, poured it into a pot, placed it on the stove, and while sitting, I composed my mind.

Seeing the five aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, and exhausting all taints (āsavas), I attained the fruit of Arahantship.

Then the bhikkhuṇīs returned and asked for the hot water; I resolved upon the fire element (tejo-dhātu) and quickly heated the water.

The bhikkhuṇīs were amazed and informed the Noble Conqueror of this matter. Hearing that, the Protector was delighted and spoke this verse:

‘Better than living a hundred years lazy and lacking effort, is living a single day putting forth firm effort.’

I have pleased the Great Hero with my good practice; that Great Sage declared me the foremost among those who put forth effort (Etadagga).

My defilements are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's Dispensation.’

Then, when the Blessed One was appointing the bhikkhuṇīs to various positions in order, he placed Therī Soṇā in the foremost position among those who put forth effort. One day, reflecting on her own practice, by the power of inspired utterance (udāna):
101:
“‘Having given birth to ten sons in this physical body, and because of that, being weak and old, I approached a bhikkhuṇī.’

‘That bhikkhuṇī taught me the aggregates, sense bases, and elements. Hearing her Dhamma, I cut off my hair and ordained.’

‘As I was practicing, the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) was purified. I also know my past lives (pubbenivāsa) where I lived before.’

‘With a concentrated and well-composed mind, I develop signless insight (animitta-vipassanā). Immediately after that, without clinging, I became cooled (attained Nibbāna) and reached Arahantship.’

‘The five aggregates are fully understood; they remain with their roots cut. Woe to you, wretched old age! Now there is no more rebirth.’”—she uttered these verses.

In those verses, ‘rūpasamussaye’ means in the collection called materiality (rūpa). This word ‘rūpa’ appears in the sense of the base of visible forms (rūpāyatana) in sentences such as “Dependent on the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises.” It appears in the sense of the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha) in sentences such as “Whatever materiality there is, past, future, or present.” It appears in the sense of nature (sabhāva) in sentences such as “One is lustful for what is of a pleasant nature, of an agreeable nature.” It appears in the sense of the kasina base in sentences such as “He sees forms externally.” It appears in the sense of fine-material absorption (rūpajhāna) in sentences such as “Possessing form, he sees forms.” It appears in the sense of the physical body (rūpakāya) in sentences such as “Dependent on bones, sinews, flesh, and skin, the space enclosed is called a physical form.” Here too, it should be understood as the physical body.

The word ‘samussaya’ is also a synonym for the skeleton or the body. It appears as a synonym for the skeleton in sentences such as “The skeletons are a hundred.” It appears in the sense of the body in sentences such as “See the body (samussaya), Nandā, diseased, impure, and putrid.” Here too, it should be understood as the body. Therefore, it is said: ‘rūpasamussaye’ means in the body which is a collection called materiality. The word ‘ṭhatvā’ (staying/remaining) is an elliptical word. ‘Asmiṃ rūpasamussaye’ is connected as: “having stayed in this collection of materiality, and depending on this physical body, having given birth to ten sons.” ‘Tato’ means because of the reason of giving birth to those ten sons. That Elder Nun, in her first stage of life...
102:
After giving birth to sons in succession, as she aged, her body became weak and she reached old age. Referring to that fact, she said: "Then I became weak and aged."

"Tassā" means "from that" (tato), or "in her presence" (tassā santike). Again, "tassā" is used as a possessive case in the sense of an instrument, meaning "by her" (tāyā). "Sikkhamānāyā" refers to one who is practicing the three trainings.

"Anantarāvimokkhāsiṃ" means she became one who possessed the liberation (fruition) that arises immediately after the Path of Arahatship. The eight liberations, such as "one possessing form sees forms," are not called "immediate liberation" (anantara-vimokkha). Although the fruit-liberations reached immediately after the path occur during the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti), they are called "immediate liberation" because they arise immediately after the first path. This is similar to how path-concentration is called "immediate concentration" (ānantarika-samādhi). "Anupādāya nibbutā" means she was quenched through the Parinibbāna of defilements without clinging to anything such as form and so on.

Having thus manifested the three knowledges and reached the summit with the fruit of Arahatship, she uttered an inspired utterance. Now, reproaching the body that had long been oppressed by old age, and to manifest the state of having transcended that old age along with the background story, she spoke the final verse beginning with "Pañcakkhandhā pariññātā." In that verse, "Dhi tavatthu jare jamme" means: "Woe to you, wretched old age, which causes the limbs to become slack; may there be reproach to you, wretched and low old age." "Natthi dāni punabbhavo" means: "Therefore, I have transcended and overcome you (old age)."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Soṇā Therī is finished.

## 9. Bhaddākuṇḍalakesātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Lūnakhesī" is the verse of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā. She too was born in a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. Upon reaching the age of discretion, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher one day, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain nun to the foremost position of those with quick intuition (khippābhiññā). She performed meritorious deeds and aspired for that position. After performing meritorious deeds for the rest of her life and wandering among devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons, in the time of Kassapa Buddha, in the house of King Kikī of Kāsi...
103:
...being one among the seven sisters, she observed the ten precepts for twenty thousand years, practicing the celibate life of a maiden, and built a monastery for the Saṅgha to reside in. After wandering only in happy realms for one Buddha-interval, she was born in a merchant family in Rājagaha during this Buddha-arising. Her name was Bhaddā Tissā. She grew up with a large retinue and, upon reaching marriageable age, she saw from a lion-window a thief named Sattuka, the son of the royal chaplain, who had been caught with stolen goods and was being led to the place of execution by the city guard on the King's order to be killed. She became infatuated with him and thought, "If I get him, I shall live; if not, I shall die," and lay face down on her bed.

Then her father, hearing of that matter and having strong affection for her as his only daughter, gave a bribe of a thousand pieces of gold and had the thief released by a trick. He had him bathed in scented water, adorned with all ornaments, and sent him to the palace. Bhaddā, her wish fulfilled, adorned herself with excessive ornaments and served him. After a few days had passed, Sattuka became greedy for her ornaments and said, "Bhaddā, as soon as I was caught by the city guard, I made a vow to the deity dwelling at the Thieves' Cliff (Corapapāta): 'If I gain my life, I will bring an offering to you.' Therefore, prepare the offering."

She, thinking "I will fulfill his wish," prepared the offering and, adorned with all ornaments, mounted a single carriage with her husband and started to climb the Thieves' Cliff, saying, "I will make an offering to the deity."

Sattuka thought, "If everyone climbs up, it will not be possible to take her ornaments." He made the retinue stay right there and, making her carry the offering bowl herself, he did not speak affectionately to her while climbing the mountain. She understood his intention by his behavior alone. Sattuka said, "Bhaddā, take off your upper robe and make a bundle of the ornaments worn on your body." She asked, "Lord, what is my fault?" He replied, "You fool, do you think I have come for the sake of an offering? I have come to take your ornaments under the pretext of an offering." She said, "Lord, for whom are the ornaments, and for whom am I?" He replied, "I do not know such distinctions." She said, "So be it, Lord, but please fulfill one wish of mine."
104:
She said, "Please allow me to embrace you in a decorative manner as well." The thief agreed, saying, "Very well." Knowing that the thief had agreed, Bhaddā embraced him from the front, and then, while pretending to embrace him from behind, she pushed him off the mountain precipice. The thief fell and was crushed to pieces. Seeing the wonder performed by Bhaddā, the deity residing on the mountain, manifesting her cleverness, spoke these verses:

"Man is not the only wise one in all circumstances;
A woman, too, is wise, being discerning in various matters.

Man is not the only wise one in all circumstances;
A woman, too, is wise, being able to quickly reflect on what is beneficial."
(Ap. Therī. 2.3.31-32)

Then Bhaddā thought, "It is not proper for me to return home in this state. I will go from here and take up a life of renunciation." She went to the monastery of the Nigaṇṭhas and requested them to ordain her. Then the Nigaṇṭhas asked her, "In what manner do you wish to be ordained?" She replied, "Perform for me that which is considered the highest in your form of renunciation." Saying "Very well," the Nigaṇṭhas plucked out her hair using a palmyra nut and ordained her. Later, when her hair grew back, it grew in curls. From that time on, she became known by the name Kuṇḍalakesā.

After learning the doctrines and methods of debate from the Nigaṇṭhas, she realized, "These people know only this much; there is no higher distinction beyond this." She left them and traveled to various places where wise people lived, learning their arts and sciences. Finding no one capable of debating with her, whenever she entered a village or a market town, she would make a heap of sand at the gate, plant a rose-apple branch on it, and give instructions to the children nearby, saying, "Whoever is able to refute my doctrine, let him trample this branch." Then she would go to her lodging. If the rose-apple branch remained there for seven days, she would take the branch and depart.

At that time, our Blessed One had appeared in the world, and having turned the noble Wheel of Dhamma, he was dwelling in the Jetavana monastery near Sāvatthī. Kuṇḍalakesā, wandering through villages, market towns, and royal capitals in the manner described, arrived at Sāvatthī. She planted a rose-apple branch in a heap of sand at the city gate, gave instructions to the children, and entered Sāvatthī.
105:
Then, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati (Venerable Sāriputta), while entering the city alone, saw that rose-apple (jambu) branch. Desiring to discipline that person, he asked the children, "Why is this rose-apple branch placed like this?" The children explained the matter to him. The Elder said, "If that is so, trample upon this rose-apple branch." The children then trampled the branch.

When Kuṇḍalakesā came out of the city after finishing her meal, she saw that the rose-apple branch had been trampled. She asked, "Who trampled this branch?" Upon learning that the Elder had ordered it to be trampled, she said, "A one-sided doctrine is not beautiful," and entered the city of Sāvatthī. Wandering from street to street, she proclaimed, "Come and see the debate between me and the Sakyaputta monks!" Then, surrounded by a great crowd, she approached the Elder Dhammasenāpati, who was sitting at the foot of a certain tree. After exchanging greetings, she stood at a suitable place and asked, "Venerable sir, why did you have my rose-apple branch trampled?" "It is true, I had it trampled," he replied. "If that is so, let there be a debate between me and you," she said. "Let it be so, sister," he replied. "Who shall ask, and who shall answer?" she asked. "The turn to ask has come to us; you ask only what you know," he said.

Kuṇḍalakesā asked all the doctrines she knew. The Elder answered all of them. When she did not know what else to ask, she remained silent. Then the Elder said to her, "You have asked much; let me also ask you one question." "Ask, Venerable sir," she said. The Elder asked this question: "What is the 'one'?" Kuṇḍalakesā, seeing neither the beginning nor the end of it, felt as if she had entered into darkness and said, "I do not know, Venerable sir." "If you do not know even this much, what else could you know?" he said, and then preached the Dhamma to her. She prostrated at the Elder's feet and said, "Venerable sir, I go to you for refuge."

"Sister, do not go to me for refuge. Go for refuge only to the Blessed One, the Supreme Person in the world including the devas," he said. "I will do so, Venerable sir," she said. In the evening, at the time of the Dhamma talk, she went to the Blessed One, paid homage with the five-point prostration, and stood at a suitable place. The Blessed One, knowing the maturity of her wisdom, spoke this verse:

"Even if there are a thousand verses,
Composed of meaningless words,
Better is a single line of a verse,
Hearing which one becomes peaceful."

At the conclusion of the verse, while standing there, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

In the city of Haṃsavatī, she was the daughter of King Ānanda. She was the half-sister of the Blessed One, born of the same father but a different mother, and was known by the name Nandā. When Princess Nandā reached maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, she saw the Blessed One appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (etadagga) among those possessing the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). Inspired, she performed great meritorious deeds and made a wish for that same position of foremost in divine eye. That Princess Nandā performed many noble meritorious deeds throughout her life and, after passing away, was reborn in the deva realm and wandered only in the happy destinations (sugati).

In the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was born into a brahmin family. Having ordained as a female wanderer (paribbājikā), she wandered alone. One day, she received oil as an alms-offering and with that oil, she performed a lamp offering at the shrine (cetiya) of the Blessed One throughout the night.
