When that female wanderer passed away from that life, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm, possessing extremely pure divine sight, and wandered only in the deva realms during the interval between two Buddhas.

In the time when this Gotama Buddha appeared, she was born into a brahmin family in the city of Sāvatthī and received the name Sakulā. When Sakulā reached maturity, on the day the Blessed One accepted the donation of the Jetavana monastery, she became a female lay follower (upāsikā) who gained faith. Later, upon hearing the Dhamma from an Arahant Elder, she was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained as a nun, and while practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she soon attained Arahantship. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

One hundred thousand aeons ago from this Bhadda-kappa, the Blessed One named Padumuttara, the Conqueror of the five Maras, who reached the further shore of all phenomena, appeared in the world. That Great Hero, the supreme among those who teach the Dhamma, practiced for the welfare, happiness, and benefit of beings in the world including the devas. The Blessed One of great glory, who reached the pinnacle of fame, was renowned for His virtues. He was worshipped by the multitudes and was famous in all directions. That Blessed One was free from doubt and uncertainty, had transcended hesitation, was of perfect intention, and had reached the noble path of Arahantship. The Blessed One, supreme among men, made known the Path that had not yet arisen, preached the Path that others could not preach, and brought into existence the Noble Path that had not yet occurred in the continuity of those to be tamed. The Blessed One knew the Path, was skilled in the Path, and was a teacher of the Path. The Blessed One, supreme among those who discipline others, was skilled in the matter of the Path. The Blessed One, possessed of great compassion, preached the Dhamma and pulled out the beings who were sinking in the mire of sensual pleasures.

At that time, I was Princess Nandā in the city of Haṃsavatī. I was very beautiful, wealthy, and possessed of glory and charm beloved by all. Being the daughter of King Ānanda, I was exceedingly graceful. I was also the half-sister of Padumuttara Buddha. Adorned together with other princesses, I approached the Blessed One and listened to the Dhamma. It was then that the Blessed One Padumuttara praised a bhikkhunī who possessed the divine eye in the midst of the assembly and placed her in the foremost position of divine eye. Having heard those words, I was filled with joy, offered gifts to the Blessed One, and made a wish for the foremost position of divine eye.

Then the Blessed One said, "Sister Nandā, you shall obtain the foremost position of divine eye for which you have prayed. It is well-decided that this position is the result of the offering of lamps and the offering of Dhamma. One hundred thousand aeons from this aeon, a Buddha named Gotama, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will appear in the world. You will be an heir to His Dhamma, a daughter born of the Dhamma, and will become a disciple named Sakulā." Due to those well-performed deeds, intentions, and aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa deva realm. In this Bhadda-kappa, the one named Kassapa, the most supreme...
106:
The Victorious Buddha named Padumuttara reached the end of all phenomena (dhammas). One hundred thousand aeons ago, that Leader of the world appeared. At that time, I was born in a merchant family in the city of Haṃsavatī. I was endowed with great happiness, illuminated by the radiance of various gems. Having approached that Great Hero, I heard the teaching of the Dhamma. Then, with faith arisen, I approached the Victorious One for refuge.

At that time, the Great Compassionate One named Padumuttara appointed a beautiful bhikkhunī to the position of those with quick intuition (khippābhiññā). Hearing that, I was delighted, and having given an offering to the Great Sage, I bowed my head at his feet and aspired for that position. The Great Hero expressed appreciation: "Sister, may all that you have aspired for be fulfilled; may you be happy and attain peace (Nibbāna)."

"One hundred thousand aeons from this aeon, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will appear in the world. His heir in the Dhamma, a breast-born daughter, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā, will come to be."

Through that well-performed deed and through my intentions and aspirations, having abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Passing away from there, I went to the Yāma heaven, then to Tusita, then to Nimmānarati, and then to the city of Vasavatti.

By the power of that merit, in whatever realm I was reborn, I was made the chief queen of kings in those various places. Passing away from there among humans, I was made the chief queen of universal monarchs (cakkavatti) and of regional kings. Having experienced prosperity among gods and humans, being happy in all births, I wandered through saṃsāra for many aeons.
107:
In this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda-kappa), the Buddha named Kassapa, of the Kassapa clan, highly renowned and the best of speakers, appeared.

In the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, the King of Kāsi named Kikī was the attendant to that Great Sage.

I was the fourth daughter of that King, and was known as Bhikkhudāyī. Having heard the Dhamma of the supreme Victorious One, I delighted in renunciation.

As our father did not grant permission, we lived diligently in the household for twenty thousand years.

The seven princesses, having grown up in comfort, practiced the celibacy of maidens (komāribrahmacariya), delighting in attending to the Buddha with joy.

They were Samaṇီ, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāyikā.

(In this present age) they are Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, myself (Bhaddā), Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.

Through those well-performed deeds and through my intentions and aspirations, when I abandoned the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Now, in my final birth, I was born in a wealthy merchant family in the supreme city of Giribbaja (Rājagaha). When I reached the age of youth,

I saw a thief being led away for execution and felt a strong attachment to him. My father released him from the death penalty by paying a thousand pieces of money.

Knowing my desire, my father gave me in marriage to him. I was very trusting of him, and served his interests with great affection.

Driven by greed for my ornaments, he, with the heart of an enemy, led me to the Thief’s Cliff (Corappapāta) and planned to kill me.

Then, having paid homage to that enemy with joined palms, and wishing to protect my own life, I spoke these words:
108:
"Take all these gold bracelets, pearls, and many lapis lazuli gems, sir; and take me as your servant," she said.

"O beautiful one, take off your ornaments; do not weep excessively; I do not desire wealth brought from others."

"Since I have known myself, since I reached the age of discretion, I have known no one dearer than you."

"Come, I will embrace you after circumambulating you to the right; now there is no more union between me and you."

"A man is not a wise person in all places; a woman too is wise, being discerning here and there."

"A man is not a wise person in all places; a woman too is wise, being a quick thinker of what is beneficial."

"I thought quickly and well when in close proximity; like a beast wearing wool, I then killed the enemy (Sattuka)."

"The foolish person who does not quickly understand the benefit that has arisen is killed like a thief in a mountain cleft."

"He who quickly understands the benefit that has arisen is released from the oppression of the enemy, just as I was then released from the enemy."

"Then, having thrown the enemy into the abyss from the mountain precipice, I approached those with white robes (Paribbājakas) and went forth as a monastic."

"Then, having plucked out all my hair with tweezers and gone forth, I constantly studied the doctrines (samaya)."

"After learning those doctrines, while sitting alone and reflecting on them, a dog took a severed human hand and dropped it near me before leaving; seeing that hand full of maggots, I obtained the sign (of impermanence).

I, having become a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), abandoned children, wealth, and grain, had my hair cut, and entered the monastic life. While a trainee (Sikkhamānā), developing the straight path, I abandoned lust, hatred, and the taints (āsavas) that reside with them (by the path of Non-returning). Having reached the state of a monk and become a bhikkhunī, I could remember the sequence of past aggregates; I also purified the stainless divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) developed by the virtuous. Seeing the conditioned things (saṅkhāras) that arise from causes and are subject to destruction as non-self (anatta), I abandoned all taints (by the path of Arahantship) and attained the cooling of defilements.

In those verses, 'Agārasmiṃ vasantīhaṃ, dhammaṃ sutvānu bhikkhuno' means: Formerly, while living in the household life, I heard the teaching of the Four Noble Truths from a monk who had destroyed the defilements. Because of the absence of the dust of lust and other defilements, I saw with the Dhamma-eye—the path of Stream-entry adorned with a thousand methods—the unconditioned state (asaṅkhata) called 'Accuta' (the Deathless), which is the escape from craving and is called Nibbāna because it is free from death and is the cause of immortality. 'Sāhaṃ' means: I am a Stream-enterer by the aforementioned method. 'Sikkhamānā ahaṃ santi' means: While practicing as a trainee and even before completing the trainee period, by developing the straight higher path which is the middle way, I destroyed the taints that reside in a single mind along with lust and hatred, which are to be abandoned by the path of Non-returning. 'Bhikkhunī upasampajjā' means: Having completed the trainee period and reached the state of a monk, I became a bhikkhunī. 'Vimalaṃ' means: I purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) which is stainless because it is free from the defilements of ignorance and other impurities, and which was developed with respect and excellence, or produced by the virtuous such as the Buddhas.

'Saṅkhāre' refers to the conditioned things in the three realms; 'parato' means as non-self (anatta); 'hetujāte' means those that arise from causes; 'palokite' means those whose nature is to be destroyed and to cease. Seeing these with the eye of wisdom, 'pahāsi āsave sabbe' means that by the path of Arahantship, I abandoned and exhausted all remaining taints. The remaining words have clear meanings. The commentary on the verses of Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā Therī ends.

## Commentary on the Verses of Soṇā Therī
The verses beginning with 'Dasa putte vijāyitvā' are the verses of Soṇā Therī. This Soṇā Therī was also born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching maturity, one day while listening to the Dhamma from the Buddha, she saw the Buddha appoint a bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who possess energetic effort. She performed meritorious deeds and aspired to that position. Having performed merits throughout her life, she passed away from that life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the time of this Gotama Buddha, she was born into a good family in the city of Sāvatthī...
109:
At that time, being stirred with agitation, I arose (from bed) and questioned my fellow practitioners. Those fellow practitioners said, "The Sakyan monks know that meaning."

Wishing to ask that meaning, I approached the Buddha's disciples; they took me into the presence of the Greatest Buddha.

The Leader of humans and gods taught me the Dhamma: the aggregates (khandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus); as foul (asubha), impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta).

Having heard the teaching of that Buddha, I purified the Dhamma-eye. From then on, being one who understood the True Dhamma, I requested the going forth and higher ordination.

When I requested, the Leader said, "Come, auspicious one (bhaddā)." At that time, I reached the state of a monk and saw a small amount of (foot-washing) water.

By washing my feet, I perceived the arising and passing away (of the water ripples); likewise, I then reflected on all conditioned things (saṅkhāras) as being of such a nature (having the nature of arising and passing away).

While reflecting thus, without clinging to anything among all phenomena, my mind was liberated in every way. Then the Victorious Buddha (Jina) made known to me the path of swift direct knowledge (khippābhiññā).

I am a master of the psychic powers. I possess the divine ear element. I know the minds of others. I am a doer of the Teacher's instruction.

I know my past lives. The divine eye has been purified. Having exhausted all taints (āsavas), I have become a very pure and stainless Arahant.

I have served the Teacher. The Buddha's bidding is done. The heavy burden is laid down. The conduit to existence (bhavanetti) is uprooted.

The purpose for which I went forth from the home life to the homeless life—that purpose has been attained: the destruction of all fetters (saṃyojanas).

In the meaning (attha), the Dhamma, the language (nirutti), and the eloquence (paṭibhāna), my knowledge is stainless and pure in the Greatest Buddha's teaching.

I have burnt up the defilements... (and so on) the Buddha's bidding is done.

Having reached Arahantship, she requested ordination at that very moment. The Teacher permitted her ordination. She went to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, ordained, and spent her time in the bliss of fruition (phala-sukha) and the bliss of Nibbāna. Reflecting on her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance (udāna)—
110:
I wandered in the past with plucked hair, covered in filth, and wearing only a single cloth. I perceived fault in the faultless and saw no fault in what was faulty.

Leaving my day-rest on Mount Gijjhakūṭa, I saw the Buddha, free from the dust of defilements, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks.

Bowing with my knees to the ground, I paid homage and raised my joined palms in his presence. The Buddha said to me, "Come, Bhaddā"; that itself was my ordination.

I wandered through the territories of Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Kāsī, and Kosala. For fifty years, I ate the alms-food of the country without being in debt.

"That lay follower who gave a robe to Bhaddā, who is liberated from all bonds, has surely generated great merit; he is indeed wise."—she spoke these verses.

In those verses, "lūnakesī" means my hair was plucked. It refers to the hair being plucked with a palm-nut during her ordination among the Nigaṇṭhas. "Paṅkadharī" means carrying the filth of dirt on the teeth due to not using a tooth-brushing stick. "Ekasāṭī" means wearing only one cloth according to the custom of the Nigaṇṭhas. "Pure cariṃ" means I wandered like this in the past as a Nigaṇṭha nun. "Avajje vajjamatinī" means perceiving fault in faultless actions such as bathing, anointing, and brushing teeth. "Vajje ca avajjadassinī" means seeing no fault in faulty things such as pride, malice, rivalry, and perversion.

"Divāvihārā nikkhamma" means coming out from her place of day-rest. This Elder, having met the Thera at midday, had her pride removed through his answers to her questions and his teaching of the Dhamma. With a confident mind, she wished to approach the Teacher. She went back to her dwelling, stayed in her day-rest, and then approached the Teacher in the evening.

"Nihacca jāṇuṃ vanditvā" means bowing with both knees on the ground in a five-point prostration. "Sammukhā añjaliṃ akaṃ" means raising the bright joined palms with ten fingernails together in the presence of the Teacher. "Ehi bhaddeti maṃ avaca, sā me āsupasampadā" means when the Buddha, after I had reached Arahantship, was requested for the Pabbajjā and Upasampadā...
111:
...the Teacher, while standing, said and commanded: "Come, Bhaddā, go to the bhikkhunīs' quarters and receive the Pabbajjā and Upasampadā in the presence of the bhikkhunīs." That command of the Teacher, being the cause of my higher ordination, became my Upasampadā.

The two verses starting with "Ciṇṇā" are verses declaring the attainment of Arahantship (aññābyākaraṇa). In those verses, "Ciṇṇā Aṅga ca Magadhā" means that in the past, I wandered through the regions of Aṅga, Magadha, Vajji, Kāsī, and Kosala, wearing a coarse cloth (sāṇā) and eating the alms-food given by the people of the country. In those very countries, from the time of meeting the Teacher, I ate the alms-food of the country for fifty years as one without debt (free from the debt of defilements), faultless, and free from defilements.

By way of praising the special merit of that lay follower who, with a very confident mind, gave his own robe, she declared her attainment of Arahantship with the final verse starting with "Puññaṃ vata pasavī bahuṃ". That verse is easy to understand.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Bhaddā Kuṇḍalakesā is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Paṭācārā

The verse starting with "Naṅgalehi kasaṃ khettaṃ" is the verse of Elder Paṭācārā. She too was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position (etadagga) among those who master the Vinaya. Having performed meritorious deeds, she made a resolution for that position. She performed wholesome deeds throughout her life and wandered through the realms of gods and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she took rebirth in the house of King Kikī of Kāsī. Being one of the seven sisters, she practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years and built a monastic cell (parivena) for the Saṅgha of monks. Passing away from that life, she was reborn in the deva world. After enjoying divine bliss for the interval between two Buddhas, she was born in the house of a merchant in Sāvatthī during the appearance of this Buddha. When she reached adulthood, she formed a defiled bond with a worker in her own house. Her parents set a date to marry her to a young man of the same social class. Knowing this, she took her valuable ornaments and fled through the city gate with that worker. While living in a small village, she became pregnant.
112: When that woman's pregnancy was mature, she said, "Lord, what is the use of living here without support? Let us go to my parents' home." Her husband delayed, saying, "We will go today, we will go tomorrow." Thinking, "This fool will not take me," she tidied the house while he was out, informed the neighbors, "Tell my husband I have gone to my parents' home," and set out alone for her parents' home. When the husband returned and did not find her, he asked the neighbors and heard she had gone. Thinking, "Because of me, this lady of good family has become helpless," he followed her tracks and caught up with her. She gave birth right there on the road. From the time of giving birth, her desire to travel subsided, and she returned with her husband. It should be understood in detail as before that she became pregnant a second time. This is the difference: when the winds of labor began while they were on the way, a great unseasonable storm arose. The sky was as if ablaze with lightning from all directions, as if breaking apart with thunder, and continuous with downpours of rain. Seeing this danger, she said, "Lord, find me a place sheltered from the rain." Looking here and there, the husband saw a thicket covered with grass. Going there, intending to cut branches with the billhook in his hand, he cut a branch growing on top of an anthill covered with grass. At that very moment, a fierce, venomous snake came out of that anthill and bit him. He fell right there and died. Suffering great misery, waiting for her husband's return, unable to bear the wind and rain, she placed her two crying sons in her bosom. Pressing the ground with her knees and hands, she passed the whole night in that position. At dawn, she placed the newborn son, who was like a lump of flesh, on a coil made of old cloth. Carrying him with her hands and bosom, she said to the elder son, "Come, dear son, your father went this way." Following the path her husband took, she saw him dead near the anthill. Crying and lamenting, "Because of me, my husband has died," she reached a river on the way, where the water was flowing knee-deep or breast-deep due to the rain all night. Because of her lack of wisdom and her weakness, she was unable to enter the water with both children, so she left the elder son on this bank...
113: ...taking the other son, she went to the far bank, spread out branches, and laid the infant on a coil made of rags upon those branches. Thinking, "I will go back for the other son," yet unable to leave the infant, she repeatedly turned back to look as she entered the river. Then, when she reached the middle of the river, a hawk saw the child and, thinking it was a piece of meat, descended from the sky. Seeing the hawk, she raised both hands and shouted loudly three times, "Shoo! Shoo!" Because of the distance, the hawk ignored her, seized the boy, and flew into the sky. The elder son, standing on the near bank, saw his mother raising both hands and shouting loudly. Thinking, "She is calling me," he quickly entered the water. Thus, the younger son was taken by the hawk, and the elder son was destroyed by the water. Lamenting, "One of my sons was taken by a hawk, one was swept away by the water, and my husband died on the road," she walked on and saw a man coming from Sāvatthī. She asked, "Friend, where do you live?" "Mother, I live in Sāvatthī." "Friend, in Sāvatthī, on such-and-such a street, there is such-and-such a family; do you know them?" "Mother, I know them, but do not ask about that; ask about something else." "Friend, I have no use for other matters; I only wish to ask about that." "Mother, though you forbid me from telling, did you not see the rain falling all night today?" "Friend, I saw it; that rain fell upon me all night long. I will tell you that reason later; for now, tell me the news of that treasurer's house." "Mother, this night, the house collapsed upon those three people—the treasurer, his wife, and his son. They are being cremated on a single pyre. Mother, that smoke you see is their smoke." At that moment, she did not even realize her clothes were falling off. Reaching a state of madness through grief, she wandered about naked, lamenting: "Both sons have died, and my husband died on the road; My mother, father, and brother are burning on a single pyre." Thus she wandered about.
114:
From that time on, because she no longer wandered even with a cloth for a lower garment and was of fallen conduct (or naked), she came to be known only as 'Patācārā'. Seeing her, some people said, "Go away, you crazy woman!" and threw rubbish on her head; others scattered dust on her, and still others threw clods of earth.

While the Blessed One was sitting in the midst of a great assembly at the Jetavana monastery preaching the Dhamma, he saw her wandering in that manner. Observing the maturity of her knowledge, he caused her to come towards the monastery. Seeing her, the assembly said, "Do not let this crazy woman come this way." The Blessed One said, "Do not forbid her," and when she came near, he said, "Sister, regain your mindfulness." At that very moment, through the power of the Buddha, she regained her mindfulness. Realizing that her garment had fallen off, she established a sense of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) and sat down in a crouching position.

A man threw her an upper garment. She put it on, approached the Blessed One, and paid homage with the five-point prostration, saying, "Venerable Sir, be my refuge. A hawk has carried off one of my sons, another was swept away by water, my husband died on the way, and my parents and brother died when their house collapsed and are being cremated on a single funeral pyre." Thus she told the cause of her grief. The Blessed One said, "Patācārā, do not worry. You have come to the presence of one who is able to be your refuge. Just as you are now shedding tears due to the death of sons and others, even so, in this beginningless Saṃsāra, the tears shed due to the death of sons and others are more than the water in the four great oceans." Showing this, he spoke this verse:

"The water in the four oceans is but a little;
The tears shed are many, not a few.
When a person is touched by suffering and grieves,
Why, dear daughter, do you neglect yourself?"

When the Blessed One spoke this discourse on the beginningless nature of Saṃsāra (Anamatagga-pariyāya) in this manner, her grief became lighter. Knowing that her grief had diminished, he said, "Patācārā,
115:
“Sons and others cannot be a protection, a shelter, or a refuge for one going to the next world.” Just as it is said, even though they exist, they are as if they do not. Therefore, a wise person should purify their own virtue and should only strive to accomplish the path leading to Nibbāna. To show this, he said:

“Sons are no protection, nor father, nor kinsmen;
For one overcome by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among relatives.”

“Knowing this fact, the wise person, restrained by virtue,
Should quickly clear the path leading to Nibbāna.”

With these verses, he preached the Dhamma. At the end of the teaching, Patācārā was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and requested the Blessed One for ordination. The Blessed One sent her to the bhikkhunīs and had her ordained. After receiving the higher ordination, while she was performing the work of insight (Vipassanā) for the sake of the higher paths, one day she took water in a jar and poured it to wash her feet. That water went a short distance and stopped. The water poured a second time went further than that. The water poured a third time went even further than that. Taking that very thing as her object of meditation, she reflected on the three stages of life: “Like the water I poured the first time, these beings also die in the first stage of life. Like the water poured the second time that went further, they die in the middle stage of life. Like the water poured the third time that went even further, they die in the last stage of life.”

While the Blessed One was staying in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), he emitted a radiance and appeared as if standing before her, saying, “Patācārā... it is just so. All these beings are subject to death. Therefore, rather than living a hundred years without seeing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates, it is better to live for even a single day or a single moment seeing that arising and passing away.” To show this meaning, he spoke this verse:

“Though one should live a hundred years
Without seeing arising and passing away,
Better is a single day of life
For one who sees arising and passing away.”

At the end of the verse, Patācārā attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). This is stated in the Apadāna:
116:
The Buddha named Padumuttara, who reached the far shore of all dhammas and is the leader of the world, appeared one hundred thousand aeons ago from this present age. At that time, I was born in the city of Haṃsavatī in a treasurer's family; I shone with the radiance of various jewels and was endowed with great wealth and happiness. Approaching that Great Hero, I heard the Dhamma teaching, and having gained faith, I took refuge in the Victorious One. 

Then the Leader praised a certain nun who was the foremost among those who bear the Vinaya, who was modest, firm, and skilled in what is allowable and what is not. At that time, with a joyful heart and greatly desiring that position, I invited the Ten-Powered One, the Protector of the World, along with the Saṅgha. After feeding them for seven days and offering the triple robes, I bowed my head at the feet of the Buddha and spoke these words: 'O Hero, O Sage, I wish to become like that nun whom you praised in the future, if it can be achieved, O Leader.' 

Then the Teacher said to me: 'Sister, do not fear; be at peace. In the future, you will obtain that heart's desire. One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama, of the Okkāka clan, will appear in the world. A female disciple named Paṭācārā, who will be an heir to his Dhamma, his heart's child, and created by the Dhamma, will arise.' 

Then, being joyful, I served that Victorious One and the Saṅgha with a heart of loving-kindness for the rest of my life. Through that well-performed deed and the aspiration of my intention, after leaving the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In this very Bhadda aeon, the famous Kassapa of noble lineage, the best of speakers, appeared.
117:
At that time, in the noble city of Bārāṇasī, the King of Kāsi named Kikī was the ruler of men and an attendant to the Great Sage. I was his third daughter, and I was well-known as a Bhikkhunī. Having heard the Dhamma of the Supreme Victor, I delighted in the state of a renunciant (and asked for permission). Our father did not permit us to ordain. At that time, we lived in the household for twenty thousand years without laziness. 

The seven princesses, who grew up in comfort, delighted in serving the Buddha and practiced the noble maidenly celibacy with joyful hearts. They were Samaṇီ, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāyikā. They became: I (Uppalavaṇṇā), Khemā, Bhaddā Bhikkhunī, Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and the seventh was Visākhā. 

Through those well-performed deeds and the intense aspiration of my intention, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. In this final birth, I was born in a treasurer's family in the noble city of Sāvatthī, which was prosperous, flourishing, and very wealthy. 

When I reached youth, following the power of my own thoughts, I saw a man who would become my lover and went away with him. I gave birth to one son, and while the second was in my womb, I firmly decided to go to my parents. At that time, while my husband was away, I left the house alone without telling him to go to the noble city of Sāvatthī. 

Then my husband followed and met me on the way. At that time, extremely painful birth-pains arose in me. At the time of my delivery, a great storm rained down. Then my husband, while going to look for wood (grass), was killed by a snake and died.
118:
At that time, helpless and pitiable due to the suffering of childbirth, I saw a small river full of water and went towards my parents' house. Carrying the infant, I crossed, and leaving him alone on the far bank, I returned to cross with the other son. On the way back, a hawk snatched the crying infant; the other son was swept away by the current. I was overcome with grief. 

Going to the city of Sāvatthī, I heard that my relatives had died. Then, oppressed by grief and overcome by great sorrow, I spoke thus: 'Both sons have died, my husband died on the road, and my mother, father, and brother are being burned on a single funeral pyre.' 

Then, thin, pale, helpless, and with a dejected mind, wandering here and there, I saw the Buddha, the Charioteer of men. Then the Teacher said to me: 'Daughter, do not grieve for your sons; be at peace. Seek only yourself; why do you suffer in vain? For one oppressed by death, sons are no refuge, nor are relatives or friends; there is no refuge among kin.' 

Hearing the words of the Sage, I first attained the fruit of Stream-entry. Not long after ordaining, I attained Arahantship. I am a master of psychic powers, I have the divine ear element, I know the minds of others, and I follow the Teacher's instruction. I know my past lives, my divine eye is purified, I have exhausted all taints and am perfectly pure and stainless. 

Then I learned the entire Vinaya teaching in detail from the All-Seeing Buddha and could answer correctly as it is. The Buddha, pleased with that quality, placed me in the foremost position: 'Among the nuns who bear the Vinaya, Paṭācārā is the foremost.'
119:
I have served the Teacher, I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching. The heavy burden has been laid down, and the craving that leads to rebirth has been uprooted.

The purpose for which I went forth from home to homelessness—that purpose, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Having attained Arahatship, while reflecting on her practice during the time she was a trainee (sekha) and illustrating how the higher distinction arose, she spoke these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

"Young men plow the fields with plows, sowing seeds in the earth; supporting their wives and children, they find wealth.

Why should I, endowed with virtue, a follower of the Teacher's instruction, diligent and not restless, not attain Nibbāna?

Having washed my feet, I stayed (focusing) on the foot-washing water. Seeing the water flowing from the high ground to the low—

I concentrated my mind on that flow of water, just as one tames a noble thoroughbred horse.

Then, taking a lamp, I entered the dwelling. Having looked at the bed, I sat down on the couch.

Then, taking a needle, I pulled out the wick; just as the lamp was extinguished, the liberation of the mind (Arahatship) occurred."

In those verses, "kasaṃ" means those who are plowing (performing the act of plowing). Here, the singular form is used in the sense of the plural. "pavapaṃ" means those who are sowing seeds. "chamā" means on the ground. Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the locative case. The summary of this meaning is: These young beings plow the fields with plows and shares, sowing various seeds of grain in the desired land, and thus supporting themselves and their wives and children...
120:
...they obtain wealth. Thus, in this world, personal effort applied appropriately is fruitful and brings increase.

Even so, why do I, though endowed with virtue, a follower of the Buddha's instruction, diligent and not restless, not attain Nibbāna? Being of very pure virtue, diligent due to aroused energy, and not restless due to a well-concentrated mind within, why do I not attain Nibbāna while practicing the Teacher's instruction known as the meditation on the Four Noble Truths? I shall certainly attain it (she thought).

Thinking thus, while applying herself to the work of insight (vipassanā), one day she took a sign (nimitta) from the foot-washing water. Therefore, she said "Having washed my feet..." and so on. Its meaning is: While I was washing my feet, seeing the foot-washing water that had been poured three times flowing from the high ground to the low, I made it a sign.

"Just as this water is of the nature to be exhausted and to perish, so too are the life-formations of beings." Thus, contemplating the mark of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa), and following that, the marks of suffering (dukkha-lakkhaṇa) and non-self (anatta-lakkhaṇa), while developing insight, I then concentrated the mind. As it is said, "like a noble thoroughbred horse," just as a skilled charioteer easily drives a noble thoroughbred horse, so I easily concentrated my mind, making it steady with insight-concentration.

While developing insight in this way, desiring suitable weather (utu-sappāya), she entered the chamber. Taking a lamp to dispel the darkness, she entered the room, placed the lamp, and as soon as she sat on the couch, she pulled the wick with a door-pin to extinguish the lamp. At that very moment, due to obtaining suitable weather, her mind became concentrated, entered the path of insight, and struck the Path. Thereafter, through the sequence of the Paths, there was the total destruction of the taints (āsavas). Therefore, it was said: "Then, taking a lamp... the liberation of the mind occurred." There, "having looked at the bed" means seeing the bed by the light of the lamp.

"Suci" means a door-pin. "I pull out the wick" means I pull the wick towards the oil to extinguish the lamp. "Liberation" (vimokkha) means liberation from defilements. Since that liberation is, in the ultimate sense, the continuity of the mind, it is said "of the mind" (cetaso). Just as a lamp, which is fit to arise when conditions such as the wick and oil are present, in their absence...
121:
It is said to be extinguished because it does not arise again. In this way, when causes such as defilements exist, the mind that is liable to arise is said to be liberated by not arising again due to the absence of those causes. Therefore, it was said: "The liberation of the mind was like the extinguishing of a lamp."

## The Commentary on the Verses of Patacara Theri is finished.

## 11. The Commentary on the Verses of the Thirty Nuns

The verse beginning with "Musalāni gahetvāna" is the verse of the thirty nuns. These nuns, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulated wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. Having gradually accumulated the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra), and being urged by their own kamma during the time of this Buddha's appearance, they were born into various families. Upon reaching maturity, they heard the Dhamma in the presence of Patācārā Therī, gained faith, and ordained. Possessing pure virtue and fulfilling their major and minor duties, they lived on. Then, one day, Patācārā Therī gave them this advice:

"Young men, taking up pestles, pound the grain;
Supporting wives and children, young men find wealth."

"Do the Buddha's bidding, which having done, one does not regret;
Quickly washing your feet, sit down to one side;
Devoted to tranquility of mind (samatha), do the Buddha's bidding."

She spoke these two verses.

The summary of the meaning in those verses is: These beings, for the sake of livelihood, take up pestles and pound the grain of others; they perform the work of the mortar. By performing other such low work, they support wives and children and collect wealth as appropriate. However, that work of theirs is low, common, worldly, painful, and unbeneficial. Therefore, avoiding such mental proliferations (papañca) that increase defilements, do the Buddha's bidding—the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One known as the Three Trainings; fulfill it and bring it into existence within your own continuity. To show the reason why it should be done, she said: "which having done, one does not regret." Because by doing that teaching, now...
122:
...and in the future, one does not come to regret. Now, to show the preliminary tasks and the method of practice in doing that work, she said the words beginning with "Quickly washing your feet." In that context, because for one who has not washed their feet or face, the comfort of sitting and the attainment of suitable weather (utu-sappāya) do not occur; whereas for one who has washed their feet and face and sits to one side, both are obtained. Therefore, without missing this moment that has been gained, quickly wash your own feet and sit down in a secluded place. Binding your mind to any one of the thirty-eight objects of meditation that pleases the mind, and being devoted to tranquility of mind (samatha), with a concentrated mind, fulfill the Buddha’s teaching, advice, and instruction through the power of meditating on the Four Noble Truths.

Then, those bhikkhunīs, standing in the advice of that Therī, established insight (vipassanā) and performed the work of meditation. Due to the ripening of their knowledge and being endowed with the necessary causes, they reached Arahatship together with the Analytical Knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Reflecting on their own practice, they recited these verses along with the verses of advice:

"Having heard her words, the instruction of Patācārā,
Having washed our feet, we sat down to one side;
Devoted to tranquility of mind, we did the Buddha's bidding.

In the first watch of the night, we recollected past lives;
In the middle watch of the night, we purified the divine eye;
In the last watch of the night, we tore asunder the mass of darkness.

Rising, we paid homage to her feet; your instruction has been carried out.
Like the thirty gods surrounding Indra, the undefeated in battle, we shall live surrounding you.
We have attained the Three Knowledges and are taint-free."

They spoke these verses.

In those verses, "Having heard her words, the instruction of Patācārā" means that those thirty bhikkhunīs, having heard the words of advice from Patācārā Therī—which are called "instruction" (sāsana) because they suppress the enemies of defilements—accepted them respectfully with their heads.
123:
Those elder nuns rose from their seats and paid homage to her feet. Saying, "The instruction has been given to you," they respectfully accepted her teaching, took it to heart, and while staying in a suitable place, they practiced meditation. Having reached the peak of meditation, they rose from their seats to report the special attainment they had achieved, approached the Elder Nun, and said, "Great Elder Nun, we have followed the instruction just as you taught us," and paid homage at her feet with the five-point prostration. Just as the thirty gods of Tāvatiṃsa surround Sakka, the conqueror who is undefeated in the battle between gods and asuras, they said, "Great Elder Nun, we shall live with you at our head, as there is no other task to be done." Therefore, they made known their gratitude, saying, "We are possessors of the threefold knowledge and are free from taints." This was indeed their declaration of Arahantship. What has not been explained here in terms of meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously mentioned.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Thirty Elder Nuns is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nun Candā

"Formerly I was poor," and so forth are the verses of the Elder Nun Candā. She too had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome roots that serve as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirths. Having gradually gathered the requisites for liberation and with her wisdom matured, she was reborn in this Buddha's era in the house of an obscure Brahmin in a certain Brahmin village. From the time of her birth, that family's wealth and possessions declined. As she gradually reached the age of discretion, she lived in hardship. Then, the plague (ahivātaro-ga) broke out in that house, and because of that disease, all her relatives met with death and destruction. When her relatives were gone, being unable to make a living elsewhere, she wandered from house to house with a bowl in hand, sustaining herself with whatever alms-food she received. One day, she arrived at the place where the Elder Nun Paṭācārā was taking her meal. The bhikkhunīs, seeing her suffering and oppressed by hunger, were moved by compassion and looked after her with kind behavior, satisfying her with the pleasant food available there. Having gained faith in the conduct and virtue of those bhikkhunīs, she approached the Elder Nun, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Elder Nun preached the Dhamma to her. Having heard that Dhamma, she gained great faith in the Dispensation and, feeling a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the cycle of rebirths...
124:
(That woman) entered the Dispensation and was ordained. After ordaining, remaining within the instruction of the Elder Nun, she began practicing insight (vipassanā) and devoted herself to meditation. Due to her previous meritorious deeds and the maturity of her wisdom, she attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

"Formerly I was poor, a widow and childless; without friends or relatives, I did not even obtain food or clothing.

"Taking a bowl and a staff, begging from house to house, I wandered for seven years, scorched by cold and heat.

"Then I saw a bhikkhunī who had obtained food and drink; approaching her, I asked for ordination into the homeless life.

"Out of compassion, that Paṭācārā ordained me; then, having instructed me, she urged me toward the ultimate goal.

"I followed the words of that Elder Nun and carried out her instruction; the Noble Lady's advice was not in vain, I am now a possessor of the threefold knowledge and free from taints."

She uttered these verses by way of an inspired utterance.

In those verses, 'duggatā' means poor. 'Pure' means in the past, before ordaining. For from the time of ordination in this Dispensation, a person should not be called rich or poor in terms of possessions. However, in terms of virtues, this Elder Nun was indeed rich. Therefore, she said, "Formerly I was poor." 'Vidhavā' means a widow because of the absence of a 'dhava' (husband), meaning one whose husband has died. 'Aputtikā' means one without children. 'Vinā mittehi' means deprived of or without friends and kinsmen. 'Bhattacoḷassa nādhigaṃ' means she did not obtain a sufficiency of food and clothing. In reality, it means she obtained only enough food and clothing in the form of alms-food and scraps of rags. Therefore, she said, "Taking a bowl and a staff," and so forth.
125:
In that verse, 'patta' refers to a vessel made of clay. 'Daṇḍa' refers to a stick for driving away or warding off cows, dogs, and so forth. 'Kulā kulaṃ' means from house to house (wandering). 'Sītuṇhena ca ḍayhanti' means being oppressed by cold and heat because of the lack of a dwelling house.

The word 'bhikkhuniṃ' refers to the Elder Nun Paṭācārā. 'Puna' means later, or in the period after the seven years.

'Paramatthe' means the highest benefit, Nibbāna, and the practice leading to Nibbāna. 'Niyojayī' means she urged her by teaching and showing the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). The rest is as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Nun Candā is finished.
## The Commentary on the Five-Verse Collection (Pañcakanipāta) is finished.
126:
## 6. Chakkanipāta
## 1. Pañcasatāmattātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Book of the Sixes, the verses beginning with "Yassa maggaṃ na jānāsi" are the verses of about five hundred bhikkhunīs. These bhikkhunīs had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that is a support for the ending of the cycle (vivaṭṭūpanissaya-kusala) in various existences. Having gradually accumulated the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra), they were born into various families in this Buddha's era. When they reached maturity, their parents sent them to their husbands' homes. While living as householders and having children in various places, because they had performed similar karma in the past, all of them became mothers whose children died. Overwhelmed by grief for their sons, they approached Therī Paṭācārā, paid respects, and sat down; then they informed her of the cause of their sorrow. The Therī, wishing to dispel their grief, said:

"You do not know the path of the being, whether coming or going;
That being, come from where you know not, you weep for, saying 'my son'.

But if you knew his path, whether coming or going,
You would not grieve for him; for such is the nature of living beings.

Uninvited he came from there, without permission he departed from here;
Having come from somewhere and stayed for a few days,
He has gone from here by one path, and from there he will go by another.

Departed in human form, he will go on wandering in saṃsāra;
As he came, so he went; what is there to lament in that?"

With these four verses, she taught the Dhamma.

Hearing her Dhamma, they were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and ordained under the Therī. After ordaining, while they were developing insight (vipassanā), because the qualities that bring liberation to maturity (vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma) had ripened, they soon attained Arahatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then, those bhikkhunīs who had attained Arahatship reflected on their own practice and, by way of an inspired utterance (udāna), along with the verses of instruction beginning with "Yassa maggaṃ na jānāsi"—
127:
"Truly, he has pulled out the dart for me, so hard to see, lodged in my heart;
He has dispelled the grief for my son, for me who was overwhelmed by grief.

Today, with the dart pulled out, I am free from craving, extinguished;
I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, the Sage."

They each recited these verses individually.

In those verses, "You do not know the path of the being, whether coming or going" means you do not know the path of arrival of the being who came to this life, nor the path of departure of the being who went from here. This is said in reference to the occurrences of past and future existences. Why do you weep, identifying as "my son" a being whose path of arrival and departure is thus unknown, who has come from some destination (gati), and who is like a man met by chance on the road with whom one has no prior acquaintance at all? The meaning is that there is no reason to weep here, because it cannot be remedied and because there is nothing to be done for the son.

"But if you knew his path" means if you knew the path of arrival and the path of departure of that being whom you consider your son. "You would not grieve for him" means in that case you would not grieve for him. Why? Because such is the nature of living beings. Even in the present life, beings have the nature of being separated and parted from all that is dear and pleasing. Since one has no control over this, how much more so in the hereafter.

"Uninvited he came from there" means he came here from the other world without being invited by anyone. There is also the Pāḷi reading "āgato," and the meaning is the same. "Without permission he departed from here" means he went to the other world from this world without asking anyone's permission. "From somewhere" means from some destination such as hell, etc. "Nūna" is used in the sense of doubt. "Staying for a few days" means staying in this life for only a few days. "He has gone from here by another" means he has gone from this existence to another; he has reached another existence by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). "From there he will go by another" means from that existence too he will go to another; he will reach yet another existence.
128:
"Peto" refers to one who, after being born in various existences, has departed from that existence (died). "In the form of a human" is merely an illustration; it means being in the state of a human, an animal, and so forth. "Wandering" means wandering by way of repeated rebirths. "Just as he came, so he has gone" means that just as he arrived from an unknown destination without being invited, so he has gone to an unknown destination without asking for permission. The meaning is: what lamentation can there be in such a situation which is not under one's control and does not happen according to one's wishes? What is the use of lamenting? The rest is as previously explained.

In this context, the first four verses were spoken individually by the Elder Patācārā to dispel the grief of those five hundred women. It should be understood that those five hundred bhikkhunīs, who stood in her instruction, ordained, and attained distinction in the Dhamma, each spoke the remaining six verses.

"The five hundred Patācārās" refers to the five hundred bhikkhunīs who received the name "Patācārā" because they received instruction from the Elder Patācārā and understood the Dhamma taught by her.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Five Hundred Elder Bhikkhunīs is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Vāseṭṭhī

The verse beginning with "Puttasokenahaṃ aṭṭā" is that of the Elder Vāseṭṭhī. She also had performed meritorious deeds of service under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. Gradually fulfilling the requisites for liberation (vimokkhasambhāra), she wandered through the realms of devas and humans. In this Buddha's era, she was born into a noble family in Vesālī. When she came of age, her parents gave her in marriage to a young man of equal status. While living happily with her husband, she gave birth to a son. When the child was at the age of running and playing about, he passed away. Afflicted by grief for her son, she became deranged. Although her relatives and husband tried to treat her, she fled without their knowledge and wandered here and there until she reached the city of Mithilā. There, she saw the Blessed One walking in the middle of the street, tamed and guarded in his senses.
129:
...seeing the Buddha, who was like a great elephant (nāga) with restrained senses, she immediately regained her normal mind as her madness vanished through the Buddha's power. Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma in brief. Having heard that Dhamma, she was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) and requested ordination from the Teacher. By the Teacher's command, she ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Having performed the preliminary duties and established herself in insight meditation (vipassanā), she strove and exerted herself. Because her knowledge had matured, she attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered these verses by way of an inspired utterance (udāna):

"Afflicted by grief for my son, with a deranged mind and lost perception, naked and with dishevelled hair, I wandered here and there.
In the junctions and crossroads, on rubbish heaps, in cemeteries and on the main roads, I wandered for three years, overcome by hunger and thirst.
Then I saw the Sugata, the Tamer of the untamed, the Awakened One who is free from fear, near the city of Mithilā.
Having regained my normal mind and having paid homage to the Buddha, I sat down nearby. Out of compassion, Gotama taught me the Dhamma.
Having heard his Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness. Exerting myself in the Teacher's instruction, I realized the peaceful state (Nibbāna).
All sorrows are cut off, abandoned, and ended here. For I have fully understood the bases from which sorrows arise."

In those verses, "aṭṭā" means afflicted. There is also this variant reading: "aṭṭitā", meaning oppressed or tormented. "Khittacittā" means having a heart deranged by the madness of grief. "Visaññinī" means being without normal perception due to that very madness. "Naggā" means being naked because of the absence of shame and dread. "Pakiṇṇakesī" means having dishevelled hair. "Tena tena" means "I wandered from village to village, from city to city, and from street to street."

"Atha" means later, when the kamma that leads to madness was exhausted. "Sugataṃ" (the Well-Gone One) is so called because of his excellent going, because he has gone to a beautiful place, because he speaks rightly, and because he has gone rightly.
130:
I saw the Blessed One, the Sugata (the Well-Spoken One). "Mithilaṃ patī" means facing Mithilā, traveling towards the city of Mithilā.

"Sacittaṃ paṭiladdhānā" means having abandoned madness through the power of the Buddha and regained one's normal mind.

"Yuñjantī satthuvacane" means making an effort in the teaching of the Fully Enlightened One, constantly practicing meditation. "Sacchākāsiṃ padaṃ sivaṃ" means I have realized the peaceful state, which is Nibbāna, secure and unassailed by the four yokes (yogas).

"Etadantikā" means these sorrows are called "ending here" because this fruition of Arahantship I have now attained is the end and conclusion of those sorrows. It means that there is no longer any arising of those sorrows. "Yato sokāna sambhavo" means the five aggregates of clinging, which are the source of the arising of sorrows characterized by internal burning and the foundation of those sorrows, have been fully understood through the three types of full understanding: full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding as abandonment (pahāna-pariññā). Therefore, it is connected that sorrows end in this fruition of Arahantship.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vāseṭṭhī is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khemā

The verse beginning with "Daharā tvaṃ rūpavatī" is the verse of the Elder Khemā. In the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, she was a servant girl in the city of Haṃsavatī, living in dependence on others. While making a living by performing services for others, one day she saw Elder Sujāta, the chief disciple of the Blessed One Padumuttara, walking for alms and offered him three cakes. On that very day, she cut off her hair (sold it) and gave an offering to the Elder, making a wish: "In the future, may I become a female disciple of great wisdom under a Buddha." Being diligent in meritorious deeds throughout her life, she wandered through the realms of gods and humans, successively becoming the chief queen of various kings of the gods in the six celestial realms. In the human world as well, she many times became the chief queen of universal monarchs and regional kings, enjoying great wealth and happiness. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, she was born in the human world, and upon reaching maturity, she heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, was moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and went forth as a nun...
131:
For ten thousand years, she practiced the holy life, became a learned Dhamma teacher, and performed meritorious deeds conducive to wisdom by preaching the Dhamma to many people. After passing away from there, she wandered only in happy realms. In this very eon, during the times of the Blessed One Kakusandha and the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, she was born into wealthy families. Upon reaching maturity, she built and donated a large monastery (saṅghārāma), offering it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha.

In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, she was the eldest daughter of King Kiki of Kāsi, a princess named Samaṇī. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, she was moved by spiritual urgency and, while remaining in the household life, practiced the holy life of celibacy for twenty thousand years. Together with her sisters, she built a delightful monastery building (pariveṇa) and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Thus, having performed noble meritorious deeds in various lives and wandering only in happy realms, she was born into the royal family in the city of Sākala in the kingdom of Madda during the time of this Buddha's appearance. She was named Khemā, and her skin was golden like the color of gold. When she reached maturity, she went to the palace of King Bimbisāra. While the Blessed One was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery, she was so infatuated with her own beauty that she did not go to see the Blessed One, having heard that "the Blessed One points out the faults of physical beauty."

The King caused people to praise the pleasantness of the Veḷuvana Monastery, thereby creating a desire in the Queen to visit the monastery. Then the Queen asked the King for permission, saying, "I will go and see the monastery." The King said, "You must not return from the monastery without seeing the Blessed One," and gave instructions to his men: "Even by force, make the Queen see the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." The Queen went to the monastery, spent about half a day there, and then prepared to leave without seeing the Blessed One. Then the King's men, despite her reluctance, led her to the presence of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, seeing her coming, used his psychic power to create a woman resembling a celestial nymph, holding a palm-leaf fan and fanning him. When Queen Khemā saw that woman, she thought, "Such women, resembling celestial nymphs, stay near the Blessed One! I am not even worthy to be their servant. I have been ruined by following the whims of my defiled mind without reason." Thinking thus, she stood staring only at that woman. While she was watching, through the power of the Blessed One's determination, that woman passed through her youth, passed through middle age, and reached old age. With broken teeth, grey hair, and wrinkled skin, she collapsed along with the palm-leaf fan.
132:
At that time, the Elder Nun Khemā, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, reflected thus: "Even a body of such a nature has come to such destruction; my body, too, will surely have such a fate." Then, the Blessed One, knowing her thoughts, spoke this verse:

"Those who are infatuated with passion follow the stream (of craving), just as a spider follows the web it has made itself. Having cut even this (bond), the wise wander forth, free from longing, having abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires."

It is stated in the Commentaries that at the end of the verse, she attained Arahantship along with the Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā). However, in the Apadāna, it is stated: "Having heard this verse, she was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala); then, having asked the King for permission, she went forth as a nun and attained Arahantship." That Apadāna Pali is as follows:

"A Conqueror named Padumuttara, the Visionary in all things, the Leader of the world, arose a hundred thousand aeons ago.

At that time, I was born in a wealthy merchant's family in the city of Haṃsāvatī; I was endowed with great happiness and the radiance of various jewels.

Approaching that Great Hero, I heard the Dhamma teaching; thereafter, with faith born in me, I went to the Conqueror for refuge.

Having asked my parents for permission, I invited the Leader (Vināyaka) and offered food for seven days to Him along with His disciples.

When the seven days had passed, the Charioteer of Men (Narāsārathi) placed a nun who was foremost in great wisdom in the position of Etadagga.

Having heard that and being filled with joy, I performed further meritorious deeds for that Great Sage (Mahesi) and, bowing down, made an aspiration for that position.

Then the Conqueror said to me: 'May your aspiration be fulfilled; the meritorious deed you have performed for Me and the Saṅgha has immeasurable fruit.

A hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by lineage, born of the Okkāka clan, will arise in the world.'"
133:
"'She will be a disciple named Khemā, an heir to that Blessed One's Dhamma, a spiritual daughter created by the Dhamma, who will attain the foremost position (Etadagga).'

Due to that well-performed deed, and because of my intention and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Passing away from there, I went to the Yāma heaven; from there I went to Tusita; from there to Nimmānarati, and then to the city of Vasavatti.

Wherever I was reborn, by the power of that merit, I became the Chief Queen of the kings in those various places.

Passing away from there and returning to the human realm, I became the Chief Queen of Universal Monarchs and regional kings.

Experiencing prosperity among gods and humans, being happy in all places, I wandered through Saṃsāra for many aeons.

Ninety-one aeons ago, the Buddha Vipassī, the Leader of the World, of beautiful appearance and the Seer of all things, arose.

Approaching that Leader of the World, the Charioteer of Men, and hearing the Dhamma he preached, I renounced the world and went forth into homelessness.

For ten thousand years, I practiced the holy life (Brahmacariya) in the Dispensation of that Hero; being devoted to practice, I became well-versed (Bahussuta).

I was skilled in the Law of Cause and Effect (Paṭiccasamuppāda), confident in the Four Noble Truths, an eloquent speaker of subtle Dhamma, and a follower of the Teacher's Dispensation.

Passing away from there, I was reborn in the Tusita heaven, possessed of great fame. There, I surpassed other deities by the fruit of my holy life.

Wherever I was reborn, I was possessed of great wealth, great riches, wisdom, virtue, and a well-disciplined retinue.

Due to that merit and my exertion in the Buddha's Dispensation, all forms of prosperity that are pleasing to the heart were easily obtained by me."
134:
"'Whoever was my husband, wherever I went, no one ever despised me because of the power of my virtuous conduct.'

In this very Bhadda Kappa (Auspicious Aeon), the Buddha named Koṇāgamana, of great fame and the best of speakers, arose.

At that time, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there were three of us: Dhanañjānī, Sumedhā, and myself, born into very wealthy families.

In the past, we were companions in giving and donated a monastery garden (Saṅghārāma) to the Saṅgha; we also built a residence (Vihāra) dedicated to the Saṅgha.

Passing away from there, we all reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven; likewise, among humans, we reached the pinnacle of fame and retinue.

In this very aeon, the Buddha named Kassapa by lineage, of great fame and the best of speakers, arose.

At that time, in the noble city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Kikī, who was an attendant to the Great Sage.

I was the eldest daughter of that king, known as Samaṇī; having heard the Dhamma of the Supreme Conqueror, I delighted in renunciation.

Our father did not permit us to go forth; at that time, we practiced diligently for twenty thousand years while still in the household life.

We seven daughters, princesses who grew up in comfort, delighted in serving the Buddha and joyfully practiced the maidenly holy life (Komāribrahmacariya).

They were Samaṇī, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāyikā.

I became Uppalavaṇṇā, (the others became) Paṭācārā, Kuṇḍalā, Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā was the seventh.

Once, that Sun of Men (the Buddha) preached the wonderful Dhamma; having heard that Mahānidāna Sutta, I mastered it."
135:
Through those well-performed deeds, and through my intentions and aspirations, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In this, my final existence, I was born in the noble city of Sākala as the daughter of King Madda. I was pleasing, beloved, and dear, a speaker of pleasant words.

At the very moment of my birth, there was peace (khema) in that city. Because of that quality, the name 'Khemā' was given to me appropriately.

When I reached maturity and was endowed with beauty and grace, my father presented me to King Bimbisāra.

I became very dear to the king and delighted in my own beauty. Having heard that the Buddha spoke of the defects of form, I did not approach the Great Compassionate One.

Then King Bimbisāra, with the intention of favoring me, praised the virtues of the Veḷuvana monastery and had singers sing to me:

'Whoever has not seen the delightful Veḷuvana, the dwelling of the Sugata, we think that person has not seen the Nandana Grove.'

'Whoever has seen Veḷuvana, which delights the hearts of men, has truly seen the Nandana Grove that delights the Lord of Devas.'

'The devas, leaving the Nandana Grove and descending to the world of men, are filled with wonder and are never satiated upon seeing the delightful Veḷuvana.'

'Who could fully describe the collection of virtues of that forest, which arose through the king's merit and is adorned by the Buddha's merit?'

Hearing of the perfection of that forest, which was pleasing to my ears, I then informed the king of my desire to see that garden.

Then the lord of the earth sent me, who was eager to see it, to that garden with a great retinue.

'Go and see the forest, O Mahābhogā, which is a nectar for the eyes, always shining with glory and illuminated by the radiance of the Sugata,' he said.
136:
When the Sage entered the noble city of Giribbaja for alms, at that very time, I approached to see the forest.

At that time, the blossoming forest was filled with the humming of various bees, accompanied by the songs of cuckoos, and graced by the dancing of flocks of peacocks.

It was quiet, not crowded with people, adorned with various walkways, filled with small huts and pavilions, and made beautiful by noble practitioners (yogis).

As I wandered about, I thought, "My eyes have truly found their purpose." In that forest, I saw a young monk engaged in practice and thought:

"In such a delightful forest, this monk stands in the prime of youth. Endowed with a pleasing form, he stands like the summer season.

Sitting at the foot of a tree, shaven-headed and clad in the double robe (saṅghāṭi), this monk is indeed absorbed in jhāna, having abandoned the delight born of the senses.

Should not one first enjoy sensual pleasures as a householder as one pleases, and only later, when old, practice this excellent Dhamma?"

Knowing it was quiet, I approached the Gandhakuti, the dwelling of the Victor (Jina), and saw the Buddha, like the rising sun.

Seeing the Buddha sitting comfortably alone, being fanned by a noble woman, I thought: "This noble one among men is not one of meager means."

That maiden had a complexion like gold, a face and eyes like lotuses, lips red like the bimba fruit, and teeth white like jasmine buds; she was a nectar for the mind and eyes.

She had earrings like golden swings, breasts like lotus buds, a waist slender like the middle of an altar, beautiful hips, and thighs like banana trunks, adorned with lovely ornaments.

She wore a red upper garment and a smooth blue lower garment, endowed with a beauty one could never tire of looking at and a smiling demeanor.

Seeing her, I thought: "Oh, how beautiful this woman is! I have never seen anyone like her with these eyes of mine."
137:
Then that woman (created by the Buddha) became oppressed by old age; her complexion faded, her face became distorted, her teeth broke, her hair turned white, saliva trickled out, and her mouth became foul.

Her ears were shriveled, her eyes were white, her breasts were sagging and unsightly, her entire body was covered in wrinkles, and her frame was covered in protruding veins.

With a bent body, using a staff as a second companion (leaning on a staff), her ribs showing, emaciated, trembling, falling down, she sighed again and again.

Then a sense of urgency (saṃvega) arose in me, wonderful and hair-raising: "Woe to this foul form, in which fools delight!"

Then the Great Compassionate One, the Sugata, seeing my mind struck with urgency, spoke these verses with a joyful heart:

"Khemā, look at this assembly of the body—ailing, impure, putrid, trickling from above and trickling from below, which is so greatly delighted in by fools.

Develop a mind that is concentrated and one-pointed on the foulness (asubha). Let there be mindfulness directed to the body; may you have much weariness (nibbidā) towards it.

As this (body) is, so is that (illusion); as that is, so is this. Dispel the desire (chanda) for the body, both internally and externally.

Develop the signless (animitta) and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit (mānānusaya). Then, through the full understanding of conceit, you shall live in peace."

"Those obsessed with passion follow the stream of craving, like a spider following the web it has made itself. Having cut even this, the wise wander forth, abandoning sensual pleasure without longing."

Then, knowing that my mind was ready, the Charioteer of Men (the Buddha) taught me the Mahānidāna Sutta for the removal of my defilements.

Hearing that excellent Sutta, I remembered my former perceptions. Standing right there, I, being peaceful, purified the Dhamma-eye.

Falling at the feet of the Great Sage at that very moment, I spoke these words to confess my fault.
138:
Homage to You, the All-Seer; homage to You, the Mine of Compassion;
Homage to You, who have crossed the ocean of Saṃsāra; homage to You, the Giver of the Deathless.

Beings who have fallen into the thicket of wrong views, and are deluded by sensual lust,
Having been disciplined by Your excellent means, now delight in the Vinaya.

Because of not seeing such Great Sages who seek the noble practice,
Beings experience great suffering in the ocean of Saṃsāra.

When I did not see You, the Refuge of the world, the One without defilements, who has reached the end of enmity,
Even though You were near, I confess that fault.

Suspecting You, the Bringer of great benefit and Giver of the Excellent [Nibbāna], to be harmful,
I did not approach You, being delighted only in my physical form; I confess that fault.

Then the Victorious One (Jina), the Great Compassionate One of sweet voice,
Said, 'Stand still, Khemā,' while sprinkling me with the Deathless Dhamma.

Then, having paid homage with my head and circumambulated Him,
I went to the King and spoke these words:

'O King, subduer of enemies, this means you devised is truly excellent.
I, who desired to see the forest, have seen the Sage who is extinguished through Nibbāna.'

'O Great King, if it pleases you, I shall go forth as a nun in the Dispensation of such a Buddha,
For I have become weary of physical form due to the words of the Sage.'

Then that Lord of the Earth, with joined palms, said:
'I permit you, lady; may your going forth be successful.'

Having gone forth, when half a month had passed,
Seeing the lighting and breaking of a lamp, with a stirred mind,

I became weary of all conditioned things (saṅkhāra). Being skilled in Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda),
I crossed the four floods and attained Arahatship.

I have mastery over psychic powers, the divine ear element,
And I am also a master of the knowledge of others' minds.
139:
I know my past lives; the divine eye is purified;
All taints (āsavas) are destroyed; now there is no more rebirth.

In the meaning (attha), the law (dhamma), the language (nirutti), and the eloquence (paṭibhāna),
My perfectly pure knowledge has arisen in the Buddha's Dispensation.

I am skilled in the purifications (visuddhi), confident in the Kathāvatthu,
And I know the methods of Abhidhamma, having reached mastery in the Dispensation.

Then at Toraṇavatthu, when questioned on subtle problems by the King, the Lord of Kosala,
I answered them exactly as they were.

Then that King approached the Happy One (Sugata) and questioned Him;
The Buddha answered in the same way as I had answered.

The Victorious One, pleased with that quality, appointed me to the foremost position:
'Monks, among my nun disciples of great wisdom, this Khemā is the foremost,' said the Best of Men.

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching is done. (Ap. Therī 2.2.289-383)

Having attained Arahatship, while this Elder Nun was dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, although other taints-destroyed Elder Nuns also possessed great wisdom, her state of 'Great Wisdom' (Mahāpaññā) became prominent due to the merit (adhikāra) she had performed in the past. Thus, while the Blessed One was seated in the midst of the Noble Assembly at the Jetavana Monastery, appointing the nuns to various positions in order, He placed her in the foremost rank of those with great wisdom, saying: 'Monks, among my nun disciples of great wisdom, Khemā is the foremost.' (A. Ni. 1.235-236). One day, while that Elder Nun Khemā was sitting under a certain tree for the day-abiding (divāvihāra), Mara the Evil One approached her in the form of a youth and tempted her with sensual pleasures, saying:

'You are young and beautiful, and I too am a young youth.
Come, Khemā, let us delight in the music of the fivefold instruments.'

The meaning of this verse is: Khemā, you have reached the prime of youth and are endowed with beauty; I too am a young youth. Therefore, let us not waste our youth; come, let us delight and play in sensual pleasures while the fivefold instruments are being played.
140:
Hearing those words, the Elder Khemā, wishing to reveal her state of detachment from sensual pleasures and all phenomena, the nature of Māra, her strong lack of confidence in beings clinging to the self, and the completion of her task, spoke these verses:

"With this foul body, diseased and fragile, I am weary and ashamed. Sensual craving has been uprooted.

Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes; the five aggregates are like a chopping block. What you call delight in sensual pleasures is now only non-delight for me.

Delight in all existences has been destroyed. The mass of darkness (ignorance) has been shattered. Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated; O Ender, you are vanquished.

Fools, worshiping the stars and tending the fire in the forest, not knowing the truth as it really is, thought it was purity.

But I, worshiping the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme Man, have been freed from all suffering, following the instruction of the Teacher."

In those verses, "tending the fire in the forest" means performing fire sacrifice in the forest of asceticism. "Not knowing the truth as it really is" means not discerning the nature of phenomena as they truly are. The remaining words are clear as explained previously.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Khemā is finished.

## 4. The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sujātā

The verse beginning with "Alaṅkatā suvasanā" is that of the Elder Sujātā. She, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome roots that serve as a powerful support for Nibbāna in various existences. Having fulfilled the requisites for liberation in due course, she was born into a merchant family in the city of Sāketa during the time of this Buddha. When she reached the proper age, her parents married her to a merchant's son of equal status, and she went to her husband's home. While living happily with her husband in that house, one day she went to a garden, enjoyed a festival of the stars, and...
141:
...while returning to the city with her attendants, she saw the Teacher in the Añjana Wood. With a confident mind, she approached, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Teacher taught her the gradual discourse and, knowing the readiness of her mind, revealed the exalted Dhamma teaching (the Four Noble Truths).

At the end of the teaching, because of her past merits and the maturity of her knowledge, and also due to the Teacher's graceful manner of teaching, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) while still sitting there. Then, having paid homage to the Teacher, she returned home, obtained permission from her husband and parents, and by the Teacher's command, went to the nunnery and was ordained among the bhikkhunīs. After ordaining, reflecting on her own practice, she uttered these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

"Adorned and well-dressed, wearing garlands and smeared with sandalwood, covered with all kinds of ornaments, and surrounded by a group of maidservants,

Taking plenty of food, drink, and snacks, I left home and went to the garden.

Having enjoyed and played there, while returning to my own home, I entered the Añjana Wood monastery in Sāketa to see it.

Seeing the Light of the World, I paid homage and sat nearby. He, the Visionary, taught me the Dhamma out of compassion.

Hearing the Truth of the Great Sage, I pierced through to the Truth. Right there, I touched the stainless Dhamma, the Deathless state (Nibbāna).
