Then, having understood the True Dhamma, I went forth into homelessness. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching is not in vain."

In those verses, 'alaṅkatā' means adorned. To show the manner of that adornment, it is said: 'suvasanā mālinī candanokkhitā'. There, 'mālinī' means one wearing garlands. 'Candanakkhitā' means smeared with sandalwood. 'Sabbābharaṇasañchannā' means one whose body is covered and decorated with all kinds of ornaments such as jewelry for the hands and so on.
142:
“Taking food and drink, snacks and meals in no small amount” means taking a large quantity of food such as Sāli rice, drinks such as mango juice, snacks such as cakes, and the remaining types of nutriment called meals. “I went to the garden” means going to the garden for the purpose of playing at a festival. It means having brought food and drink there, she enjoyed herself and played along with her attendants.

“In Sāketa, the Añjana Wood” means she entered the Añjanavana Monastery near the city of Sāketa.

“The Light of the World” refers to the Buddha, who is like a lamp for the world through the light of his knowledge.

“I touched” means I experienced or attained. The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sujātā is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Anopamā

The verse beginning with “In a high-born family” is that of the Elder Anopamā. This elder had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome roots that serve as a strong support for the cessation of suffering in various lives. Having gradually developed the qualities that bring liberation to maturity, she was born in this Buddha’s era as the daughter of a treasurer named Majjha in the city of Sāketa. Because of her perfection of form, she was named “Anopamā” (Incomparable).

When she reached the proper age, many sons of treasurers, royal ministers, and kings sent messengers to her father, saying, “Give your daughter Anopamā to me; I will give you this much and that much wealth.” When she heard those words, being one who possessed the necessary supporting conditions, she thought, “Household life is of no use to me.” She went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma, and as her knowledge matured, she practiced insight meditation according to the teaching. Through the sequence of the paths, she was established in the third fruit (Anāgāmi).

She requested ordination from the Teacher. By the Teacher’s command, she went to the nunnery and was ordained among the bhikkhunīs. On the seventh day, she realized Arahantship. Reviewing her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance:

“I was born in a high-born family, with much wealth and great riches. Endowed with beauty and form, I am the own daughter of the treasurer Majjha.”
143:
“Desired by princes, longed for by sons of treasurers, they sent messengers to my father, saying: ‘Give Anopamā to me.’

‘Whatever weight your daughter Anopamā is worth, I will give eight times that amount in gold and jewels.’

Then I, having seen the Fully Enlightened One, the Supreme, the Eldest in the World, having paid homage to his feet, sat down to one side.

That Gotama, the Blessed One, out of compassion, taught me the Dhamma. While sitting right there on that seat, I attained the third fruit (Anāgāmi-phala).

Then, having cut off my hair, I went forth from the home life into homelessness. Today is the seventh night for me since craving was completely destroyed.” She spoke these verses.

In those words, “In a high-born family” means in a very noble Vessa (Vaishya) family. “With much wealth” means having many possessions such as ornaments. “With great riches” means it should be connected as: “I was born into a family with great wealth amounting to forty crores of buried treasure.” “Endowed with beauty and form” means being endowed with both complexion and physical appearance, possessing a smooth and radiant skin, and being endowed with bodily parts enhanced by clothes and ornaments. “Daughter of the treasurer Majjha” means the biological daughter of the treasurer named Majjha.

“Desired by princes” means greatly desired by royal princes, thinking, “How can we obtain her?” “Longed for by sons of treasurers” means similarly greatly desired and hoped for by sons of treasurers. “Give Anopamā to me” means princes and others sent messengers to her father saying, “Give Anopamā to me, give her to me.”

“Whatever weight she is worth” means it should be connected as: messengers were sent to the father saying, “Whatever the value of your daughter Anopamā is,” as determined by those skilled in signs (physiognomists), “I will give eight times that wealth.” The rest is as explained before.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Anopamā is finished.
144:
## 6. Commentary on the Verses of Mahāpajāpatigotamī Therī

The verse beginning with “Buddha vīra namo tyatthu” is that of Mahāpajāpatigotamī. It is said that during the time of Padumuttara Buddha, she was born into a noble family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Upon reaching maturity, while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those of long standing (rattaññū). She performed a great act of merit and aspired for that very position. Throughout her life, she performed meritorious deeds such as giving (dāna) and wandered through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand aeons. In the interval between Kassapa Buddha and our Buddha, during a Buddhasuñña period (an era without a Buddha) in the world, she was born in the city of Bārāṇasī as the leader of five hundred maidservants.

At that time, during the season for entering the rains-retreat (vassa), she saw five Paccekabuddhas descending from the Nandamūlaka cave to Isipatana. After they had wandered for alms in the city and returned to Isipatana, she found them seeking manual laborers to build small huts for the rains-retreat. She encouraged those maidservants and their husbands to build five small huts complete with walkways (caṅkama) and other amenities. Having prepared couches, stools, drinking water, and water for general use, she invited the Paccekabuddhas to reside there for the three months of the retreat and established a rotation for offering alms-food. If anyone was unable to offer alms on their designated day, she would personally provide it from her own house. Having thus cared for them for three months, when the time for the Pavāraṇā ceremony arrived, she had each maidservant offer one cloth, resulting in five hundred cloths. She exchanged those cloths to make triple robes (ticīvara) for the five Paccekabuddhas and offered them. While they were watching, the Paccekabuddhas departed through the air to Mount Gandhamādana.

All of them performed meritorious deeds throughout their lives and were reborn in the deva realm. Their leader, after passing away from there, was reborn in the house of a head weaver in a weavers' village not far from Bārāṇasī. Upon reaching maturity, she saw five hundred Paccekabuddhas, who were the sons of Padumavatī. Filled with great devotion and affection, she paid homage to all of them and offered alms-food. After finishing their meal, those Paccekabuddhas also departed for Mount Gandhamādana. She too performed meritorious deeds throughout her life and wandered through the realms of devas and humans. Before the appearance of our Teacher, she took conception in the house of Mahāsuppabuddha in the city of Devadaha. Because she came from the Gotama clan, her name was simply Gotamī; she was the younger sister of Mahāmāyā Devī. The physiognomists also predicted, “The sons residing in the wombs of both these women...”
145:
“...will become Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti).” When they reached maturity, King Suddhodana performed the two auspicious marriage ceremonies and brought them to his palace.

Later, when our Teacher had appeared and was favoring teachable beings (veneyya) in various places with the noble Dhamma-wheel discourse he had set in motion, and while he was residing in the Kūṭāgārasālā monastery near the city of Vesālī, King Suddhodana realized the fruit of Arahatship under the white parasol and attained Parinibbāna. At that time, Mahāpajāpatigotamī, desiring to ordain, requested the Teacher for ordination once but did not receive it. On the second occasion, she had her hair cut, donned saffron-dyed robes, and at the conclusion of the teaching of the Kalahavivāda Sutta, she departed from the palace. Together with the attendants (wives) of the five hundred Sakyan princes who had already ordained, she went to Vesālī. She had the Venerable Ānanda request the Teacher on her behalf and obtained the status of a nun and the higher ordination (upasampadā) by accepting the Eight Heavy Rules (garudhamma). All the other women also received the higher ordination at the same time. This is a summary here; the detailed account of this story appears in the Pāḷi Canon itself.

Having thus obtained the higher ordination, Mahāpajāpatigotamī approached the Teacher, paid homage, and stood in a suitable place. Then the Teacher taught her the Dhamma. Taking a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Teacher and applying herself to meditation, she soon attained Arahatship together with the direct knowledges (abhiññā) and analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The remaining five hundred bhikkhunīs also became Arahats with the six direct knowledges at the conclusion of the Nandakovāda Sutta. Then, one day, while the Teacher was seated in the midst of the assembly of noble ones at the Jetavana Monastery, as he was appointing the bhikkhunīs to various positions, he placed Mahāpajāpatigotamī in the foremost position (etadagga) among the bhikkhunīs of long standing (rattaññū). While spending her time in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, and remaining established in gratitude, she one day declared her attainment of Arahatship by way of illustrating the Teacher’s help, preceded by praise of the Teacher’s virtues:

“O Heroic Buddha, homage to You, the Most Excellent of all beings, who has delivered me and many other people from suffering.

All suffering is fully understood; craving, the cause, is dried up; the Eightfold Path has been developed; and Cessation (Nibbāna) has been realized by me.”
146:
“Because I did not know the truth, I have been a mother, a son, a father, a brother, and a grandmother. I have wandered through the endless cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra) without rest.

“I have seen that Blessed One; this is my last body. The cycle of rebirth is exhausted; now there is no further becoming.

“Behold the disciples who are energetic, resolute, always firm in effort, and united. This is the worship of the Buddhas.

“For the benefit of many, Māyā gave birth to Gotama. He dispelled the mass of suffering for beings afflicted by disease, old age, and death.” Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, 'Buddhavīra' (Hero of the Buddhas) means the courageous one among the Buddhas who have realized the Four Truths. All Buddhas are called heroes (vīra) because they have achieved victory through supreme energy, or because they are Buddhas who have realized the Four Truths, or because they have accomplished the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna). The Blessed One, in particular, deserves to be called a hero (vīra) because he fulfilled the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramī), undertook the fourfold energy, and accomplished the extraordinary task of the fourfold right effort. Furthermore, he is called a hero because he firmly established that energy in the mental continuities of those to be tamed.

'Namo tyatthu' means 'May there be homage to you.' 'Sabbasattānamuttamā' means the Blessed One is supreme among beings, such as those without feet, through virtues like morality (sīla). To show a portion of the Teacher's helpful qualities, she said, “The Blessed One who liberated me from suffering, and also many other people,” and wishing to clarify her own liberation from suffering, she spoke the verse beginning with “Sabbadukkha” (All suffering).

Again, to show a portion of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) from which she was liberated, she spoke the verse beginning with “Mātā putto” (Mother, son). In that verse, 'yathābhiccamajānanti' means not knowing the truth as it is, such as the cause of existence (samudaya-sacca). 'Saṃsariṃhaṃ anibbisanti' means wandering through successive births without finding a footing or support in the ocean of saṃsāra. It means that in one life she was the mother of this person, in another life she was the son of that same person, and in other lives she was the father or brother.
147:
By the verse “I have seen,” she also clarifies her own state of being liberated from suffering. In that verse, “I have seen that Blessed One” means that I have seen the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, clearly with the eye of wisdom (ñāṇacakkhu), which is the seeing of the supramundane Dhamma realized by oneself. For he who sees the Dhamma, sees the Blessed One. As it is said (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya): “Vakkali, he who sees the Dhamma sees me,” and so forth.

“Energetic” (āraddhavīriye) means those with upheld energy. “Resolute” (pahitattte) means those whose minds are directed toward Nibbāna. “Always firm in effort” (niccaṃ daḷhaparakkame) means those who have steadfast effort at all times for the attainment of what has not yet been attained and for the increase of what has been attained. “United” (samagge) means those who are united by the commonality of virtue (sīla) and view (diṭṭhi). Because they arose at the end of hearing the Teacher’s instruction, they are called disciples (sāvake); she sees them as they truly are, thinking, “These are those established in the Path, these are those established in the Fruition.” “This is the worship of the Buddhas” means that the personal realization of the supramundane Dhamma—which is the Dhamma-body of the Teacher and the noble state of the noble disciples—is the true worship of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas and the Disciple-Buddhas (Arahants), characterized by bowing to their virtues as they truly are.

By the final verse, “For the benefit of many,” she also clarifies the Teacher’s great helpfulness to the world. What is not specifically analyzed here in terms of meaning is easily understood.

Then, at one time, while the Teacher was staying in the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) near Vesālī, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was herself staying in the Bhikkhunī monastery in Vesālī. In the morning, after wandering for alms in Vesālī and eating her meal, she spent the designated time of her day-rest in the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Emerging from the attainment of fruition, she reflected on her own practice and, filled with joy, she turned her attention to her life-span (āyu-saṅkhāra). Knowing that her life-span was exhausted, she thought: “What if I go to the monastery, ask the Blessed One's permission, and after taking leave of the venerable elders who are inspiring to the mind and all my fellow practitioners, I return here and attain Parinibbāna?” Just as the elder nun thought this, the five hundred bhikkhunīs who were her followers had the same thought. Therefore, it is said in the Apadāna:

“Once the Light of the World, the Charioteer of Men, was staying in the Gabled Hall in the Great Wood near Vesālī.”
148:
At that time, the bhikkhunī Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the stepmother of the Victorious Buddha, resided in the bhikkhunīs' quarters in that beautiful city of Vesālī.

While she was in seclusion with five hundred bhikkhunīs who were liberated from defilements, this thought arose in her:

"I do not wish to see the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, nor that of the pair of chief disciples, nor of the Venerables Rāhula, Ānanda, and Nanda.

Before the Parinibbāna of the Buddha, the pair of chief disciples, and the Venerables Mahākassapa, Nanda, Ānanda, and Rāhula, it would be well if I, having relinquished the life-force in advance and with the permission of the Lord of the World, the Great Sage, were to go to Nibbāna."

Similarly, such a thought arose in the five hundred bhikkhunīs, starting with Khemā.

Then there was an earthquake, and the celestial drums of the devas resounded. The deities residing in the monastery were oppressed by grief.

Those deities, lamenting most piteously, shed tears. Those bhikkhunīs, who were her companions, approached Gotamī.

Bowing their heads at her feet, they spoke these words: "Lady, while we were in seclusion, we were drenched with tears there.

This earth has shaken and trembled, the celestial drums have resounded, and the sound of wailing is heard. Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, for what reason is this?"

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī told them all that she had thought. Those bhikkhunīs also told her all that they had thought.

"Lady, if you wish to go to the supreme, peaceful Nibbāna, O one of good vows, we all shall also attain Parinibbāna with the Buddha's permission.

We went forth together from the household life and from existence; we shall go together to the supreme state of Nibbāna."
149:
Saying, "What shall I say to these bhikkhunīs who are going to Nibbāna?" Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī then departed from the bhikkhunīs' residence with all of them.

"May the deities residing in the bhikkhunīs' residence forgive me; this is my final sight of the bhikkhunīs' residence."

"I shall go to the Unconditioned Nibbāna, where there is no old age or death, no meeting with the unpleasant, and no separation from the beloved."

Hearing those words, the daughters of the Buddha (the nuns) who were not yet free from passion, oppressed by grief, lamented: "Alas, how little is our merit!"

"This bhikkhunīs' residence has become empty without those theras; like stars at dawn, the daughters of the Victor (the theras) are no longer seen."

As five hundred rivers go to the ocean with the Ganges, so Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī went to Nibbāna with her retinue of five hundred theras.

Seeing the theras walking along the road, the faithful laywomen came out of their houses, bowed at their feet, and spoke these words:

"O lady of great wealth, please have compassion and do not leave us helpless; it is not yet fitting for you to attain Nibbāna." Thus those laywomen lamented, their desired welfare being lost.

To dispel their grief, she spoke these sweet words: "Dear daughters, there is no use in weeping; today is a time for you to rejoice."

"I have fully understood the Truth of Suffering (Dukkha), I have abandoned the Truth of the Cause (Samudaya), I have realized the Truth of Cessation (Nirodha), and I have well-developed the Truth of the Path (Magga)."

"I have served the Teacher, the Buddha; I have carried out the Buddha's teaching; I have laid down the heavy burden; the craving that leads to new existence has been uprooted."

"The purpose for which I went forth from home to homelessness—that purpose, the destruction of all fetters (Arahatship), has been attained by me."

"While the Buddha and his True Dhamma remain complete, it is time for me to attain Nibbāna. Dear daughters, do not grieve for me."
150:
"Koṇḍañña, Ānanda, Nanda, and others, as well as the Victorious Rāhula, remain. The Saṅgha is happy and united. The heretics have been defeated."

"The fame of the descendant of the Okkāka dynasty, the crusher of Māra, is high. Dear daughters, is it not now the time for my Nibbāna?"

"The aspiration I have held since long ago is fulfilled today. This is the time to beat the drum of joy. Dear daughters, why are you shedding tears?"

"If you have compassion for me, and if you have gratitude, all of you should exert firm effort for the endurance of the True Dhamma."

"At my request, the Fully Enlightened One allowed the going forth for women. Therefore, just as I rejoice, you too should abide in that Dispensation."

Having thus exhorted them, surrounded by the bhikkhunīs, she approached the Buddha, paid homage, and spoke these words:

"O Blessed One, I am your mother, and you, O Hero, are my father. O Lord, giver of the happiness of the True Dhamma, O Gotama, I was born (spiritually) because of you."

"O Blessed One, this physical body (rūpa-kāya) of yours was nurtured by me. But my faultless Dhamma-body (dhamma-kāya) was nurtured by you."

"I gave you the milk that quenched your thirst for a moment. But you gave me the milk of the Dhamma which is exceedingly peaceful."

"O Great Sage, you are not in debt to me for my protection and care. Women who desire a son pray to obtain a son like you."

"The mothers of kings such as Mandhātu are submerged in the ocean of existence. O Son, you have saved me from the ocean of existence."

"The title 'Mother of a King' or 'Great Queen' is easily obtained by women. But the title 'Mother of a Buddha' is extremely difficult to obtain."

"O Great Hero, I have obtained that title and my aspiration because of you. Whatever aspiration I had, small or great, has all been fulfilled by me."
152:
## 
“O Noble One among men, those who behold your face as you roar like a lion in the midst of the assembly, subduing various doctrines, are indeed blessed. O Bearer of virtues, those who bow at your feet, endowed with long fingers, copper-red nails, and beautiful long heels, are also blessed. O Supreme among men, those who hear your words—sweet, joyful, dispelling the stains of defilements, and beneficial—are also blessed.

O Great Hero, I, who have been constantly devoted to worshipping your feet, have crossed the desert of Saṃsāra through your auspicious words, O Glorious One.” Then, that virtuous Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, having paid homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and to Rāhula and Prince Nanda, spoke thus:

“I am weary of this body, which is like a dwelling of venomous snakes, an abode of diseases, a mass of suffering, and the hunting ground of old age and death. I wish to go to Nibbāna with this body, which is filled with various impurities, dependent on others, and devoid of essence. O sons, please give me your permission.”

Nanda and the venerable Rāhula, free from sorrow and without taints (āsavas), remained firm and unshakable, contemplating the nature of the Dhamma. “Woe to the unstable conditioned things (saṅkhāras), which are essence-less, like the trunk of a banana tree, similar to an illusion or a mirage, transient and unsteady! Since even Gotamī, the foster mother of the Conqueror (Jina) who nurtured the Buddha, must come to an end, indeed all conditioned things are impermanent.”

At that time, Ānanda, who was still a trainee (sekha) and dearly loved the Conqueror, wept piteously with tears flowing. “Alas! Gotamī goes to the state of peace. Surely the Buddha, too, will soon enter Nibbāna, like a fire whose fuel is exhausted,” he lamented. To Ānanda, who was thus lamenting, Gotamī said: “O Ānanda, deep as the ocean of heard Dhamma, ever devoted to the service of the Buddha...”
153:
“My son, it is not proper to grieve when a time of joy has arrived. Because of you, my son, I have reached Nibbāna, my refuge.

Dear son, because of your request and urging, the Buddha permitted our ordination. My son, do not be distressed; your effort has been fruitful.

That state of Nibbāna, which was not seen by the ancients or even by the teachers of other sects (titthikas), has been realized even by delicate young girls of seven years.

O Protector of the Buddha's Dispensation, this is my last sight of you. My son, I am going to the place that is unseen (Nibbāna).

Once, while the Leader of the World (Lokagganāyaka) was teaching the Dhamma, he sneezed. At that time, out of compassion, I uttered a blessing:

‘O Great Hero, may you live long! O Great Sage (Mahāmuni), may you remain for an aeon (kappa)! For the benefit of all beings, may you remain free from old age and death.’

To me, who spoke thus, the Buddha said: ‘Gotamī, Buddhas should not be honored in the way you are honoring them.’

‘O All-Knowing One (Sabbaññū), how then should the Tathāgatas be honored? How should they not be honored? Being asked, please explain this to me.’

‘Look at the disciples who are harmonious, who have aroused energy, who are resolute, and who are always firm in their exertion. This is the honoring of the Buddhas.’

Then, having returned to the monastery, I reflected alone: ‘The Protector, who has reached the end of the three worlds, has shown that a harmonious assembly is the highest worship.’

‘Now, I shall attain Parinibbāna; let me not see the decline of the Dispensation.’ Having reflected thus and having seen the Seventh of the Sages (Isisattama)—

I informed the Leader (Vināyaka) of the time of my Parinibbāna. Then the Buddha permitted me, saying: ‘Gotamī, you know the time.’

My defilements are burnt away; all births are destroyed. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live without taints (anāsava).”
154:
“Truly, my coming into the presence of the Buddha was a good coming. The three knowledges (tisso vijjā) have been attained; the instruction of the Buddha has been fulfilled.

The four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the eight liberations (vimokkha), and the six higher powers (chaḷabhiññā) have been realized; the instruction of the Buddha has been fulfilled.

‘O Gotamī, display your psychic powers (iddhi) to dispel the wrong views of those fools who have doubts about women's realization of the Dhamma.’

Then Gotamī, having paid homage to the Fully Enlightened One and having ascended into the sky, displayed many psychic powers with the Buddha's permission.

From being one, she became many; from being many, she became one. She manifested and disappeared; she passed through walls and mountains.

She dived into the earth without obstruction and walked on water without it breaking, as if on solid ground.

Like a bird, she traveled through the sky sitting cross-legged; she exercised mastery with her body as far as the Brahma realm.

Making Mount Sineru her staff and the great earth her umbrella, she turned them upside down with their roots and walked to and fro in the sky holding them.

She made the world filled with smoke as if six suns had risen; she made the world filled with blazing flames as if at the end of an aeon.

She held Mount Mucalinda, Mount Mahāsela, the base of Mount Meru, and everything in the valleys in a single fist like mustard seeds.

With the tip of her finger, she covered the sun and the moon; she wore thousands of moons and suns like a floral garland.

She held the waters of the four oceans in one hand; she caused a great rain to fall like the rain at the end of an aeon.

In the sky, she created a Cakkavatti king with his retinue; she displayed the roars of Garuḍas, elephants, and lions.”
155:
Having created a single form, and then manifested an immeasurable group of bhikkhunīs, I made them disappear again and, as a single person, addressed the Sage.

"O Great Hero, your foster mother, a follower of your teaching, has reached her goal (Arhatship). O Visionary One, I pay homage at your feet."

Having displayed various miracles and descended from the sky, that Theri paid homage to the Buddha, the Light of the World, and sat in a suitable place.

"O Great Sage, I am one hundred and twenty years of age. O Hero, O Leader, this is enough; I shall now attain Parinibbāna."

At that time, the entire assembly, being greatly amazed, joined their hands in reverence and asked, "How did such incomparable psychic power and effort come to be?"

One hundred thousand aeons ago, the Conqueror named Padumuttara, the Visionary One in all things, the Leader, arose in the world. At that time, I was born in the city of Haṃsāvatī in the family of a minister, which was endowed with all necessities, wealthy, prosperous, and of great riches.

Once, together with my father and escorted by a group of maidservants, I approached that Best of Men with a great retinue. I saw the Buddha, who was like Sakka raining down the rain of Dhamma, free from taints, and who shone with a net of rays like the autumn sun. Having gained confidence in my heart and heard His well-spoken Dhamma, I heard the Leader of Men appointing a bhikkhunī, His foster mother, to the foremost position.

Having heard this, I gave a great gift (mahādāna) for seven days to that Tathāgata, the Best of Men, along with the Saṅgha, providing many requisites. Prostrating at His feet, I aspired for that position. Then, the Best of Sages spoke in the midst of the great assembly:

"I shall describe the woman who has served and made offerings to the Leader of the World along with the Saṅgha for seven days; listen to my words."
156:
"One hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka line, will arise in the world. His heir in the Dhamma, a breast-born daughter, created by the Dhamma, a disciple of the Teacher named Gotamī, will come to be.

Being the foster mother of that Buddha and the one who nurtured His life, she will attain the foremost position among the bhikkhunīs of long-standing (rattaññū)."

Having heard that prophecy and being delighted, I served the Conqueror (Padumuttara) with the four requisites for the rest of my life. After passing away from that life—

I was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, where all desires are fulfilled. I surpassed others in ten attributes: in form, sound, smell, taste, and touch; and also in lifespan, beauty, happiness, and fame.

Likewise, I shone, surpassing others in sovereignty. There, I was the beloved chief queen of the King of Gods (Sakka).

As I wandered through saṃsāra, driven by the wind of kamma, I was born in a servant village in the kingdom of the King of Kāsi. At that time, no fewer than five hundred maidservants lived there. I was the wife of the one who was the head of them all.

Five hundred Paccekabuddhas entered the village for alms. Seeing them, I was delighted along with all the women. We all, as a group, served them for the four months of the rainy season. Having offered the triple robes, we wandered through saṃsāra together with our husbands.

When we all passed away from there, we went to Tāvatiṃsa. Now, in this final birth, I was born in the city of Devadaha. My father was Añjana Sakka and my mother was Sulakkhaṇā. From there, I went to the house of King Suddhodana in Kapilavatthu.
157:
The remaining women were born in the Sakyan clan and came to the houses of the Sakyans. I was the most distinguished among all of them, being the foster mother who raised the Conqueror (Jina).

My son, having gone forth, became the Buddha, the Guide of the world. Later, I went forth as a nun together with five hundred women. Along with the wise Sakyan women, I touched the peace of Nibbāna. Those who were our husbands in a previous life—

Who performed meritorious deeds together with us and were the cause for the preaching of the Mahāsamaya Sutta—they reached Arhatship, being shown compassion by the Sugata.

Then, the other bhikkhunīs ascended into the sky. Possessing great psychic power, they shone like a cluster of stars. They displayed many kinds of psychic powers, just as a well-trained goldsmith creates various ornaments from gold.

Having displayed many wonderful miracles and having gladdened the Buddha, the Best of Speakers, along with the assembly, they descended from the sky and paid homage to the Best of Sages. With the permission of the Best of Men, they sat in their respective places.

"Our foster mother Gotamī, who is very compassionate toward us, has nurtured us for a long time. Being cultivated by your merit, we have reached the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya)."

Our defilements are burnt away; all births are uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, we live free from taints. Our coming to the presence of the Buddha, the Most Excellent, was indeed a good coming. The Three Knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

O Great Sage, we are masters of psychic powers, the divine ear element, and the knowledge of others' minds.
158:
We know our past lives; the divine eye has been purified. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

O Great Hero, the knowledge of the meaning, the Dhamma, the linguistics, and the intuition has arisen in us in your presence.

O Leader, we have served you with a heart of loving-kindness. O Great Sage, please permit us all to enter Nibbāna.

To those bhikkhunīs who said, 'We shall attain Parinibbāna,' the Victorious Buddha said, 'Now you know the time [for it].'

Led by Gotamī, those bhikkhunīs paid homage to the Victor, rose from their seats, and departed.

The Leader, the supreme in the world, accompanied his foster mother to the gate of the monastery along with a great multitude.

Then Gotamī, together with all those [bhikkhunīs], prostrated at the feet of the Buddha, the kinsman of the world, for the final time.

'This is my final sight of the Lord of the World; I shall not see your face, which is like the deathless nectar, again.

O Great Hero, O Supreme in the World, my salutation shall no longer touch your very tender feet; today I go to Nibbāna.

What is the use of this physical body, when the Dhamma is seen as it truly is? All conditioned things are indeed without refuge and transitory.'

She, along with those bhikkhunīs, went to her own nunnery and sat in the noble posture of half-cross-leggedness.

Then the laywomen, who were devoted to the Buddha's Dispensation, having heard of her situation, came to pay homage at her feet.

Striking their breasts with their hands, they fell to the ground like uprooted creepers, weeping piteously, overcome by grief.
159:
'O Noble Lady, giver of refuge, do not leave us and go to Nibbāna yet. We all entreat you, bowing our heads.' Stroking the head of the foremost among those laywomen, who was endowed with faith and wisdom, she spoke these words: 'Enough, daughters, do not despair by following the snare of Māra. All conditioned things are impermanent, ending in separation, and unstable.'

Then Gotamī, having dismissed them, entered the noble first jhāna, the second, the third, and the fourth in succession. Likewise, she entered the attainments of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in order. Gotamī then entered the jhānic attainments in reverse order down to the first jhāna, and from there again up to the fourth jhāna. Emerging from that fourth jhāna, she attained Parinibbāna, free from taints, like the flame of a lamp going out. Then there was a great earthquake, and streaks of lightning fell from the sky. The celestial drums (thunder) resounded loudly. The deities lamented. Showers of flowers fell from the sky, covering the earth. Even Mount Meru, the king of mountains, shook like a dancer in the middle of a stage. The ocean roared with grief like one who is extremely distressed. Devas, Nagas, Asuras, and Brahmas were terrified at that moment, saying, 'Alas, these conditioned things have come to destruction; indeed, conditioned things are impermanent!'

The five hundred bhikkhunīs who surrounded me, followers of the Teacher's instruction, also attained Parinibbāna without clinging, like the flame of a lamp. 'Alas, union ends in separation! Alas, all conditioned things are subject to decay! Alas, life ends in destruction!'—thus the sounds of lamentation arose. Then the Devas and Brahmas approached the Great Sage (the Buddha) and performed the duties appropriate for the occasion, in accordance with the nature of the world.
160:
Then the Teacher addressed the Venerable Ānanda, who was like an ocean of learning: 'Go, Ānanda, and inform the monks of the Parinibbāna of my foster mother.'

Then Ānanda, devoid of joy and with eyes full of tears, said with a trembling voice: 'Let the monks assemble!'

'O monks, sons of the Sugata, residing in the East, South, West, and North, listen to my words.

She who carefully nurtured the final body of the Sage, that Gotamī has gone to peace, like stars disappearing at sunrise.

Even the mother of the Buddha, leaving behind only her name, has gone to the state of peace, where even the Leader with five eyes cannot see her destination.

Whoever has faith in the Sugata, whoever loves the Great Sage, and whoever is a son of the Sugata, let him perform the funeral rites for the Buddha's mother.'

Hearing those words, monks living even in very distant places arrived quickly; some by the power of the Buddha, and some being proficient in psychic powers.

They placed the couch on which Gotamī lay upon a delightful, golden, and beautiful gabled mansion.

The four world-guarding kings (Lokapālas) carried it evenly on their shoulders; the remaining deities, led by Sakka, supported the mansion.

There were five hundred such mansions in total, having the color of the autumn sun, created by Vissakamma.

All those five hundred bhikkhunīs were also lying on couches; carried on the shoulders of deities, they departed in succession.

The entire sky was covered with a canopy; the moon, sun, and stars were fashioned of gold as ornaments.

Many banners were hoisted, and nets made of flowers were spread out. Lotus flowers fell from the sky, and flowers bloomed from the earth.
161:
The moon and sun are seen; the stars also shine. Even when the sun reaches the zenith, it does not cause heat, just like the moon.

The devas worshipped with divine scents and fragrant garlands, and with music, dance, and songs.

Nāgas, Asuras, and Brahmās, according to their power and effort, worshipped the mother of the Buddha who had attained Parinibbāna and was at peace.

All the bhikkhunīs, the heart-born daughters of the Sugata who had attained Parinibbāna, were carried in front.

But Gotamī, who had nurtured the Buddha and was worthy of worship, was carried behind.

In front followed devas and humans, along with Nāgas, Asuras, and Brahmās.

Behind, the Buddha, together with his disciples, went to pay homage to his mother.

The Parinibbāna of the Buddha was not like this.

Only the Parinibbāna of Gotamī was so exceedingly wonderful.

Although the Buddha did not arrange [ceremonies] for his own Parinibbāna, for the Parinibbāna of Gotamī, the Buddha himself and monks such as Sāriputta made the arrangements.

Having prepared those pyres (citaka) made of all kinds of scents and scattered with scented powders, they cremated those bhikkhunīs right there.

The remaining parts were consumed by fire; only the bones (relics) remained entirely.

Then the Venerable Ānanda spoke words that inspire urgency (saṃvega):

"Gotamī has gone to her death, and her physical body has been burned. The sign of the Buddha's Parinibbāna will also occur before long."

Then, at the Buddha's urging, Ānanda presented those relics of Gotamī, which were placed in a bowl, to the Buddha, the Lord of the World.

The Buddha, the best among sages, holding those relics aloft with his hand, spoke:

"Just as a great, substantial tree standing firm, if a very large branch should break due to impermanence, even so, from the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha, Gotamī has attained Parinibbāna."
162:
“Oh, how wonderful it is to me! Although my mother has attained Parinibbāna and only her body remains, there is no more sorrow or lamentation.

Having crossed the ocean of Saṃsāra, having abandoned the heat of defilements, being cooled and well-quenched, the foster-mother is not one to be grieved for by others.

O monks, that foster-mother was wise, possessed of great wisdom, and likewise of wide wisdom. Monks, remember her as the senior (rattaññū) among the bhikkhunīs.

Gotamī was a master of psychic powers; she was also a master of the divine ear element (dibba-sota) and the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa).

She knew her past lives; her divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) was purified. All her taints (āsavas) were exhausted; for her, there is no further rebirth.

Her knowledge was perfectly pure in the analytical insights of meaning, truth, language, and eloquence (paṭisambhidā). Therefore, she is not one to be grieved for.

Just as the destination of a glowing spark, struck by an iron hammer and gradually extinguished, cannot be known,

Even so, for those who are well-liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sensual desires, and who have reached the unshakable bliss [of Nibbāna], there is no destination that can be designated.

Therefore, be islands unto yourselves (attadīpa), having the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) as your domain. Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), you shall make an end of suffering.” (Thus he spoke).

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Guttā

The verse beginning with “Gutte yad-atthaṃ pabbajjā” is that of the Elder Guttā. She too, having performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various lives, gradually fulfilled the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra). With mature wholesome roots, she wandered only in happy realms (sugati) and in this Buddha's era, was reborn in a Brahmin family in Sāvatthī, and was named Guttātissā. When she reached the age of discretion, urged by her store of merit (upanissaya-sampatti) and feeling revulsion for household life, she asked permission from her parents and ordained in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī.
163:
After ordaining, while she was applying herself to insight meditation (vipassanā) and devoted to mental development (bhāvanā), her mind, due to long-standing habit, wandered toward external objects and did not become one-pointed. The Teacher, seeing this and wishing to assist her, while remaining seated in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), emitted a radiance and showed himself as if seated in the air near her. Admonishing her, he spoke these verses:

“Guttā, for whatever purpose you went forth, leaving behind your dear son and wealth, cultivate that very purpose; do not go under the power of the mind.

Beings are deceived by the mind, delighting in the realm of Māra. Lacking knowledge, they wander through the Saṃsāra of many births.

Sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (byāpāda), self-identity view (sakkāya-diṭṭhi), adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbata-parāmāsa), and fifthly, doubt (vicikicchā).

A bhikkhunī who has abandoned these lower fetters will not come back to this world again.

Having abandoned lust (rāga), conceit (māna), ignorance (avijjā), and restlessness (uddhacca), and having cut the fetters, you will make an end of suffering.

Having exhausted the Saṃsāra of births, and having fully understood further existence, you will live in this very life, free from craving and at peace.”

In these verses, “tam-eva anubrūhehi” means for whatever purpose—the Nibbāna of defilements and the Nibbāna of the aggregates—[you ordained, cultivate that purpose]. “Hitvā puttaṃ vasuṃ piyaṃ” means having abandoned the circle of relatives and the mass of wealth that should be cherished, the going forth and the holy life in my Dispensation (Sāsana) was desired; you should increase and fulfill that very purpose. “Mā cittassa vasaṃ gamī” means do not go under the power of the crooked mind, which has been developed through the influence of sense objects like forms for a long time.

Because the mind is like a magician's trick, blind worldlings (puthujjana) deceived by it follow the will of Māra and cannot escape from Saṃsāra. Therefore, it was said: “Beings are deceived by the mind,” and so on.
164:
"These fetters" refers to the five fetters mentioned as "sensual desire and ill-will," etc., so called because of their nature of binding. *Pajahitvāna* means having completely cut them off through the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). *Bhikkhunī* is an address to that elder nun. *Orambhāgamanīyāni* means those that are beneficial or conducive to human life in the sensual realm (*kāmadhātu*), which is the lower part of the fine-material and immaterial realms, because they serve as the cause for rebirth there. The letter 'm' is a euphonic conjunction. There is also a Pali reading *oramāgamanīyāni*, which has the same meaning. *Nayidaṃ punarehisi* means that by abandoning the lower fetters, one will not return again to this sensual existence, the sensual realm, by way of rebirth. The letter 'r' is a euphonic conjunction. There is also a Pali reading *itthaṃ*, which simply means this human existence or sensual existence.

*Rāgaṃ* refers to lust for fine-material existence and lust for immaterial existence. *Mānaṃ* refers to the conceit that is to be abandoned by the path of arahantship. The same method applies to *avijjā* (ignorance) and *uddhacca* (restlessness). *Vivajjiya* means having set aside through insight (*vipassanā*). *Saṃyojanāni chetvāna* means having completely cut off these five higher fetters, such as lust for fine-material existence, etc., through the path of arahantship. *Dukkhassantaṃ karissasi* means you will reach the end or the conclusion of all suffering in the round of rebirths.

*Khepetvā jātisamsāraṃ* means having brought to an end the process of the round of births along with its roots. *Nicchātā* means one who is free from craving. *Upasantā* means one who is at peace through the complete subsiding of all defilements. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

When the Teacher had spoken these verses, at the conclusion of the verses, the Elder Nun attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) and, by way of an inspired utterance (*udāna*), recited these verses exactly as spoken by the Blessed One. Therefore, these verses became known as the verses of that Elder Nun.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Guttā Therī is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Verses of Vijayā Therī

The verse beginning with 'Catukkhattuṃ' is the verse of the Elder Nun Vijayā. She, too, had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and, accumulating merit that serves as a support for the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) in various existences, had her roots of merit gradually matured. While wandering through the realms of gods and humans, she was reborn in a certain family home in Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha. Upon reaching the age of discretion...
165:
...she was a friend of Khemā Therī during her lay life. When she heard that Khemā Therī had ordained, she thought, "If even such a Great Queen ordains, why should someone like me not be able to?" With the desire to ordain, she approached Khemā Therī. The Elder Nun, knowing her inclination, taught her the Dhamma in such a way that she would develop a mind full of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding the round of rebirths and become deeply devoted to the Dispensation. Having heard that Dhamma, she was moved by spiritual urgency, gained faith, and requested ordination. The Elder Nun then ordained her. After ordaining, she performed the preliminary duties and began practicing insight (*vipassanā*). Due to her possession of sufficient supporting causes, she attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) before long. Reviewing her own practice, she spoke these verses by way of an inspired utterance—

“Four or five times I went out from the monastery,
Without obtaining peace of mind, having no control over my heart.

Approaching a bhikkhunī (Khemā Therī), I questioned her respectfully;
She taught me the Dhamma, the elements, and the sense bases.

The Four Noble Truths, the faculties, and the powers,
The factors of enlightenment, and the Eightfold Path, for the attainment of the highest goal.

Having heard her words and following her instruction,
In the first watch of the night, I recollected my past lives.

In the middle watch of the night, I purified the divine eye;
In the last watch of the night, I tore asunder the mass of darkness.

Pervading my body with rapture and happiness, I then dwelt;
On the seventh day, I stretched out my legs, having torn asunder the mass of darkness.”

In those verses, “bhikkhuniṃ” refers to Khemā Therī.

“Bojjhaṅgaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ” refers to the seven factors of enlightenment and the Eightfold Noble Path. “Uttamatthassa pattiyā” means for the sake of attaining the fruit of Arahantship or for the attainment of Nibbāna.
166:
"Pītisukhena" means with the rapture and happiness included in the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*). "Kāyaṃ" refers to the mental body (*nāmakāya*) associated with that rapture and happiness, and also the physical body (*rūpakāya*) that follows the course of that mental body. "Pharitvā" means having touched or having pervaded. "Sattamiyā pāde pasāresiṃ" means that on the seventh day from the day she began practicing insight, she broke her cross-legged posture and stretched out her legs.

How (did she stretch out her legs)? By tearing asunder the mass of darkness; having torn asunder the mass of delusion (*moha*)—which had never been torn asunder before—with the sword of the knowledge of the path of Arahantship (*arahattamaggañāṇa*). The rest of the sequence of words is just as explained below.

## The Explanation of the Verses of Vijayā Therī is finished.

## The Explanation of the Book of Sixes is finished.
167:
## 7. Sattakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sister Uttarā

In the Book of the Sevens, the verse beginning with "Musālāni gahetvāna" is the verse of Elder Sister Uttarā. This elder sister had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Accumulating wholesome merit that serves as a powerful support for liberation (vivaṭṭa-upanissaya) in various existences, she gradually established the roots of merit and gathered the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra). Having matured the qualities that ripen into liberation (vimutti-paripācanīya-dhamma), she was born in this Buddha's era into a certain family in the city of Sāvatthī and was named Uttarā. Upon reaching maturity, she approached Elder Sister Paṭācārā. The elder sister taught her the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, she felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), gained great faith in the Dispensation, and ordained as a nun.

After ordaining and performing the preliminary duties, she practiced insight meditation (vipassanā) under Elder Sister Paṭācārā. While devoted to meditation, because she was endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (upanissaya) and her spiritual faculties (indriya) had reached maturity, she soon intensified her insight and attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Having attained Arahatship, she reviewed her own practice and uttered these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna):

"Young men take pestles and pound grain;
Supporting their wives and children, young men acquire wealth.

Strive in the Dispensation of the Buddha, which once done brings no regret;
Quickly wash your feet and sit to one side.

Establishing the mind, one-pointed and well-concentrated,
Contemplate conditioned things as 'other' (anatta), and not as 'self' (atta).

Having heard the words of instruction from that Elder Sister Paṭācārā,
I washed my feet and sat to one side.

In the first watch of the night, I remembered my past lives;
In the middle watch of the night, I purified the divine eye.

In the last watch of the night, I shattered the mass of darkness that is ignorance;
Then, having attained the three knowledges (tevijjā), I arose; your instruction has been carried out."
168:
"Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods live with Sakka, the undefeated king of gods, at their head, so shall I live with wisdom at my head. I am endowed with the three knowledges and am free from taints (āsavas)." Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, 'cittaṃ upaṭṭhapeṭvāna' means firmly establishing the meditative mind on the object of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). How? 'Ekaggaṃ susamāhitaṃ paccavekkhaṭha' means, with a well-concentrated mind, contemplate your own practice; it means to practice insight meditation on conditioned things through the three marks of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta). These words were spoken as a repetition of the advice given by the Elder Sister to herself and other bhikkhunīs at the time of instruction. 'Paṭācārānusāsaniṃ' refers to the instruction of Elder Sister Paṭācārā. There is also a variant reading 'Paṭācārāya sāsanaṃ'.

Then, 'vuṭṭhāsiṃ' means that after attaining the state of the three knowledges, she arose from her seat. This elder sister also, one day, after clarifying her meditation subject with Elder Sister Paṭācārā, entered her own dwelling and sat down cross-legged. She made a resolution: 'I will not break this cross-legged posture as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging.' She then began the contemplation of mental and physical phenomena, and gradually intensifying her insight, she attained Arahatship along with the supernormal knowledges (abhiññā) and analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) through the sequence of the paths (magga). When the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arose, she felt joyful, thinking, 'Now my task is done,' and after uttering these verses as an inspired utterance, she stretched her legs at the time of dawn. Then, when the night had fully brightened into day, she approached the Elder Sister and recited these verses back to her. Therefore, it is said, 'Your instruction has been carried out,' and so on. All the remaining meanings are exactly as explained previously.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sister Uttarā is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sister Cālā

The verse beginning with 'Satiṃ upaṭṭhapeṭvāna' is the verse of Elder Sister Cālā. This elder sister had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas. Having accumulated wholesome merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences, she was born in this Buddha's era in the village of Nālaka in the Magadha country, in the womb of the brahmin lady Rūpasārī. On the day of her naming, they gave her the name Cālā. Her younger sister was named Upacālā, and then her younger sister...
169:
Sīsūpacālā means that all three of these were the younger sisters of the General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta). The names of their three sons were also these same names. Referring to them, it is stated in the Theragāthā: "Cāla, Upacāla, Sīsūpacāla."

These three sisters, upon hearing that "the General of the Dhamma (our elder brother) has ordained," thought, "That Dhamma-Vinaya in which our noble brother has ordained cannot be inferior, nor can that monkhood be inferior." Filled with zeal and intense desire, they left their weeping relatives and kinsfolk and ordained. Having ordained, they strove and exerted themselves, and before long, they attained Arahantship. Having attained Arahantship, they dwelt in the bliss of Nibbāna and the bliss of the attainment of fruition.

Among them, one day, after her meal, Cālā Bhikkhunī returned from her almsround, entered the Andhavana forest, and sat down for her day-rest. Then Māra approached her and tempted her with sensual pleasures. Referring to that incident, it is said in the Sutta:

"Then, Cālā Bhikkhunī, having dressed in the morning and taking her bowl and robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī and returned from her almsround after her meal, she approached the Andhavana forest for her day-rest. Having entered deep into the Andhavana forest, she sat down at the foot of a certain tree for her day-rest. Then the Evil Māra approached Cālā Bhikkhunī and said this to her" (as recorded in the Saṃyutta Nikāya).

Māra approached Cālā Bhikkhunī, who was sitting for her day-rest in the Andhavana forest, and wishing to make her fall away from the holy life, asked, "On account of whom have you shaved your head?" and so on. Then, she declared the qualities of the Teacher and the nature of the Dhamma as leading out (of Saṃsāra), and by explaining that her task was completed, she made it known that she had transcended his realm. Hearing those words, Māra, becoming sorrowful and dejected, vanished right there. Then, Cālā Bhikkhunī, uttering the verses spoken by herself and Māra as an inspired utterance (udāna), said:

Having well established mindfulness, the bhikkhunī with developed faculties,
Pierced the peaceful state, the bliss of the stilling of formations.
170:
"To whom dedicated do you shave your head? You appear like a nun. You do not delight in the sects (pāsaṇḍa). Why do you wander thus like one who is utterly deluded?"

"The sects outside this [dispensation] are dependent on wrong views. They do not know the Dhamma; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.

There is the Buddha, born in the Sakyan clan, an incomparable individual. He taught me the Dhamma for the overcoming of views.

Suffering (dukkha), the origin of suffering (dukkhasamudaya), the overcoming of suffering (dukkhanirodha), and the Noble Eightfold Path (magga) leading to the subsiding of suffering (he taught).

Having heard the word of that Buddha, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation. The three knowledges (vijjā) have been attained; the Buddha's bidding has been done.

Delight (nandī) in all objects has been destroyed; the mass of darkness (tamokkhandha) has been shattered. Know thus, O Evil One, you are defeated, O Ender!" she uttered these verses.

In those verses, 'satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvāna' means establishing mindfulness well through the power of Satipaṭṭhāna meditation on the body (kāya), etc., by way of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self. 'bhikkhunī' is said referring to herself. 'bhāvitindriyā' refers to those who possess the five faculties such as faith, etc., developed through the meditation on the Noble Path. 'paṭivijjhi padaṃ santaṃ' means she has penetrated and realized the peaceful state of Nibbāna through realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha). 'saṅkhārūpasamaṃ' refers to Nibbāna, which is the cause of the subsiding of all conditioned things. 'sukhaṃ' refers to ultimate bliss (accanta-sukha).

The verse beginning with 'kaṃ nu uddissa' was spoken by Māra. The summary of its meaning is: In this world, there are many doctrines (samaya), and there are many teachers (titthakara) who teach those doctrines. Among them, to whom dedicated do you shave your hair and become bald? Not only are you bald, but by wearing the saffron-colored robe, you also appear like a nun. 'na ca rocesi pāsaṇḍe' means you do not delight in those various doctrines regarded as the correct practice by ascetics (tāpasa), wanderers (paribbājaka), and so forth. 'kimi'daṃ carasi momuhā' means why is this so? Having abandoned the straight path to Nibbāna prescribed in the doctrines, why do you now enter upon a useless wrong path and wander like one who is utterly deluded? (Thus Māra asked).
171:
Hearing the words of Māra, the Elder Nun, rebuking him by way of a reply, spoke the verse beginning with "Outside this [Dispensation]." In that verse, "outside this [Dispensation]" means outside the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened Buddha, referring to false doctrines (pāsaṇḍa) such as those of the Kuṭīsaka and Bahukāra. These are called "pāsaṇḍa" because they set and lay the snare of craving (taṇhā-pāsa) and the snare of views (diṭṭhi-pāsa) for sentient beings. Therefore, it is said, "They are devoted to views." This means they have approached and relied upon views such as eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) and have adopted those views. To the extent that they rely on views, to that same extent they rely on false doctrines.

"They do not know the Dhamma" means that those sectarians (pāsaṇḍins) who rely on eternalism do not truly know even the nature of the process of existence (pavatti-dhamma), thinking, "This process occurs in this way." "They are not skilled in the Dhamma" means they are also not proficient in the nature of the cessation of existence (nivatti-dhamma), thinking, "This cessation occurs in this way." Indeed, they are confused even about the path of the process of existence, so what need is there to mention the nature of cessation?

Having thus shown the inability of false doctrines to lead out of Saṃsāra, she now spoke the verse beginning with "There is one born in the Sakyan clan..." to answer the question, "On whose account have you become a shaven-headed one?" In that verse, "transcending views" means the one who has untangled the net of views, which is the means to transcend all views (referring to the Buddha). The remaining words are as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Cālā Therī Ends.

## 3. Upacālātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

The verse beginning with "Mindful and possessing the eye [of wisdom]" is the verse of the Elder Nun Upacālā. Her story is the same as that told in the story of the Elder Nun Cālā. Like Cālā, she entered the Order, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. While expressing her solemn utterance, she spoke this verse:

"The bhikkhunī, mindful and possessing the eye [of wisdom], with faculties developed,
Has penetrated the state of peace, not frequented by ignoble men."

In that verse, "satimatī" means endowed with mindfulness; it means being endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection in the preliminary stage, and later, through the development of the Noble Path, reaching the fullness of mindfulness and thus being endowed with the highest mindfulness. "Cakkhumatī" means endowed with the eye of wisdom; it means being endowed with the noble, penetrative wisdom that sees the rise and fall [of phenomena] from the beginning...
172:
...being endowed with [noble wisdom], and through reaching the fullness of wisdom, she is said to be endowed with the supreme eye of wisdom. "Akāpurisasevita" means not frequented by low people, but frequented by superior persons, the Noble Ones such as the Buddhas.

The verse beginning with "Why do you not delight in birth?" was spoken by Māra, who wished to entice the Elder Nun toward sensual pleasures. When asked by Māra, "Bhikkhunī, what is it that you do not delight in?", the Elder Nun replied, "Friend, I do not delight in birth."

Then Māra, wishing to show that one who is born enjoys sensual pleasures, and therefore birth should be desired and sensual pleasures should be enjoyed, spoke this verse:

"Why do you not delight in birth?
One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures.
Enjoy the delights of sensuality,
Lest you be one who regrets later."

The meaning of that verse is: Upacālā, for what reason do you not delight, or would you not delight, in birth? There is no such reason. Because one who is born in this world enjoys sensual happiness by indulging in visual objects and so forth associated with the cords of sensual pleasure. For one who is not born, that happiness does not exist. Therefore, enjoy the delights of sensual play. "While youth exists and wealth is present, I did not enjoy sensual happiness"—do not be one who regrets later in this way. The intended meaning is that in this world, what is called 'Dhamma' is only for the sake of attaining an objective, and that objective is clearly for the sake of sensual happiness.

Hearing those words, the Elder Nun, explaining the nature of birth as a cause of suffering and her own transcendence of that realm, rebuked Māra and said:

"For one who is born, there is death,
The cutting off of hands and feet,
Execution, imprisonment, and affliction;
One who is born only encounters suffering.

There is the Fully Enlightened Buddha, born in the Sakyan clan,
Who is unconquered by others.
He taught me the Dhamma,
The transcendence of birth."

The Blessed One, who is the seventh among the Sages, with his hand, those [relics]...
173:
“Suffering, the origin of suffering, the overcoming of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the subsiding of suffering (I have realized).

Having heard the words of that Blessed One, I dwelt delighting in the Dispensation; the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.

Delight (nandī) in all sense objects has been destroyed, the mass of darkness has been shattered; know this, O Evil One, you are defeated (by me).” Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, the phrase ‘jātassa maraṇaṃ hoti’ means that for a being who is born, death occurs; it does not occur for one who is not born. Not only death, but all other misfortunes such as aging and sickness also occur for one who is born, due to the cause of birth. Therefore, the Blessed One said: “With birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.” For that very reason, when it is said “the cutting off of hands and feet,” such cutting occurs only for one who is born, not for one who is not born. It should be understood that by the mention of cutting off hands and feet, the thirty-two types of torture (kammakaroiṇs) are also indicated here. Therefore, He said: “One who is born encounters the suffering of slaughter, bonding, and affliction.” One who is born alone experiences the affliction of slaughter, such as being deprived of life or being struck with fists, the affliction of bonding, such as being bound in shackles, and all other forms of suffering; one who is not born does not experience them. Therefore, it means “I do not delight in birth (rebirth).”

Now, wishing to show from the very root how she has completely transcended birth and sensual pleasures, she said: “Atthi sakyakule jāto,” and so on. Therein, ‘aparājito’ (the Unconquered One) refers to one who cannot be conquered by any Māra, such as the Māra of defilements. The Blessed One is called ‘aparājito’ because He remains having truly overcome the world including the devas, by surpassing all phenomena. The remaining words are clear according to the method already stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Upacālā is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of the Sevens is finished.
175:
It is said that "Tāvatiṃsa" is merely the name of those devas. They are called "Yāma" because they have reached, attained, and are endowed with divine bliss that is superior to the two lower deva realms. They are called "Tusita" because they are delighted and joyful with divine prosperity. They are called "Nimmānarati" because, when they wish to enjoy themselves beyond the naturally prepared objects, they create their desired enjoyments and delight in them. They are called "Vasavatti" because they know the desires of others' minds and exercise control over the enjoyments created by others.

"Set your mind on that heaven" means place your mind in that assembly of devas starting with Tāvatiṃsa; develop a longing for rebirth there. Only Tāvatiṃsa and the higher realms are mentioned with the implication that the prosperity of the Cātumahārājikā devas is inferior to the others. "Where you have lived before" means in those deva assemblies where you have previously resided. It is said that this Elder Nun, having been born in the deva realms before, had passed through the five heavens of the sensual sphere starting from Tāvatiṃsa in succession, then descending again, stayed in the Tusita realm, and after passing away from there, has now been reborn in the human world.

Hearing those words, the Elder Nun said, "Mara, let be the world of desires you speak of. The entire rest of the world is also ablaze and fully ignited by the fires of lust and so forth. The minds of the wise do not delight in that world." Thus, showing her mind's withdrawal from both the sensual desires and the world, she threatened Mara and spoke thus:

169. There are the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the Yāma devas, and the Tusita devas, the Nimmānarati devas, and those devas who are Vasavatti.

170. (Those devas), always preoccupied with identity (sakkāya) from existence to existence, unable to transcend identity, run along the course of birth and death.

171. The whole world is ablaze, the whole world is fully ignited, the whole world is flaming, the whole world is trembling.

172. The Buddha has taught the Dhamma—Nibbāna—which is unshakeable, incomparable, and not frequented by worldlings; in that Dhamma, my mind delights.

173. Having heard the word of that Buddha, I have lived delighting in the Dispensation; the three knowledges have been attained, and the Buddha's bidding has been done.
176:
“Delight (nandī) has been destroyed in every respect; the mass of darkness (delusion) has been torn asunder. Know this, O Evil One: you are defeated, O Ender!”—she spoke these verses.

Therein, ‘kālaṃ kālaṃ’ means at those various times. ‘Bhavā bhavaṃ’ means from one existence to another existence. ‘Sakkāyasmiṃ’ means in the group of the five aggregates. ‘Purakkhatā’ means those who act by placing [something] in front (preoccupied). This is what is meant: Mara, the devas such as those of Tāvatiṃsa whom you mentioned, while going from existence to existence, are established in identity (sakkāya) which is cluttered with many disadvantages such as impermanence. Therefore, at the time of birth in that existence, at the middle time, and at the final time—at those various times—they remain placing only identity in the forefront. For that very reason, being unable to transcend identity, not facing towards the escape from identity, and only running around the shore of identity, they wander through birth and death. Because they are followed by lust and so forth, they repeatedly encounter birth and death; they are not liberated from that saṃsāra.

‘The whole world is ablaze’ means: Mara, not only the world of desires you mentioned, but the entire world known as the three realms (dhātuttaya) is ablaze with the eleven fires such as the fire of lust. Because it is repeatedly set ablaze by those very fires, it is ‘padippita’ (fully ignited). Because it has become a single mass of flame without interruption, it is ‘pajjalita’ (flaming). Because it is shaken and moved here and there by craving and all defilements, it is ‘pakampita’ (trembling).

In such a world that is ablaze, flaming, and trembling, Nibbāna is called ‘akampiya’ (unshakeable) because it cannot be shaken or moved by anyone. It is called ‘atuliya’ (incomparable) because it cannot be measured by its qualities as being “this much,” and because there is nothing equal to it. It is called ‘aputhujjanasevita’ (not frequented by worldlings) because it is frequented only by the Noble Ones (Ariyas) like the Buddhas through the attainment of meditative development of the object. The Blessed Buddha, with a mind urged by great compassion, taught, spoke, and proclaimed the ninefold supramundane Dhamma consisting of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna to the world including the devas. ‘In that Noble Dhamma, my mind is greatly delighted; it does not turn back from it’—this is the meaning. The rest of the sequence of words is just as explained previously.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sīsupacālā Therī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of the Eights is finished.
177:
## 9. Navakanipāta
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vaḍḍhamātā

In the Book of the Nines, the verse beginning with "Mā su te vaḍḍha lokamhi" is that of the Elder Nun Vaḍḍhamātā. This elder nun had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and, accumulating wholesome deeds that serve as a support for the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births, she gradually gathered the requisites for liberation (vimokkhasambhāra). In this Buddha's era, she was born into a respectable family in the city of Bharukaccha. Upon reaching maturity, she went to her husband's house and gave birth to a son. The son was named Vaḍḍha. From that time on, she was known as Vaḍḍhamātā (Vaḍḍha's mother).

Having heard the Dhamma from the monks and gaining faith, she entrusted her son to her relatives, went to the nunnery, and ordained. The events following this are exactly as recorded in the story of the Elder Vaḍḍha (in the Commentary on the Theragāthā). When her son, the Elder Vaḍḍha, approached the nunnery alone with his upper robe to see her, this elder nun, wishing to admonish him by questioning, said:

"Vaḍḍha, may the forest of defilements never be yours in the world at any time;
Dear son, do not be a partaker of the mass of suffering again and again.

Vaḍḍha, the sages, free from agitation, with doubts cut off,
Cooled and having attained self-mastery, dwell happily, free from taints.

Vaḍḍha, for the sake of making an end of suffering and for attaining the vision of the Path,
Cultivate the path trodden by the seers."

She spoke these three verses.

In those verses, in the phrase "Mā su te vaḍḍha lokamhi," the word "su" is merely a particle. Vaḍḍha, dear son, in the entire world of beings and the world of formations, may the forest of defilements (kilesa-vanatha) never be yours at any time. She stated the reason for this with "Mā pุuttaka punappunaṃ bhāgimā." If one cannot cut off the forest of defilements, for that reason, do not be a partaker of the mass of suffering, such as birth and so forth, again and again.
178:
## Commentary on the Verses of Elder Vaḍḍhamātā

Having thus shown the danger of not cutting off the forest of craving (vanatha), she now speaks the words beginning with "Sukhañhi vaḍḍha" to show the benefits of cutting it off. The meaning is: Dear son Vaḍḍha, those called sages (munayo) because they are endowed with the qualities of a sage (moneyya-dhamma); those free from agitation (aneja) because of the absence of craving known as agitation (ejā); those whose doubts are cut off (chinnasaṃsayā) because doubt has been abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry; those who are cooled (sītibhūtā) because of the absence of the heat of all defilements; and those who have attained self-mastery (damappattā) because they have reached the supreme restraint—these taintless ones (anāsavā) who have destroyed the taints dwell happily. For them, there is no mental suffering now, and in the future, all suffering will certainly not arise.

Because it is so, she said, "Tehānuciṇṇam isīhi... anubrūhaya." The meaning is: Dear son Vaḍḍha, you should cultivate and develop the path of Samatha and Vipassanā, which was trodden and practiced by those taintless seers for the attainment of knowledge and vision and for making an end of the entire suffering of the cycle of rebirth.

Hearing these words, the Elder Vaḍḍha thought, "Surely my mother is established in Arahantship," and wishing to make that matter known, he recited this verse:

"My mother who gave birth to me speaks this meaning boldly.
I think that in my mother, the forest of craving no longer exists."

In that verse, "Visāradāva bhaṇasi, etamatthaṃ janetti me" means: "Dear son Vaḍḍha, may the forest of craving never be yours in the world at any time"—this advice, mother, you speak to me without fear, being unattached and unclinged to anything. Therefore, he said, "Maññāmi nūna māmike, vanatho te na vijjati." Mother, I think that in you, there is no longer even the forest of craving consisting of household affection toward me. "Māmikā" means "my mother."

Hearing those words, the elder nun said, "Not even a tiny bit of defilement exists in me regarding any object," and wishing to manifest the completion of her task, she said:

"Vaḍḍha, whatever formations there are—low, high, or middling—
not even a tiny bit, not even the slightest forest of craving exists in me."
179:
“All my taints are exhausted; for me, meditating diligently, the three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.” — He spoke these two verses.

In those verses, ‘ye keci’ is an indefinite term. ‘Saṅkhārā’ refers to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata-dhamma). ‘Hīnā’ refers to low and loathsome things. ‘Ukkaṭṭhamajjhimā’ refers to excellent and middle things. Among them, unconditioned phenomena (asaṅkhata) are [sometimes considered] low, while conditioned phenomena related to birth (jāti-saṅkhata) are excellent, and a mixture of both is middle. Alternatively, those produced by low desire (chanda) etc., are low; those by middle [desire] are middle; and those by excellent [desire] are excellent. Or, unwholesome states (akusala dhamma) are low, supramundane states (lokuttara dhamma) are excellent, and the rest are middle. ‘Aṇūpi aṇumattopi’ means not only in you, but in all conditioned things that are divided into categories such as low, etc., even the smallest, minute thicket of craving (vanatha) no longer exists for me.

He stated the reason for this: “All my taints are exhausted; for me, meditating diligently.” There, ‘appamattassa jhāyato’ means for [the Therī] who is meditating diligently; this is spoken with a change of gender (using the masculine). Here, because the three knowledges have been attained, the Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled. The connection should be understood as: because of meditating diligently, all my taints are exhausted, and even the smallest, minute thicket of craving no longer exists for me.

Taking the advice thus spoken as a goad, the Elder, having developed spiritual urgency (saṃvega), went to the monastery, sat in his daytime quarters, developed insight (vipassanā), and reached Arahantship. Reviewing his own practice and being filled with joy, he went to his mother and, declaring his attainment, spoke these three verses:

“My mother has indeed applied a great goad to me; she spoke verses connected with the ultimate truth (paramattha), like a compassionate mother.

Having heard her words, the instruction of my progenitor, I attained spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) for the sake of reaching the security from bondage (yogakkhema).

I, with a mind directed toward striving, being untiring day and night, and urged by my mother, touched the supreme peace (santi), the state of peace.”
180:
Then the Therī, having made her own words a goad and being delighted in heart by her son's attainment of Arahantship, herself repeated the verses spoken by him. Thus, these verses also became known as the verses of the Therī.

In those verses, ‘uḷāraṃ’ means vast or great. ‘Patodaṃ’ means the goad of instruction. ‘Samavassarī’ should be connected as “indeed, she has properly applied.” If one asks what that goad is, it says: “verses connected with the ultimate truth.” This refers to the verses beginning with “Do not, Vaḍḍha, in the world...” Just as others who are supportive, so too my mother applied a great goad, a driving stick in the form of verses explaining the process of arising and ceasing, to stimulate the speed of my wisdom—this is the meaning.

“Dhamma-saṃvegaṃ āpādiṃ” means that because of seeing the fearful through wisdom, I attained a very great and terrifying spiritual urgency.

“Padhānapahitatto” means one whose mind is sent towards Nibbāna by means of the fourfold right effort (sammappadhāna). “Aphusiṃ santimuttamaṃ” means I have touched, I have attained, the peerless peace of Nibbāna.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Vaḍḍhamātutherī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of Nines is finished.
181:
## 10. Ekādasakanipāta (Book of Elevens)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Kisāgotamī Therī
In the Book of Elevens, the verse beginning with ‘kalyāṇamittatā’ is the verse of Kisāgotamī Therī. It is said that in the time of the Buddha Padumuttara, she was born into a good family in the city of Haṃsāvatī. When she came of age, one day while listening to the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, she saw the Teacher appoint a certain bhikkhunī to the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes.
