She performed a great merit and aspired for that position. Wandering through heavens and the human world for a hundred thousand aeons, she was born into a poor family in Sāvatthī during the time of this Buddha. Her name was Gotamī. However, because of her thin body, she was called ‘Kisāgotamī’.

When she went to her husband's family, she was looked down upon because she was the daughter of a poor family. She gave birth to a son. Only after obtaining a son did they treat her well. However, that son died at the age when he could run and play about. Because of that, madness due to grief for her son arose in her.

Thinking, “Previously I was looked down upon, and only from the time my son was born did I receive honor; these people are now trying to throw my son outside,” she, under the influence of madness from grief, took the dead corpse on her hip and wandered from door to door in the city saying, “Give me medicine for my son.” People rebuked her, saying, “Where can medicine be found?” but she did not heed their words. Then a wise man thought, “This woman has reached a state of mental distraction due to grief for her son; only the Dasabala (the Buddha) will know the medicine for her,” and said, “Mother, go to the Fully Enlightened Buddha and ask for medicine for your son.”

She went to the monastery at the time of the Teacher's Dhamma desanā and said, “Blessed One, give me medicine for my son.” The Teacher, seeing her supporting conditions (upanissaya), said, “Go, enter the city, and from a house where no one has ever died, bring a mustard seed.” She, with a joyful heart, saying “Very well, Bhante,” entered the city and at the very first house said, “The Teacher has me bring a mustard seed as medicine for my son. If no one has ever died in this house, give me a mustard seed.” [They replied,] “Who can count the dead here? What use are those mustard seeds?” She went to a second and third house, and through the power of the Buddha, her madness vanished. Established in her normal mind, she thought thus:
182:
“This very nature will prevail in the entire city; the Blessed One, who is compassionate for the welfare of beings, must have seen this matter.” Having gained spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she went out from there, discarded her son in the raw charnel ground (āmaka-susāna), and recited this verse:

“It is not a law of a village, nor a law of a market town,
Nor is it a law of a single family;
For the entire world including the devas,
This very law is indeed impermanence (aniccatā).”

Having said this, she went to the presence of the Teacher. Then the Teacher asked her, “Gotamī, did you obtain the mustard seed?” She replied, “Venerable Sir, the matter of the mustard seed is finished; please be my refuge.” Then the Teacher recited this verse:

“Death takes away that person
Whose mind is clinging and intoxicated with children and cattle,
Just as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.”

At the conclusion of the verse, while standing right there, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and requested the Teacher for ordination. The Teacher permitted her ordination. She circumambulated the Teacher three times, paid homage, went to the bhikkhunīs' quarters, and after being ordained and receiving higher ordination, she soon developed insight (vipassanā) by practicing with wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra). Then the Teacher, emitting an aura, recited this verse:

“Better is a single day of life for one who sees the deathless state (amata pada),
Than living a hundred years without seeing the deathless state.”

At the conclusion of the verse, she attained Arahantship. She became most excellent in the use of requisites and lived wearing robes endowed with the three types of coarseness. Then the Teacher, while seated in the Jetavana monastery and appointing the bhikkhunīs to their respective positions in order, placed her in the foremost position among those who wear coarse robes (lūkha-cīvara-dhārī). Reflecting on her own practice, she spoke these verses in praise of the Teacher as a good friend (kalyāṇamitta), saying, “Depending on the Teacher, I have obtained this distinction”:
184:
One becomes a friend; that person is called a good friend (kalyāṇamitta). The state of that person is having a good friend (kalyāṇamittatā) and being endowed with a good friend (kalyāṇamittavantatā). "Muninā" refers to the Buddha, the Teacher. "Lokaṃ ādissa vaṇṇitā" means praised with reference to the world of beings, saying, "One should follow a good friend."

It is praised thus: "Ānanda, this entire holy life (brahmacariya) is indeed good friendship, good companionship, and good comradeship" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.2). And, "Meghiya, for a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good comrade, it is to be expected that he will be virtuous, and will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha" (Udā. 31), and so forth.

"Kalyāṇamitte bhajamāno" and so forth shows the benefits of associating with a good friend. In that regard, a person who associates with a good friend, even if he were a fool (bāla) previously due to a lack of learning (suta) and such, may become a wise person (paṇḍita) through hearing the Dhamma (assutasavana) and so forth.

Since they are the cause for even a fool to become wise, virtuous persons (sappurisa) such as the Buddha should be associated with by approaching them from time to time. For those who associate with a good friend, wisdom grows, flourishes, and reaches fulfillment in that way. Among those people, whether one is of the warrior caste (khattiya) or otherwise, if one associates with a virtuous person, one can be liberated from all sufferings such as birth (jāti); thus should the connection be understood.

To show the method of liberation through the power of a good friend, "Dukkhañca vijāneyya" (one should also know suffering) and so forth is stated. In that regard, it means one should know or penetrate these Four Noble Truths (ariyasacca): the Truth of Suffering (dukkha), the Truth of the Origin of Suffering (dukkhasamudaya), the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (nirodha), and the Noble Eightfold Path (magga).

The two verses beginning with "Dukkho itthibhāvo" (Womanhood is suffering) were spoken by a certain female spirit (yakkhinī) who was disparaging the state of womanhood. In that regard, the statement that womanhood is suffering was spoken by the Blessed One, the incomparable charioteer of men to be tamed, because of such disadvantages as fickleness, bearing a child in the womb, and always living in dependence on others. "Sapattikampi dukkhaṃ" means living with a co-wife is also suffering; living together with a co-wife...
185:
...living together is also suffering; the meaning is that this too is a disadvantage of womanhood. "Appekaccā sakiṃ vijātāyo" means some women have given birth only once, being unable to endure the suffering of childbirth in their first pregnancy. "Galake api kantanti" means they even cut their own throats. "Sukhumāliniyo visāni khādanti" means women with delicate bodies, unable to endure the exhaustion due to their delicate nature, even consume poisons. "Janamārakamajjhagatā": a fetus in obstructed labor (mūḷhagabbha) is called a "killer of people" (janamāraka) because it kills women. The meaning is that they have come into the midst of a fetus in obstructed labor within the womb. Both the fetus and the pregnant mother experience the suffering of death and the calamities leading to death.

Other teachers, however, say that both husband and wife, having fallen into the midst of defilements (kilesa) called "janamāraka" and having fallen into the sequence of defilements, meet with ruin in this life through the power of the fever of defilements, and in the future through the power of the afflictions of the miserable realms (duggati). It is said that that female spirit (yakkhinī) spoke these two verses by recollecting the suffering she herself had experienced in a previous existence. The Elder Nun (Therī), however, spoke them again to clarify the disadvantages of womanhood.

The two verses beginning with "Upavijaññā gacchanti" were spoken concerning the life story of the Elder Nun Paṭācārā. In that regard, "Upavijaññā gacchanti" means going on a journey when the time for giving birth was near; the connection is to be understood as: "Before reaching my own home, having given birth on the way, I saw my husband dead."

"Kapaṇikāyā" means one with a pitiable body. These two verses were spoken by the Elder Nun to clarify the disadvantages of womanhood by imitating the manner of Paṭācārā, who was then insane with grief.

Taking both of those as examples, she now spoke the verse beginning with "Khīṇakuline" wishing to clarify the suffering she herself had experienced. In that regard, "Khīṇakuline" means one born in a family that has reached ruin in terms of wealth and so forth. "Kapaṇe" means one who has reached the state of being utterly despised. Both of these are words addressing herself. "Anubhūtaṃ te dukhaṃ aparimāṇaṃ" means you have experienced much suffering either in this life or in lives prior to this. Now, to show that suffering in parts, "Assū ca te pavattaṃ" (and your tears have flowed) and so forth is stated. Its meaning is: in this beginningless Saṃsāra (anamatagga)...
186:
The tears shed by her as she wandered through the round of rebirths, oppressed by sorrow in many thousands of lives, if spoken of generally, would indeed be more than the water in the great ocean.

'Lived in the midst of a cemetery' means having lived in the midst of a cemetery as a female dog or a female jackal that eats human flesh. 'Ate the flesh of sons' means having eaten the flesh of her own sons in lives such as a tiger, leopard, or cat. 'Hatakulikā' means one whose family lineage is destroyed. 'Sabbagarahitā' means one who is reproached or worthy of reproach by all householders. 'Matapatikā' means a widow whose husband has died. She speaks referring to these three conditions that befell her in previous existences. Even though she reached such a state, by associating with a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) found through a fortunate opportunity, she attained the Deathless, reaching Nibbāna.

Now, to make that attainment of the Deathless clear, the words beginning with 'Bhāvito' are spoken. Therein, 'Bhāvito' means the Path that is manifested, produced, developed, and penetrated by the power of meditative realization. 'Dhammādāsaṃ avekkhiṃ' means 'I have looked into, I have seen, the mirror of the Dhamma.'

'Ahamaṃhi kantasallā' means 'I am one whose thorns, such as lust, have been eradicated by the Noble Path.' 'Ohitabhārā' means one whose burdens—the cords of sensual pleasure, the aggregates, the defilements, and the volitional formations—have been laid down. 'Katañhi karaṇīyaṃ' means the sixteenfold task, such as full understanding (pariññā), has been done and completed. 'Suvimuttacittā imaṃ bhaṇီ' means the Elder Kisāgotamī, whose mind is completely liberated, spoke this meaning in the form of verses beginning with 'Kalyāṇamittatā,' referring to herself as if she were another person. In this regard, this is the Apadāna (biographical account) of this Elder:

'The Conqueror named Padumuttara, the one who reached the end of all phenomena, the Leader, arose in this world a hundred thousand aeons ago.

At that time, I was born into a certain family in the city of Haṃsavatī. Approaching that Best of Men, I went to him for refuge.

I heard his Dhamma, which is connected to the Four Noble Truths, sweet, supremely delightful, and bringing the happiness of peace from the round of rebirths.

At that time, the Hero, the Best of Men, while appointing a nun who wore coarse robes to the foremost position (etadagga), praised her.'
187:
'Generating no small amount of joy upon hearing the virtues of that nun, I made offerings to the Buddha according to my ability and strength.

Bowing respectfully to that Excellent Sage, I aspired for that position. Then the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Leader, gave his approval for the attainment of that position.

"A hundred thousand aeons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka family, will arise in the world.

You will be a female disciple of that Teacher, named Kisāgotamī, an heir to his Dhamma, a legitimate daughter created by the Dhamma."

Hearing that prophecy, I became joyful and, from then on, with a heart of loving-kindness, I served that Conqueror, the Leader, with the four requisites for the rest of my life.

Due to that well-performed meritorious deed and my intentional aspiration, after leaving the human body, I went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In this Auspicious Aeon (Bhadda Kappa), the famous Buddha named Kassapa by clan, born of the Brahman lineage, the best of speakers, arose.

At that time, there was a king named Kikī in the excellent city of Bārāṇasီ, who was an attendant to the Great Sage (Kassapa Buddha).

I was his fifth daughter, well-known by the name Dhammā. Having heard the Dhamma of the Excellent Conqueror, I delighted in going forth (ordination).

Our father did not grant us permission to ordain. At that time, we lived in the household for twenty thousand years, practicing without sloth.

The seven daughters, though raised in the comfort of princesses, delighted in serving the Buddha and joyfully practiced the celibate life of a maiden.

They were Samaṇီ, Samaṇaguttā, Bhikkhunီ, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saṅghadāyikā.

(In this present life) they are Khemā, Uppalavaṇṇā, Paṭācārā, Kuṇḍalā, myself (Kisāgotamī), Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.'
188:
Through those well-performed deeds and through my intentions and aspirations, I left the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

In this final life, I was born into a merchant's family. When we became poor and our wealth was destroyed, I went to a wealthy family.

Except for my husband, others looked down on me as a poor woman. But when I gave birth to a son, I became beloved by all.

When that son of mine—young, beautiful, tenderly raised, and as dear to me as my own life—fell into the power of Yama (death).

With a face worn out by grief and a tearful, weeping face, I went about wailing, embracing the dead corpse.

Then, meeting a virtuous person, I approached the supreme Physician and requested, "Venerable Sir, please give me the medicine that can bring my son back to life."

The Victorious Buddha, skilled in the means of discipline, said, "Bring a mustard seed from a house where no one has ever died."

Then, having gone to Sāvatthī, I did not find such a house. Therefore, how could I obtain the mustard seed? It was then that I regained mindfulness.

After discarding the corpse, I approached the Lord of the World (Lokanātha). Seeing me from afar, he spoke with a sweet voice:

"Better is a single day's life of one who sees the rise and fall than a hundred years of life of one who does not see the rise and fall."

"This law of impermanence is not the law of a village, nor the law of a market town, nor the law of a single family. It is the law for the entire world including the devas."

Having heard these verses, I purified the eye of Dhamma. After thus realizing the True Dhamma, I left the household life and ordained.

Having thus ordained and being at peace, I strove in the Dispensation of the Victor. Within a short time, I attained Arahantship.
189:
I am one who has attained mastery in psychic powers; I possess the divine ear element (dibbasota); I know the minds of others; I am a follower of the Teacher's instruction.

I know my past lives (pubbenivāsa); my divine eye (dibbacakkhu) is purified; having exhausted all taints (āsavas), I am a perfectly pure and stainless Arahant nun.

I have served the Teacher; I have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation; I have laid down the heavy burden (the burden of the aggregates); I have uprooted craving that leads to rebirth (bhavanetti).

The purpose for which I went forth from the household life to the homeless life—that goal, the destruction of all fetters, has been attained by me.

By the power of the Buddha, my knowledge in the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) of meaning (attha), doctrine (dhamma), language (nirutti), and eloquence (paṭibhāna) is stainless and pure.

Having collected rags from dust heaps, cemeteries, and streets, I made a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) from those rags and wore coarse robes.

The Victorious Buddha, pleased with that quality of wearing coarse robes, appointed me to the foremost position (etadagga) in wearing coarse robes (lūkhacīvaradhāraṇa) in the midst of the fourfold assembly.

My defilements have been burnt away... the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Kisāgotamī Therī is finished.

## The Commentary on the Eleventh Section is finished.
190:
## 11. Dvādasakanipāta (The Book of the Twelves)
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī

In the Dvādasakanipāta, the verse beginning with "Ubho mātā ca dhītā ca" is the verse of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī. This Elder Nun was also born into a good family in the city of Haṃsavatī during the time of Padumuttara Buddha. When she came of age, she went to the Buddha with a group of people and listened to the Dhamma. Seeing the Teacher appoint a certain nun to the foremost position in psychic powers, she gave a great offering for seven days to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha and aspired for that position. She performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, wandering through the realms of devas and humans. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, she was conceived in the house of King Kiki of Kāsi in the city of Bārāṇasī, becoming one of the seven sisters. For twenty thousand years, she practiced the holy life, donated a monastery precinct to the Saṅgha, and was reborn in the deva realm.

Passing away from there and coming back to the human world, she was born in a small village in a place where she had to work with her own hands for her livelihood. One day, while going to a field hut, she saw a lotus flower blooming early in the morning in a pond along the way. She went down into the pond and took the lotus flower and a lotus leaf to hold puffed rice. She harvested ears of Sāli rice in the field, sat in the hut, parched the rice, and prepared five hundred portions of puffed rice. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha, who had arisen from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) on Mount Gandhamādana, arrived and stood not far from her. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, she took the lotus flower along with the puffed rice, came down from the hut, poured the puffed rice into the Paccekabuddha's bowl, and offered it, covering the bowl with the lotus flower.

Then, when the Paccekabuddha had gone a little way, this thought occurred to her: "Renunciants have no need for flowers; I will take the flower and wear it." Thinking thus, she went and took the flower back from the Paccekabuddha's hand. Then she reconsidered: "If the Noble One had no need for the flower, he would not have allowed it to be placed on top of the bowl; surely the Noble One must have a use for it." Thinking thus, she went back, placed it on top of the bowl, and asked for the Paccekabuddha's forgiveness. She made an aspiration: "Venerable Sir, by the merit of this puffed rice, may I have as many children as the number of grains of puffed rice. By the merit of this lotus flower, may lotus flowers spring up at every step I take in every life I am born." While she was watching, the Paccekabuddha...
191:
She traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana and placed that lotus as a foot-wipe near the stairs used by the Paccekabuddhas at the Nandamūlaka cave. 

Due to the result of that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the celestial realm. From the time of her birth in the celestial realm, a large lotus appeared at every step she took. After passing away from that celestial realm, she was reborn inside a lotus bud in a lotus pond at the foot of a mountain. A hermit lived depending on that pond. Early in the morning, the hermit went to the pond to wash his face, and seeing that lotus, he thought: "This lotus is much larger than the others; while the others have bloomed, this one is still a bud. There must be a special reason for this." He waded into the water and picked the lotus. As soon as he touched it, it bloomed. The hermit saw a little girl sleeping inside the lotus bud.

From the moment he saw her, a fatherly love for a daughter arose in him. He took her along with the lotus to his leaf-hut and laid her on a small couch. Then, by the power of her merit, milk emerged from her thumb. When the old lotus withered, the hermit brought a new one and laid her to rest on it. Later, when she reached the age where she could run and play about, lotuses appeared at every step she took. Her complexion was like a heap of saffron (kuṅkuma). She had not yet attained divine beauty, but she far surpassed human beauty. When her father, the hermit, went to search for various fruits, she remained behind in the leaf-hut.

One day, when she had reached the age of maturity and while her father was away searching for fruits, a forest-dweller saw her and thought: "Humans do not possess such beauty; I will investigate." He sat waiting for the hermit's return. When the father hermit returned, she went to meet him on the path, took the carrying pole and baskets from his hands, and after returning, she performed her usual duties for the seated hermit. Then, the forest-dweller, realizing she was indeed human, paid homage to the hermit and sat down. The hermit invited the forest-dweller to partake of roots and various fruits and offered him drinking water, then asked: "Good man, will you stay here or will you go?" "Venerable sir, I will go. What would I do here?" he replied. "When you go from here, will you be able to refrain from telling others about what you have seen?" the hermit asked. "Venerable sir, if you do not wish it, why would I tell?" he said. He paid homage to the hermit and departed, making marks on branches and trees to recognize the path should he return in the future.
192:
He went to the city of Bārāṇasī and saw the King. The King asked: "Why have you come?" "Great King, I am your forest hunter. I have come after seeing a wonderful woman-treasure (itthi-ratana) at the foot of the mountain," he reported the whole matter. Hearing the hunter's words, the King went quickly to the foot of the mountain, established a camp nearby, and after providing a meal for the hermit along with the hunter and other men, he approached the hermit when he was seated, paid homage, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side.

The King placed the requisites for a monk at the hermit's feet and said: "Venerable sir, what shall we do in this place? Let us return." "Go, Great King," the hermit replied. "Yes, I shall go, venerable sir. However, we have heard that there is an incompatible person (a woman) near you. This is unsuitable for those who have gone forth. Therefore, venerable sir, let her go with me." "The human heart is difficult to satisfy; how will she live in the midst of many people?" the hermit asked. "From the moment she is to our liking, we shall place her in the position of chief over the others and look after her, venerable sir," the King replied.

Hearing the King's words, the hermit called his daughter by the name given in her childhood: "Dear Padumavatī." At his call, she immediately came out of the leaf-hut, paid homage to her father, and stood there. Then the father said: "Dear, you have reached maturity. From the moment the King has seen you, it is no longer proper for you to stay in this place. Go with the King, my dear." She accepted her father's words, saying, "Very well, father," paid homage, and stood weeping. The King, thinking, "I will satisfy this father's heart," performed the consecration ceremony (abhisheka) right there, placing her upon a heap of Kahāpaṇa coins.

Then he took her and returned to his city. From the time of his arrival, he did not look at other women but delighted only with her. Those other women, overcome by jealousy and wishing to create a rift between the King and her, spoke thus: "Great King, this one is not of human birth. Where have you ever seen lotuses springing up in places where humans walk? She is certainly an ogress (yakkhiṇī). Cast her out, Great King." Hearing the words of those women, the King remained silent.

Later, a rebellion broke out in the border region. The King, saying, "Padumavatī is heavily pregnant," left her in the city and went to the border. Then those women gave a bribe to her attendant and said: "As soon as her child is born..."
193:
They said, "Remove a wooden pot, smear it with blood, and place it nearby." Not long after, Padumavatī gave birth. Prince Mahāpaduma alone was conceived in the womb. The remaining four hundred and ninety-nine children were moisture-born (saṃsedaja), appearing at the time Prince Mahāpaduma emerged from his mother's womb and lay there. Then, realizing that she had not yet regained consciousness, the attendant smeared a wooden pot with blood, placed it nearby, and gave a signal to those women. Each of those five hundred women took a child, sent for baskets from the basket-makers, placed the children they had respectively taken into those baskets, sealed them from the outside, and set them aside.

When Padumavatī regained consciousness, she asked the attendant, "Mother, what have I given birth to?" The attendant, threatening her, said, "Where would you get a child from?" and placed the blood-smeared wooden pot before her, saying, "This is the child that came out of your womb." Seeing it, she was overcome with sorrow and said, "Quickly split it and take it away; if anyone sees it, it will be shameful." Hearing her words, the attendant, acting as if she desired her welfare, split the wooden pot and threw it into the stove.

The King, having returned from the border, was waiting for an auspicious constellation and remained encamped outside the city. Then those five hundred women came to welcome the King and said, "Great King, you do not believe us; it is as if what we say is without cause. Please summon the Chief Queen's attendant and question her; your Queen gave birth only to a wooden pot." Without investigating the matter, the King said, "She must be of non-human birth," and drove her out of the house. As soon as she left the royal palace, the lotus flowers disappeared, and her complexion became dull. She wandered alone in the backstreets. Then, an elderly woman of age saw her, felt a motherly affection for her, and asked, "Mother, where are you going?" "I am a stranger, wandering in search of a place to stay," she replied. "Come here, mother," she said, giving her a place to stay and preparing food for her. While she was living there in this manner, those five hundred women, being of one mind, said to the King, "Great King, for you..."
194:
"Great King, while you were away at war, we made a vow to the deity of the Ganges: 'When our lord returns victorious from battle, we shall make an offering and play in the water.' Great King, we wish to inform you of this matter." Pleased by their words, the King went to play in the water in the Ganges. Those women also took the baskets they had respectively seized, concealing them, and went to the river. To hide the baskets, they wrapped themselves in robes, entered the water, and released the baskets. All those baskets floated away together and got caught in a net spread downstream. After playing in the water, when the King came out, the fishermen hauled in the net, saw the baskets, and brought them to the King.

Looking at the baskets, the King asked, "Friends, what is in these baskets?" "Great King, we do not know," they replied. He had the baskets opened and, while looking, first had the basket of Prince Mahāpaduma opened. By the power of their merit, from the very day they were placed in the baskets, milk emerged from the thumbs of those princes. Sakka, the King of Devas, in order to dispel the King's doubt, had letters inscribed inside the baskets: "These princes are the sons of the King of Bārāṇasī, born in the womb of Queen Padumavatī. Then, the five hundred women who were Padumavatī's rivals placed them in baskets and threw them into the water. Let the King know this fact." As soon as the basket was opened, the King read the letters and, seeing the children, picked up Prince Mahāpaduma. He quickly had the chariot harnessed and said, "Prepare the horses; today I shall enter the city and deal with certain women as they deserve." He ascended the noble palace, placed a bundle of a thousand coins on an elephant's neck, and had the drum beaten throughout the city, proclaiming, "Whoever can find Padumavatī, let that person take this thousand."

Hearing those words, Padumavatī gave a sign to her mother, saying, "Mother, take the thousand from the elephant's neck." "I do not dare to take such wealth," the mother said. When Padumavatī spoke a second and third time, she asked, "Mother, what shall I say when I take it?" "Say, 'My daughter sees Queen Padumavatī,' and take it." The mother, saying "Whatever happens, happens," went and took the bundle of a thousand coins. Then people asked the old mother, "Mother, do you see Queen Padumavatī?" "I do not see her, but my daughter says she sees her," she replied. They said, "Mother, where is that daughter?" and along with that mother...
195:
(The royal officials) went and, recognizing Padumavatī, prostrated at her feet. At that time, the old nurse, realizing, "This lady is Queen Padumavatī," said, "The karma of women is indeed very heavy; despite being the chief queen of such a king, she had to live in such a place without protection."

Those royal officials had Padumavatī's residence surrounded with white curtains, stationed guards at the door, and went to inform the King. The King sent a golden palanquin. Padumavatī said, "I do not wish to go like this. From my residence to the palace in Rājagaha, let excellent painted carpets be spread in this interval, and above, let a cloth canopy decorated with golden stars be hung. Only when all the ornaments are sent for my decoration will I go on foot. Only by going thus will the city dwellers see my prosperity." The King said, "Do as Padumavatī desires."

Then Padumavatī, having adorned herself with all the ornaments, set out on the road, saying, "I will go to the palace." Then, wherever she stepped, lotus flowers sprang up, breaking through the excellent painted carpets. Having shown her prosperity to the multitude, she ascended to the palace and gave all those cloth carpets to the old woman as payment for her care.

The King also summoned those five hundred women and said, "O Queen, I give these women to you as your slave-women." She replied, "Very well, Great King, let the whole city know that these women have been given to me." The King had a drum beaten throughout the city, announcing, "The five hundred women who wronged Padumavatī have been given as slave-women to this Queen." Knowing that "the whole city has noted their status as slaves," she asked the King, "O King, may I be allowed to make my slave-women free?" "As you wish, O Queen," he replied. "If so, call back that same drummer and have the drum beaten again, announcing: 'All five hundred women given as slaves to Queen Padumavatī have been made free.'" After she had freed those women, she gave four hundred and ninety-nine of her sons—one less than five hundred—into the hands of those very women to be raised, while she herself took only Prince Mahāpaduma.

At another time, when those princes reached the age for playing, the King had various playgrounds built in the park. When they reached their sixteenth year, they were all together in the park, covered with lotuses...
196:
While playing in the auspicious pond, seeing new lotuses blooming and old lotuses falling from their stalks, they took it as an object of meditation, thinking: "Even in these inanimate things, such old age is reached; what then of our bodies? This body, too, will surely have such a fate." All of them then brought forth the knowledge of a Silent Buddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) and, rising up, sat cross-legged on the lotus hearts.

Then the royal officials who had accompanied those princes, knowing that much of the day had passed, said, "O Princes, please know the time." Those princes remained silent. The officials went and reported to the King, "Great King, the princes are sitting on the lotus hearts; even though we speak, they do not utter a word." "Let them sit as they please," the King replied. Those officials kept guard all night and let the dawn break while they were still sitting on the lotus hearts. The officials approached again the next day and said, "O Lords, please know the time." "We are no longer princes; we are Paccekabuddhas," they replied. "O Lords, why do you speak such difficult words? Those called Paccekabuddhas are not like you; they have hair and beards two finger-breadths long and carry the eight requisites on their bodies," the officials said. Those princes stroked their heads with their right hands, and at that very moment, their lay appearance vanished. The eight requisites appeared on their bodies. Then, in the presence of the multitude who were watching, they flew through the air to the Nandamūlaka Cave.

That Queen Padumavatī also fell into a state of heart-rending grief, thinking, "I, who had many sons, have now become sonless." Passing away due to that very grief, she was reborn in a gate-keeper village in the city of Rājagaha, in a place where she had to live by working with her own hands. At another time, having gone to her husband's house, one day while carrying gruel to her husband's field, she saw eight Paccekabuddhas—who had been her sons—flying through the air at the time for alms. She went quickly and said to her husband, "O Lord, look! Let us invite the Paccekabuddhas and feed them." That husband said, "Those called 'monk-birds' wander like this in other places too; these are not Paccekabuddhas." While they were speaking, the Paccekabuddhas descended at a place not far away. That woman, having offered her rice and food that day to those Lords, said, "Tomorrow also, may the eight of you accept my alms." "Very well, laywoman, let your hospitality be only this much, and let there be only eight seats. Many others..."
197:
“May your mind be clear upon seeing the Paccekabuddhas,” he said. On the following day, that woman prepared eight seats and arranged offerings for the eight Paccekabuddhas, and sat waiting.

The invited Paccekabuddhas gave a signal to the remaining Paccekabuddhas, saying, “Friends, today do not go elsewhere; all of you should show favor to your mother.” Having heard those words, all of them came together through the air and appeared at the door of the mother’s house. Since she had already received the signal beforehand, the woman was not shaken even though she saw many Paccekabuddhas. She invited all those Paccekabuddhas into the house and had them sit on the seats. While those Paccekabuddhas were sitting in order, the ninth Paccekabuddha created eight other seats and sat himself in the chief seat; as the seats increased, the house also expanded in size.

Thus, while all those Paccekabuddhas were seated, the woman offered the gifts prepared for eight Paccekabuddhas to all five hundred Paccekabuddhas until they were satisfied. Then, bringing eight handfuls of blue lotuses, she placed them at the feet of the invited Paccekabuddhas and made a wish: “Venerable sirs, in every life I am born, may my complexion be like the color of the inner petals of these blue lotuses.” After giving their blessing (anumodanā) to the mother, the Paccekabuddhas departed for Mount Gandhamādana.

That woman, having performed meritorious deeds throughout her life, passed away from that existence and was reborn in the celestial realm. In this Buddha's era, she took rebirth in a merchant family in the city of Sāvatthī. Because her complexion was like the inner part of a blue lotus, she was named Uppalavaṇṇā. When she reached maturity, kings and merchants from all over the island (Jambudīpa) sent messengers to the merchant, saying, “Give your daughter to us.” There was almost no one who did not send a messenger.

Then the merchant thought, “I cannot satisfy everyone’s mind; I will devise a plan.” He summoned his daughter and asked, “Dear daughter, would you be able to go forth as a nun?” Since she was in her final existence, her father’s words were like pouring oil that had been cooked a hundred times onto her head. Therefore, she said to her father, “Father, I will go forth.” The merchant honored his daughter and, taking her to the nunnery, had her ordained.

Not long after her ordination, it became her turn to perform duties in the Uposatha hall. She lit the lamp, swept the Uposatha hall, and taking the sign (nimitta) from the flame of the lamp, she stood repeatedly gazing at it. She attained jhāna with the fire-kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa) as its object, and using that jhāna as a basis, she reached the fruit of Arahantship. Together with the fruit of Arahantship...
198:
...the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) were also accomplished. In particular, she became one who had mastery (vasībhāva) in the performance of psychic powers. Therefore, it is stated in the Apadāna (Ap. Therī 2.2. Uppalavaṇṇātherī-apadāna):

Padumuttara was the name of the Victor (Jina), who reached the far shore of all dhammas; a hundred thousand eons ago, that Leader appeared in the world.

At that time, I was born in a merchant family in the city of Haṃsavatī, endowed with great happiness and the radiance of various jewels.

Approaching that Great Hero, I heard the Dhamma teaching; then, with faith arisen, I went to the Victor for refuge.

The Blessed One, the Leader, praised a certain nun who was foremost among those with psychic powers, who was modest, possessed of the quality of 'tādi', and skilled in concentration and jhāna.

Then, with a joyful heart, I greatly desired that position; I invited the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), the World Leader, along with the Saṅgha.

Having fed them for seven days and offered the triple robe, I took a seven-tiered garland fragrant like the scent of blue lotuses.

Placing it at the Teacher’s feet, I made an offering to his knowledge; bowing my head at his feet, I spoke these words:

"O Hero, the nun whom you praised as being in the eighth position from here; O Leader, if it may be accomplished, may I become like her."

Then the Teacher said to me, "Be confident, young girl; in the future, you will obtain that heart's desire."

"A hundred thousand eons from now, a Teacher named Gotama by clan, born of the Okkāka dynasty, will appear in the world."

"You will be his heir in the Dhamma, a daughter of his heart, created by the Dhamma, named Uppalavaṇṇā, and famous for your beauty."

"Having reached mastery in the higher knowledges, a doer of the Teacher’s bidding, with all taints (āsavas) exhausted, you will be the Teacher’s female disciple."
199:
At that time, I was filled with joy, and from then on, for the rest of my life, I served the Buddha, the Leader of the World, along with the Saᅉgha, with a heart of loving-kindness.

Through that well-performed deed, intention, and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiᅃsa heaven.

Passing away from that heaven and being reborn in the human world, I offered alms-food covered with lotuses to the Self-Enlightened One (Sayam-bhū).

Ninety-one aeons ago, the Leader named Vipassī, who was beautiful to behold and possessed the eye of wisdom regarding all phenomena, appeared in the world.

At that time, I was the daughter of a merchant in the noble city of Bārāᅃasī. Having invited the Buddha, the Leader of the World, along with the Saᅉgha,

and having given a great gift, I honored the Leader (Vināyaka) with lotuses and, in my heart, made an aspiration for beauty of complexion.

In this auspicious aeon (Bhadda-kappa), the Buddha named Kassapa, of great fame and a kinsman of Brahmā, the best of speakers, appeared.

At that time, King Kikī of Kāsi, in the noble city of Bārāᅃasī, was the attendant of the Great Sage (Mahesi).

I was his second daughter, named Samaᅃaguttā. Having heard the Dhamma of the Foremost Conqueror, I delighted in renunciation.

Our father did not grant us permission to ordain, so we lived in the household for twenty thousand years, practicing diligently without laziness.

The seven princesses, who grew up in comfort, delighted in serving the Buddha and joyfully practiced the noble life of a maiden (virginity).

They were Samaᅃī, Samaᅃaguttā, Bhikkhunī, Bhikkhudāyikā, Dhammā, Sudhammā, and the seventh, Saᅉghadāyikā.

They are [now] myself, the wise Khemā, Paᅭācārā, Kuᅃᅃalā, Kisāgotamī, Dhammadinnā, and Visākhā is the seventh.
200: Through those well-performed meritorious deeds, intentions, and aspirations, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiᅃsa heaven. Passing away from that heaven, I was born into a noble family among humans. I offered a precious, soft, and smooth cloth to an Arahant. Passing away from there, I was born into a brahmin family in the city of Ariᅭᅭhapura. I was the daughter of the brahmin Tiriᅭivaccha, named Ummādantī, who delighted the hearts of others. Passing away from there, I was born into a certain family in the countryside. In that life of modest means, I guarded a field of hill-paddy. At that time, having seen a Paccekabuddha, I offered five hundred portions of popped rice covered with lotus flowers. I also obtained five hundred sons. I made an aspiration, and those sons also made aspirations after offering honey to the Self-Enlightened One (Sayam-bhū). Passing away from there, I was born inside a lotus in a forest. I became the queen of the King of Kāsi and was one who was honored and respected. I gave birth to five hundred princes endowed with all auspicious marks. When they reached youth, while playing in the water, they saw a fallen lotus and became Paccekabuddhas. Separated from those sons, who were heroes of great learning, I was filled with grief. Passing away, I was born in a small village on the side of Mount Isigili. Understanding the welfare of my sons and husband, while I was going along carrying gruel (yāgu), I saw eight Paccekabuddhas. Seeing those noble ones coming for alms, I remembered my sons, and out of love for them, milk flowed from me. Then, with a confident heart, I offered the gruel to those noble ones with my own hands. Passing away from there, I was born in the Tāvatiᅃsa heaven, where the Nandana Grove is located. Having experienced happiness and suffering and wandered through various lives, O Great Hero of valiant effort, I have even sacrificed my life for your sake.
201:
## The Apadāna of the Elder Nun Yasodharā

Great Hero, O Buddha, the Wise One, the Bearer of Light, I am your daughter. I have performed many difficult deeds, very hard to accomplish.

Rāhula and I, throughout many hundreds of births, were born together in a single existence, with the same aspirations and minds.

We were born together in every birth, even of the same status. Now, having reached this final birth, we are both born in different circumstances.

Great Sage, I have shown my many services in the presence of the former supreme Victors for your sake.

Sage, remember the meritorious deeds I have fulfilled. Great Hero, I have accumulated merit for your sake.

Avoiding improper places and restraining from misconduct, Great Hero, I have sacrificed many lives for your sake.

Thus, there were many kinds of suffering and many kinds of success. Having reached this final birth, I was born in the city of Sāvatthī.

I was born in a wealthy merchant family, prosperous and well-adorned, shining with the light of various jewels, and fulfilled in all sensual desires.

Respected, honored, esteemed, and revered, I was endowed with the glory of beauty and highly honored among families.

I was greatly desired for the glory of my beauty; even by hundreds of merchant sons, I was desired.

Having renounced the household life, I entered the homeless life. Before even half a month had passed, I realized the Four Noble Truths.

Having created a square chariot through psychic power, I shall pay homage to the feet of the Buddha, the Protector of the World, the One Endowed with Equanimity.

Great Sage, I am a master of psychic powers, the divine ear element, and the knowledge of others' minds.

(Background story from the Nissaya)
Having practiced the holy life for twenty thousand years and served the community of monks, she was reborn in the celestial realm. Passing away from that realm and returning to the human world, she was born in a small village where she earned her living by her own labor. One day, while going to a field-watch hut, she saw a lotus flower blooming early in a pond along the way. She waded into the pond, plucked the lotus, and took a lotus leaf to hold popcorn. Harvesting stalks of rice in the field and sitting in the hut, she roasted popcorn and prepared five hundred grains. At that moment, a Paccekabuddha, having arisen from the attainment of cessation on Mount Gandhamādana, arrived and stood not far from her. Seeing the Paccekabuddha, she took the popcorn along with the lotus, descended from the hut, poured the popcorn into his bowl, and offered it, covering the bowl with the lotus flower.

Then, as the Paccekabuddha walked a short distance away, she thought, "Monks have no need for flowers; I will take the lotus back and wear it." However, she reconsidered, "If the Venerable One did not want the flower, he would not have allowed it to stay on top of the bowl; he must surely want it." She went back, replaced it on the bowl, and asked for forgiveness. Then she prayed, "Venerable Sir, by the result of this popcorn, may I have as many sons as there are grains; by the result of this lotus, may a lotus flower appear at every step in every birth I take." While she watched, the Paccekabuddha traveled through the air to Mount Gandhamādana and placed that lotus as a foot-wipe near the walkway in the Nandamūlaka valley.

By that merit, she was reborn in the celestial realm. From the time she became a goddess, large lotus flowers appeared at every step. When she passed away from there, she was born inside a lotus in a lotus pond at the foot of a mountain. A hermit living near that pond, going to wash his face early in the morning, saw the lotus and thought, "This lotus is much larger than the others; while others have bloomed, this one is still a bud; there must be a reason." He waded in to take it. As soon as he touched it, the lotus bloomed, and he saw a young girl lying inside. Loving her like a daughter, he took her to his hermitage and cared for her. Milk flowed from her thumbs. When the lotus withered, he brought a new one for her to sleep in. When she grew up and could run and play, lotus flowers appeared at every step. Her complexion was as beautiful as a cluster of saffron, resembling a goddess and surpassing human beauty. One day, while her father, the hermit, was away searching for fruit, a forest hunter saw her. Of the people...
202:
“I know my past lives; my divine eye is purified; all taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

“By the power of the Great Sage, my knowledge is stainless and pure in the analytical insights of meaning, truth, language, and wit.

“Robes, almsfood, medicinal requisites, and lodgings—thousands of people from all directions offer these in an instant.

“The Victorious Buddha, pleased with those qualities, placed me in the foremost position. The Leader of the world, in the midst of the assembly, declared, ‘She is the foremost among those with great psychic power.’

“I have served the Teacher; I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching; the heavy burden has been laid down; the conduit to existence has been uprooted.

“The goal for which I renounced the household for the homeless life—the destruction of all fetters, the fruit of Arahantship—has been attained by me.

“My defilements have been burnt away... I have fulfilled the Buddha's teaching.”

When the Blessed One went to the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī to perform the Twin Miracle, this elder nun approached the Buddha, paid homage, and roared a lion's roar, saying, “Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One permits, I shall perform a miracle.” Based on this event, while the Buddha was residing in the Jetavana Monastery in the midst of the Noble Saṅgha, he assigned the nuns to their respective positions and placed this elder nun in the foremost position (Etadagga) among the nuns with great psychic power. She spent her time in the bliss of meditative absorption, the bliss of fruition, and the bliss of Nibbāna. One day, while reflecting on the danger, lowliness, and impurity of sensual pleasures, she recited the verses spoken by the mother and daughter living on the banks of the Ganges, who were moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega) due to living as co-wives of the same husband:

“Both mother and daughter, we were co-wives. Because of that, a wonderful and hair-raising spiritual urgency arose in me.

“Woe to the impure, foul-smelling, and many-thorned sensual pleasures, because of which even a mother and daughter became co-wives!”
203:
## 
“Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, and seeing renunciation as safety, I went forth from the home life into homelessness in Rājagaha.” — She spoke these three verses. In those verses, the phrase “Both mother and daughter, we were co-wives” means that both of us, mother and daughter, had been co-wives to one another.

It is said that in the city of Sāvatthī, the wife of a certain merchant conceived a child in her womb at the time of dawn. She herself was unaware that she was pregnant. When the night had brightened into day, the merchant loaded goods onto carts and departed for Rājagaha. As time passed, her pregnancy matured. Then her mother-in-law said to her, “My son has been away for a long time, yet you are pregnant; you have committed a wicked deed.” She replied, “I know no man other than your son.” Although she heard this, the mother-in-law did not believe her and drove her out of the house. While searching for her husband, she eventually reached Rājagaha. At that very time, her birth-pains began, and she entered a certain rest house near the road where she gave birth. Having given birth to a son who resembled a golden image, she laid him down in the alms-hall and went outside for the sake of water. 

Meanwhile, a certain childless caravan leader traveling along that road thought, “This is an ownerless child; he shall be my son,” and handed him over to a nurse. When the child's mother returned after finishing her business with the water, she did not see her son. Overcome by grief and lamenting, she did not enter Rājagaha but continued along the road. Midway, a certain chief of thieves saw her and, becoming infatuated, made her his wife. While living in his house, she gave birth to a daughter. 

One day, while she was holding the daughter, she had a quarrel with her husband and threw the daughter onto the couch, causing a small wound on the girl's head. Later, fearing her husband, she returned to Rājagaha and lived as she pleased. When her son reached early youth, not knowing she was his mother, he made her his wife. Later, not knowing that the daughter of the chief of thieves was his sister, he married her and brought her to his home. Thus, that man lived making both his mother and his sister his wives. Therefore, both of them lived as co-wives. One day...
204:
The mother, while loosening her daughter’s hair to look for lice, saw the scar on her head and asked, “Could this be my daughter?” Becoming struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), she went to the Bhikkhunī quarters in Rājagaha and went forth. Having performed the preliminary duties and living in seclusion, she reflected on her past conduct and recited the verses beginning with “Both mother and daughter.” This Elder (Therī), repeating those very verses spoken by the mother through the power of seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, spoke the verses beginning with “Both mother and daughter.” Therefore, it is said: “That Elder, passing the time in the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of fruition, and the bliss of Nibbāna, spoke these three verses.”

In those verses, ‘impure’ (asuci) means impure due to the oozing of the impurities of defilements. ‘Foul-smelling’ (duggandhā) means having a putrid odor like the smell of poison. ‘Having many thorns’ (bahukaṇṭakā) means having many thorns of defilements because they arise like stakes and pierce through wholesome conduct. Indeed, it is said that those sensual pleasures are like spears and stakes. ‘Wherein’ (yattha) means in those sensual pleasures which are to be enjoyed. ‘Co-wives’ (sabharīya) means having the same husband, which has the same meaning as ‘sapattī’.

“I know my past lives; the divine eye has been purified.
The knowledge of encompassing the minds of others and the divine ear element have been purified.

Psychic power has been realized by me; I have attained the destruction of the taints.
The six higher knowledges have been realized; the Buddha’s teaching has been fulfilled.”

The Elder, having reflected on the specific distinction she had attained and being filled with joy and gladness, spoke the two verses beginning with “I know my past lives.” In those verses, ‘knowledge of encompassing the minds’ (cetopariccañāṇa) refers to cetopariyañāṇa; it should be connected with ‘realized’ or ‘attained’.

“Having created a four-cornered chariot by psychic power,
I paid homage at the feet of the Buddha, the Protector of the World, the Such-like One.”

This verse was spoken with a heart of faith when the Blessed One approached the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree to perform the Twin Miracle. At that time, this Elder created such a chariot and went to the Teacher’s presence with it, saying, “Venerable Sir, I shall perform a miracle to crush the pride of the heretics; please give me permission,” and stood in the Teacher’s presence. In that verse, ‘Having created a four-cornered chariot by psychic power’ means that she created a chariot yoked with four horses by psychic power, paid homage at the feet of the Buddha, the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
205:
“Approaching the tree well-blossomed at the top, you stand alone at the foot of the Sāla tree;
You have no companion whatsoever;
O foolish girl, do you not fear the rogues?”

In that verse, 'su-pupphitaggaṃ' means well-blossomed at the top, meaning fully blossomed starting from the top. 'Pādapaṃ' refers to a tree; here, a Sāla tree is intended. 'Ekā tuvaṃ' means you are standing here alone. 'Na cāpi te dutiyo atthi koci' means you have no protector as a companion. Or, it means there is no second person equal to you in beauty; being of incomparable beauty, you stand alone in this place secluded from people. 'Bāle na tvaṃ bhāyasi dhuttakānaṃ' means, O young woman, why do you not fear the rogues who are negligent in sensual pleasures?

It is said that one day, Māra, seeing the Therī sitting for the day's abiding in a Sāla grove where the trees were well-blossomed, approached her, wishing to distract her from her seclusion and to test her. Then the Therī, threatening Māra by the power of her own majesty, said:

“Even if a hundred thousand rogues like these should come together,
Not a single hair of mine would stir or tremble;
O Māra, what can you alone do to me?

I shall disappear,
Or I shall enter your belly;
I shall stand between your eyebrows,
And you will not see me standing there.

I am a master of my mind,
The bases of power (iddhipāda) have been well-developed,
The six direct knowledges (abhiññā) have been realized,
The Buddha's teaching has been fulfilled.

Sensual pleasures are like swords and stakes,
The five aggregates are like a chopping block (for them);
That delight in sensual pleasures of which you speak
Is now for me only non-delight.

Delight has been destroyed in every way,
The mass of darkness (tamokhandha) has been shattered;
Know this, O Evil One,
O Death, you are defeated.”

She spoke these verses.
206:
In that verse, "Sataṃ sahassānipi dhuttakānaṃ, samāgatā edisakā bhaveyyuṃ" means even if many hundreds of thousands of rogues of such a nature as you should come together. "Lomaṃ na iñje napi sampavedhe" means not even a single hair would stir, nor would there be any trembling. "Kiṃ me tuvaṃ māra karissaseko" means, O Māra, being alone, what can you do to me?

Now, wishing to make clear that Māra is unable to do anything to her, she spoke the verse "Esā antaradhāyāမိ." The meaning of that verse is: O Māra, I shall disappear even while standing before you and become invisible; while you are unaware, I shall enter your belly or stand between your eyebrows; you will not be able to see me standing thus.

Why is that? Because I am a master of my mind, and the bases of power (iddhipāda) have been well-developed. O Māra, my mind has attained mastery, and the four bases of power have been well-developed and frequently practiced by me; therefore, I am capable through the aforementioned range of psychic power (iddhivisaya). All the remaining words are clear in meaning as they follow the method already explained below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Numerical Section of Twelves is finished.
207:
## 12. The Numerical Section of Sixteens
## 1. Commentary on the Verses of Puṇṇā Therī

In the Section of Sixteens, the verse beginning with "Udahārī ahaṃ sīte" is the verse of Puṇṇā Therī. This Puṇṇā Therī had also performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas, accumulating merit that serves as a support for the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. In the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, she was born in a good family. Upon reaching maturity, being endowed with sufficient causes, she felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). She approached the bhikkhunīs, heard the Dhamma, and having gained faith, she ordained. Being of pure virtue, she learned the three Piṭakas and became learned (bahussuta), a bearer of the Dhamma (dhammadhara), and a teacher of the Dhamma (dhammakathika). Just as in the dispensation of the Blessed One Vipassī, she also ordained in the dispensations of the Blessed Ones Sikhī, Vessabhū, Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, becoming one endowed with virtue, learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, and a teacher of the Dhamma. However, due to having a latent tendency of pride (māna), she was unable to completely eradicate the defilements.

Because she had performed actions based on pride, in this Buddha's era, she was born in the womb of a domestic slave in the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, and her name was Puṇṇā. After hearing the discourse of the Sīhanāda Sutta, she became a stream-enterer (sotāpanna). Later, after disciplining a Brahmin who believed in purification by water (udakasuddhika), she was honored by the merchant, who released her from slavery and granted her the status of a free person. Having asked the merchant for permission to ordain, she ordained and, while practicing vipassanā, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) before long. This is stated in the Apadāna:

"In the dispensations of the Blessed Ones Vipassī, Sikhī, and Vessabhū,
And in the dispensations of the sages Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and others;
And in the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, having ordained,
I was a bhikkhunī endowed with virtue, wise, and with restrained faculties.
I was learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, one who questioned the meaning of the Dhamma,
A learner of the teachings, and one who attended to hearing the Dhamma.
I used to preach the Dhamma in the midst of people in the dispensation of the Conqueror;
Because of that great learning, I looked down upon those who were dear to virtue."
208:
In this final existence, I was born as a water-carrier slave in the house of Anāthapiṇḍika in the noble city of Sāvatthī.

While going to fetch water, I saw the Brahmin Sotthiya shivering in the middle of the water due to the cold, and I spoke these words:

"I am a water-carrier; I always enter the water because I fear the punishment of my masters and am oppressed by the fear of their verbal abuse.

Brahmin, whom do you fear that you always enter the water, with your limbs trembling, experiencing such intense cold?"

"Puṇṇikā, you surely know me, yet you ask—I who am performing wholesome deeds and blocking the evil deeds I have done.

Whether old or young, if one has committed an evil deed, one can be freed from that evil deed by bathing in water."

To that Brahmin as he emerged from the water, I spoke words connected with the Dhamma. Having heard them, he was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and became an Arahant.

Since I was born when one was lacking to complete a hundred, my name is Puṇṇā. They freed me from slavery.

Then, having asked permission from the merchant, I went forth into homelessness. In no long time, I attained Arahantship.

Great Sage, I am a master of various psychic powers, the divine ear-element, and the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others.

I know my former lives; my divine eye is purified; all taints (āsavas) are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth.

Through the grace of the Buddha, the Best of Beings, my knowledge is stainless and pure regarding the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) of meaning, doctrine, language, and eloquence.
209:
Through meditation (bhāvanā), there is great wisdom; through learning alone, one becomes learned. Because of pride, I was born into a low family; indeed, kamma does not perish.

My defilements (kilesas) are burnt away... I have followed the Buddha's teaching.

Having attained Arahantship, reflecting on her own practice, she uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"I was a water-carrier; I always entered the water in the cold, fearing the punishment of my mistresses and oppressed by the fear of their verbal abuse."

"Brahmin, whom do you fear that you always enter the water? You are experiencing intense cold with trembling limbs."

"Lady Puṇṇikā, you know me, yet you ask—I who am performing wholesome kamma and blocking the evil kamma I have done."

"Whether old or young, if one has committed an evil deed, one can be freed from that evil deed by bathing in water."

"Who told you this—the ignorant telling the ignorant—that 'one can be freed from evil deeds by bathing in water'?"

"If that were so, then all the frogs, turtles, nagas, crocodiles, and other water-dwelling creatures would surely go to heaven."

"Sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, fishermen, hunters, thieves, executioners, and other evildoers would also be freed from their evil deeds by bathing in water."

"If these rivers could wash away the many evil deeds you have done in the past, they would wash away your merit (puñña) as well. In that case, you would be devoid of merit."

"Brahmin, whatever (evil) you fear that makes you always enter the water, just do not do that evil. Do not let the cold water destroy your skin."

"You have led me, who was on the wrong path, to the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). Lady, I give you this robe for this (service of) cleansing by water."
210:
“Let that robe be yours alone; I do not desire the robe. If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,

Do not commit an evil deed, whether openly or in secret. If you will do or are doing an evil deed,

There is no escape from suffering for you, even if you run away. If you fear suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,

Go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha of such quality. Undertake the precepts (sīla); that will be for your benefit.

I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha of such quality. I undertake the precepts; that will be for my benefit.

Formerly I was a 'Brahmin by kin' (in name only), but today I am a true Brahmin. I am one with the threefold knowledge (tevijja), accomplished in the Vedas, a 'Sotthiya' (one who has washed away evil), and a 'Snātaka' (one who is cleansed of defilements).” — Thus he spoke these verses.

In that context, “Udāhārī” means one who carries water with a jar (a water-carrier). “Entered the water then in the cold” means she entered the water even in the winter season, at all times, day and night. Whenever the masters needed water, she entered the water; the meaning is that she went down into the water and brought it back. “Fearing the punishment of the masters” means fearing the danger of being beaten by the masters. “Oppressed by the fear of verbal abuse” means being oppressed and tormented by the fear of verbal punishment and the fear of anger; connect this with “entering the water even in the cold.”

Then one day, the slave girl named Puṇṇā went to the landing place to fetch water with a jar. There, at a time of intense cold when snow was falling, she saw a certain Brahmin who believed in purification by water. He had entered the water early in the morning, submerged himself including his head, recited mantras, and emerged from the water, shivering with wet clothes and wet hair, his teeth chattering. Seeing him, her mind was moved by compassion, and wishing to turn him away from that wrong view, she asked with a verse: “Brahmin, whom do you fear?” In that verse, “Brahmin, whom and for what reason of fear are you afraid...” (is the meaning).
211:
He constantly descends into the water; at all times, both evening and morning, he descends into the water. Having descended into the water, he experiences extreme cold with shivering limbs; he experiences the suffering of cold that is very difficult to endure.

'The lady indeed knows me,' (the Brahmin said). 'O Puṇṇikā, you ask me, saying that I am performing a wholesome deed by descending into the water in this way, which is capable of preventing the accumulated evil deeds.'

Is this matter not well-known in the world? Wishing to show, 'We shall also speak words to you,' she spoke the verse beginning with 'Yo ca vuḍḍho'. The meaning of that verse is: Whether old, young, or middle-aged, whoever commits evil deeds such as harming excessively—even such a person who delights in evil deeds is freed from those evil deeds by bathing through water-sprinkling; he is completely liberated.

Hearing those words, Puṇṇikā, wishing to reply to that Brahmin, spoke the verse beginning with 'Ko nu te'. In that verse, 'Ko nu te idamakkhāsi' means: To you who do not know the result of kamma, who is the foolish one, totally ignorant of the result of kamma, that told you this matter: 'One is freed from evil deeds because of water-sprinkling'? That person's words are not to be believed, nor is this practice appropriate—this is the meaning.

Now, wishing to clarify that inappropriateness, she spoke the verse beginning with 'Saggam nūna gamissanti'. In that verse, 'nāgā' means large fish. 'Susumārā' means crocodiles. 'Ye caññe udake carā' means other creatures that frequent the water, such as fish, makaras, turtles, and so on. The meaning is: If liberation from evil deeds occurs through water-sprinkling, then I suppose those creatures will also go to heaven, arising in the celestial realm.

'Orabbhikā' means sheep-slaughterers. 'Sūkarikā' means pig-slaughterers. 'Macchikā' means fishermen. 'Migabandhakā' means hunters. 'Vajjhaghātā' means those employed in the act of execution.

'Puññampi mā vaheyyum' means: If these rivers, such as the Aciravatī, could carry away and remove the evil you previously committed through water-sprinkling, then in the same way, these rivers would also carry away and wash away the merit you have performed. Therefore, you...
212:
...would then be one who is devoid of that meritorious kamma, an outsider to it; the meaning is that this is not appropriate. Otherwise, just as the merit of one who descends into the water cannot be washed away by water, so too evil cannot be washed away. Why? Because bathing is not the opposite of the causes of evil. That which destroys something is its opposite. Just as light is the opposite of darkness, and knowledge (vijjā) is the opposite of ignorance (avijjā), bathing is not the opposite of evil. Therefore, a conclusion should be reached here: 'There is no liberation from evil through water-sprinkling.' Thus, the Blessed One said:

'One is not pure by water; many people bathe in this water. He in whom there is truth and Dhamma, he alone is pure, and he is a Brahmin.'

Now, wishing to show, 'If you desire to wash away evil, do not commit any evil at all,' he spoke the verse beginning with 'Yassa brāhmaṇa'. In that verse, 'Tam-eva brahme mākāsi' means: O Brahmin, do not commit that very evil of which you are afraid. Descending into the water in such a winter season only troubles the body. Therefore, he said: 'Mā te sītaṃ chaviṃ hane'—the meaning is: Let not the cold arising from bathing in such a winter season destroy your skin or trouble you.

'Kummagga-paṭipannaṃ maṃ' refers to me, who was established in and practicing this wrong path, this false view that 'purity comes through bathing'. 'Ariyamaggaṃ samānayi' means: You have well-led and brought me to this path traversed by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddha, which is 'the non-doing of all evil, the undertaking of the wholesome'. Therefore, Lady... as a teacher's share given out of joy, I give this robe to you; please accept that robe—this is the meaning.

That woman, rejecting the robe and preaching the Dhamma to establish him in the Refuges and the Precepts, said, 'Let this robe be yours alone; I do not desire the robe,' and spoke the verse beginning with 'Sace bhāyasi dukkhassa'. The meaning of those words is: If you fear the suffering of the entire lower realms and the suffering such as discomfort and misfortune that can occur in the happy realms; if that suffering is unloved and unpleasant to you; whether openly or clearly to others...
213:
Do not do even the slightest evil or base deed, whether openly by body or speech, or secretly in private by mind through covetousness and so forth. If you will do that evil deed in the future, or are doing it now, even if you run away intentionally with the thought, "Even if I flee from here to there, the suffering which is the fruit of that deed will not follow me in the four planes of misery such as hell or among humans," there is no escape or release for you from that evil. It will surely ripen when there is a conjunction of other causes such as destination (gati) and time (kāla). The word "uppaccā" is also a variant reading, meaning "having flown up."

Having shown the absence of suffering by not doing evil, he now says "Sace bhāyasi" etc., to show that same absence of suffering by doing good. In that verse, "tādinaṃ" refers to the Blessed One who has reached the state of "tādi" (steadfastness) regarding sights and so forth. Or else, because he is to be seen like the previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, he is called "Tādi"; the connection is: "approach that Buddha as a refuge." The same method applies to the Dhamma and the Saṅgha. Approach the Dhamma of the noble Buddhas who are "tādi", and the Saṅgha, the group of the eight noble persons, as a refuge. "Taṃ" refers to the established going for refuge and the undertaking of the precepts. "Hehiti" means "it will be."

That Brahmin, established in the refuges and precepts, later heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, gained faith, ordained, and through striving and effort, before long became one with the three knowledges (tevijja). Reviewing his own practice, he uttered an exultation (udāna) with the verse beginning with "Brahmabandhu."

The meaning of that verse is: "Formerly, I was a Brahmin in name (Brahmabandhu) merely by birth in a Brahmin family. Likewise, I was called one with the three knowledges (tevijja), endowed with the Vedas (vedasampanna), a learned one (sottiya), and a cleansed one (nhātaka) merely by the study of the Rigveda and so forth. Now, I am a true Brahmin, a Brahmin in the ultimate sense (paramattha-brāhmaṇa), because of having discarded all evil. I am a tevijja because of attaining the three knowledges. I am vedasampanna because of being endowed with the Veda known as the knowledge of the Path (magga-ñāṇa). And I am a nhātaka because of having crossed over all evil." Here, both the verse spoken by the Brahmin and the verse spoken by herself were later recited individually by the Therī; thus, all the verses became the verses of the Therī alone.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Puṇṇā Therī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Book of the Sixteens is finished.
215:
The hair growing on my head used to be like a fragrant casket, filled with flowers and scented with perfume. Now, due to old age, it smells like the fur of a wild animal. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My hair was thick like a well-planted forest, beautiful with tips adorned with combs, pins, and hairpins. Now, due to old age, it is sparse here and there. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My hair was black in color, as if adorned with gold, and beautiful when decorated with fine braids. Now, due to old age, the head has become bald. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My eyebrows were beautiful in the past, like lines well-drawn by a painter. Now, due to old age, they are wrinkled and drooping. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My eyes were bright and very beautiful like jewels, deep dark blue and long. Now, oppressed by old age, they are no longer beautiful. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My nose was smooth and beautiful in my youth, like a high mountain peak. Now, due to old age, it is like something withered. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

My earlobes were beautiful like well-crafted bracelets. Now, due to old age, they are wrinkled and drooping. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.
216:
In the past, my teeth were very beautiful, resembling the color of trumpet flower buds. Now, due to old age, they are broken and dark in color. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, I used to sing as sweetly as a cuckoo wandering in the forest. Now, due to old age, that voice falters here and there. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, my neck was very beautiful, like a smooth, well-polished conch shell. Now, due to old age, it is broken and bent. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, both my arms were very beautiful, like rounded door-bars. Now, due to old age, they are shriveled like dried sesame stalks. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, my hands were very beautiful, adorned with smooth gold rings. Now, due to old age, they are like old, decaying roots. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, both my breasts were very beautiful, full, rounded, and firm. Now, due to old age, they hang down like empty water-skins. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, my body was very beautiful, like a well-polished gold plate. Now, due to old age, it is covered with fine wrinkles. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.
217:
In the past, both my thighs were very beautiful, like the trunk of an elephant king. Now, due to old age, they have become like bamboo poles. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise (it is very true).

In the past, my calves, adorned with golden anklets, were very beautiful. Now, due to old age, they have become like dried sesame stalks. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

In the past, both my feet were very beautiful and soft, as if stuffed with cotton wool. Now, due to old age, they are wrinkled and cracked. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise.

This aggregate of a body was once of such a nature. Now, however, it is decayed and worn out, a dwelling place of many sufferings. It is like an old house with its plaster of old age peeling off. The word of the Buddha, the speaker of truth, is not otherwise. Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, 'kāḷakā' means having a black color. 'Bhamaravaṇṇasadisā' means that although they are black, they have a glossy blue color like the color of a bee; it means a smooth dark blue. 'Vellitaggā' means having curled tips; it means curled and wavy from the root to the tip. 'Muddhajā' means the hair. 'Jarāyā' means because of old age, having an appearance destroyed by old age. 'Sāṇavākasadisā' means like hemp or like bark; it also means like hemp and like makaci bark. 'Saccavādivacanaṃ anaññathā' means the word of the Blessed One, who speaks the truth and whose word is not false, such as "All form is impermanent, overcome by old age," is not otherwise, but is exactly as it is; it means there is nothing false in that word.

'Vāsitova surabhī karaṇḍako' means it is fragrant like a perfume casket scented and infused with flower scents, aromatic powders, and so on. 'Pupphapūra mama uttamaṅgajo' means my mass of hair in the past, which was filled with flowers such as jasmine, great jasmine, and Arabian jasmine...
218:
“Nimmala” means free from impurities. “Taṃ” refers to the hair growing on the head. That hair has now reached a state of smelling like fur, having only its natural animal scent. Alternatively, “salomagandhika” means having a scent similar to sheep’s wool. Some also say “the scent of goat’s hair.”

“Kānanaṃva sahitaṃ suropitaṃ” means (it was formerly) like a small garden well-planted, densely situated, growing only upwards, with straight and long branches. “Kocchasūcivicitaggasobhitaṃ” means in the past, the ends of the hair were beautiful and ornate by combing and using golden hairpins to arrange the tresses. Or, because of its thickness, it was like a comb, and the hair ends were beautiful because they were adorned with ivory hairpins. “Taṃ” refers to the hair growing on the head itself. “Viralaṃ tahiṃ tahiṃ” means the hair has become sparse and broken in various places.

“Kaṇhakhandhakasuvaṇṇamaṇḍitaṃ” refers to the mass of black hair adorned with gold, diamonds, and so on. For those who read “saṇhakaṇḍakasuvaṇṇamaṇḍitaṃ,” it means adorned by arranging the tresses with smooth golden hairpins. “Sobhate suveṇīhilaṅkataṃ” means it was beautiful in the past, being adorned with lovely braids of hair resembling garlands of golden cassia flowers. “Taṃ jarāya khalitaṃ siraṃ kataṃ” means that head, which was once so beautiful, has now become bald and has sparse, broken hair here and there due to old age.

“Cittakārasukatāva lekhikā” means beautiful like lines well-painted by a skilled artist with blue pigment. “Su bhamukā pure mama” means in the past, my lovely eyebrows attained beauty. “Valibhippalambitā” means (now) they remain hanging down due to the wrinkles that have appeared on the surface of the forehead.

“Bhassarā” means radiant. “Surucirā” means very beautiful. “Yathā maṇī” means (beautiful) like a ruby ring. “Nettahesuṃ” means they were beautiful eyes. “Abhinīlamāyatā” means they were very dark blue and long. “Te” refers to those eyes. “Jarāyabhihatā” means they have been afflicted by old age.
