“Saṇhatuṅgasadisī ca” means smooth, high, and fitting with the other parts of the face. “Sobhate” means my nose is beautiful like a rounded stick of yellow orpiment. “Su abhiyobbanaṃ pati” means although that nose was beautiful in the time of early youth, now, because its beauty has been obstructed by old age, it has become withered and like a leather thong.
219:
“Like a well-fashioned, well-finished bracelet” refers to the roundness like a well-crafted gold bracelet. “Sobhare” means they are beautiful. Alternatively, there is a variant reading “sobhante.” “Su” is merely an expletive particle. “Kaṇṇapāḷiyo” refers to the tips of the ears. “Hanging down with wrinkles” means they hang down, sagging like pieces of cloth pressed by a roller, being wrinkled by the lines that have appeared in various places.

“Resembling the color of a plantain bud” means having the color and shape similar to a plantain bud. “Broken” means they have reached a state of being jagged due to breaking and falling out. “Blackened” means they have become black due to the discoloration.

“Like a cuckoo that wanders in search of food within the forest, dwelling in the forest edge, and singing in the woods, I used to speak sweet words.” “Taṃ” refers to such warbling speech. “Faltering occurs in various places” means the voice has become faltering in various places due to broken teeth and so on.

“Well-polished like a smooth conch shell” means like a smooth golden conch shell that has been well-polished. “Broken and bent” means they have become as if broken and are bent due to the mass of veins becoming prominent because of the wasting away of the flesh.

“Having a comparison like a round door-bolt” means being exactly like a round door-bolt. “Tā” refers to both those arms. “Like a withered Pāṭalī branch” means they are like a Pāṭalī branch that is white and grey due to decay.

“Adorned with smooth rings and gold” means adorned with smooth, radiant rings made of gold. “Like a radish” means they are like radishes.

“Full and round, they rose up together side by side.” “Both my breasts were beautiful in the past” means both my breasts were formerly beautiful like golden jars, as described. Here, the singular form “sobhate” expresses a plural meaning, and the present tense expresses the past sense. “Hanging down like empty bags” means both those breasts of mine, no longer having liquid (milk) and having been drained, hang down like empty water-skins hung on a bamboo pole.
220:
It was as beautiful as a well-polished gold plate, or like a gold plate that had been rubbed with natural cinnabar and polished for a long time. 'That body of mine is now covered with fine wrinkles' means that my body is now spread with fine wrinkles here and there, having reached the state of wrinkled skin.

'The comparison is like an elephant's trunk' means it was just like the trunk of a noble elephant. In this context, the trunk is called 'bhoga' because it is used for eating. 'Te' refers to the thighs. 'Like bamboo tubes' means they have now become like bamboo joints.

'Adorned with smooth golden anklets' means they were decorated with bright and smooth golden anklets. 'Jaṅghā' refers to the shin bones. 'Tā' refers to those shins. 'Like dried sesame stalks' means that due to the lack of flesh and blood, they have become like dried sesame stalks left over after being harvested, in a state of emaciation. The letter 'ra' is for euphonic junction (padasandhi).

'The comparison is like being filled with silk-cotton' means they were like shoes filled and padded with soft and smooth silk-cotton. Those feet of mine are now cracked, split, and full of wrinkles.

'Such as this' means of such a nature. 'Ahu' means it has been. 'This heap of a body' refers to this body of mine. 'Jajjaro' means the bonds are loosened. 'The dwelling of many pains' means it is the abode of many sufferings caused by old age and so on. 'Apalepapatito' means this heap of a body is heading towards collapse and destruction because the 'plastering' of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) has been exhausted. It can also be analyzed as 'sopī alepapatito', with the same meaning. 'Jarāgharo' means it is like an old house, or it has become the house of old age. Therefore, the words of my Teacher, the Perfectly Enlightened One, who speaks the truth, who knows the true nature of things as they are and teaches them, and who speaks without deviation, are true and do not lead to any other state.

Thus, this Elder Nun, by contemplating the mark of impermanence in her own person, considered impermanence in all things of the three planes. Following that sequence, she applied the marks of suffering and non-self to those things, and by exerting herself in insight meditation, she reached Arahatship through the stages of the Path. This is stated in the Apadāna:

'The Great Sage named Phussa, who was wreathed in rays, appeared. I was the sister of that Blessed One, born into a kshatriya family.

I became a preacher of the Dhamma among the people in the Buddha's Dispensation and attended upon the Buddha. Because of that great learning (bāhusacca), I looked down upon the bhikkhunīs who cherished virtue. In this final existence, I was born in the noble city of Sāvatthī in the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, in the womb of a water-carrying slave.

When I went to fetch water, I saw a Brahmin in the middle of the water, tormented by the cold, reciting and chanting the Vedas. Seeing that Brahmin, I spoke these words:

"Venerable sir, I am a water-carrier who must always descend into the water in the cold season because I fear the danger of the staff of my masters, and because I am tormented by the danger of their verbal abuse and anger."

"O Great Brahmin, fearing what danger do you always descend into the water? Why do you endure the intense cold with limbs trembling?"

"O young girl Puṇṇā, why do you ask me when you already know that I am performing meritorious deeds that can block and prevent the evil kamma already committed?"

"Whether old or young, whoever commits an evil deed, that person can be liberated from the evil committed through bathing in water," the Brahmin replied.

I then spoke words of Dhamma concerning cause and effect to the Brahmin who had come up from the water. Hearing that Dhamma, the Brahmin was struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, and became an Arahant.

Because I was born when one person was needed to complete a hundred slaves, they named me Puṇṇā. Those masters gave me my freedom from slavery.

Then, after asking permission from the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, I entered the monkhood and soon reached Arahatship.

O Buddha, I am proficient in the field of psychic powers, in the divine ear (dibba-sota), and in the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa).

I know the succession of aggregates (khandha) lived in previous lives. I have purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). I have exhausted all taints (āsava). Now, there is no further rebirth for me. By the power of the Buddha—

My knowledge has become stainless and pure in the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight of Dhamma, the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and likewise in the analytical insight of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).

Through the practice of meditation, I possess great wisdom. Through much hearing, I possess great learning. Because of pride, I was born in a low caste. Truly, the kamma one has committed does not disappear. We have burned away the defilements. The Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.'

Having reached Arahatship and reflecting on her own practice, she recited these verses as an inspired utterance (udāna): "I am a water-carrier in the cold season... I am a Veda-knower who has bathed."

236. I am a water-carrier who must always descend into the water in the cold season because I fear the danger of the staff of my masters, and because I am tormented by the danger of their verbal abuse and anger.

O Great Brahmin, fearing what danger do you always descend into the water? Why do you endure the intense cold with limbs trembling?

O Puṇṇā, why do you ask me when you already know that I am performing meritorious deeds that can block and prevent the evil kamma already committed?

Whether old or young, whoever commits an evil deed, that person can be liberated from the evil committed through bathing in water.

O Great Brahmin, what ignorant person, not knowing the fruit of kamma, told you, who also do not know the fruit of kamma, that "one is liberated from evil through bathing in water"?

If that were so, then all the frogs, turtles, nagas, crocodiles, and other fish and sea monsters that live in the water would also go to heaven.

Sheep-butchers, pig-butchers, fishermen, hunters, thieves, executioners, and all other evildoers would also be liberated from their evil deeds through bathing in water.

If these rivers, such as the Aciravatī, could wash away the many evil deeds you have committed in the past...
221: Having heard the Dhamma of that Blessed One, with a heart full of faith, I gave a great gift and made a wish to be endowed with beauty. Thirty-one aeons ago from now, the Buddha Sikhī, the supreme leader of the world, the light of the world, the refuge of the three worlds, the Conqueror, appeared. At that time, in the delightful city of Aruṇapura, having been born into a Brahmin family, I insulted a bhikkhunī whose mind was liberated, out of anger. Having insulted her thus, "You are like a prostitute of bad conduct, a destroyer of the Buddha's Dispensation," because of that evil deed, I went to a dreadful hell and experienced great suffering. Passing away from there, I was born in the human world in poverty. For ten thousand births, I had to be a prostitute. I could not escape from that evil deed, just like one who has swallowed poison. I practiced the holy life in the Dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa. Due to the result of that deed, I was born in the celestial city. In my final birth, I was born spontaneously (opapātika). Because I was born among the branches of a mango tree, I am called "Ambapālī." Surrounded by tens of millions of beings, I went forth in the Buddha's Dispensation. Now I have reached the unshakable state of Nibbāna, and I am the heart-born daughter of the Buddha. I have mastery over psychic powers and the divine ear element. I have mastery over the knowledge of encompassing the minds of others, O Great Sage. I know my past lives, and my divine eye is purified. All taints are exhausted; now there is no more rebirth. In the analytical insights of meaning, truth, language, and eloquence, my knowledge is stainless and pure by the grace of the Buddha. My defilements are burnt away; all existences are uprooted. Like an elephant that has broken its bonds, I live free from taints.
222:
"My coming to the presence of the Buddha was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been accomplished.

The four analytical insights, these eight liberations, and the six supernormal powers have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been accomplished." (She said thus).

Having reached Arahantship and reflecting on her own practice, she uttered these very verses as an inspired utterance (udāna).

## The Commentary on the Verses of Ambapālī Therī is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Verses of Rohiṇī Therī

The verse beginning with "Samaṇā" is the verse of Rohiṇī Therī. This Elder Nun also had performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas and accumulated merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth in various existences. Counting back ninety-one aeons from now, during the time of the Buddha Vipassī, she was born in a good family. When she reached the age of discretion, one day, seeing the Blessed One wandering for alms in the city of Bandhumatī, she took his bowl, filled it with cakes, and offered it. Filled with joy and happiness, she paid homage with the fivefold prostration.

Due to that meritorious deed, wandering among devas and humans, and having accumulated the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra) in due course, she was born in this Buddha's era in the city of Vesālī in the house of a wealthy Brahmin. Named "Rohiṇī," when she reached the age of discretion, while the Teacher was staying in Vesālī, she went to the monastery, heard the Dhamma, and became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). She preached the Dhamma to her parents, inspired faith in them for the Dispensation, and after obtaining their permission, she herself went forth. Practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights before long. Regarding that, it is said (in the Apadāna):

"In the city of Bandhumatī,
while the Great Sage Vipassī
was wandering for alms,
I then offered him a cake.

Due to that well-performed deed,
and because of my intention and aspiration,
having inspired faith in my heart for that Buddha,
I reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven."
223:
I have been the chief queen of thirty-six kings of gods; I have been the chief queen of fifty universal monarchs. Everything I desired in my mind was fulfilled for me. I enjoyed prosperity among both gods and humans. Having reached my final existence, I was born into a Brahmin family and was cherished by my relatives under the name Rohinī. Having gone to the presence of the monks and heard the Dhamma as it truly is, with a mind full of spiritual urgency, I renounced the world and went forth into homelessness. Striving with wise reflection, I attained Arahatship. Because of the gift of a cake I gave ninety-one aeons ago, I have never known a miserable rebirth. This is the fruit of giving a cake. My defilements are burnt away... the Buddha's teaching has been accomplished.

After attaining Arahatship, reflecting on her own practice, she uttered as an inspired utterance the verses spoken between her father and herself when she was previously a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna):

'O lady, you say "monk" when you sleep, and you say "monk" when you wake. You only praise the virtues of monks; surely you will become a nun. You give abundant food and drink to the monks. Rohinī, I ask you now: why are those monks dear to you?

They do not desire work, they are lazy, they live on what others give, they are full of longing and desire for delicious things. Why are those monks dear to you?'

'Father, you have questioned me about the monks for a long time. I shall describe to you their wisdom, virtue, and effort. They desire work, they are not lazy, they perform the noblest of deeds. They abandon lust and hatred; therefore, those monks are dear to me.

Those who perform pure deeds destroy the three roots of evil. All evil is abandoned in them; therefore, those monks are dear to me.'

(Nissaya Commentary) At various desired times, one had to descend into the water. Descending into the water, one had to fetch water. This is the meaning. Because of being oppressed by the fear of the master's rod, the fear of verbal punishment such as abuse, and the fear of anger, one had to descend into the water even in cold weather.

237. Then one day, when a slave girl named Puṇṇā went to the landing place to fetch water with a pot, she saw a Brahmin who, despite the intense cold of the snowy season, had descended into the water early in the morning, immersed himself including his head, recited mantras, and was now shivering with his teeth chattering as he came out of the water. Seeing that Brahmin, with a compassionate heart and wishing to free him from that wrong view, she asked: 'Brahmin, because of what fear do you always descend into the water, both evening and morning? Why are you enduring the suffering of this extreme cold which is so hard to bear?'

238. The Brahmin said: 'O Puṇṇā, I am performing wholesome kamma by bathing in this way, which can prevent the bad kamma I have committed. Why do you ask when you already know this? Is this reason not well-known in the world? Whether an adult or a youth, if someone has committed a bad deed, they can surely be liberated from that bad deed by bathing.'

240. Hearing those words, Puṇṇā replied: 'What fool told you this, you who do not know the fruit of kamma? The words of such a person are not to be believed, nor are they logical. If one could be liberated from bad deeds by bathing, then the nagas, crocodiles, fish, and tortoises in the water would all go to heaven. Would the sheep-slaughterers, pig-slaughterers, fishermen, hunters, and executioners also be liberated from their bad deeds? If these rivers could carry away the bad deeds you committed in the past, could they not also carry away your good deeds?'
224:
Their bodily actions are pure, their verbal actions are likewise pure, and their mental actions are pure. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They are stainless like a well-polished conch shell, pure both internally and externally, and full of bright, wholesome qualities. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They are very learned (bahussuta), they are bearers of the Dhamma (dhammadhara), they are noble (ariya), they live according to the Dhamma, and they teach the meaning and the Dhamma. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They are very learned, they are bearers of the Dhamma, they are noble, they live according to the Dhamma, they have one-pointed minds, and they are endowed with mindfulness. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They possess wisdom that can reach distant objects, they are mindful, they speak with reflection, they are not restless, and they know the end of suffering. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

From whatever village they depart, they do not look back at anything; they go away without any attachment. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They do not store alms-food in granaries, nor in pots, nor in baskets; they seek only food that is already prepared. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

They do not accept gold, nor coins, nor silver; they subsist only on what they receive in the present. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

Though they have gone forth from various families and various regions, they love one another. For that reason, those monks are dear to me.

Rohinī, you were indeed born in our family for our welfare. You have faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and you have intense respect for them.

You truly know the incomparable, supreme field of merit (puññakkhetta). May these monks also accept our offerings.

Our noble sacrifice will be enduring and abundant. If you are afraid of suffering, if suffering is unpleasant to you,

Then go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, who are endowed with such qualities. Undertake the precepts. That will lead to your welfare.
225:
"I go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saᅅgha of the Stable One (Tādi). I undertake the precepts; that will be for my benefit.

In the past, I was a 'relative of Brahmins' (Brahmabandhu) merely by birth; but now, I am a true Brahmin. I am one with the three knowledges (tevijja), a master of lore (sottiya), a knower of the Vedas (vedagũ), and one who has bathed (snātaka)." He recited these verses.

Among those verses, the first three were spoken by the Brahmin who did not wish for his daughter to have faith in the monks. In that verse, "monks" means: O lady, even while you are asleep, you sleep praising them, saying "monks, monks," speaking only words related to monks. "You wake up saying 'monks'" means that even when rising from bed, you wake up and rise from sleep saying "monks." "You praise only the monks" means that at all times, you praise and extol either the monks themselves or the virtues of the monks. "You will surely become a nun (samaᅇĩ)" means that although you remain in the form of a layperson, he thinks you will surely be a nun in mind. Alternatively, "You will surely become a nun" means that although you remain in the form of a layperson now, because your nature is inclined only toward the monks, he thinks you will surely become a nun before long.

"Gives" means bestows. "Rohiᅇĩ, now I shall ask" means: Dear daughter Rohiᅇĩ, I shall now ask you—thus the Brahmin spoke while questioning his daughter. "Why are the monks dear to you?" means: Dear daughter Rohiᅇĩ, whether you are sleeping, waking, or at other times, you only praise the virtues of the monks; for what reason have the monks become ones who should be loved and cherished by you? This is the meaning.

Now, the Brahmin, wishing to tell his daughter the faults of the monks, spoke the verse beginning with "Akammakāmā." In that verse, "akammakāmā" means they do not desire work; they have no desire to perform any task that brings benefit to themselves or others. "Alasā" means they are lazy. "Those who live depending on what others give" means those whose nature is to live only on the requisites donated by others. "Āsaᅃsukā" means those who hope for and expect alms-food, robes, and so on from those very people. "Sādukāmā" means those who desire only delicious and sweet food. In all these words, the Brahmin, not knowing the virtues of the monks, spoke of faults he had imagined himself.
226: Upon hearing those words, Rohiᅇĩ thought, "Now I have gained the opportunity to speak of the virtues of the noble ones," and with a joyful heart, wishing to praise the virtues of the monks, she first expressed the joy of such praise and spoke the verse: "Father, it is only after a long time (that you ask me)." In that verse, "cirassaᅃ vata" means only after a long time. "Tātā" is an address to the father. "Samaᅇānaᅃ" means questioning about the monks or about the monks whom I love and cherish. "Tesaᅃ" means of those monks. "Paāsĩlaparakkamaᅃ" refers to wisdom, virtue, and energetic effort. "Kittayissāmi" means I shall tell. Having promised to speak (of their virtues), she first cleared away the faults spoken by her father, such as "those who do not want to work, the lazy ones," and to show the virtues that are the opposite of those faults, she spoke the verse beginning with "Kammakāmā." Therein, "kammakāmā" means they are "those who desire work" because they wish to fulfill the duties of a monk, such as the major and minor obligations (vatta-paᅩivatta). Since they are endowed with endeavor in those monastic duties and strive with rising energy, they are not lazy, and thus are called "analasā—the not-lazy." Because they perform only that work which is noble and leads to Nibbāna, they are called "doers of the best work." In doing so, because their practice is blameless, they abandon lust and hatred. The monks perform their work in this way so that lust and hatred may be eliminated. "Tena me samaᅇā piyā" means that because of such right practice, the monks are loved and cherished by me. "Tĩᅇi pāpassa mũlāni" refers to the three roots of unwholesome action: greed, hatred, and delusion. "Dhunanti" means they shake off or abandon. "Sucikārino" means those who habitually perform blameless deeds. "Sabbaᅃ pāpaᅃ pahĩnesaᅃ" means that through the attainment of the Path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga), all evil has been abandoned by those monks. In this way, to explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as "the monks are performers of pure deeds," she spoke the verse beginning with "Kāyakammaᅃ." That verse is very easy to understand. "Vimalā saᅃkhamuttāva" means they are free from stains like a well-washed conch or a pearl, being free from the stains of defilements such as lust. "Suddhā santarabāhirā" means they are pure both internally and externally, meaning they have pure intentions (āsaya) and efforts (payoga). "Puᅇᅇā sukkāna dhammānaᅃ" means they are full of purely bright and blameless qualities, being endowed with the aggregates of virtue (sĩlakkhandha) and so on of an Asekha (one beyond training).
227: ## Because of having heard much of the Dhamma such as Sutta and Geyya, or because of the arising of wisdom through hearing, one is called 'learned' (bahussuta). It means being endowed with the great learning of the scriptures (pariyatti-bāhusacca) and the great learning of penetration (paṭivedha-bāhusacca). Because of bearing that twofold Dhamma, one is called a 'bearer of the Dhamma' (dhammadhara). Because they are far from defilements through the training rules of conduct and behavior for beings, they are called 'Noble Ones' (ariya). Because of living by the Dhamma and in a righteous way, they are called 'living by the Dhamma' (dhammajīvī). 'They teach the meaning and the Dhamma' means they speak and reveal the meaning of what is spoken and the Dhamma of the teaching. Alternatively, they teach and point out the Dhamma that is not devoid of meaning and the meaning that is not devoid of Dhamma. 'Ekaggacittā' means those with a concentrated mind. 'Satimanto' means those with established mindfulness. 'Dūraṅgamā' (far-going) means those who have gone to the forest, leaving the vicinity of humans and going far away. Or, they are called 'dūraṅgamā' because they can go to a distant place as they wish by means of psychic power. 'Mantā' refers to wisdom; because of the habit of speaking with that wisdom, one is called a 'wise speaker' (mantabhāṇī). 'Na uddhatā' means those who are not restless, having a peaceful mind free from agitation (uddhacca). 'Dukkhassantaṃ pajānanti' means they penetrate Nibbāna, which is the end of the suffering of the round of rebirths. 'Na vilokenti kiñcanaṃ' means that from whichever village they depart, they do not look back with a sense of attachment at any being or conditioned thing in that village, but rather they go and depart with detachment. 'Na te saṃ koṭṭhe openti' means those monks do not put or store their own property in granaries, because they do not have such possessions. 'Kumbhiṃ' means in a pot. 'Khaḷopiyaṃ' means in a basket. 'Pariniṭṭhitamesānā' means they seek only the food that has been prepared in the houses of others for the sake of others. 'Hirañña' means coins (kahāpaṇa). 'Rūpiya' means silver. 'Paccuppannena yāpenti' means they do not sorrow over the past nor do they long for the future, but they subsist on the present and maintain their existence. 'Aññamaññaṃ pihayanti' means they develop loving-kindness toward one another. There is also a variant reading 'pihāyanti', which has the same meaning. Thus, that Brahmin, having heard the virtues of the monks from his daughter, with a confident mind, praised his daughter, saying, 'It is indeed for our benefit,' and so on. 'Amhampi' means 'for us also'. 'Dakkhiṇā' means a gift to be offered (deyyadhamma).
228:
"Ettha" means "among these monks." "Yañña" means the practice of giving. "Vipula" means having extensive fruits. The rest is as previously stated.

Thus, that Brahmin, established in the refuges and the precepts, later experienced spiritual urgency (saṃvega), ordained, developed insight (vipassanā), and became established in the fruit of Arahantship. Reflecting on his own practice and uttering an exclamation of joy (udāna), he spoke the verse beginning with "Brahmabandhu." The meaning of that verse is the same as what was stated below.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Rohinī Therī is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Verses of Cāpā Therī

The verse beginning with "Laṭṭhihattho pure āsi" is that of Cāpā Therī. This Therī had also performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome merit that serves as a support for liberation from the cycle of rebirth (vaṭṭa) in various existences. Having the root of merit accumulated in succession and having the requisites for liberation (vimokkha) fulfilled, she was born in this Buddha's era as the daughter of a head hunter in a certain hunter village in the Vanga country. Her name was Cāpā. At that time, Upaka the Ājīvaka met the Blessed One, who was traveling from the Bodhi tree towards Vārāṇasī to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. He asked the Blessed One: "Friend, your faculties are very clear, your complexion is pure and bright. Under whom, friend, have you ordained? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you prefer?"

"I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all, unstained by all things, having renounced all, liberated in the destruction of craving. Having realized it myself, whom should I point to as a teacher?

I have no teacher, no one like me exists. In the world with its devas, there is no person to rival me."
229:
“I am indeed the Arahant in the world; I am the incomparable Teacher. I alone am the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha); I am cooled and extinguished (nibbuta). To set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, I go to the city of Kāsī. In this world become blind, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless (Amata).”

When the Blessed One thus announced his state of Omniscient Buddhahood and his intention to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, Upaka the Ājīvaka, with a settled mind, said, “It may be so, friend; you deserve to be the Infinite Victor (Anantajina).” Having said this, he turned away from the path and departed, going to the region of Vangahāra. There, he lived depending on a certain hunters' village. The head hunter of that village attended to him. One day, as the head hunter was about to go far for hunting, he instructed his daughter Cāpā, “Do not neglect my Arahant,” and went away with his sons and brothers. That hunter's daughter was very beautiful and lovely to behold.

Then, at the time for alms-round, Upaka the Ājīvaka went to the hunter's house. Seeing Cāpā approaching to serve him, he was overcome by lust. Unable even to eat, he took his bowl of food, went back to his dwelling, placed the food aside, and lay down without eating, thinking, “If I get Cāpā, I shall live; if not, I shall die.” On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter, “Did you attend to my Arahant without neglect?” She replied, “He came only on the first day and has not returned since.” The hunter immediately went to Upaka's dwelling and, massaging his feet, asked, “Venerable sir, what is your ailment?” Upaka only groaned and rolled about. The hunter said, “Tell me, venerable sir; whatever I can do, I will do it all.” Upaka revealed his desire through a certain means. The other asked, “But do you know any craft, venerable sir?” “I do not,” he replied. “Venerable sir, it is not possible to maintain a household without knowing any craft.” Upaka said, “Though I know no craft, I will carry meat for you and sell it as well.” The hunter said, “We also like this idea.” He gave him an upper garment, let him stay in a friend's house for a few days, and on a suitable day, brought him home and gave him his daughter.
230:
Then, as time passed, a son was born to them through their living together; they named him Subhadda. When the child cried, Cāpā mocked Upaka with a lullaby, saying, “Son of Upaka, son of the Ājīvaka, son of the meat-carrier, do not cry, do not cry,” and so on. Upaka said, “Cāpā, do not think of me as one without support; I have a friend named Anantajina (Infinite Victor). I shall go to him.” Knowing that he would get angry when she spoke thus, Cāpā continued to say the same thing repeatedly. One day, being provoked by Cāpā's words, he became angry and prepared to leave. Although she tried to appease him with various words, he remained unsatisfied and departed, heading towards the West.

At that time, the Blessed One, while staying at Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, told the monks, “Monks, if anyone comes to this monastery today and asks, ‘Where is Anantajina?’, send him to me.” Upaka, asking here and there, “Where does Anantajina live?”, eventually reached Sāvatthī. Entering the monastery and standing in the middle, he asked, “Where is Anantajina?” The monks led him to the Blessed One. Upon seeing the Blessed One, he said, “Does the Blessed One recognize me?” “Yes, I recognize you. But where have you been living all this time?” “In the region of Vangahāra, Bhante.” “Upaka, you have now grown old; will you still be able to ordain?” “I will ordain, Bhante,” he replied. The Teacher commanded a certain monk, “Come, monk, ordain this man.” That monk ordained him.

Having ordained and taken a subject of meditation from the Teacher, he applied himself to meditation and before long was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala). When he passed away, he was reborn in the Aviha realm, and at the very moment of rebirth, he attained Arahantship. Among the seven individuals who attained Arahantship upon being reborn in the Aviha realm, this Upaka was one. Thus it was said:

“Seven monks, reborn in Aviha, are liberated;
With lust and hatred destroyed, they have crossed over the attachment to the world.

Upaka, Phalagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti—these three,
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhuraggi, and Singiya;
Having abandoned the human body, they have transcended the divine bond.”
231:
When Upaka had departed, Cāpā, with a weary heart, entrusted her young son to his grandfather. Then, following the path previously taken by Upaka, she arrived at Sāvatthī and was ordained in the presence of the bhikkhunīs within the Buddha's Dispensation. While practicing insight meditation (Vipassanā), she attained Arahantship in due course. Reflecting on her own practice, she combined the verses previously spoken by Upaka and herself into an inspired utterance (udāna) and spoke thus:

“Formerly, he was one who held a staff in his hand; now, that same person has become a hunter. Sunk in the terrible mire of craving, he was unable to cross to the other shore.

Thinking of me as one who was deeply attached, Cāpā tried to please me with our young son. Having cut the bond of Cāpā, I shall go forth again.

O Great Hero, do not be angry with me. O Great Sage, do not be angry with me. For one overcome by anger, there is no purity; how then can there be ascetic virtue (tapo)?

I shall depart from Nālā village; let anger remain only in Nālā. Women bind with their feminine form those monks who live according to the Dhamma.

O Kāla, please come! Please return! Enjoy sensual pleasures as before. Both I and my relatives will submit to your will.

Cāpā, even if it were a quarter of what you say, to a man captivated by you, that would indeed be most delightful.

Like a Kālaṅginī tree (Takkarī) blooming on a mountain peak, like a young pomegranate tree in bloom, or like a Pāṭalī tree flowering in the middle of an island.

With my body anointed with red sandalwood, wearing the finest garments of Kāsī, endowed with beauty and tranquility—for whose sake will you abandon me and go?

Just as a fowler wishes to bind a bird, you shall no longer trouble me with this feminine form.

O Kāla, you have fathered this precious son with me. For whose sake will you abandon me, who has a son and is tranquil, and go?”
232:
“The wise abandon sons; then they abandon kinsmen and then wealth. Great heroes go forth from the world, just as a great elephant breaks its bonds.

Now I shall strike this son of yours with a stick or a knife, or dash him upon the ground; you shall not be able to go because of grief for your son.

O vile woman, even if you give the son to jackals or dogs, you will not be able to make me turn back for the sake of a son.

Well then, Venerable Kāla, where will you go now? To which village, market town, city, or royal capital?

Formerly we were leaders of a sect, not being monks but claiming to be monks; we wandered from village to village, and to cities and royal capitals.

This Blessed Buddha, near the Nerañjarā river, is teaching the Dhamma to living beings for the abandoning of all suffering. I shall go to that Blessed One; He shall be my Teacher.

Now, please convey my salutation to the Peerless Lord of the World. Having circumambulated Him, please dedicate the merit (dakkhiṇā) to me.

We can indeed do this matter as you say to me. Now I shall convey your salutation to the Peerless Lord of the World. Having circumambulated Him, I shall dedicate the merit to you.

Thereupon, Kāla departed toward the Nerañjarā river. He saw the Fully Enlightened One teaching the path to the Deathless (Nibbāna).

He taught suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcending of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Having paid homage to the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated Him, and having dedicated the merit to Cāpā, I have reached the state of a monk, free from the home life. The Three Knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled.” She spoke these verses.
233:
In this verse, ‘lāṭṭhihattho’ means a person with a staff in his hand (one who holds a staff with his hand). ‘Pure’ means in the past, during the time he was a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka), he used to wander around carrying a staff in his hand to ward off fierce oxen, dogs, and so on. ‘So dāni migaluddako’ means that this Upaka has now become a deer hunter (māgavika) who kills deer, living and eating together with other hunters. ‘Āsāya’ means because of craving (taṇhā). There is also a variant reading ‘āsayā,’ which means because of his disposition (ajjhāsaya). ‘Palipā’ refers to the mire of sensuality (kāma) and the mire of wrong views (diṭṭhi). ‘Ghorā’ means terrible or dreadful because it brings about many unknown harms; thus it is intense (ghora). ‘Nāsakkhi pārametave’ means he was unable to reach, or could not attain, Nibbāna, which is the other shore of that mire; Upaka says this referring to himself.

‘Sumattaṃ maṃ maññamānā’ means thinking of me as one who is well-intoxicated, or stuck through attachment to sensuality, or negligent. ‘Cāpā puttamatosayī’ means Cāpā, the daughter of the deer hunter, teased and played with the son, provoking me by saying, "Son of an Ājīvaka," and so on. There is also a reading ‘supati maṃ maññamānā,’ which means thinking that I am asleep. ‘Cāpāya bandhanaṃ chetvā’ means having cut the bond of defilements (kilesa) that had arisen within you towards Cāpā. ‘Pabbajissaṃ punopahaṃ’ means I shall go forth (become a monk) for a second time.

Now he says to Cāpā, "I have no need [for you] anymore." Hearing these words, Cāpā apologized and spoke a verse: "Do not be angry with me." In that verse, ‘mā me kujjhi’ means do not be angry with me just for making fun. She addresses Upaka as ‘Mahāvīra’ (Great Hero) and ‘Mahāmuni’ (Great Sage). This is because she knew that he had been a monk before and now wished to go forth again; thus, hoping for his forgiveness, she said ‘Mahāmuni.’ Therefore, it was said: "For one overcome by anger, there is no purity; how can there be ascetic virtue (tapa)?" The meaning is: if you cannot endure even this much, how will you restrain your mind, or how will you practice asceticism?

Then, when Cāpā asked, "Do you wish to go to Nālā village to make a living?" Upaka replied, "I shall depart from Nālā as well; who would live in Nālā?" Who indeed would live here in Nālā? I shall certainly depart from Nālā. That Nālā village was his birthplace; he left that village and went forth. That village is in the Magadha country, in a place near the Bodhimaṇḍa (the site of Enlightenment); it is said in reference to that village. ‘Bandhantī itthirūpena, samaṇe dhammajīvino’ means: Cāpā, you stand binding righteous monks who live according to the Dhamma with your female form and feminine gestures. Because of such binding, I have now become like this (a hunter); therefore, I renounce you—this is the meaning.
234:
When this was said, Cāpā, wishing to make him turn back, spoke the verse beginning with ‘Ehi, kāḷa.’ The meaning of that verse is: O Upaka, called Kāḷa because of your dark complexion, come, turn back, do not go away; enjoy sensual pleasures as before. I and all my relatives will be under your control (made to follow your will) because of our desire for you not to leave.

Hearing this, Upaka spoke the verse beginning with ‘Etto cāpe.’ In that verse, ‘cāpe’ is an address to Cāpā. She received the name Cāpā because her body was like a bow-string (cāpa); therefore, she is called Cāpā. O Cāpā, as you speak now, and what you say now—you should perform such pleasant conduct, which is only a fourth part of these sensual pleasures. To a man who is attached to you and overcome by lust, those words might indeed be excellent. But I am now disillusioned with you and with sensual pleasures; therefore, I do not abide by Cāpā's words—this is the meaning.

Again, Cāpā, wishing to arouse his attachment to her, spoke the verse beginning with ‘Kāḷaṅgini.’ In that verse, ‘kāḷā’ is an address to him. ‘Aṅgini’ means being endowed with [beautiful] limbs. ‘Iva’ is a particle used for comparison. It means like a young pomegranate tree in full bloom standing on a mountain top. Some also read ‘ukkāgāri,’ meaning like the structure of the body's limbs. The word ‘giri-muddhani’ (on the mountain top) is said to show a beauty that cannot be destroyed by anyone. Some read ‘kāliṅgini’ and say it means like a pumpkin vine. It means like a pomegranate tree in bloom, or like a flowering citron vine, or like a Pāṭali tree (trumpet flower tree) in bloom in the middle of an island. The mention of an island here is to show the extraordinary nature of the beauty.

‘Haricandanalittaṅgi’ refers to one whose entire body is smeared with red sandalwood. ‘Kāsikuttamadhārini’ refers to one wearing excellent cloth from the Kāsi country. ‘Taṃ maṃ’ refers to me, who is like that. ‘Rūpavatiṃ santiṃ’ means although being endowed with beauty. ‘Kassa ohāya gacchasi’ means for which being, or for what reason, or for what purpose do you leave, abandon, and renounce me?

After this, there are verses of their dialogue, and at the end, there are three verses. In those verses, ‘sākuntiko va’ means like a bird-hunter. ‘Āharimena rūpena’ means by decorating the body, such as dressing the hair, and so on...
235:
It means through physical appearance prepared with clothes, ornaments, and so forth, through reputation, and through skill and cleverness. "You will no longer be able to obstruct me" means that just as before, you are now unable to obstruct me.

'Puttaphala' means the fruit known as a son (childbirth).

'Sappaññā' means those who possess wisdom; the meaning is those endowed with wisdom that perceives the disadvantages in Saṃsāra. They renounce, leaving behind a circle of relatives and a mass of wealth, whether small or great. Therefore, it is said: "Great heroes go forth into homelessness, like an elephant (nāga) having broken its bonds." The meaning is that just as a great elephant breaks the bond of iron chains, only those with great energy go forth after breaking the bonds of household life, not those with inferior energy.

'Daṇḍena' means with any kind of stick. 'Churikāya' means with a razor. I will harass [him] by throwing [him] on the ground and beating or stabbing him, etc. "You shall not go because of grief for your son" means you will not go due to the cause of grief for your son.

'Padāhisi' means you will give. 'Puttakatte' means because of the son. 'Jammī' is an address to that woman, meaning a low or wretched woman.

Now, having permitted his departure, he spoke the verse beginning with "Handa kho" to let her know the place he is going.

The other person, showing "Formerly, I stood upholding a teaching that does not lead to liberation; but now, I wish to stand in the teaching of the Infinite Victor (Anantajina) which leads to liberation; therefore, I will go to that Buddha," spoke the words beginning with "Ahumbhā." Therein, 'gaṇino' means teachers of a group. 'Assamaṇā' means those with unpacified faults. 'Samaṇamānino' means those who imagine themselves to be those with pacified faults (recluses). "We wandered" is said by including himself among teachers such as Pūraṇa [Kassapa].

'Nerañjaraṃ pati' means near the Nerañjarā River, on its bank. 'Buddha' means one who has reached the knowledge of the Path of Arahatship and Omniscience. It is said with the meaning that the Blessed One resided right there for the entire time while he was enlightened and preaching the Dhamma.

"Now tell him of my salutation" means "Convey to the peerless Lord of the World (Lokanātha) my words of respect." "Having performed a circumambulation, point out the gift" means having circumambulated the Blessed Buddha three times, in the four...
236:
...places, having paid homage and sharing the portion of merit obtained therefrom, one should point out the circumambulation. He says this because of having heard of the Buddha's virtues before and because of being endowed with the right cause.

This indeed can be obtained by us means "This merit of performing circumambulation can be given to you by us, but returning [to household life] cannot be given, nor can the enjoyment of sensual pleasures as before." "Te vajjanti" means "I will speak of your salutation."

"So" means the time. "Addasāsī" means he saw.

In the teaching of the Blessed One, the talk on the Four Noble Truths is primary, and since there is nothing devoid of it, he spoke starting with "Dukkha" (suffering). The remaining meanings are just as previously explained.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Elder Cāpā is finished.

## 4. Commentary on the Verses of Elder Sundarī

The verse beginning with "Petāni bhoti puttāni" is the verse of Elder Sundarī. This elder also had performed meritorious services (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and accumulated wholesome deeds that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. Thirty-one aeons ago, during the time of Buddha Vessabhū, she was born in a good family home. Upon reaching the age of discretion, one day she saw the Teacher wandering for alms and, with a confident mind, offered alms-food and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. The Teacher, knowing the clarity of her mind, gave a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) and departed. Due to that meritorious deed, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, stayed there for the full lifespan enjoying divine bliss, and after passing away from there, wandered only in happy destinations (sugati). When her wisdom matured, in this Buddha's era, she was born as the daughter of a Brahmin named Sujāta in the city of Vārāṇasī. Because of her physical beauty, she was named Sundarī. When she reached the age of maturity, her younger brother passed away. Then her father, overcome by grief for his son, wandered from place to place and met Elder Vāsiṭṭhī. When he asked about the cause for dispelling grief, she spoke the two verses beginning with "Petāni bhoti puttāni." The elder, knowing that the Brahmin was overcome by grief and wishing to dispel his grief, spoke the two verses beginning with "Bahūni puttasatāni" and told him about her own state of being free from grief.
237:
Hearing those words, the Brahmin asked, "Lady, how have you become so free from sorrow?" The Theri then explained the virtues of the Triple Gem to him.

Then the Brahmin asked, "Where does the Teacher reside?" and hearing that "He is currently staying in Mithilā," he immediately had the chariot prepared and went to Mithilā by chariot. Approaching the Teacher, he paid homage, engaged in pleasant conversation, and sat at a respectful distance. The Teacher taught him the Dhamma. Having heard the Dhamma, he gained faith, ordained, and while practicing insight meditation with great effort, he attained Arahantship on the third day.

Then the charioteer took the chariot back to Bārāṇasī and informed the Brahmin woman of these events. When Sundarī heard that her father had ordained, she asked her mother for permission, saying, "Mother, I too will ordain." The mother said, "All the wealth in this house belongs to you. You are the heir to this family; take possession and enjoy all this wealth. Do not ordain." She replied, "Mother, wealth is of no use to me. I will certainly ordain." Having obtained her mother's permission, she renounced the great wealth like a glob of spit and ordained.

After ordaining, while still a trainee (sikkhamānā), she developed insight meditation and strove hard. Because her past perfections were complete and her wisdom had matured, she attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Regarding this, it is said in the Apadāna:

"While the Great Sage Vessabhū was walking for alms, I took a spoonful of food and offered it to the Excellent Buddha.

Having accepted it, the Fully Enlightened One, Vessabhū, the Leader of the World, standing in the street, the Teacher gave me a blessing (anumodanā).

By giving a spoonful of alms, you will go to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. You will be the chief queen of thirty-six kings of the gods.

You will be the chief queen of fifty wheel-turning monarchs. Whatever you desire in your heart, you will always obtain it all.

Having enjoyed prosperity, you will ordain without anxiety. By fully understanding all taints (āsavas), you will attain Nibbāna, free from taints."
(Thus he spoke).
238:
"Having said this, the Fully Enlightened One, Vessabhū, the Leader of the World, the Hero, rose into the sky like a king of swans in the air.

My gift was well-given, a supreme offering; the perfection of the gruel offering was well-sacrificed. By giving a spoonful of alms, I have reached the unshakable state (Nibbāna).

Counting from now, thirty-one aeons ago, I gave that gift. Because of the merit of that gift of alms, I have never known a miserable rebirth (duggati).

My defilements are burnt up... the Buddha's teaching has been carried out."

Having thus attained Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of fruition (phalasukha) and the bliss of Nibbāna, she later thought, "I will utter a lion's roar (sīhanāda) in the presence of the Teacher." Having asked permission from her preceptor (upajjhāya), she departed from Bārāṇasī. Accompanied by many bhikkhunīs, she gradually reached Sāvatthī and approached the Teacher. After paying homage to the Teacher, she stood at a respectful distance. Having received the Teacher's welcome, she made known her Arahantship by manifesting her status as the Teacher's heart-born daughter and so on. Then, her relatives and attendants, led by her mother, ordained. Later, reflecting on her own practice, she uttered these inspired verses (udāna), beginning with the verse spoken by her father:

"O Lady, in the past you used to eat (grieve for) your dead sons; day and night, you suffered excessively.

O Brahmin woman Vāseṭṭhī, today, though you have 'eaten' a hundred sons, why do you not suffer intensely?"

"O Brahmin, in the past, hundreds of my sons and hundreds of my relatives have been 'eaten' by you and me (in saṃsāra).

Having known the escape from birth (jāti) and death (maraṇa), I no longer sorrow, I no longer weep, nor do I suffer."

"O Vāseṭṭhī, it is truly wonderful! You speak such words. Having understood whose Dhamma do you speak such words?"

"O Brahmin, this Fully Enlightened One, who has arrived at the city of Mithilā, teaches the Dhamma to living beings for the abandonment of all suffering."
239:
"O Brahmin, having heard the Dhamma from that Arahant who is free from acquisitions (upadhi), and having understood the True Dhamma therein, I have dispelled the sorrow for my son.

I, too, shall go towards the city of Mithilā. Perhaps that Blessed One will release me from all suffering."

The Brahmin saw the Buddha, who is fully released and free from acquisitions. The Sage (muni), who has reached the far shore of suffering, taught the Dhamma to that Brahmin.

(He taught) suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcending of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering.

Having understood the True Dhamma therein, he delighted in ordination. Sujāta the Brahmin attained the three knowledges (tevijjā) in just three days.

"Come, charioteer, go! I hand over this chariot to you. Tell the Brahmin woman of my well-being: 'Now the Brahmin has ordained; Sujāta has attained the three knowledges in just three days.'"

Then the charioteer, taking the chariot and a thousand pieces of money, told the Brahmin woman of his well-being: "Now the Brahmin has ordained; Sujāta has attained the three knowledges in just three days."

"O charioteer, having heard about the Brahmin who possesses the three knowledges, I give you this horse-drawn chariot and a thousand pieces of money as a gift."

"O Brahmin woman, let the horse-drawn chariot and the thousand pieces of money be yours alone. I, too, shall ordain in the presence of the One of Excellent Wisdom."

"O Sundarī, your father has renounced elephants, cattle, horses, jeweled earrings, and this abundant household wealth to ordain. You are the heir in this family; enjoy the wealth."
240:
“Having abandoned elephants, cattle, horses, jewels, earrings, and this delightful household wealth, my father, tormented by grief for his son, has gone forth [into homelessness]. I too shall go forth, tormented by grief for my brother.”

“O Sundarī, may that intention you desire be fulfilled for you. Scraps of food obtained by alms, gleaning, and rag-robes—those who can master these are free from taints (āsavas) in the next life.”

“O Noble Lady, while I was practicing as a trainee (sikkhamānā), the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) was purified. I know my past lives, where I lived before.”

“O beautiful Elder Nun, who graces the Saṅgha, depending on you, I have attained the three knowledges (tevijjā) and fulfilled the Buddha's teaching.”

“O Noble Lady, please grant me permission. I wish to go to Sāvatthī. I shall roar a lion's roar in the presence of the Great Buddha.”

“Sundarī, behold the Teacher, of golden hue and bright skin, the tamer of the untamed, the Fully Enlightened One, who is fearless.”

“Behold this Sundarī coming, liberated, free from acquisitions (nirūpadhi), free from lust, detached, having done what was to be done, and free from taints.”

“O Great Hero, having departed from Bārāṇasī, I have come into your presence. Your disciple Sundarī pays homage at your feet.”

“You are the Buddha, you are the Teacher. O Brahmin, I am your daughter, born of your breast, born from your mouth [the Dhamma], having done what was to be done, and free from taints.”

“O auspicious one, welcome to you; your coming is not ill-fated. For thus do the tamed come to pay homage at the Teacher's feet—free from lust, detached, having done what was to be done, and free from taints.” Thus, he spoke these verses in response.

“I am the incomparable, supreme, and unique Fully Enlightened One, the Teacher of gods and men. I am cooled, having extinguished the fires of defilements. I shall go to Bārāṇasī of the Kāsi people to set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. In this world shrouded in darkness, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.” When the Blessed One made known his state of omniscience and his intention to preach the Dhammacakka, that Upaka the ascetic, with a clear mind, said, “Friend, you are worthy to be the Infinite Victor (Anantajina),” and taking a path that was not the main road, he departed and went to the Vaṅgahāra country. In that Vaṅgahāra country, he lived depending on a small hunter's village, and the head hunter attended to him. One day, when the head hunter was about to go to a distant forest, he instructed his daughter Cāpā, “Do not be negligent toward my Arahant,” and went away with his sons and brothers. That daughter was very beautiful and lovely to behold. Then, when Upaka the ascetic went to the hunter's house at the time of alms-round, he saw Cāpā who came to serve him. Overcome and tormented by lust, he could not even eat the alms-food; he took the food back to his place and lay there without eating or drinking, thinking, “If I get Cāpā, I shall live; if not, I shall die.” On the seventh day, the hunter returned and asked his daughter, who said, “He came only one day and has not returned since.” The hunter went to Upaka's place, massaged his feet, and asked about his illness. As Upaka was groaning and tossing about, the hunter said, “Venerable sir, tell me; I will do everything I can.” Upaka then expressed his desire through a pretext. The hunter said, “Venerable sir, do you know any craft? It is not possible to live in a house without knowing a craft.” Upaka replied, “Even if I know no craft, I will be your meat-carrier and meat-seller.” The hunter agreed, gave him an upper garment, and married him to his daughter. As time passed, a son named Subhadda was born to them. When the child cried, Cāpā would mock Upaka with a lullaby, saying, “Hey, son of Upaka, son of the meat-carrier, do not cry.” Upaka said, “I have a friend named Anantajina; I shall go to him.” But as Cāpā continued to mock him repeatedly, Upaka became angry and set out toward the west. At that time, while the Blessed One was staying at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, he told the monks, “Monks, today there will be someone coming to ask, 'Where is the Anantajina?'”
241:
In that Pali, 'petāni' means those who have died. 'Bhotī' is a word used to address that woman. 'Puttāni' is spoken with a change of gender and refers to the dead sons. In reality, although only one son of that woman had died, the Brahmin spoke in the plural because he perceived, 'This woman has been wandering about tormented by grief for a long time; I think many of her sons have died.' Therefore, he said, 'Having today eaten all hundred sons.' 'Khādamānā' (eating) is merely a word of reproach according to worldly usage. In the world, when the children of a certain woman die as soon as they are born, those who blame her usually say 'child-eater' and so on. 'Atīva' means exceedingly. 'Paritappasi' means you grieve or burn, and it should be connected with the word 'pure' (formerly). The summary meaning here is: 'Lady Vāseṭṭhī, formerly you wandered through villages, towns, and royal capitals, being extremely overwhelmed by grief, mourning and weeping because you had a dead son.'

'Sājjā' is 'sā ajja', meaning 'that you today', and it implies 'that you now'. There is also a variant reading 'sajjā'. 'Kena vaṇṇena' means 'for what reason'. The Elder Nun also uses the word 'khāditāni' in the same metaphorical sense as the Brahmin. Or, she says 'khāditāni' referring to species such as tigers, leopards, and cats. 'Atītaṃse' means in the past portion, in past lives. 'Mama tuyhañca' means 'of mine and of yours'. 'Nissaraṇaṃ ñatvā jātiyā maraṇassa ca' means because of penetrating and knowing through Path-knowledge Nibbāna, which is the escape from birth, aging, and death. 'Na cāpi paritappayiṃ' means there is no more grieving, no more intense distress; it means 'I no longer reach the state of intense distress'.

'Abbhutaṃ vata' means 'how wonderful indeed'. Something that has never happened before is called 'abbhuta'. 'Edisiṃ' means of such a nature, referring to the words showing the absence of grief, etc., such as 'I no longer grieve, I no longer weep, I no longer burn intensely'. 'Kassa tvaṃ dhammamaññāya' means that since it is impossible to obtain such a Dhamma from anyone else, 'Having known whose Teacher's Dhamma do you speak such words?'—thus asking about the Teacher and the Dispensation. 'Nirūpadhiṃ' means free from suffering. 'Viññātasaddhammā' means having penetrated and realized the Dhamma of the Noble Truths. 'Vyapānudiṃ' means having removed or dispelled.
242: "Vippamutta" means one who is completely liberated, free from all defilements and all existences. "Swassa" means may that Fully Enlightened One be the refuge of that Brahmin. "Tattha" means in that teaching of the Four Noble Truths. "Rathaṃ niyyādayāhimaṃ" means hand over this chariot to the Brahmin woman. "Sahassañcāpi" means take also the thousand Kahāpaṇas brought for travel expenses and hand them over. "Assarathaṃ" means a chariot yoked with horses. "Puṇṇapattaṃ" means a gift given with joy. While this joyful gift was being given to the Brahmin woman, the charioteer did not accept the gift and, saying the verse "May it be yours alone," went to the Buddha and ordained. When the charioteer had ordained, the Brahmin woman called her daughter Sundarī and, urging her toward the household life, spoke the verse beginning with "Hatthī gavassaṃ." In that verse, "Hatthī" means elephants. "Gavassaṃ" means cattle and horses. "Maṇikuṇḍalañca" means gems and earrings. "Phītañcimaṃ gahavibhavaṃ pahāya" means having abandoned this abundant household wealth, including elephants and the like, as well as the aforementioned or unmentioned fields, plots, gold, silver, and all other household items and male and female servants, your father has ordained. "Bhuñja bhogāni Sundarī" means Sundarī, enjoy these pleasures. "Tuvaṃ dāyādikā kule" means you are the one worthy of the inheritance in this family. Hearing those words, Sundarī, expressing her desire for renunciation, spoke the verse beginning with "Hatthīgavassaṃ." Then the mother, encouraging her daughter in renunciation itself, spoke a verse and a half beginning with "So te ijjhatu." In that verse, "Yaṃ tvaṃ patthesi Sundarī" means Sundarī, what you now aspire to and desire. "So te pabbajjāya saṅkappo" means may that intention and desire of yours for ordination be fulfilled without obstacle. "Uttiṭṭhapiṇḍo" means alms-food obtained by standing at house after house. "Uñcho" means the wandering from house to house for that alms-food and standing at the intended places. "Etāni" means those alms-gathering activities and so forth. "Abhisambhontī" means accomplishing and carrying out without weariness, relying on the strength of one's feet. Then Sundarī, consenting to her mother's words saying "Very well, mother," left the house, went to the bhikkhunī monastery, and while still a sikkhamānā, realized the Three Knowledges...
243: "I shall go to the presence of the Buddha," she informed her preceptor and went to Sāvatthī together with the bhikkhunīs. Therefore, it was said: "Sikkhamānāya me, ayye," and so forth. There, "Sikkhamānāya me" means by me, who am a sikkhamānā. "Ayye" is the addressing of her own preceptor. "O beautiful Elder who graces the midst of the Saṅgha, relying on you..." means she is called "Saṅghattherī" because of her seniority in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and her possession of the quality of steadfastness, "Sobhane" (the beautiful one) because she is endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), and "Kalyāṇi" (the noble friend). The sentence should be connected as: "O Noble Lady, relying on you, I have attained the Three Knowledges and have fulfilled the Buddha's Dispensation." "Icche" means I wish. "Sāvatthi gantave" means to go to the city of Sāvatthī. "Sīhanādaṃ nadissāmī" is said in reference to the declaration of the fruit of Arahantship. Then the Elder Sundarī went to Sāvatthī in due course, entered the monastery, and seeing the Buddha seated upon the Dhamma-seat, experienced great joy and happiness, and addressing herself, said: "Sundarī, look!" "Hemavaṇṇaṃ" means having a complexion like the color of gold. "Harittacaṃ" means having skin like gold. Here, the Buddha is called "golden-colored" because of his bright yellow complexion. Furthermore, "Hemavaṇṇaṃ" is said followed by "Harittacaṃ" to show that he is like a well-polished golden mirror that has been thoroughly rubbed and smeared with natural vermilion. "Look at this Sundarī coming" means look at me, named Sundarī, who is coming to the presence of the Buddha. With the words "Vippamuttaṃ" and so forth, she spoke with a surge of joy, declaring the fruit of Arahantship. To dispel the doubts of those who wondered, "Where did this Sundarī come from? Where is she going? What is her nature?", she spoke the verse beginning with "Bārāṇasito," and to make the meaning of "Sāvikā ca" in that verse clearer, she spoke the verse beginning with "Tuvaṃ Buddho." The meaning of that verse is: In this world with its devas, you alone are the one Omniscient Buddha. Because you instruct appropriately regarding the benefits of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, you are my Teacher. I am an Arahant Brahmin woman, your "breast-born" daughter, born from the effort generated in your bosom. I am "mouth-born" because I was born from the sound of the Dhamma proceeding from your mouth and from the Noble Path which is the mouth of the Dispensation. I have "done what was to be done" because I have completed the tasks of full comprehension and so forth. I am "canker-free" because all taints have been entirely exhausted.
244:
At that time, the Blessed One, joyfully accepting the arrival of Sundarī Therī, spoke the verse beginning with "Tassā te svāgataṃ." The meaning of that verse is: You have realized the Dhamma as I have attained it, just as it truly is. Dear daughter Sundarī, for such a one as you, this coming into my presence is a good coming (svāgataṃ). For that very reason, this coming of yours is not an ill-coming (durāgataṃ), but only a good coming (adurāgataṃ). Why is that? Because those who are thus tamed are bound to come. Sundarī, you have been tamed by the noble discipline of the Noble Path; therefore, you come to pay homage to the feet of the Teacher, being one who is dispassionate in all places, who has completely cut off all fetters, who is detached, who has completed what was to be done, and who is free from taints (āsavas). Therefore, the connection is made that such a coming of yours is a good coming and not an ill-coming.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Sundarī Therī ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Verses of Subhā Therī, the Goldsmith's Daughter

The verses beginning with "Daharāhaṃ" are the verses of the Elder Subhā, the daughter of a goldsmith. This Elder also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas and had accumulated merit that serves as a support for the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences. Having gradually matured her roots of merit and accumulated the requisites for liberation (vimokkha), she wandered only in the happy realms (sugati). Having reached maturity of knowledge, she was reborn in this Buddha's era in the city of Rājagaha as the daughter of a certain goldsmith. Because she was endowed with the beauty of physical appearance, her name was "Subhā."

When she gradually reached the age of discretion and became an adult, she developed faith in the Teacher while He was entering the city of Rājagaha. One day, she approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. The Teacher, seeing the maturity of her spiritual faculties (indriya), preached the Dhamma concerning the Four Noble Truths in accordance with her inclination. At that very moment, she was established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), adorned with a thousand methods. Later, seeing the faults of the household life, she attained the status of a Buddhist nun in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. Established in the bhikkhunī precepts, she devoted herself to meditation for the sake of the higher paths. Her relatives approached her from time to time, tempting her with sensual pleasures and showing her great wealth and possessions to allure her. One day, wishing to reveal the danger of the household life and sensual pleasures to the relatives who had come to her, she preached the Dhamma with twenty-four verses beginning with "Daharāhaṃ," making them lose hope and sending them away. While she was striving in the work of insight (vipassanā), purifying her faculties...
245:
...purifying the faculties and exerting herself in meditation, she attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Having attained Arahatship, she uttered this inspired utterance:

When I was young, wearing white garments, I heard the Dhamma in the past. To me, being diligent, there was the penetration of the Truths.

Since then, I have found great dissatisfaction in all sensual pleasures. Seeing fear in the group of existence (sakkāya), I longed only for renunciation (nekkhamma).

I abandoned the circle of relatives, and the male and female servants, and the prosperous, delightful, and pleasant villages and fields.

Having given up no small amount of wealth, I ordained. Thus, I went forth from the world out of faith in the well-proclaimed True Dhamma.

It would not be proper for one who aspires to nothingness (the goal) to return again after having discarded gold and silver.

Neither silver nor gold leads to awakening (bodhi) or to peace (nibbāna). This is not suitable for recluses (samaṇa); this is not the wealth of the Noble Ones (ariya).

This (gold and silver) causes greed, intoxication, and delusion, and increases the dust of defilements. It is full of danger and great toil; there is no stability or permanence in it.

Men who are attached to this and negligent, with defiled minds, being at odds with one another, create many quarrels.

Killing, binding, suffering, loss, grief, and lamentation—many such calamities are seen for those who are immersed in sensual pleasures.

O my relatives, you are like enemies; why do you join me to sensual pleasures? Know me as one who has ordained, seeing danger in sensual pleasures.

The taints (āsavas) cannot be exhausted by gold and silver. Sensual pleasures are like murderous enemies, like hostile thorns and bonds.

O my relatives, you are like enemies; why do you join me to sensual pleasures? Know me as one who has ordained, with a shaven head and wearing the outer robe (saṅghāṭi).
246:
Almsfood obtained by standing, almsfood obtained by gleaning, and rag-robes—these alone are suitable for me, who relies on the homeless life.

Sensual pleasures, both divine and human, have been abandoned by the Great Sages; those noble ones are liberated in the place of safety, Nibbāna, and have reached unshakable happiness.

May I not encounter those sensual pleasures in which there is no refuge; sensual pleasures are like enemies, like killers, like a great mass of fire, and they bring suffering.

This [sensual pleasure] is an obstacle, a danger, accompanied by distress, and is like a thorn; this craving is very harsh, great, and is the gateway to delusion.

It is a terrifying calamity; sensual pleasures are like the heads of snakes; foolish worldlings, who are like the blind, take great delight in those sensual pleasures.

Many ignorant people in the world, immersed in the mire of sensual pleasures, do not know the end of birth and death.

Many people follow the path leading to an unhappy destination (duggati) caused by sensual pleasures, bringing disease upon themselves.

Thus, sensual pleasures give rise to enemies, cause burning, and are defiling; they are like the bait of the world, a bond, and the bond of death.

They cause madness, they deceive, and they destroy the mind; Māra has quickly set the snare of sensual pleasures for the defilement of beings.

Sensual pleasures have endless faults, much suffering, and are like a potent poison; they have little sweetness, cause enmity, and wither the wholesome side (sukka-pakkha).

Seeing such ruin caused by sensual pleasures, I shall not return to them; I shall always delight only in Nibbāna.

Having crossed over the enmity of sensual pleasures, desiring the state of coolness, I shall live heedfully for the exhaustion of all fetters.

I follow the path of the Noble Eightfold Path—sorrowless, stainless, secure, and straight—by which the Great Sages have crossed over.
247:
“Look at this daughter of a blacksmith, established in the Dhamma and beautiful. Free from craving, she has reached [meditative absorption] and meditates at the foot of a tree.

It has been eight days since she went forth; she has faith and is beautiful through the True Dhamma. Disciplined by the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā, she possesses the Triple Knowledge (tevijjā) and has abandoned death.

This bhikkhunī, the daughter of a blacksmith, is free from slavery, free from debt, with developed faculties, detached from all yokes, has completed her task, and is free from taints (āsavas).

Sakka, the King of Gods, together with the host of devas, approaches by psychic power and pays homage to the beautiful daughter of the blacksmith.” — Thus he spoke these verses.

In those verses, “Daharāhaṃ suddhavasanā, yaṃ pure dhammamassuṇiṃ” means: Because formerly, while I was still a young girl, wearing pure clothes and being adorned, I heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One. Having heard the Dhamma, I reflected on it as I had heard it, and being heedful with established mindfulness, undertaking virtue and devoting myself to meditation, I attained the penetration (paṭivedha) of the Four Noble Truths, starting with “This is suffering.”

“Tato'haṃ sabbakāmesu, bhusaṃ aratimajjhagā” means: Because of that realization of the Truths, I felt a great lack of delight (arati) in all sensual pleasures of both humans and devas. Seeing the danger in the “identity” (sakkāya), which is the five aggregates of clinging, with the eye of wisdom, I yearned only for renunciation (nekkhamma), which is the state of a monk/nun, and for Nibbāna.

“Dāsakammakārāni ca” refers to slaves and workers (here the gender is changed in the expression). “Gāmakhettāni” refers to villages and fields where crops are grown, or fields included within a village. “Phītāni” means prosperous and wealthy. “Ramaṇီye” means delightful. “Pamodite” means joyful. “Bhogakkhandhe hitvā” should be connected as “having abandoned the mass of wealth.” “Sāpateyyaṃ” refers to one's own property, such as gems, gold, silver, and other stored items. “Anappakaṃ” means great or much. “Pahāya” means having abandoned. “Thus, having gone forth with faith” means “having abandoned the circle of relatives,” and so on...
248:
Having renounced a great circle of relatives and a great mass of wealth in the manner described, and having gone forth from home, believing with faith in the objects of faith—namely, kamma, the results of kamma, and the Triple Gem—I have gone forth in the Noble Discipline (Ariya-vinaya) well-proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One.

For me, who has thus gone forth, it is not proper to return to the sensual pleasures that have been discarded. "Ākiñcaññañhi patthaye" means I aspire only to the state of having nothing (akiñcana-bhāva) and the state of non-possession (apariggaha-bhāva). If a person, after discarding gold, silver, or any other kind of wealth, were to take it back again, how could that person lift their head in the midst of the wise?

This is because silver or gold does not lead to the realization (of the Four Noble Truths), nor to peace, nor to the knowledge of the Path, nor to Nibbāna. "Netaṃ samaṇasāruppaṃ" means that this object of possession, such as gold and silver, or the act of possessing it, is not suitable for recluses. Thus it has been said: "Gold and silver are not allowable for the recluses who are sons of the Sakyans," and so forth (Cullavagga). "Na etaṃ ariyadhanaṃ" means that this aforementioned object of possession is not wealth consisting of the Noble Dhamma, like the wealth of faith and so on, nor does it bring about the state of being a Noble One (Ariya). Therefore, it is said, "lobhanaṃ" and so forth.

In that passage, "lobhanaṃ" means producing greed. "Madanaṃ" means bringing about intoxication. "Mohanaṃ" means producing delusion. "Rajavaḍḍhanaṃ" means increasing the dust of passion and so on. It is called "sāsaṅkaṃ" in the sense that it is accompanied by apprehension, because it brings fear of danger to the one who possesses it. It means it brings apprehension from somewhere or other to the one who possesses it. "Bahu-āyāsaṃ" means much toil through the preparation and protection (of wealth) and so on. "Natthi cettha dhuvaṃ ṭhiti" means that in this wealth, there is no state of permanence or stability; it has only a nature of being unstable and unsteady.

"Ettha rattā pamattā ca" means those who are lustful, having passion arisen for this wealth, are negligent due to being devoid of mindfulness regarding the ten wholesome dhammas. They are indeed those with defiled minds due to defilements such as greed. Furthermore, being at odds with one another, many beings cause quarrels. Even a mother with her son, and a son with his mother—thus being at odds with one another, many beings cause quarrels...
249:
(They) engage in quarrels and disputes. For that reason, the Blessed One said: "Furthermore, monks, with sensual pleasures as the cause, sensual pleasures as the source, sensual pleasures as the basis... a mother disputes with her son, and a son disputes with his mother," and so forth (Majjhima Nikāya).

"Vadha" means death. "Bandha" means bonds such as being bound in shackles. "Pariklesa" means falling into affliction such as the cutting off of hands. "Jāni" means the loss of wealth and the loss of followers. "Soka-parideva" means sorrow and lamentation. "Adhipannānaṃ" means those who are obsessed (with sensual pleasures). "Dissate vyasanaṃ bahu" means that many and various kinds of ruin and misfortune are clearly seen in sensual pleasures, such as the aforementioned death and bonds, as well as the unmentioned grief, despair, and so on, pertaining to both this life and the life to come.

"To such a one as me, relatives are like enemies;
Why do you join me to sensual pleasures?"
This means: why do you, being my relatives, yet like enemies who wish for my harm, urge and join me to sensual pleasures—me, who is already disgusted with sensual pleasures? "Know me as one who has gone forth, seeing danger in sensual pleasures" means: know me as one who has gone forth, seeing sensual pleasures as a danger; do you not know even this much? This is the meaning.

"The taints are not exhausted by bullion and gold,"
This means that the taints of sensual desire (kāmāsava) and so forth are never exhausted by bullion and gold; on the contrary, they only increase because of them. Therefore, it was said:
"Sensual pleasures are enemies, they are killers,
They are adversaries, bonds of darts."
Sensual pleasures are called enemies because they bring harm and lack loving-kindness. They are called killers because they are like executioners with raised swords, being the cause of death. They are called adversaries because they bring harm even while following after one, like an adversary who pursues a grudge. They are called bonds of darts because they bind one to the darts of passion and so forth.

"Muṇḍa" means having a shaven head. "Saṅghāṭipāruta" means one who is clad in the outer robe (saṅghāṭi) by taking rags from here and there and wearing them.

"Uṭṭhiṭṭhapiṇḍa" means alms-food obtained by standing at the doors of houses that are open. "Uñcha" means the practice of seeking alms for that food. "Anagārūpanissaya" means the requisite for livelihood which is a support, because it is to be depended upon by those who have gone forth into the homeless life. Indeed, depending on that, those who have gone forth live.
250:
“Vantā” means things that are discarded. “Mahesīhi” means by those who seek the great practice, such as the Buddha and others. “Khemaṭṭhāne” means in Nibbāna, which is the place of safety from the yoke of sensual pleasures (kāmayoga) and so forth. “Te” means those persons who seek the great practice have reached the unshakeable and steady happiness of Nibbāna (acalaṃ sukhaṃ). Therefore, it means that one who desires that happiness of Nibbāna should renounce sensual pleasures.

“Māhaṃ kāmehi saṅgacchiṃ” means “May I never associate or meet with sensual pleasures at any time.” Why is this? He said, “Yesu tāṇaṃ na vijjati” and so forth. When those sensual pleasures are examined, there is not even one that can provide protection from danger. They are like a great mass of fire because of their intense burning. They are sufferings because of their painful nature.
