These sensual pleasures are obstacles and dangers because people do not know that they bring about many disadvantages. They are accompanied by distress because they cause the mind to be weary and exhausted. They are like thorns because they pierce. “Gedho suvisamo ceso” means they are called “gedha” (greed) because they are the cause of attachment. That sensual pleasure is a very uneven and great obstacle. It is great because it is difficult to overcome. It is the beginning of delusion because it is the cause of falling into bewilderment.

“Upasaggo bhīmarūpo” means they have a very terrifying nature, like the danger of great demons, because they bring about harm and suffering. Sensual pleasures are like the head of a snake because of their fearsome nature.

“Kāmapaṅkena sattā” means beings who are stuck in the mire called sensual pleasures.

“Duggatigamanaṃ maggaṃ” means it is the path leading to woeful states such as hell. “Kāmahetukaṃ” means it is caused by the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. “Bahu” means many kinds of unwholesome acts such as killing living beings. “Rogamāvahaṃ” means they bring about the suffering of the present life called disease because of their painful nature.

“Evaṃ” means in the manner stated as “enemies, killers,” and so forth. “Amittajananā” means they bring about the state of being an enemy. “Tāpanā” means they cause burning; it has the meaning of being tormenting. “Saṅkilesikā” means they bring about the impurities of defilements. “Lokāmisā” means they are like bait in the world. “Bandhaniyā” means they are to be increased by the fetters that are bonds; it has the meaning of being connected with fetters. “Maraṇabandhanā” means they are the bonds of death because they function as the sign for arising in existence and as the root cause of arising.
251: “Ummādanā” means things that cause grief and madness due to separation from things that are subject to change, or things that bring about intoxication increasingly as sensual pleasures grow. “Ullapanā” means things that cause one to cry out repeatedly, “Oh, what happiness! Oh, what happiness!” There is also a variant reading “Ullolanā.” It means things that entice beings increasingly for the sake of bait (sensual pleasures), like a dog wagging its tail for a morsel of food, and lead them to ruin and degradation. “Cittappamāthino” means things that have the nature of crushing the mind in the present and in the future by causing burning and so forth. There is also a reading “Cittappamaddino,” which has the same meaning. For those who say “Cittappamādino,” it means things that bring about the mind's negligence. “Saṅkilesāya” means for the sake of oppression or torment. “Khippaṃ mārena oḍဍိtaṃ” means these sensual pleasures should be regarded as a trap (or net) set by Māra because they bring harm to beings. “Anantādīnavā” means things that have endless faults and many disadvantages, as taught in the Cūḷadukkhandha Sutta and others, in the manner of “This is a lure, this is an intoxication,” and “Here, one is confronted by cold, confronted by heat,” and so forth. “Bahudukkhā” means things followed by many kinds of suffering, such as those of the woeful states. “Mahāvisā” means things that are like the potent halāhala poison because their results are bitter and unbearable. “Appassādā” means things that have only a little gratification, like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword. “Raṇakarā” means things that increase the impurities of defilements and so forth. “Sukkapakkhavisosanā” means things that destroy the faultless group of wholesome states of beings. “Sāhaṃ” means “That I.” It means that, as stated below, having heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, I gained faith, renounced sensual pleasures, and became ordained. “Etādisaṃ” means of such a nature, in the manner already described. “Katvā” means having done so, meaning for the reasons already mentioned. “Na taṃ paccāgamissāmi” means “I will not again enjoy those sensual pleasures that I have previously vomited out.” “Nibbānābhiratā sadā” should be connected as: “Because I delight in Nibbāna at all times from the time of ordination, I will not return to those sensual pleasures.” “Raṇaṃ taritvā kāmānaṃ” means having crossed over the impurity of sensual pleasures, and I have done that crossing by abandoning them through the Noble Path. “Sītibhāvābhikaṅkhinī” means desiring Arahantship, which is called the state of coolness because of the subsiding of all the distress and burning of defilements. “Sabbasaṃyojanakkhaye” means delighting in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of all fetters.
252:
"By which the Great Sages have crossed" (Yena tiṇṇā mahesino) means: by which Noble Path the Great Sages (Mahesī—seekers of the great practice), headed by the Buddha, have crossed the great ocean of Saṃsāra. "I also follow the path they have gone, and reach it through the practice of virtue and so forth" is the meaning. "Established in the Dhamma" (Dhammaṭṭhaṃ) means standing in the Noble Fruition. "Unshaken" (Anejaṃ) refers to the Fruition of Arahantship, which is named "Aneja" because the agitation of craving has been stilled. "Having attained" (Upasampajja) means having reached it through the attainment of the Path of Arahantship. "She meditates" (Jhāyati) means she is closely contemplating that very Fruition-meditation (Phala-jhāna).

"Ordained eight days ago" (Ajjaṭṭhamī pabbajitā) means today is the eighth day since her ordination; counting back from today, she was ordained on the eighth day. "Faithful" (Saddhā) means being endowed with faith. "Beautiful through the True Dhamma" (Saddhammasobhanā) means being beautiful through the attainment of the True Dhamma.

"Free" (Bhujissā) means being a free person because of the abandoning of defilements which are like slavery. She is "debtless" (Anaṇā) because of the disappearance of debts such as sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and so forth.

These three verses were spoken by the Blessed One while praising the Elder Nun (Therī) and showing her to the monks, as she sat at the foot of a certain tree, having entered the attainment of Fruition (Phala-samāpatti) after reaching Arahantship on the eighth day of her ordination.

Then, Sakka, the Lord of Devas, saw this matter with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and thought, "This Elder Nun, who is thus praised by the Teacher, should also be attended upon by the devas." At that very moment, he approached together with the Tāvatiṃsa devas, paid homage, and stood with joined palms. Referring to this, the Recorders of the Council (Saṅgītikāras) said: "Sakka, the Lord of Beings, having approached with a host of devas by his psychic power, pays homage to the beautiful daughter of the smith."

In that verse, "Lord of Beings" (Bhūtapati) refers to Sakka, the King of Devas, who is so named because he is the lord and master of beings born in the three realms of sense-existence (kāma-bhava). That Sakka, together with the host of devas, approached the beautiful daughter of the smith by his divine power and paid homage; the meaning is that he worshipped her with the fivefold prostration.

## The Commentary on the Verses of the Elder Nun Subhā, the Goldsmith's Daughter, is finished.

## The Commentary on the Book of Twenties is finished.
253:
## 14. Tiṃsanipāta
## 1. Subhā Jīvakambavanikātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Book of the Thirties, the verse beginning with "Jīvakambavanaṃ rammaṃ" is the verse of the Theri Subhā Jīvakambavanikā. This Theri had also performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas and had accumulated wholesome deeds that serve as a support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various births. Having strong wholesome roots, she gradually developed the requisites for liberation (vimokkhasambhāra) and, with matured knowledge, was reborn in a wealthy Brahmin family (brāhmaṇamahāsāla) in Rājagaha during the time of this Buddha. Her name was Subhā. It is said that her limbs were endowed with beautiful complexion and form; therefore, the name 'Subhā' (Beautiful) arose in accordance with its meaning.

That Subhā gained faith when the Teacher entered Rājagaha and became a lay follower (upāsikā). Later, she developed a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding saṃsāra, and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and perceiving renunciation (nekkhamma) as safety, she went forth in the presence of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. While performing the work of insight (vipassanā), she was established in the Fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala) in just a few days.

Then one day, a certain rogue, a resident of Rājagaha who was in his first youth, saw the Theri going to Jīvaka's Mango Grove for her day-rest. With a mind obsessed with lust, he blocked her path and tempted her with sensual pleasures. The Theri preached the Dhamma to him, making known the danger of sensual pleasures in various ways and her own inclination toward renunciation. Even after hearing the Dhamma talk, he did not retreat but persisted. The Theri, seeing that he did not abide by her words and was extremely infatuated with her eyes, said, "Here, take the eye you admire," and plucking out one of her eyes, she offered it to him. Then that man was struck with terror and spiritual urgency; his lust vanished right there, and after asking the Theri's forgiveness, he departed. The Theri went to the presence of the Teacher. Merely upon seeing the Teacher, her eye became as it was before. Then the Theri stood there, continuously suffused with the joy (pīti) born of mindfulness of the Buddha. The Teacher, knowing the movement of her mind, preached the Dhamma and taught her a meditation subject for the sake of the Highest Path. She suppressed the joy and, developing insight at that very moment, reached Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having reached Arahantship and dwelling in the bliss of fruition and the bliss of Nibbāna, she reviewed her own practice and uttered these verses, spoken by herself and that rogue, by way of an inspired utterance (udāna):
254:
"A rogue blocked the beautiful nun Subhā as she was going to the delightful Mango Grove of Jīvaka. Then the nun Subhā spoke thus to that rogue:

'O friend, what wrong have I done to you that you stand blocking my way? It is not proper for a man to touch a woman who has gone forth.

In the teaching of my Teacher, the training rule taught by the Sugata is very grave to me. Why do you stand blocking me, who have a pure step and am free from blemish?

You, with a turbid mind, why do you stand blocking me who am untroubled, free from dust, free from blemish, and whose mind is liberated in every way?

You are young and innocent; what will going forth do for you? Cast off the saffron robe. Come, let us delight in this well-flowered forest.

The trees, stirred by the pollen, waft sweet scents in all directions. This season, the beginning of spring, is pleasant. Come, let us delight in this well-flowered forest.

The trees with flowering tops seem to roar as they are stirred by the wind. What pleasure will you have if you enter the forest alone?

This great forest is frequented by herds of wild beasts and haunted by elephants in rut and their mates. Do you wish to go without a companion into this lonely, terrifying great forest?'"
255:
“O young maiden with skin like the color of gold, you wander in the Cittalata Grove like a celestial nymph. Clad in incomparable fine garments of Kāsī silk, you shine with exquisite beauty.

“If we were to delight in the midst of the forest, I would be one who follows your will. O one with eyes like those of a Kinnarī, there is no life dearer to me than you.

“If you would do as I say, come and live happily in a household. Residing in a wind-protected palace, let women wait upon you.

“Wear fine garments of Kāsī silk, and adorn yourself with garlands and unguents. I shall provide you with various ornaments of much gold, jewels, and pearls.

“Ascend a new and costly couch, spread with well-washed silver-colored covers, soft woolen carpets, and cotton down, and perfumed with the scent of sandalwood.

“Just as a lotus risen from the water stands in a place unfrequented by people, so too will you, living the holy life, reach old age in your own limbs.

“What essence do you see in this body, which is filled with corpses, which increases the cemetery, and which is of a nature to break, that you look upon it with a bewildered mind?”
256:
Your eyes are beautiful like musical instruments, and like the eyes of the kinnarīs in the mountain clefts. Seeing your eyes, my delight in sensual pleasure increases greatly.

Seeing your eyes, which are like lotus buds in your pure, gold-like face, my sensual desire increases greatly.

Even when you have gone far away, we remember your eyes with long lashes and pure vision. O Subhā, with eyes as round as a kinnarī's, there is no one more beloved to me than you.

As for you who seek a son of the Buddha, you wish to travel by a path that is no path. You seek the moon as a toy. You wish to leap over Mount Meru.

In this world with its devas, there is no longer any place where lust could arise in me. I do not even know what that lust is like; indeed, it has been destroyed, along with its roots, by the Path.

It is like something cast into a pit of glowing coals, or like being struck by a poisoned arrow. I do not even know what that lust is like; indeed, it has been destroyed, along with its roots, by the Path.

Tempt one who lacks reflection, or one who has not attended upon a teacher. You will only trouble yourself by tempting me who knows.

(Background History and Other Verses)
Subhā the Elder was born as the daughter of a goldsmith. She was named Subhā because of her perfect and beautiful appearance. When she came of age, while the Buddha was entering the city of Rājagaha, she developed firm faith in the Buddha. One day, she approached the Buddha, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place. Seeing the maturity of her faculties, the Buddha preached the Four Noble Truths according to her inclination. At that moment, she was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), adorned with a thousand methods.

Later, seeing the faults of household life, she ordained under the Great Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. While established in the bhikkhunī's virtue, she practiced meditation for the higher paths. Her relatives approached her from time to time, inviting her with sensual pleasures and tempting her by showing great wealth and possessions. One day, she clearly showed the faults of household life and sensual pleasures to those who came to her, preaching the Dhamma with twenty-four verses beginning with "Daharahāṃ". Having sent them away without hope, she practiced insight meditation (vipassanā), purified her faculties, developed her meditation, and soon reached Arahantship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

After reaching Arahantship, she recited these verses: "I, being young and wearing pure white clothes, heard the Dhamma when I was a layperson. Therefore, being diligent, the penetration of the Four Noble Truths occurred for me. Thus, I attained great disenchantment with all sensual pleasures. Seeing danger in the manifest five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā), I cherish and long only for the state of a monk which is the escape from sensual pleasures, and for Nibbāna which is the liberation. I have renounced my circle of relatives, servants, and workers, as well as the pleasant, delightful, and prosperous villages and fields. Abandoning great wealth, I have gone forth from home, believing in kamma, its results, and the Triple Gem, and have ordained in the True Dhamma (Saddhamma) which the Buddha has perfectly made known."
257:
“In abuse and veneration, in pleasure and pain, my mindfulness is established before me. Knowing conditioned things (saṅkhata) as unattractive (asubha), my mind is not smeared by any object.

“I am a female disciple of the Sugata, traveling in the vehicle of the Eightfold Path. With the dart pulled out, without taints (anāsava), I delight in a secluded dwelling.

“I have seen well-painted puppets and small wooden dolls. They are bound with strings and pegs, and they perform various dances.

“When the strings and pegs are pulled out from that puppet, and it is scattered, defective, and broken into pieces, one cannot find any essence. In what should one settle the mind there?

“These bodies are also like those puppets. They do not exist without those phenomena (dhammas). If they do not exist without those phenomena, in what should one settle the mind in that body?

“Just as one sees a painting on a wall smeared with yellow orpiment, your vision of that form is distorted. The perception of humans is in vain.

“O blind one, you approach a hollow form, which is like an illusion created before you, like a golden tree seen in a dream, or like a silver figure made in the midst of a crowd.”
258:
The eye is like a small bubble in the middle, accompanied by tears, like a sphere placed in a hollow. In that eye, various parts of the eye are gathered and formed. Subhā the nun, who had a mind free from attachment, did not tremble as she plucked out that eye of beautiful appearance. Saying, "Here, take this eye that you desire," she gave it to that man at that very moment.

At that very moment, his lust vanished, and he paid obeisance to the nun, asking for forgiveness. "O lady who practices the noble life, may you be safe; I will never do such a thing again," he said. "I have offended such a person, as if embracing a blazing mass of fire, or as if grasping a venomous snake. May we be safe; please forgive us," he pleaded.

Having been freed from that man's hands, the bhikkhunī went into the presence of the Excellent Buddha. Upon seeing the excellent marks of merit (puññalakkhaṇa), her eye became as it was before. She recited these verses.

In those passages, "Jīvakambavanaṃ" refers to the mango grove of the physician Jīvaka Komārabhacca. "Rammaṃ" means delightful. That mango grove was extremely pleasant and delightful due to the excellence of the ground, the excellence of shade and water, and the systematic planting of trees. "Gacchantiṃ" refers to the nun who was heading towards the mango grove to stay for the day's rest. "Subhaṃ" is the nun of that name. "Dhuttako" refers to a rogue who is a womanizer. He was the son of a wealthy goldsmith living in Rājagaha, a handsome young man and a rogue who wandered about intoxicated. He... to that nun...
259:
Seeing her on the way, with an obsessed mind, he stood blocking the path. For that reason, it is said, "The rogue obstructed her," meaning he prevented my going. Subhā the bhikkhunī spoke to that rogue who stood obstructing her. In this context, by saying, "Subhā spoke to the bhikkhunī Subhā who was going," the Elder nun speaks of herself as if she were another person. The editors of the Council (Saṅgītikāras) spoke this verse to show the connection of the verses uttered by the Elder nun.

After saying, "Subhā spoke," in order to show how she spoke, she said, "What have I offended you?" and so forth. In that speech, "What have I offended you?" means "Friend, what wrong have I done to you?" "That you stand blocking me" means the reason for which you stand blocking me who am going and preventing my passage—that offense simply does not exist. Furthermore, if you act this way with the perception of me as a 'woman,' she said, "Friend, it is not proper for a man to touch a nun," to show that such behavior is also inappropriate. Friend, son of the goldsmith, even by worldly custom, it is not proper for a man to touch those who have gone forth. For a nun, it is not proper for a man to touch her even if he were an animal; let alone the touch of a man, the touch of a man who is liable to a Nissaggiya offense due to lust is certainly not proper.

Therefore, she said, "Weighty in my Teacher's Dispensation," and so forth. Its meaning is: In my Teacher's Dispensation, which should be respected like a stone parasol, there are training rules (sikkhā) prescribed and laid down by the Sugata, the Fully Enlightened One, for the nuns. Why do you stand blocking me who am going, who have a pure state through those training rules, who am without blemish because of the total absence of blemishes such as lust?

You, who have a clouded mind due to sensual thoughts and the like which cause the mind to be clouded; why do you stand blocking me, whose mind is unclouded due to the absence of those, who am free from dust and blemish because of the absence of the dust of lust and the like, and whose mind is liberated by the liberation of cutting off (samucchedavimutti) in regard to the entire group of five aggregates?

When the Elder nun spoke thus, the rogue, revealing his own intention, spoke ten verses beginning with "You are young." In those verses, "daharā" means a young woman standing in the first stage of life. "Apāpikā casi" means you are also not of inferior beauty.
260:
"Asi" means one who bears excellent beauty. "What will monkhood do for you?" means: what can monkhood do for you who are in your youth and endowed with beauty? It is spoken with the meaning that one should only become a monk when one is old and of repulsive appearance. "Nikkhipa" means discard. If there is a variant "Ukkhipa," it means remove.

"Madhura" means beautiful or having a good scent. "Pavanti" means they blow. "Sabbaso" means from all around. "Trees rising with pollen" means these trees, with pollen rising as the cool wind blows, seem to rise up by themselves with their own pollen and blow fragrantly all around. "The first spring season is a pleasant season" means this first month of spring is a season of pleasant touch.

"With flowering tops" means (trees) with well-blossomed tops. "As if roaring when stirred by the wind" means they stand moving and roaring, as if thundering, when the wind blows. "If you descend into the forest alone" means "If you enter the forest alone, what kind of delight will you find there?" He says this because he himself is deeply attached to the pleasure of sensual desires.

"Frequented by herds of wild beasts" means (a forest) frequented in various places by herds of wild beasts such as lions and tigers. "Disturbed by rutting bull elephants and cows" means a place (a forest) disturbed by rutting bull elephants and cows, by frightening the minds of other animals and by breaking the branches of trees and bushes. In fact, though such danger did not exist in that forest at that time, he says this wishing to frighten her, saying "a forest is of such a nature." "Rahita" means a forest devoid of people, secluded. "Bhimsanaka" means a forest that causes terror.

"Like a doll made of red gold" means you wander like a doll decorated with red gold, or like a golden statue fashioned by a highly skilled master mechanic through the power of machinery; even now you move here and there. "Like a goddess in the Cittalatā garden" means like a celestial nymph in the garden named Cittalatā. "With very delicate clothes from the Kāsi kingdom" means with extremely fine garments produced in the Kāsi country. "Vaggu" means smooth and glossy clothes. "You look beautiful in incomparable robes" means "With incomparable, matchless lower and upper garments, you now look beautiful following my will." He speaks as if it is actually happening, based on his own desire for what might happen in the future.

"I will be one who follows your will" means "I too will be one who follows your will, an obedient servant." "If we live in the midst of the forest" means "If we both..."
261:
“Let us live together in the midst of the forest; let us enjoy ourselves. There is no one dearer to me than you.” He states the reason for following her will. “Pāṇo” means a being; it means “There is no other being dearer to me than you.” Alternatively, “Pāṇo” refers to his own life; it means “There is no life of mine dearer than you.” “Kinnarimandalocane” means one with soft and wide eyes like a Kinnarī.

“If you do as I say, live happily in the household.” This means “If you do as I say, come, leaving behind the suffering of the holy life, which is sitting alone and sleeping alone; being happy with sensual pleasures, dwell in the household.” Some read “Sukhitā heti agāramāvasantī”; according to them, it means those who dwell in the household will be happy. “Pāsādanivātavāsinī” means one who dwells in palaces where the wind does not blow (sheltered). There is also a variant “Pāsādavimānavāsinī,” meaning one who dwells in palaces like celestial mansions. “Parikammaṃ” means service (attending to duties).

“Dhāraya” means “wear”; use it as both a lower garment and an upper robe. “Abhiropehi” means “place on the body by way of decoration”; it means “decorate.” “Mālavannakaṃ” means flowers and fragrant ointments. “Kañcanamaṇimuttakaṃ” means associated with gold, gems, and pearls; it means “adorned with gems and pearls made of gold.” “Bahu” means many kinds, such as hand ornaments. “Vividhaṃ” means various types, due to the distinction in craftsmanship.

“Sudhotarajapacchadaṃ” means an upper coverlet from which dust has been removed because it has been well washed. “Subhaṃ” means beautiful. “Gonakatūlikasanthataṃ” means spread with a black, long-haired woolen rug and with a mattress stuffed with swan down and the like. “Navaṃ” means new. “Mahārahaṃ” means very precious. “Candanamaṇḍitasāragandhikaṃ” means having a fragrant scent because of being adorned with heartwood sandalwood such as Gosīsa. It means “Ascend such a bed; having ascended that bed, sleep and sit as you please.”

“Uppalaṃ cudakā samuggataṃ” means in this phrase, the letter “ca” is merely a particle; like a well-blossomed lotus that has emerged from the water, risen, and stands high above. “Yathā taṃ amanussasevitaṃ” means since that lotus grows in a pond possessed by rakkhasas (demons), it is not frequented by humans and thus remains unenjoyed by anyone. “Evaṃ tvaṃ brahmacārinī” means “In this way, you are a practitioner of the holy life, like that well-blossomed lotus. You will reach old age while your own bodily limbs remain unenjoyed by anyone; you will become old and decrepit in vain.”
262:
Thus, when that man, who was frivolous in sensual pleasures, clearly expressed his desire, the Elder Nun, wishing to cut off his lust right there by revealing the nature of the body, spoke the verse beginning with "Kiṃ te idha" (What is there for you here?). The meaning of that verse is: "Friend, son of a goldsmith (Suvaṇṇakāraputta), in this impure carcass called the body, which is filled with corpses such as hair and so forth, which is certainly of the nature of decay, and which increases the cemetery—what do you consider to be the essence and hold in high esteem? Having seen what, do you become distracted and devoid of mental focus on other objects, or do you gaze with joy upon this very body without distraction? Tell me that."

Upon hearing those words, although the Elder Nun's appearance was beautiful with grace, that man, whose mind had been obsessed with her since the first sight, spoke the words beginning with "Your eyes are like those of a doe..." referring to that very gaze. In truth, because this Elder Nun was well-restrained, she possessed peaceful faculties. In those eyes, which were produced by the power of merit, adorned with the five clear sensitivities (pañcappasāda), and were steady, serene, and tranquil, an extraordinary beauty and graceful appearance were found. Because that rogue was himself deceived by his own imaginings of gestures, manners, and charms, the lust in his gaze grew particularly extensive.

In that verse, "akkhīni ca tūriyāriva" means "tūri" refers to a doe. The word "ca" is merely a particle. The meaning is "your eyes are like those of a young deer." There is also a Pāli reading "koriyāriva," which means like a young hen. "Kinnariyāriva pabbatantare" means your eyes are like those of a Kinnarī wandering in a mountain cleft. "Having seen your eyes, which are endowed with the aforementioned special qualities, my delight in sensual pleasures increases more and more."

"Uppalasikharopamāni te" means your eyelashes are like the tips of blue lotuses. "Vimala" means being free from impurities. "Hāṭakasannibhe" should be connected as "having seen the eyes in your face, which is like the face of a golden statue." "Api dūragatā" means even when gone to a distant place, I constantly remember your eyes without thinking of anything else. "Āyatapamhe" means having long eyelashes. "Visuddhadassane" means having clear eyes. "Na hi matthi tayā piyattaro nayanā" means there is nothing else more dear to me than your eyes. Here, the instrumental case "tayā" is used in the sense of possession (sāmī).
263:
Thus, wishing to overturn the desire of that man who was babbling various things like one maddened by the perfection of her eyes, the Elder Nun spoke twelve verses beginning with "Apathena." Among those verses, "Apathena payātumicchasi" means: "Friend, son of a goldsmith, while other young women exist, why do you long for me, the breast-born daughter of the Buddha? You, who long thus, are like one wishing to travel by a wrong path (apathā) that is obstructed by thorns and dangerous, even though there is a safe and straight path. It is like seeking the moon as a toy and wishing to make the lunar disc a play-ball, or like wishing to cross over Sineru, the king of mountains, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, to reach the other side. You, being such a person, are longing for me, the daughter of the Buddha"—this is how the meaning should be connected.

Now, to show that he is unworthy of her and that his longing will only bring distress, she spoke the verses beginning with "Natthi." In that verse, "rāgo yatthapi dāni me siyā" means: "The object upon which my lust might now arise does not exist at all in the world including the devas." "Napi naṃ jānāmi kīriso" means: "I no longer even know what kind of nature that lust has." "Atha maggena hato samūlako" means: "Lust, together with its root known as improper attention (ayoniso manasikāra), has been utterly destroyed by the Noble Path." "Iṅgālakuyā" means in a pit of glowing embers. "Ujjhito" means like being blown away by the wind, or like burning fuel in a fire. "Visapattoriva" means like a cup of poison. "Aggito kato" means like being removed from the embers, or like poison being removed and destroyed without any remainder.

"Yassā siyā apaccavekkhitaṃ" means: "For whichever woman this fivefold aggregate has not yet been reflected upon with wisdom, nor fully understood." Or, "for whichever woman, due to not seeing the Dhamma-body (Dhamma-sarīra), has not yet been disciplined." "Friend, you should entice with sensual pleasures only such a woman whose conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāras) have not been subdued and who has not reflected on the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara-dhamma)." "Jānantiṃ so imaṃ vihaññasi" means: "You, who are trying to entice me who already knows and understands thus, will only be weary."
264:
By relying on this beautiful bhikkhunī, who knows cessation as it truly is and has penetrated the Four Noble Truths, you have come to distress and suffering. You will encounter the suffering of distress both now and in the future.

Desiring to explain the cause of his falling into distress at the present time, she spoke the words beginning with "Mayhaṃ hi." Therein, the word "hi" is a particle indicating cause. "Akkutthavandite" means in both abuse and worship. "Sukhadukkhe" means in both happiness and suffering, or in the encounter with pleasant and unpleasant objects. "Satī upaṭṭhitā" means that mindfulness associated with reflection is clearly present at all times. "Saṅkhatamasubhanti jāniyā" means knowing the conditioned phenomena of the three realms as loathsome (asubha) due to the oozing of the impurities of defilements. "Sabbattheva" means that in all three realms, my mind is not smeared by the stickiness of craving and so forth.

"Maggaṭṭhaṅgikayānayāyinī" means one who goes to the city of Nibbāna by the noble vehicle known as the Eightfold Path. "Uddhatasallā" means one who has pulled out the darts of lust (rāga) and so forth from her own continuity.

"Sucittitā" means well-fashioned or prepared with parts such as hands, feet, and face. "Sombhā" refers to puppet makers. "Dārukapillakāni vā" refers to figures made of wooden sticks and so forth. "Tantīhi" means with strings made of sinews. "Khīlakehi" means with small pegs fixed for the purpose of hands, feet, back, ears, and so forth. "Vinibaddhā" means bound in various ways. "Vividhaṃ panaccakā" means making it dance by pulling and releasing the mechanical strings; it is to be understood as being seen as if it were dancing.

"Tamuddhaṭe tantikhīlake" means in that which is designated as a figure with a specific structure, if the strings and pegs are removed from their places, if the binding is loosened, if they are separated and defective from one another, and if they are scattered and thrown here and there. "Na vindeyya khaṇḍaso kate" means if the parts of the puppet figure are cut into pieces, the puppet figure cannot be found or obtained. If this is so, where in that part of the puppet figure would one place the mind? Would one place the mind or the perception of the mind on the peg, or on the string, or on the lump of clay? The meaning is that when the parts are disassembled, that perception of a "figure" would never arise.

"Tathūpamā" means similar to that puppet figure. How so? She said the words beginning with "Dehakāni." Therein, "dehakāni" means the parts of the body such as hands, feet, and face. My mind remains attached to those parts. "Tehi dhammehi" means by those phenomena...
265:
...apart from the elements such as earth and phenomena such as the eye, the body does not exist. Apart from such and such arranged phenomena like earth, there is no such thing as a body. In saying it does not exist apart from phenomena, it means the body does not exist and cannot be found apart from the constituent parts and the phenomena of those parts. This being so, where in that body would one place the mind? In what? In the earth element, or in the water element and so forth? Would one place the mind or the perception of the mind in the thought of "body" or "hands and feet"? Since this designation such as "body," "hands and feet," "being," "woman," or "man" exists only in the mere phenomena of elements like earth and sensitive matter, therefore, for one who knows, there is no attachment in this matter.

It is like seeing a woman's figure painted by a skilled artist on a wall smeared with yellow orpiment. The perception "Is this a human woman?" relying on that wall is vain because the essence of a human being is absent there. The perception of it as a woman is merely a distorted vision; it is not a grasp of it as it truly is. The meaning is that the perception of "woman" or "man" in a mere heap of phenomena should be understood in the same way as this metaphor.

"Like magic performed in one's presence" means similar to the illusion shown by a magician in front of one. "Like a golden tree in a dream" means like a tree made of gold that appears in a dream. "O blind fool, you approach this empty, essence-less body, which is devoid of internal core, as if it had essence, thinking 'This is mine', and you become attached to it." "Like a silver figure in the midst of a crowd" means like a silver figure shown by a magician in the midst of a great crowd, which appears as if it has essence but is actually essence-less.

"Like a round object" means like a small ball made of lac. "Placed in a hollow" means placed in a hollow of a tree. "Like a bubble in the middle" means like a water bubble situated in the middle of the eyelids. "With tears" means accompanied by tear-water. "Eye-filth" (pīḷakoḷikā) refers to the impurity of the eye. It arises at the two corners of the eye-socket, emitting a foul smell. Or, the pustules that arise on the eyelids are called "pīḷakoḷikā." "Various" means having many varieties by way of the white and blue circles and the seven layers such as red, yellow, and so forth. "Eye-types" means the parts of the eye or the types of eyes, because of its nature of consisting of many groups (kalāpas). "Massed" means gathered together.
266:
In this way, she made clear to that man, who was intensely lusting after her eye, the foulness (asubha) of the eye and its impermanence (anicca) due to its instability. Having made this clear, she used an analogy: just as someone carrying desirable goods through a forest path inhabited by thieves, being obstructed by them, gives up those goods and proceeds; likewise, the Therī, being obstructed by that man who was intensely lusting after her eye, plucked out her own eye and gave it to him. With reference to that matter, it was said: "Uppāṭiya cārudassanā," and so forth.

In that verse, "Uppāṭiya" means having plucked it out and removed it from the eye socket. "Cārudassanā" means one who has a lovely, attractive, and mind-captivating appearance. "Na ca pajjitthā" means she did not fall into attachment to that eye. "Asaṅgamānasā" means one whose mind is unattached to any object whatsoever. "Handa te cakkhu" means: "Since you desired it, and because I have given it for that very reason, take this impure mass of flesh called an eye; take it and carry it away; lead it to whatever place you desire, full of clarity."

"Tassa ca viramāsi tāvade" means at the very moment the eye was plucked out, the lust of that rogue vanished. "Tattha" means in the eye, or in that Therī, or in that very place. "Khamāpayī" means he asked for forgiveness. "Sotthi siyā brahmacārinī" means: "O holy practitioner (brahmacārinī) of noble conduct, may you be safe and healthy." "Na puno edisakaṃ bhavissati" means from now on, such improper conduct will not occur; I will not do it again.

"Āsādiya" means having offended or struck against. "Edisaṃ" means such a person who is free from lust in all respects. "Aggim pajjalitaṃva liṅgiya" means like embracing a blazing fire.

"Tato" means from that rogue. "Sā bhikkhunī" refers to the nun Subhā. "Agamī buddhavarassa santikaṃ" means she approached the presence of the Fully Enlightened Buddha. "Passiya varapuññalakkhaṇaṃ" means having seen the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) produced by the supreme accumulation of merit. "Yathā purāṇakaṃ" means the eye became restored to its original state, just as it was before being plucked out. In this commentary, whatever has not been mentioned in between should be understood easily according to the method already stated.

## The Commentary on the Verses of Subhā Jīvakambavanikā Therī is finished.
## The Commentary on the Section of Thirty is finished.
267:
## 15. Cattālီsanipāta
## 1. Isidāsītherīgāthāvaṇṇanā
In the Section of Forty, the verse beginning with "Nagaramhi kusumanāme" is the verse of the Therī Isidāsī. This Therī also had performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Buddhas. While existing in the male form in various births, she accumulated wholesome merit that serves as a strong support for liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya). In the seventh birth before her final life, depending on bad friends, she committed the act of adultery (paradārikakamma). Upon the breaking up of the body, she was reborn in hell. Having suffered in that hell for many hundreds of years, she passed away from there and was reborn in the animal kingdom for three births. Passing away from there, she was reborn as a hermaphrodite (napuṃsaka) in the womb of a slave woman. Passing away from there again, she was reborn as the daughter of a poor cart-driver. When she reached maturity, Giridāsa, the son of a certain merchant, took her to his home as his wife. He already had a wife who was virtuous and of good conduct. Out of jealousy towards that wife, she made her husband hate that wife. Having lived there until the end of her life, upon the breaking up of the body, she was reborn in this Buddha's era in the city of Ujjenī as the daughter of a wealthy merchant who was highly esteemed for his lineage, virtue, and conduct. She was named Isidāsī.

When she reached maturity, her parents gave her in marriage to another merchant's son who was equal in lineage, appearance, age, and wealth. She lived in that merchant's house for about a month as a devoted wife (patidevatā) who revered her husband like a deity. Then, due to the power of her past karma, her husband became disgusted with her and expelled her from the house. All of this can be understood from the Pali text itself. Due to being disliked by various husbands, she became disenchanted (saṃvega), asked her parents for permission, and went forth as a nun in the presence of the Therī Jinadattā. While practicing insight meditation (vipassanā), she attained Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) before long. Spending her time in the bliss of fruition (phalasukha) and the bliss of Nibbāna, one day, after wandering for alms in the city of Pāṭaliputta and returning from the alms-round, she sat on the sandy bank of the great Ganges river. When her friend, the Therī named Bodhi, asked about her former practice, she answered that matter in the form of verses beginning with "Ujjeniyā puravare." To show the connection between those questions and answers:

In the city named Kusuma, which is Pāṭaliputta, the ornament of the earth,
There were two virtuous bhikkhunīs born of the Sakyan clan.
268:
Among those Elder Nuns, Isidāsī was one, and the second was Bodhī, who was endowed with virtue. These Elder Nuns delighted in the practice and cultivation of jhāna; they were very learned and had shaken off the defilements.

Having wandered for alms and finished their meal, they washed their bowls and were sitting comfortably in a secluded place when they spoke these words.

These three verses were placed here by the Recorders (Saṅgītikāras).

"Noble Lady Isidāsī, you are lovely to behold, and your youth has not yet faded. What suffering did you see that led you to be devoted to renunciation (nekkhamma)?" (Thus asked the Elder Nun Bodhī).

Being thus questioned, the Elder Nun Isidāsī, who was skilled in teaching the Dhamma, spoke these words: "Listen, Bodhī, to the reason why I went forth into homelessness."

## From here onwards are the verses of her reply.

"In the noble city of Ujjenī, my father was a merchant who was restrained in virtue. I was his only daughter, beloved, cherished, and the joy of his heart.

Then, suitors of noble lineage came from the city of Sāketa to ask for me. My father, a merchant of great wealth, gave me to them as a daughter-in-law.

I would approach my parents-in-law morning and evening and, as I had been instructed, I would bow my head to their feet in salutation.

Whenever I saw my husband's sisters, brothers, or attendants, even for a moment, I would respectfully offer them a seat with trepidation.

I served them with whatever food, drink, and snacks were available in the house, and I shared and distributed what was appropriate for each.

When it was time, I would wait at the entrance of the house, wash my husband's hands and feet, and approach him with joined palms.

Taking a comb, cosmetics, eye-salve, and a mirror, I would personally adorn my husband like a handmaid.

I cooked the rice myself and washed the dishes myself. Just as a mother cares for her only son, so did I serve and attend to my husband."
269:
"In this way, although I was devoted to my husband, affectionate, dutiful, humble, energetic, not lazy, and endowed with virtue, my husband hated me.

That husband said to his mother and father, 'I will take my leave and go; I do not wish to live with Isidāsī, nor do I wish to dwell in the same house with her.'

'Dear son, do not speak thus. Isidāsī is wise, very clever, energetic, and not lazy. Dear son, what is it that displeases you?' (the parents said).

'She does not harm me in any way, yet I do not wish to live with Isidāsī. My hatred alone is enough for me. I will take my leave and go,' (the husband replied).

Hearing his words, my mother-in-law and father-in-law asked me, 'What fault have you committed? Speak boldly according to the truth.'

'I have not committed any fault, nor have I caused any harm, nor have I spoken any harsh words. If my husband hates me, what can I do?' (I replied).

Those parents-in-law, being dejected and overcome by sorrow, sent me back to my father's house. By following the whims of their son, they lost a beautiful and auspicious wife.

Thereafter, my father gave me in marriage to the house of a second wealthy family. On that occasion, a merchant obtained me as a wife for half the dowry.

I lived in his house for a month, but then he too discarded me. Even though I served him like a slave and was faultless and endowed with virtue, (I was abandoned again).

Then my father said to a young man who was wandering for alms, one who was self-controlled and calm, 'Become my son-in-law; set down your bowl and water-pot.'

He too, after staying for half a month, said to my father, 'Give me back my bowl, water-pot, and cup; I will go wandering for alms again.'

Then my father said to him, 'Friend, I and my entire circle of relatives are here. What is not provided for you here? Speak quickly, and I shall have it done for you.'

When he was thus spoken to, he replied, 'If I can manage on my own, that is enough for me. I do not wish to live with Isidāsī, nor do I wish to dwell in the same house with her.'"
270:
"That husband abandoned me and left. I, being alone, thought to myself: 'I will ask permission from my parents and go; I will either die or I will renounce the world.'

At that time, the Noble Lady Jinadattā, who was a bearer of the Vinaya, very learned, and endowed with virtue, came to our house while wandering for alms.

Seeing that Noble Lady, I rose and prepared a seat for her. I bowed at the feet of the seated Noble Lady and offered her alms-food.

Having satisfied her with whatever rice, drink, and snacks were in the house, I said, 'Noble Lady, I wish to go forth as a nun.'

Then my father said to me, 'Dear daughter, practice the Dhamma right here in this house; satisfy the ascetics and brahmins with food and snacks.'

Then, weeping and with joined palms, I said to my father, 'I have committed evil kamma in the past; let me work to exhaust that kamma.'

Then my father said, 'Dear daughter, may you attain the Enlightenment (Bodhi), the Supreme Dhamma, and Nibbāna, which was realized by the Best of Bipeds (the Buddha).'

Having paid homage to my parents and all my relatives, I went forth. On the seventh day of my renunciation, I attained the Three Knowledges (Tevijjā).

I know my own seven past lives. I shall tell you of which kamma this life is the fruit; listen to it with an undistracted mind.

In the city of Erakaccha, I was once a goldsmith of great wealth. Intoxicated by the pride of youth, I committed adultery with the wives of others.

Passing away from that life, I suffered in hell for a long time. Having been cooked there and then emerging, I entered the womb of a female monkey.

When I was only seven days old, the great monkey who was the leader of the troop castrated me. This was the fruit of the kamma of committing adultery.

Passing away from that life and dying in the Sindhu forest, I again entered the womb of a female goat that was blind in one eye and lame."
271:
For twelve years, because of the karma of committing adultery with another's wife, I was born as a castrated boy and had to carry others on my back. I lived like a worm, unhealthy and miserable.

Passing away from that life, I was born in the womb of a cow belonging to a cattle merchant. I was a calf with a complexion as red as lac, and for twelve months, I underwent castration.

I had to pull the plow and the cart. Because of the karma of committing adultery with another's wife, I was blind, lived miserably, and was unhealthy.

Passing away from that life, I was born in the house of a female slave in an alley. Because of the karma of committing adultery with another's wife, I was born as a neuter, neither woman nor man.

At the age of thirty, I passed away and was born as a young girl in a family of cart-drivers. I was born into a poor family with few possessions, heavily oppressed by many creditors.

Then, a merchant, due to the excessively high interest, forcibly dragged me away from my family home while I was weeping.

Later, in my sixteenth year, when I reached the bloom of youth, a merchant's son named Giridāsa saw me and took me as his wife.

He already had another wife who was virtuous, reputable, and devoted to her husband. I harbored ill-will toward that senior wife.

Even though I served him like a slave, they abandoned me and left. This is indeed the result of that karma of harboring ill-will. I have now brought an end to that karma.

In that verse, 'in the city named Kusuma' means in the city known by the name 'Kusumapūra'; now he shows that city itself as 'in Pāṭaliputta'. 'In the center of the earth' means in the city which is like the center of the entire earth. 'Born in the Sakya clan' refers to those who were daughters of the Sakya clan and entered the dispensation of the Blessed One, the Son of the Sakyas, as Buddhists.

'Among them' means among those two bhikkhunīs. 'Bodhi' is the Elder nun (Therī) of that name. 'Delighting in the contemplation of jhāna' means those who greatly delight in the practice of both mundane and supramundane jhāna. 'Possessing great learning' (bahussuta) means those endowed with extensive knowledge of the scriptures (pariyatti). 'Who have shaken off defilements' means those who have completely eradicated all defilements through the Path of Arahatship. For the sake of alms...
272:
After finishing the meal, while sitting comfortably in a secluded place with the bliss of renunciation and the bliss of solitude, they engaged in pleasant conversation through questions and answers, which will now be told.

The verse beginning with 'Pāsādikāsi' was spoken by the Elder nun Bodhi as a question. The verse beginning with 'Evamanuyuñjiyamānā' was spoken only by the Recorders (Saṅgီtikāras). All the remaining verses beginning with 'Ujjeniyā' were spoken only by the Elder nun Isidāsī. In that verse, 'Pāsādikāsi' means being endowed with physical beauty, she was able to inspire confidence and devotion in those who saw her. 'Your youth has not yet faded; you are one who stands in the first stage of life' is the meaning of the phrase 'vayo pi te aparihīno'. 'What fault or danger did you see in household life?' is the question asked by the phrase 'kiṃ disvāna byālikaṃ'. In 'athāsi nekkhammamanuyuttā', 'atha' is merely a particle; it means she became one devoted to the state of a renunciant, which is nekkhamma.

'Anuyuñjiyamānā' means when being questioned; it should be connected with 'that Elder nun Isidāsī in a secluded place'. 'Listen, Bodhi, to how I ordained, listen to that story of the past,' is the meaning of the phrase 'suṇa bodhi yathāmhi pabbajitā'.

'Ujjeniyā puravare' means in the noble city named Ujjeni in the kingdom of Avanti. Being an only daughter, she was one to be loved and cherished, pleasing due to her virtues and conduct, and worthy of compassion. Later, when I reached the proper age, suitors from the city of Sāketa came to ask for me. They were from the highest family in that city; the merchant who sent them was one of great wealth. My father gave me as a daughter-in-law to that Sāketa merchant's son.

In the evenings and mornings, I would approach my mother-in-law and father-in-law and pay homage with my head; I would bow at their feet. 'I did exactly as they instructed; I did not transgress their advice,' is the meaning of the phrase 'yathāmhi anusiṭṭhā'. I also served my only beloved husband. Being one who was respectful and cautious, I would offer the appropriate seat to whichever person it was suitable for.
273:
In that verse, "tattha" means in the place of serving or feeding. "Sannihitaṃ" means being present and ready. "Chādemi" means I cover; having covered, I bring near; having brought near, I give; and in giving, I give only what is appropriate for that person.

"Ummāre" means on the threshold. "Dhovantī hatthapāde" should be connected as: she was one who washed her hands and feet, and after washing, she approached the house.

"Kocchaṃ" refers to a comb for grooming the beard and hair. "Pasādaṃ" means anointing the face with scented powder and so on. There is also a variant reading "pasādhanaṃ," which means ornaments or cosmetics. "Añjaniṃ" refers to a collyrium tube. "Parikammakārikā viya" means that although she was born of a noble family and possessed wealth, she served her husband like a servant girl.

"Sādhayāmi" means I cook. "Bhājanaṃ" refers to bronze vessels and the like. "Dhovantī paricarāmi" should be connected as: washing and serving.

"Bhattikataṃ" means having shown devotion to the husband. "Anurattaṃ" means being constantly affectionate. "Kārikaṃ" means performing various duties that ought to be done. "Nihatamānaṃ" means having abandoned pride. "Uṭṭhāyikaṃ" means being endowed with energetic effort. "Analasaṃ" means being free from laziness due to that very effort. "Sīlavatiṃ" means being endowed with virtue and good conduct. "Dussate" means offending, or speaking in anger.

"Āpucchahaṃ gamissāmi" (I will take leave and go) means that my husband said to his parents, "I will take leave of you and go somewhere." If asked what he said: "I cannot live with Isidāsī; it is impossible for me to live together in the same house." In this context, "vacchaṃ" means I shall dwell.

"Desso" means an unloved person. "Alaṃ me" means "I have no further use for that woman." "Apucchahaṃ gamissāmi" means "If you wish me to live with that woman, I will take leave of you and depart for another place."

"Tassa" means to my husband. "Kissā" means "What happened to your husband?" It implies, "Did you commit some fault or act deceitfully?"

"Napihṃ aparajjhaṃ" means "I did not commit even a single fault against that husband." This is the text itself. "Napi hiṃsemi" means "I did not cause any harm either." "Dubbacanaṃ" refers to bad speech. "Kiṃ sakkā kaatuyye" means "Noble lady, what can I do?" "Yaṃ maṃ viddessate bhattā" means "Because the husband, for no reason at all, is angry with me and feels aversion toward me."
274:
"Vimanā" (displeased) means having an unhappy heart. "Puttamanurakkhamānā" (protecting the son) means protecting by way of guarding the mind of her son, who is my husband. "Jitāmhase rūpiniṃ lakkhiṃ" (we have lost the beautiful Lakkhī) means we have lost the beautiful glory; it means we have been deprived of the Goddess of Fortune who wanders in human form.

"Aḍḍhassa gharamhi dutiyakulikassa" (in the house of a wealthy second husband) means that starting from the first husband, I was given to the house of a second wealthy son of a good family. In giving me, I was given with a dowry that was half of the first dowry. "Yena maṃ vindatha seṭṭhī" (by which dowry the merchant obtained me) means the merchant first obtained me with a certain dowry; it should be connected as: (given to the second husband) with half of that dowry.

"Sopi" (he too) refers to the second husband. "Maṃ paṭiccharayi" (he abandoned me) means he drove me out; he expelled me from the house. "Upaṭṭhahantiṃ" (while serving) means while I was performing service like a slave girl. "Adūsikaṃ" (without fault) means without having committed any offense.

"Damakaṃ" (a tamer) means one who tames the minds of others based on compassion. It refers to one who wanders for alms given by others, having made his own body and speech tamed and peaceful so that others might give something. "Jာမာတာ" (son-in-law) means the daughter's husband. "Nikkhipa poṭṭhiñca ghaṭikañca" (put down the rags and the pot-shard) means "Discard the pieces of rags you are wearing and the alms-bowl shard."

"Sopi vasitvā pakkhāṃ" (he too, having stayed, went) means that beggar man also left after staying with me for about half a month. Then the father spoke to him (atha naṃ bhaṇati tāto) means my father, mother, and all my relatives gathered in groups and spoke to that beggar. How? "What is not done for you here? What indeed is not provided or accomplished? Speak quickly. We will do that for you."

"Yadi me attā sakkoti" (if my self is able) means if my self follows my own will and is free: "I have had enough of Isidāsī; I have no need for her. Therefore, I do not wish to live with her; I cannot dwell with her in the same house."

"Vissajjito gato so" (released, he went) means that beggar, having been permitted by the father, went wherever he pleased. "Ekākinī" (alone) means being all by oneself. Having asked permission (āpucchitūna)...
275:
"Gacchanti" means "I will go after taking leave of my father." "Marituye" means for the purpose of dying. "Vā" is a particle used in the sense of an alternative (vikkappattha). "Gocarāya" means for the purpose of alms-food; it should be connected as "came to the father's family home."

"Taṃ" refers to the Elder Nun Jinadattā. "Rising, I prepared a seat for that Elder Nun" means that after getting up, I prepared a place for that Elder Nun to sit. "Right here" means staying in this very house. "Dear child" (Puttakā) is a common term used to address a daughter out of compassion. "Practice the Dhamma" means to practice the Dhamma such as the holy life (brahmacariya) that should be practiced after ordaining. "Dvijāti" means the Brahmin caste. "I shall exhaust" means I shall make it age or destroy it.

"Bodhi" refers to the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) that penetrates the Four Noble Truths. "The Supreme Dhamma" refers to the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). "The Buddha, the best of bipeds, realized which Dhamma" means that the Perfectly Enlightened One, the supreme among humans and gods, realized the supramundane Dhamma known as the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna; it should be connected as "may you attain that Dhamma."

"Having been ordained for seven days" means within seven days after ordaining. "I have touched" (Aphassayim) means I have touched or realized. "This is the result (vipāka) of that unwholesome deed" means this is the resultant effect (nissandaphala) of that base deed, characterized by being unpleasant to the husband. "I will tell that to you" means I will tell that karma to you. "Taṃ" refers to that karma being told, or to my words. "With a single mind" means with a concentrated mind. This is the text itself.

"In the city of Erakaccha" means in the city of that name. "He committed adultery with another's wife" means that I committed adultery with another's wife. "Cooked for a long time" means being burned by the fires of hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. "Rising from there" means after passing away and rising from that hell. "I entered the womb of a female monkey" means I took conception in the womb of a female monkey.

"Yūthapa" is the leader of the herd, the monkey king. "Castrated" (Nillacchisi) means he removed the testicles, which are the marks of masculinity. "This is the fruit of that karma" means this is the fruit of the karma I performed in the past. "Just as going to another's wife" means just as I transgressed with another's wife.
276:
"Tato" means from the monkey species (from the life of a monkey). "Sindhavāraññe" means in a forest area in the Sindhavā region. "Eḷakiyā" means by a female goat (or ewe).

"Carrying the children" (Dārakaṃ parivahitvā) means carrying the young ones on the back. "Kimināvaṭṭo" means being surrounded by worms in the place of birth and thus suffering distress. "Akallo" means being ill; the word "ahosi" (was) is the remaining part of the sentence.

"Govāṇijakassa" means of one who makes a living by selling cows. "Lākhātambo" means one endowed with hair as red as if dyed with lac-dye.

"Voḍhūnā" means by carrying. "Naṅgalaṃ" means the plow, and "sakaṭañca dhārayāmi" means I have to pull the cart. "Andhovaṭṭo" means being blind in one eye and thus oppressed and weary.

"Vīthiyā" means in the city street. "Born in the house of a maidservant" means born from the womb of a domestic maidservant. Some also say "from a prostitute" (vaṇṇadāsiyā). "Neither woman nor man" means I was neither a woman nor a man, but a congenital eunuch (jātinapuṃsaka).

"Died at the age of thirty" means dying at the age of thirty while being a eunuch. "In a family of carters" means in a family of charioteers or cart-drivers. "In a family frequently beset by creditors" means in a family overwhelmed and oppressed by many creditors.

"Ussannāya" means accumulated. "Vipulāya" means great. "Vaḍḍhiyā" means the increase of debt interest. "Okkaḍဎati" means being dragged out. "Kulagharasmā" means from the family home where I was born.

"The son of Orundhata" refers to the son of that merchant leader; a man named Giridāsa, who had an attached mind toward me, kept me in his house as his possession.

"Devoted to her husband" (Anurattā bhattāraṃ) means one who follows the will of her husband. "I caused enmity for her" means I performed an act to make that husband hate that wife, my co-wife. I acted in such a way that the husband would be angry with her.
277:
"They abandon me and go away," in this phrase, it means that husbands abandon me, discard me, and leave without any regard, even though I serve them respectfully like a maidservant in various places. This being abandoned is the resultant effect (nissandaphala) of the karma of committing adultery (paradārika-kamma) and the karma of causing hatred toward a co-wife, which I performed at that time.

"I have also made an end to that karma," in this phrase, it means that I, who have now attained the supreme Path of Arahantship, have made an end to that terrible, base karma that was once so enticing. From now on, there is not even the slightest bit of suffering. Whatever has not been explained in detail here and there is clear in meaning according to the method already mentioned.

## The Explanation of the Verses of the Elder Nun Isidāsī is finished.

## The Explanation of the Section of the Forties is finished.
278:
## 16. Mahānipāta
## 1. Sumedhātherīgāthāvaṇṇanā

In the Mahānipāta, the verse beginning with "Mantāvatiyā nagare" is that of the Elder Nun Sumedhā. This Sumedhā had also performed meritorious deeds under previous Buddhas, accumulating wholesome roots conducive to liberation (vivaṭṭūpanissaya) in various existences, and respectfully fulfilling the requisites for liberation (vimokkha-sambhāra). During the time of the Blessed Koṇāgamana Buddha, she was born into a noble family. Upon reaching the age of discretion, she and her female companions of similar status shared a common aspiration; they built a large monastery (ārāma) and offered it to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Due to that meritorious deed, when her body perished, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Having enjoyed divine bliss there for the full lifespan, she passed away and was reborn in the Yāma heaven. From there, she passed away and was reborn in Tusitā; then in Nimmānarati; and then in Paranimmitavasavatti. Thus, she was reborn successively in the five celestial realms of the sense sphere, serving as the chief queen of the kings of those realms. After passing away from there, during the time of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha, she was born as the daughter of a very wealthy merchant. Upon reaching maturity, she became a devoted follower of the Dispensation and performed noble meritorious deeds dedicated to the Triple Gem.

In that life, she lived righteously until the end of her days, delighting in wholesome states. After passing away, she was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and wandered through the cycle of rebirth only in happy destinations (sugati). In this current Buddha's era, she was born in the city of Mantāvatī as the daughter of King Koñca. Her parents named her Sumedhā. When she grew up and reached marriageable age, her parents consulted each other, saying, "We shall give her in marriage to King Anikaratta of the city of Vāraṇavatī." However, from her youth, she had gone to the nunnery with princesses of her own age and attendants to listen to the Dhamma from the bhikkhunīs. Because of the meritorious deeds she had performed over a long period, she felt spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the cycle of rebirth and became deeply devoted to the Dispensation. By the time she reached maturity, her mind was turned away from sensual pleasures. Therefore, upon hearing her parents' and relatives' consultation, she said, "I have no need for household life; I will ordain." Although her parents urged her toward household life and pleaded with her in various ways, they were unable to convince her. She [thought], "In this way...
279:
"May I be allowed to ordain," she thought, and taking a sword, she cut her own hair. Taking those very hairs as her object, she developed the reflection on foulness (paṭikkūlamanasikāra). While reflecting thus, due to her past meritorious deeds and having previously heard the method of reflection from the bhikkhunīs, she produced the sign of foulness (asubha-nimitta) and attained the first jhāna in that object. Having attained the first jhāna, she inspired her parents, who had come to urge her toward household life, as well as the household members, attendants, and the entire royal family, to have great faith in the Dispensation. She then left home, went to the nunnery, and ordained. After ordaining, she practiced insight meditation (vipassanā). As her knowledge matured and because of her excellence in the qualities that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya-dhamma), she soon attained Arahatship along with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). This is stated in the Apadāna:

## Apadāna (Ap. Therī 2.1.1-19)
During the time of the Blessed Koṇāgamana Buddha, in the new settlement of the Saṅghārāma, three female friends gave the gift of a monastery.

Ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, and more than a hundred thousand times, we were reborn in the celestial realms; what need is there to mention the human realm?

In the celestial realms, we were possessed of great psychic power; what need is there to mention the human realm? I was the "Woman-Treasure" (itthi-ratana), the chief queen of a Wheel-turning Monarch.

In this life, having accumulated merit and being born into very prosperous families, there were three of us: Dhanañjānī, Khemā, and myself.

Having built a well-constructed monastery, adorned with all its parts, and having offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, we were filled with joy.

By the power of that meritorious deed, in every place we were reborn, we reached the highest status among both gods and humans.

In this very eon, there arose the Great Renowned One, a kinsman of Brahmā, Kassapa by clan, the best of speakers.

At that time, in the supreme city of Bārāṇasī, there was a King of Kāsi named Kikī, who was the attendant of that Great Sage.
280:
That king had seven daughters, princesses who grew up in comfort. Delighting in serving the Buddha, they lived the holy life.

Being a companion to those princesses, well-established in virtue, having respectfully given gifts, I practiced the religious life even while in the household.

Due to that well-performed deed, and because of my intention and aspiration, I abandoned the human body and reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

When I passed away from that heaven, I reached the Yāma heaven. From there, I went to the Tusita heaven. From there, I reached the Nimmānarati heaven and the Vasavatti heaven.

In whatever life I was reborn, being endowed with merit, I attained the position of chief queen to kings in those very lives.

When I passed away from those heavens and was born in the human world, I attained the position of chief queen to Universal Monarchs and to kings who ruled over nations.

Experiencing prosperity and happiness among gods and humans, being happy in all states, I wandered through Saṃsāra for many births.

That merit is the cause, that merit is the origin, that merit is the root; it is the faith in the Dispensation. That merit is the first meeting; for me, who delights in the Dhamma, it leads to Nibbāna.

My defilements have been burned away; all existences have been uprooted. Like a female elephant having broken her bonds, I live without taints.

My coming to the presence of the Excellent Buddha was indeed a good coming. The three knowledges have been attained; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

The four analytical insights, the eight liberations, and the six direct knowledges have been realized; the Buddha's teaching has been carried out.

Having attained Arahantship and reviewing her own practice, she spoke thus by way of an inspired utterance:

In the city of Mantāvatī, I was the daughter named Sumedhā, born to the chief queen of King Koñca. I was one who was inspired by the Buddhas, the makers of the Dispensation.

Virtuous, eloquent, learned, and disciplined in the Buddha's Dispensation, that Sumedhā approached her parents and said, 'Mother and father, please listen to me.'
281:
Delighting in Nibbāna, I do not delight in existence, even if it be divine, for it is impermanent. What need is there to speak of empty sensual pleasures, which provide little gratification and much suffering?

Sensual pleasures are like poison and are bitter. Fools who are infatuated with those sensual pleasures fall into hell for a long time and are painfully oppressed.

Fools who are unrestrained in body, speech, and mind, who increase evil, and who have bad kamma, always grieve in the states of deprivation.

Those fools, lacking wisdom and mindless, blocked by the cause of suffering, do not know or see the Noble Truths taught by the Buddhas.

Mother, those who do not know the Truths taught by the Excellent Buddha are many. They delight in existence and long for rebirth among the gods.

Even rebirth among the gods is included in the round of existence and is therefore impermanent. Fools do not fear the danger of being reborn again and again.

The four states of deprivation and the two [good] destinations are obtained with difficulty. For those who have gone to the states of deprivation, there is no opportunity for renunciation in the hells.

O parents, please allow me to renounce in the teaching of the Buddha, the Ten-Powered One. I will strive without anxiety to abandon birth and death.

What is the use of delighting in existence with this essence-less, flawed body? I will renounce for the cessation of craving for existence; please grant me permission.

The arising of Buddhas is rare; having avoided the wrong times, the rare and opportune moment has been obtained. I shall not defile virtue and the holy life as long as I live.

Sumedhā said to her parents, 'As long as I remain a householder, I will no longer take food; I shall only go towards death.'

The mother and father wept in distress. While Sumedhā, being greatly oppressed, lay fallen on the ground on the palace floor, the parents tried to persuade her to understand.
282:
“Rise, dear daughter, why do you grieve? You have already been given [in marriage] in the city of Vāraṇavatī. King Anīkaratta is handsome; you have been given to him.

You will be the wife and chief queen of King Anīkaratta. Dear daughter, the undertaking of virtue, the living of the holy life, and renunciation are very difficult.

In the kingdom, there are power, wealth, and sovereignty. Sensual pleasures are delightful, and you are still young. Enjoy sensual pleasures; let there be a marriage ceremony for you.”

Then Sumedhā said to her parents: “Do not speak such words regarding the essence-less round of existence. For me, there will be either renunciation or death, but marriage shall never be.

Why should I embrace this foul body, which is like a bag of skin full of impurity, constantly leaking, frightening, like a rotting corpse, and smelling of stench?

Knowing this body to be essence-less—smeared with flesh and blood, an abode for swarms of worms, and food for birds—why is it being given [in marriage]?

Before long, relatives who loathe this body, devoid of consciousness, will discard it like a log and carry it to the cemetery.

After discarding it in the cemetery, even one's own parents, loathing it, will bathe [as if touched by another's filth]. What then to say of ordinary people?

People are attached to this essence-less, foul body, which is a collection of bones and sinews, filled with saliva, excrement, and sweat.

If one were to dissect this body and turn the inside out, even one's own parents would loathe it, unable to bear the smell.

The aggregates, elements, and bases are only conditioned phenomena; they are merely sufferings rooted in rebirth. Why should I, who reflects with wise consideration, desire marriage?

Let three hundred fresh spears fall upon this body every single day; even being oppressed like that for a hundred years is better, if by such means the end of suffering [Nibbāna] can be achieved.”
283:
One who understands the Teacher's word in this way should accept even being killed. For those who are killed again and again, saṃsāra is indeed long.

Among gods, humans, animals, asuras, petas, and in hells, immeasurable instances of being killed are seen.

For one who has fallen into hell and is being tormented, the instances of being killed in hell are many. Even among the gods, there is no refuge other than the bliss of Nibbāna.

Those who are joined with the teaching of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) have reached Nibbāna. Free from anxiety, they strive for the abandonment of birth and death.

"Dear father, I shall go forth this very day; what is the use of these essence-less riches? I am disgusted by sensual pleasures; they are like vomit, and like a palm tree with its head cut off, their roots are already severed."

When the time for the marriage arrived in the city of Vāraṇavata, she spoke in this way to her father and to Prince Anīkaratta, to whom she had been given.

Then Sumedhā, having cut off her dark, soft, and thick hair with a sword and having closed the palace door, entered and dwelt in the first jhāna.

While she was thus absorbed in attainment, Prince Anīkaratta arrived at the city. On the palace, Sumedhā was developing the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā).

While she was reflecting in her mind, Prince Anīkaratta, his body adorned with jewels and gold, quickly ascended and, with palms joined, entreated Sumedhā:

"Royal power, wealth, sovereignty, enjoyments, and happiness are still with you in your youth. Enjoy sensual pleasures; in this world, sensual happiness is difficult to obtain.

I hand over the kingdom to you; enjoy the riches and give gifts. Do not be dejected; your parents are in distress."

Sumedhā replied to that prince: "I have no need for sensual pleasures; I am one who is free from delusion. Do not delight in sensual pleasures; see the danger in them.

King Mandhātu, who ruled over the four great islands, was the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures. Yet he passed away unsatisfied, his desires unfulfilled."

After death, I was born as a girl in a family of carters, who were poor and possessed few riches, and were constantly oppressed by creditors. Later, a merchant, due to the accumulation of heavy interest, forcibly took me from my parents' house, dragging me away while I was weeping and lamenting.

Then, when I reached the age of sixteen, the son of that merchant named Giridāsa, seeing me as a grown maiden, took me as his wife. Besides me, Giridāsa had another senior wife who was endowed with virtue, merit, and a retinue, and who served her husband respectfully. I caused that husband to hate his senior wife.

Even though I served them as I did, husbands would abandon me and leave. This being abandoned by husbands is the consequence of my evil kamma of destroying others' marriages and causing hatred between husband and wife. Now, I have brought that terrible consequence of evil kamma to an end through the Path of Arahantship.

In those verses, "in the city named Kusuma" means in the city called Kusumapura. Now, that city is specifically shown as Pāṭaliputta. It is called "Maṇi" (Gem) because it is like an ornament of the entire earth. She is called "Sakyakulakulīnā" because she is a noble daughter of the Sakyan clan and because she went forth in the dispensation of the Buddha, who was a Sakyan prince.

Among those two bhikkhunīs, the Elder Bodhī was greatly devoted to the attainment of mundane and supramundane jhānas. She was very learned in the scriptures (pariyatti). She had completely eradicated all defilements through the Path of Arahantship. When the meal was finished, while they were staying happily in a secluded place with the bliss of recluseship and the bliss of seclusion (or the bliss of Nibbāna), they recited these verses while engaging in questions and answers. The verse beginning with "Pāsādikāsī" was spoken as a question by the Elder Bodhī. The verse "Evamanuyuñjiyamānā" was inserted by the Elders who conducted the Council. All the remaining verses starting from "Ujjeniyā" were spoken only by the Elder Isidāsī.

In those verses, "Pāsādikāsī" means that because she was perfect in form, she was inspiring to those who saw her. "Vayo pi te aparihīno" means that your age has not yet declined and you are still in your first youth. When asked what fault she saw in household life that she repeatedly strove for the state of a recluse, which is the escape from sensual pleasures, that Elder Isidāsī said in that secluded place, "O Noble Lady Bodhī, listen to the former causes of my going forth."

In Ujjenī, the noble city of the Avanti kingdom, I was an only daughter, beloved, endowed with virtue, one who gladdened the heart, and one to be cherished. Later, when I reached the proper age, suitors arrived from the city of Sāketa. The one sent by the noble clansmen of that city to ask for me was a great merchant who was wealthy and possessed many jewels. My father gave me as a daughter-in-law (as a wife) for the son of that Sāketa merchant.

Every evening and morning, I had to approach my parents-in-law and bow to them with my head. I had to bow at their feet. I acted according to their instructions and did not transgress their advice. Even if I saw someone familiar, I would be startled and offer them a suitable seat. I had to store and preserve the items prepared in the service area, and I had to bring and give what should be brought near. In giving, I gave only the objects suitable for that person.

I was the one who washed their hands and feet at the doorway. Only after washing them did I enter the house. Carrying a comb to comb the beard and hair, as well as scented powder, face powder, and a collyrium stick, like a handmaid...
284:
Even if the seven jewels were to rain down from all around like rain in the ten directions, there would still be no satisfaction in sensual pleasures. Humans die while still unsatisfied.

Sensual pleasures are like a slaughterhouse; they are like the head of a snake. They burn like a torch and are like a heap of bones.

Sensual pleasures are impermanent, unstable, and full of much suffering; they are like a potent poison. Like a heated iron ball, they are the basis of misfortune and yield painful results.

Sensual pleasures are like fruit, like a piece of meat, causing suffering. They are deceptive like a dream and like borrowed goods.

Sensual pleasures are like a spear or a stake; they are like disease, an ailment, a danger, and destruction. They are like a pit of glowing coals, the root of evil, a source of fear, and a means of slaughter.
