Thus, sensual pleasures have been declared to involve much suffering; they create obstacles. Go away! I no longer have any confidence in my own existence.

If one's own head were on fire, or if old age and death were following closely behind, what could another do for me? One should only strive to destroy that old age and death.

Having opened the door and seen my parents and all my relatives sitting on the ground weeping, I said these words:

Saṃsāra is long for the foolish who weep again and again. In this beginningless saṃsāra, the death of fathers, the killing of brothers, and one's own killing have been many.

Remember the tears, the mother's milk, and the blood that have flowed since the beginningless saṃsāra. Remember also the heap of bones of beings who have wandered in saṃsāra.

Remember that when compared to the tears, milk, and blood that have been shed, the four oceans are small. Remember that the heap of bones accumulated in a single aeon is as large as Mount Vipula.

While wandering in the beginningless saṃsāra, if the earth of Jambudīpa were made into small clay balls the size of jujube seeds to count one's mothers, the mothers would be more numerous than those clay balls; they would not be enough.

If grass, wood, branches, and leaves were made into four-inch pieces to count one's fathers since the beginningless saṃsāra, the fathers would be more numerous than those pieces of wood; they would not be enough.
285:
Remember the one-eyed turtle in the eastern ocean and the yoke hole coming from the west. The turtle's head entering that yoke hole is a simile for the difficulty of obtaining human birth.

Remember the physical form of this body, which is like a mass of foam, essence-less, and faulty. Behold the impermanent aggregates. Remember hell, where there is much torment.

Remember that which causes the cemetery to grow again and again in various births. Remember the dangers of crocodiles and remember the Four Noble Truths.

While the Deathless Nibbāna exists, what benefit is there for you in drinking the five bitters? All delights in sensual pleasures are more bitter than the five bitters.

While the Deathless Nibbāna exists, what benefit is there for you in sensual pleasures that are burning? All delights in sensual pleasures are burning, boiling, trembling, and agonizing.

While the enemy-less Nibbāna exists, what benefit is there for you in sensual pleasures that have many enemies? Sensual pleasures are shared with kings, fire, thieves, water, and the unloved; they have many enemies.

While the liberation of Nibbāna exists, what benefit is there for you in sensual pleasures where there is killing and binding? Those who lust after sensual pleasures experience the suffering of being killed and bound.

Just as a person holding a burning grass torch is burned if they do not let it go, so do sensual pleasures, which are like a torch, burn those who do not let them go.

Do not give up great happiness for the sake of a small amount of sensual pleasure. Do not be like a fish that swallows a hook and suffers later.

Discipline yourself regarding sensual pleasures. Do not be like a dog bound by an iron chain. Sensual pleasures will destroy you just as hungry outcasts kill a dog.

One associated with sensual pleasures will experience immeasurable suffering and much mental distress. Give up impermanent sensual pleasures.

While the ageless Nibbāna exists, what benefit is there for you in sensual pleasures where there is aging? In all births, all beings everywhere are oppressed by death and disease.

This Nibbāna is ageless, it is deathless; it is the state free from aging and death, free from sorrow, without enemies, without confinement, without failure, safe, and without distress.
286:
This Deathless Nibbāna has been attained by many; this Deathless Nibbāna is still attainable even now. He who strives wisely [attains it]; but one who does not strive cannot possibly attain [Nibbāna].

Sumedhā, finding no delight in conditioned things, spoke thus. While persuading Prince Anikaratta, Sumedhā cast her hair upon the ground.

That Prince Anikaratta, having risen and with palms joined in reverence, entreated Sumedhā's father: "Please grant permission for Sumedhā, who wishes to see the truth and the Nibbāna of liberation, to go forth as a monastic."

When permitted by her parents, Sumedhā, fearing the danger of sorrow, went forth. Practicing the three trainings, that Sumedhā realized the six supernormal powers and the highest fruit of Arahatship.

The attainment of Nibbāna by Sumedhā, the princess, was truly wonderful and marvelous. How did she explain her past conduct in her final days?

In the time of the Blessed Buddha Koṇāgamana, in a newly built Saṅghārāma monastery, three women friends gave the gift of a monastery.

We were reborn in the deva realms ten times, a hundred times, a thousand times, and a hundred thousand times; what need is there to mention rebirth in the human realm?

We were of great power in the deva realms; what need is there to mention the human realm? I was once the Chief Queen of a Universal Monarch, a jewel of a woman.

That gift was the cause, that gift was the origin, that gift was the root, and that gift was the delight in the Dispensation. That was the first meeting; for me, who delights in the Dhamma, that gift was the cause for Nibbāna.

"Those who believe the words of the Buddha of incomparable wisdom act in this way. They become weary of existence; having become weary, they become dispassionate." Thus she spoke these verses.

In those verses, "Mantavatiyā nagare" means in the city named Mantavatī. "Rañño Koñcassa" means she was the daughter born from the womb of the Chief Queen of the King named Koñca. By name, she was Sumedhā. "Pasāditā sāthanakarehi" means she was one who was inspired to have faith in the Dispensation through the Dhamma teaching of the Noble Ones who carry out the Dispensation of the Buddha, and was made to have faith in the Triple Gem.
287:
Sīlavatī means being endowed with conduct and virtue. Cittakathā means having fascinating Dhamma talk. Bahussutā means being endowed with hearing the scriptural Dhamma in the presence of the bhikkhunīs. Disciplined in the Buddha's Dispensation (Buddhasāsane vinītā) means being one whose body, speech, and mind are disciplined and restrained in the Buddha's Dispensation because of being free from defilements temporarily (tadaṅga) through wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra) in accordance with the Suttas, such as: "Thus is arising, thus is ceasing; this is virtue, this is concentration, this is wisdom." The phrase "Listen, both of you" should be connected as approaching the parents and speaking, "Both of you, listen to my words."

Even though it is an attainment of existence within the deva world, all existence is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. What need is there to mention empty human sensual pleasures? All those sensual pleasures are empty and void because they lack essence; they provide little gratification, like a drop of honey on the edge of a sword. They involve much exhaustion due to great suffering both now and in the future.

Kaṭukā means disagreeable. They are compared to a cobra because of their fearsome nature. "Infatuation in those sensual pleasures" means being deeply attached. Samappitā means entirely surrendered, cast down, or arisen due to one's own kamma. Haññante means they are oppressed.

Vinipāte means in the realms of misery (apāya).

Acetanā means "without intention" because of the absence of intention directed toward one's own benefit. Dukkhasamudayoruddhā means they are imprisoned in Saṃsāra, which has craving as its root cause. When the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths is being preached, they do not know the meaning and thus do not understand the Noble Truths such as suffering.

"Ammā" is an address made with the mother as the primary recipient. It should be connected as: those who delight in reaching existence, who long for rebirth among the devas, and who do not know the Truths preached by the Excellent Buddha—those very people are the most numerous in this world.

All existence is impermanent; rebirth among the devas is also not eternal. Even though this is so, fools are not terrified, they do not fear, and they do not gain a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). "To be born again and again" means arising repeatedly.

The four downfalls (vinipāta) are: hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and the asura realm. These four are called "destinations of downfall" (vinipātagati) because they destroy happiness.
288:
The two destinations known as rebirth among humans and devas are obtained with great difficulty and hardship through some means, because meritorious deeds are difficult to perform. "Nirayesu" means in the woeful planes which are devoid of happiness.

"Appossukkā" means being free from concern for other matters (strive on). "Ghaṭissaṃ" means I will strive, I will practice meditation. The connection is: "Why should I delight in existence with a body that is like essence-less impurity?"

"Bhavataṇhāya nirodhā" means because of the cause of the cessation of craving for existence, for the sake of cessation.

The connection is: The arising of the Buddhas has been obtained; the eight inopportune moments, such as rebirth in hell, have been avoided; and the ninth opportune moment has been obtained. "Sīlāni" refers to the Fourfold Purification Morality (catupārisuddhisīla). "Brahmacariyaṃ" refers to the noble holy life in the Sasana. "Na dūseyyaṃ" means I shall not violate (or defile) it.

The connection is: Sumedhā said to her parents, "I will not yet eat food as a layperson. If I do not obtain ordination, I will surely face death."

"Assā" refers to Sumedhā's (tears). "Sabbaso samabhihato" means having a face completely struck by tears. "Ghaṭenti saññāpetuṃ" means the parents strive and persuade Sumedhā, who is lying on the ground on the palace floor, to remain in the lay life. There is also a variant reading "Ghaṭenti vāyamanti", which has the same meaning.

"Kiṃ socitena" means why do you worry, thinking "I will not obtain ordination"? "Dinnāsi Vāraṇavatimhi" means you have been given (to King Anikaratta) in the city of Vāraṇavatī. After saying "Dinnāsi", saying "Tvaṃ dinnā" again is to show the firmness of the fact that she has been given.

"Rajje āṇā" means your authority will spread in the kingdom of King Anikaratta. "Dhanamissariyaṃ" means the mastery of wealth and the most delightful pleasures and happiness in this family and in the husband's family have reached your hands. "Daharikāsi" means you are still of a young age, so enjoy sensual pleasures. The connection is: For that reason, let there be a marriage for you with sons.

"Ne" refers to the parents. "Mā edisikāni" means let there not be such things as royal authority. Why? She said, "Bhagavatam asāraṃ" (the body is essence-less), and so on.
289:
'Like a worm' (kimi vā) means just like a maggot. 'Foul body' (pūtikāyaṃ) refers to this putrid carcass. 'Spreading stench' (savaṇagandhaṃ) means having a foul odor that spreads out. 'Fearful' (bhayānakaṃ) means causing fear to those who are not yet free from lust. 'One should enter a bag of corpses' (kuṇapaṃ abhisaṃviseyyaṃ bhastaṃ) is like entering a leather bag filled with a putrid corpse. Should one always be attached to and delight in this body, thinking 'this is mine', when it is full of various impurities and constantly leaking?

In the phrase 'knowing it to be like a worm' (kimi va tahaṃ jānantī), 'loathsome' (vikūlakaṃ) refers to the body which is extremely disgusting, smeared with lumps of flesh and blood, an abode for many families of worms, and food for birds. In the reading 'kimikulālasakuṇabhattaṃ', the meaning is food for worms and the remaining birds. I stand knowing that carcass. She shows: 'Why and for what reason is that [body] of mine now being given by way of marriage?' The connection should be seen as: 'How is that gift of his like a worm?'

'The body is carried to the cemetery, soon the body is without consciousness' (nibbuyhati susānaṃ, aciraṃ kāyo apetaviññāṇo) means this body, with consciousness departed, will soon be carried or brought to the cemetery. 'Discarded' (chuddho) means thrown away. 'Like a log' (kaḷingaraṃ viya) means like a useless piece of wood. Even being loathed by relatives, it is taken to the cemetery.

'Having discarded it in the cemetery' (chuddhūna naṃ susāne) means having thrown that carcass in the cemetery. 'Food for others' (parabhattaṃ) means becoming food for others such as dogs and jackals. 'They bathe, being disgusted' (nhāyanti jigucchantā) means being so disgusted that they think, 'I have come from behind this carcass,' and they bathe by submerging their heads; what to say of those who actually touched it? Even one's own parents are disgusted. What need is there to mention how other people would be disgusted?

'Attached' (ajjhositā) means being obsessed through the power of craving. 'In the essenceless' (asāre) occurs in the body which is devoid of essence such as permanence.

'Having separated' (vinibbhujitvā) means having made it separate from consciousness. 'Unable to endure the stench' (gandhassa asahamānā) means because they cannot endure the smell of this body. Even one's own mother would be extremely disgusted when the body parts are separated, because the loathsome nature becomes clearly manifest.
290:
Aggregates, elements, and bases mean these five aggregates such as the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha), these eighteen elements such as the eye element (cakkhudhātu), and these twelve bases such as the eye base (cakkhāyatana). Thus, all this collection of mental and physical phenomena, known as aggregates, elements, and bases, is called 'conditioned' (saṅkhata) because it is produced by the combination and coordination of causes. This conditioned thing is the suffering (dukkha) that occurs in that existence; because it has the cause of being born, it has birth (jāti) as its root. Reflecting and thinking repeatedly with wise means in this way: "For what reason should I desire marriage?"

In response to the parents' words, "Observing virtue (sīla), practicing the holy life (brahmacariya), and ordaining (pabbajjā) are difficult," the words beginning with "Day by day" (divase divase) were spoken. In that context, "Let three hundred spears fall upon the body every day" means that every day, three hundred sharp spears should fall upon the body. "Even being tortured for a hundred years is better" means that even being tortured by the aforementioned spear strikes continuously for a hundred years is better. "Thus suffering is exhausted" means that if the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha) would be exhausted in this way, one should endure even such great occurring suffering and make an effort to attain Nibbāna.

"Ajjhupagacche" means one should accept. "Evaṃ" is in the manner already described. The meaning is: if a person, understanding the words of the Teacher who shows the beginningless Saṃsāra and the immeasurable suffering of the round of rebirths, remains firm, they should accept the aforementioned suffering of spear strikes; by such acceptance, the suffering of the round of rebirths would be exhausted. Therefore, it is said: "Long is their Saṃsāra, they are being struck again and again." This means those who are oppressed by repeated birth, aging, sickness, death, and so on.

"Asurakāya" refers to the assembly of peta-asuras such as the Kālakañjikas. "Ghātā" means the destruction or killing of both body and mind.

"Bahū" means many instances of oppression occurring through the power of the fivefold bonds and other such punishments (kammakāraṇa). "Vinipātagatassa" refers to one who has reached the downfall (vinipāta) known as the remaining lower realms. "Pīḷiyamānassa" refers to one being oppressed in an existence such as that of an animal. Even among the devas, there is no refuge (atāṇa) because there is suffering and distress due to the fever of lust (rāga) and so on. There is no other supreme bliss beyond the bliss of Nibbāna; worldly bliss is...
291:
...due to its nature of suffering in change (vipariṇāma) and suffering in formations (saṅkhāradukkha). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Nibbāna is the highest bliss" (Dhp. 203-204).

"They have reached Nibbāna" means they are indeed those who have reached Nibbāna. Alternatively, only they have reached Nibbāna. "Those who are devoted to the teaching of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)" means those who are well-exerted and devoted to the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Fully Enlightened One.

"Nibbindā" means those who are weary and detached. "Me" means 'by me'. "Vantasamā" means those who are like a dog's vomit. "Tālavatthukatā" means those who are made like a palmyra stump.

"Atha" means 'afterwards', after informing her parents of her intention and hearing about the arrival of King Anikaratta. "Asitanicitamuduke": 'black' (asita) because of the color like sapphire and large bees; 'thick' (nicita) because of being densely packed; 'soft' (mudu) because of the touch like silk-cotton. "Cutting the hair with a sword" means cutting her own hair with a well-sharpened sword. "Closing the palace" means closing the auspicious chamber in the palace where she lived and locking its door. "Enters the first jhāna" means placing her hair cut by the sword in front of her, developing the reflection on foulness (paṭikkūlamanasikāra) upon that hair, and after gaining mastery (vasībhāva) over the first jhāna that arose from the sign (nimitta) as it appeared, she entered the meditative attainment.

The meaning is that Sumedhā entered jhāna in that palace. "Develops the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā)" means that after emerging from jhāna, using jhāna as a basis and establishing insight (vipassanā), she thoroughly develops the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) by way of "Whatever form...", etc. It should be understood that by taking the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering (dukkhasaññā) and others are also included here.

"Maṇikanakabhūsitango" means one whose body is adorned with golden garland ornaments variegated with jewels.

"Authority in the kingdom" and so on are demonstrations of the manner of entreaty. There, "authority" (āṇā) means sovereignty. "Issariya" means fame and the accomplishment of wealth. "Bhogā sukhā" means the enjoyment of sensual pleasures that are desirable and pleasing. "You are now a young maiden" is what is meant.

"My kingdom is surrendered to you" means "My entire kingdom of three yojanas is surrendered to you; accept that kingdom and enjoy the riches." (Sumedhā reflected:) "Indeed, this king is inviting me only with sensual pleasures."
292:
Do not be dejected. "Give gifts" means to provide grand offerings to recluses and brahmins as you desire. Your parents, having heard of your intention to ordain, have fallen into suffering and distress; therefore, they indulge in sensual pleasures. Serve those parents as well, and free their minds from suffering. This is how the connection of the meaning of the words should be understood here.

"Do not delight in sensual pleasures" means do not delight in objective sensuality (vatthukāma) and subjective sensuality (kilesakāma). Furthermore, observe the danger and fault in those sensual pleasures with the eye of wisdom, following my words.

"Cātuddīpa" refers to the ruler of the four great islands, such as Jambudīpa. "Mandhātu" is the name of a king who was the foremost, the supreme, among those who enjoy sensual pleasures. Thus, the Blessed One said: "Just as Rāhu is the foremost among those with an individual existence, Mandhātu is the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures." King Mandhātu spent 84,000 years in childhood play, 84,000 years as viceroy, and 84,000 years as a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), enjoying pleasures similar to those of the gods. Even after enjoying heavenly bliss in the Tāvatiṃsa realm for a duration equal to the lifespan of thirty-six Sakkas, he passed away still unsatisfied with sensual pleasures. The wishes of King Mandhātu were not fulfilled, and his craving for sensual pleasures did not reach an end.

"Even if it rained the seven gems" means that even if the rain-god were to rain down the seven gems, pervading the ten directions and all around according to the wishes of men—just as it rained for the Great King Mandhātu—even then, there is no satisfaction in sensual pleasures; humans die while still unsatisfied. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Not by a rain of coins is satisfaction found in sensual pleasures."

Sensual pleasures are like a sword and a chopping block because of the sense of being oppressed. They are like a snake's head because of the sense of being fearful. They are like a grass torch because of the sense of burning repeatedly. Therefore, it is said, "anudahanti" (they burn repeatedly). They are like a skeleton because of the sense of having little gratification.

"Mahāvisa" means they are like great poisons such as Halāhala. "Aghamūla" means they are the root or cause of misery (agha). Therefore, it is said, "dukkhapphala" (having suffering as their fruit).

They are like a fruit-bearing tree because of the sense of breaking limbs and parts of the body. They are like a piece of meat because of the sense of being common to many. They are like a dream because of the sense of appearing only momentarily and because of deceiving like an illusion.
293:
Therefore, it is said, 'they are deceptive,' meaning they have the nature of deceiving. 'They are like borrowed goods' means they are like borrowed items because of their temporary nature.

They are like spears and stakes because of their nature of piercing. They are called 'disease' because of their nature of causing pain and because suffering is easily obtained through them. They are called 'boils' (gaṇḍa) because the impurities of defilements flow from them. They are called 'calamity' (agha) because of their nature of producing suffering. They are called 'destruction' (nigha) because they lead to death. They are like a pit of glowing coals because of their nature of burning intensely. They are called 'danger' and 'execution' (vadha) because they are the cause of fear and because there are many executioners; thus should sensual pleasures (kāma) be understood.

'They are declared as obstacles' means that the Buddhas and others who possess vision have taught that 'they create obstacles to the path to heaven and the path to Nibbāna.' Saying 'Go forth,' he dismissed King Anīkaratta along with his retinue.

'What good can another do for me?' means what benefit can another person possibly provide for me while my own head, the highest limb, is constantly burning with the eleven fires? Therefore, it is said, 'while aging and death follow.' Effort should be made to destroy and eradicate that aging and death, which is like the burning of one's head.

'Chamaṃ' means on the ground. 'Spoke these words' refers to the words that arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega), such as 'Long is the saṃsāra for fools.'

'Long is the saṃsāra for fools' means that saṃsāra, which is the continuous succession of the aggregates (khandha) and bases (āyatana) consisting of the round of defilements, kamma, and results, is very long for the blind fools who do not understand the truth; it cannot be delimited even by the Buddha's knowledge. Just as the prior end of the continuity of existence is not known because ignorance (avijjā) and craving (taṇhā) are not cut off, so too is the latter end. 'They weep again and again' refers to those who weep repeatedly due to sorrow. By this, he demonstrates that their ignorance and craving are not yet severed.

'Tears, milk, and blood' refers to the tears of those who weep when struck by the loss of relatives and so on, the milk drunk from a mother's breast during infancy, and the blood shed when killed by enemies (all of which are vast). 'Because the beginning of saṃsāra is not known' is said because even when searching with knowledge, the beginning of saṃsāra cannot be found. Reflect on how much living beings have wandered in this long period of saṃsāra; contemplate and reflect on the accumulation of skeletons.

My foul body is like a worm; it is impure, oozing with putrid fluids, foul-smelling, terrifying, and like a corpse. Fools wrongly cling to it as 'my body'; it is like a leather bag filled with rot. Putrid liquids flow from it many times, and it is full of excrement and filth. I remain aware of this corpse, which is as loathsome as a worm, smeared with flesh and blood, the dwelling place of many worms, and the food for crows and vultures. Why is this corpse being given in marriage?

Before long, this body will be devoid of consciousness and carried to the cemetery. Disgusted relatives will discard it like a useless log. Even parents will abandon this corpse in the cemetery to be food for dogs and jackals, and then bathe themselves out of disgust. How could the assembly of relatives not be disgusted? Fools cling with craving to this essence-less corpse of a body, which is full of saliva and excrement, and is a collection of bones and sinews. If one were to dissect this corpse and look inside, even one's own mother would be unable to bear the foul smell and would be disgusted.

Why should I desire marriage, I who rightly contemplate the conditioned phenomena (saṅkhata)—the aggregates, elements, and bases—which are full of suffering and rooted in birth (jāti)? Let three hundred spears fall upon my body every single day; if the suffering of the round of rebirths would end through such pain, then being pierced by spears for a hundred years would be noble indeed. One who knows the words of the Blessed One can endure such suffering. Long is the saṃsāra only for the fools who do not know the Dhamma.

In the realms of devas, humans, animals, asuras, petas, and hell, there are immeasurable oppressions and killings. For beings suffering in the four lower realms, there is no refuge; even in the celestial realms, there is no ultimate security. There is no happiness superior to the bliss of Nibbāna. Those who strive to abandon birth and death in the Dispensation of the Buddha reach Nibbāna.

'O parents... I shall go forth and become a monastic this very day. What is the use of these essence-less sensual pleasures? I am weary of sensual pleasures, which are like dog vomit; I have made them like a palm tree cut down at the root.' Thus spoke Princess Sumedhā to her parents. King Anīkaratta arrived from the city of Vāraṇavatī as the time for the wedding approached. Then Sumedhā cut her dark, soft hair with a knife, locked the door of her room, and while entering the first jhāna, she developed the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā). King Anīkaratta, adorned with jewels, ascended the palace and pleaded with joined palms:

'All my sovereign power and wealth are now in your hands. You are still young, so please enjoy sensual pleasures. In this world, sensual pleasure is difficult to obtain. I grant you a kingdom of three yojanas. Give alms and live happily; do not be dejected,' he said.
294:
Now, in order to show the abundance of the faults of Saṃsāra by way of similes, he spoke the verse beginning with "Remember the four oceans." In that verse, "sara caturodadhi upanīte assuthanyarudhiramhi" means: For each and every one of these beings wandering in the beginningless Saṃsāra, the four great oceans are cited as a comparison by the Buddhas to the amount of tears shed, milk drunk, and blood flowed throughout Saṃsāra; remember those oceans. "Ekakappamaṭṭhīnaṃ sañcayaṃ vipulena samaṃ" means: Remember the pile of bones of a single person produced within a single aeon (kappa), which is compared to Mount Vepulla.

In connection with this matter:
"The pile of bones of a single person produced within a single aeon, if heaped up, would be a mountain-like mass; so said the Great Sage (the Buddha).
That great Mount Vepulla, which is said to be the pile of bones, clearly exists to the north of Gijjhakūṭa Mountain in Giribbaja of the Magadha country."

The earth of Jambudīpa is cited as a simile. "Kolaṭṭhimattaguḷikā mātā mātusveva nappahontī" means: If the great earth called Jambudīpa were made into small pellets the size of jujube seeds (kola) and if one were to count them saying, "This is my mother, this is my grandmother," those pellets would not be enough for the number of mothers and grandmothers. While the mothers and grandmothers of a being wandering in the beginningless Saṃsāra would not yet be exhausted, those pellets alone would reach an end and be depleted. In this way, reflect upon the earth of Jambudīpa being cited as a simile to show the length of Saṃsāra.

"Tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ" refers to grass, wood, branches, and leaves. "Upanītaṃ" means cited as a simile. "Anamataggato" is because of the beginningless nature of Saṃsāra. "Caturaṅgulikā ghaṭikā" refers to pieces about four inches in size. "Pitupitusveva nappahontī" means those pieces would not be enough for the number of fathers and grandfathers. The meaning is: If all the grass, wood, branches, and leaves in this world were made into four-inch pieces, and if one were to count them saying, "This is my father, this is my grandfather," those pieces alone would reach an end and be depleted, but the fathers and grandfathers of a being wandering in the beginningless Saṃsāra would not be exhausted. In this way, remember the grass, wood, branches, and leaves being cited to show the length of Saṃsāra. In this place, however—
295:
"Monks, this Saṃsāra is without a discoverable beginning. A first point is not discerned for beings hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving who roam and wander on. What do you think, monks, which is more: the stream of tears you have shed while roaming and wandering this long time—weeping and wailing because of being united with the unloved and separated from the loved—or the water in the four great oceans?" and so forth; the Anamatagga Pāḷi should be cited. "Remember the turtle blind in both eyes" means constantly remember the turtle that is blind in both eyes. "A single hole in a yoke circling by the force of the wind in the eastern ocean and other (western, northern, southern) oceans" means a single hole in a yoke that revolves by the force of the wind in the eastern ocean or in the other western, northern, and southern oceans. "The head of that turtle entering that hole" means remember the blind turtle's head entering the hole of the yoke when it surfaces once every hundred years. "The simile for obtaining human birth" means, just as in the appearance of Buddhas and the teaching of the Dhamma, remember with wisdom all this as a simile for obtaining human status, because that human status is of a nature extremely difficult to obtain and because it is of a nature that transcends the fear of dread. For it has been said: "Monks, suppose a man were to throw a yoke with a single hole into the great ocean," and so forth.

"Remember the body which is like a lump of foam" means remember the impurity, foul smell, and loathsomeness of the body, which is like a lump of foam because it cannot withstand pressure, which is called the body (or "the foul one") because it is a collection of many misfortunes, and which is without essence because it is devoid of permanent substance and so on. "See the aggregates as impermanent" means look with the eye of wisdom at all five aggregates of clinging as impermanent in the sense of being destroyed after having come to be. "Remember the hells with much affliction" means constantly remember the eight great hells and the sixteen prominent (Ussada) hells with their much affliction, much suffering, and great pain.

"Remember those who increase the cemetery" means constantly remember the beings who, by repeatedly taking birth in various existences, repeatedly increase the cemetery or the cremation ground. Or, if the Pāḷi is "vaḍḍhanto," it should be construed as "you, increasing [the cemetery]." "The dangers of crocodiles" refers to the dangers of gluttony (being "belly-led") by doing what should not be done for the sake of nourishing the stomach. For it has been said: "Monks, 'danger of crocodiles' is a designation for gluttony." Remember.
296:
The Four Noble Truths are: 'This is the Noble Truth of Suffering... This is the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.' Reflect and contemplate upon these Four Noble Truths as they truly are.

Thus, the princess, having shown the danger in sensual pleasures and in saṃsāra by means of recollecting in various ways, now says 'Amataṃhi vijjamāne' and so forth to show that danger by way of exclusion (vyatireka). In that verse, 'Amataṃhi vijjamāne' means while the Deathless Nibbāna, which is the True Dhamma brought by the Buddha through His great compassion, is clearly present. 'Kiṃ tava pañcakaṭukena pītena' means: What benefit is there for you in consuming the taste of the five sensual pleasures, which are like five bitters, because they are accompanied by sharp suffering, distress, and intense fever in the five stages of seeking, acquiring, guarding, enjoying, and the ripening of results? To make the aforementioned meaning clearer, she says: 'Sabbā hi kāmaratiyo, kaṭukatarā pañcakaṭukena.' It means all delights in sensual pleasures are far more bitter than the five bitters.

'Ye pariḷāhā' means those sensual pleasures which have great destruction because they occur with the fever of defilements in the present and the fever of results in the future. 'Jalitā kuthitā kampitā santāpitā' means they are ablaze and boiling with the eleven fires, causing those possessed of them to tremble and burn.

'Asapattamhi' refers to renunciation (nekkhamma) which is free from enemies. 'Samāne' means while it exists. Having said 'Bahusapattā' (having many enemies), she says 'Rājaggi' and so forth to show those many enemies. Because they are common to kings, fire, thieves, water, and unpleasant heirs, the metaphor is applied to those sensual pleasures themselves.

'Yesu vadhabandho' means in those sensual pleasures, because of them, there occur afflictions such as killing and beating, and bindings such as being fettered in chains. 'Kāmesu' and so forth is to clarify the stated meaning. Therein, 'hi' is a particle indicating cause. Because beings experience the suffering of killing and binding in sensual pleasures due to the cause of sensual pleasures, she says 'Asakāmā.' It means these sensual pleasures are the nature of the ignoble, being low and base. There is also a variant reading 'Ahakāmā,' which has the same meaning. The word 'aha' is a synonym for baseness, as in 'ahalokitthiyo nāma' and so forth.
297:
'Ādīpita' means ablaze. 'Tiṇukkā' means a torch made of grass. 'Those beings who do not renounce sensual pleasures but always grasp them, those sensual pleasures burn them' means they cause them to burn both in the present and in the future.

'Mā appakassa hetu' means do not forsake or discard the vast, lofty, and sublime supramundane happiness for the sake of a trifling sensual pleasure which is like the fleeting enjoyment of a flower. 'Mā puthulomova baḷisaṃ gilitvā' means do not suffer later by being unable to renounce sensual pleasures, like the fish named 'Puthuloma' who meets destruction by swallowing a hook out of greed for bait; do not come to ruin later.

'Sunakhova saṅkhalābaddho' means just as a dog bound by a leather strap cannot go elsewhere because it is firmly tied to a post and must circle around that very spot, so too are you bound by the craving for sensual pleasures. Even if you now delight in sensual pleasures, restrain your faculties. In the sentence 'Kāhinti khu taṃ kāmā, chātā sunakhaṃva caṇḍālā,' 'khu' is merely a particle. It means those sensual pleasures will treat you just as hungry outcasts (caṇḍālas) would bring destruction upon a dog if they caught one.

'Apari mitañca dukkhaṃ' refers to the bodily suffering in hell and so forth, which cannot be measured as 'this much.' 'Bahūni ca cittadomanassāni' refers to the many and various mental distresses and sorrows that arise in the mind. 'Anubhohisi' means you will experience them. 'Kāmayutto' refers to one who is joined with sensual pleasures, one who cannot renounce them. 'Paṭinissaja adduve kāme' means renounce and remove the impermanent sensual pleasures.

'Jarāmaraṇabyādhigahitā, sabbā sabbattha jātiyo' means births in all states of existence, distinguished by being low and so forth, are oppressed by old age, death, and disease; they are not free from these dangers. Therefore, the connection is: while there is Nibbāna which is free from old age, what use do you have for sensual pleasures which are not free from old age and so forth?

Thus, having shown the danger in sensual pleasures and in states of existence by way of showing the virtues of Nibbāna, she now spoke two verses beginning with 'Idamajaraṃ' wishing to show only the virtues of Nibbāna that have arisen. Therein, 'Idamajaraṃ' means this Nibbāna alone is ageless because there is no old age in itself and because it is not a cause for old age once attained. 'Idamamaraṃ' here also means deathless.
298:
This is also in the same manner. 'This Dhamma is free from aging, free from death'—she speaks by way of praise, combining these two. 'Pada' (the state) refers to Nibbāna, which should be attained by those wishing to be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) by going forth as monastics. It is called 'Asoka' (sorrowless) because of the absence of causes for sorrow and the absence of sorrow itself. It is called 'Asapatta' (without enemies) because of the absence of things that act like enemies. It is called 'Asambādha' (without obstruction) because of the absence of the crowding of defilements. It is called 'Akhalita' (without stumbling) because of the absence of misconduct known as stumbling. It is called 'Abhaya' (fearless) because of the total absence of dangers such as self-reproach and the danger of the round of rebirths. It is called 'Nirupatāpa' (without distress) because of the absence of defilements that cause suffering and distress. All this is said in reference to the Great Deathless Nibbāna. When that Nibbāna appears to one through the manner of what has been heard traditionally, she said 'this Dhamma' as if showing it directly to them.

'This deathless has been attained by many' means that this deathless Nibbāna has been attained, known, and personally realized by many Noble Ones (Ariyas) beginning with the Buddha. It is said not only in reference to their attainment but also to the fact that it can still be obtained today, can be attained now, and that it is possible to attain it. To the question 'Who can obtain it?', she said: 'Whoever strives by appropriate means.' This should be understood as: 'Whoever, standing in the advice given by the teacher, strives with appropriate methods and makes the right effort, can obtain it.' In saying that one who does not strive is unable to obtain it, the meaning is that if one does not strive appropriately, such a person who does not strive can never obtain it.

'Sumedhā speaks thus' means that in the manner described, Princess Sumedhā gives a Dhamma discourse that illustrates her own spiritual urgency (saṃvega) regarding the round of rebirths and causes disenchantment with sensual pleasures. 'Without finding delight in conditioned things (saṅkhāras)' means without finding even a slight delight in the process of formations. 'Persuading King Anikaratte to understand' means making King Anikaratte understand. 'She also threw her hair on the ground' means she threw and discarded the hair she had cut with her sword onto the ground.

'The King pleaded with her father' means that King Anikaratte pleaded with King Koñca, the father of Sumedhā. As for how he pleaded, he said: 'Release Sumedhā to go forth as a monastic so that she may see the true liberation.' The meaning is: 'Please allow Princess Sumedhā to go forth; having gone forth, may she be one who sees the true Nibbāna without distortion.'
299:
'Sokabhayabhītā' (frightened by sorrow and fear) refers to those who are afraid due to causes such as separation from relatives and the danger of the entire round of rebirths, and who are terrified by the power of noble knowledge. 'Sikkhamānāyā' means that while still a probationary nun (sikkhamānā), she realized the six direct knowledges (abhiññās); moreover, she realized the highest fruit, Arahantship.

'That was a wonder and a marvel, the Nibbāna of the princess' means that for Princess Sumedhā, the extinguishment of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna) was a wonderful and marvelous event. Regarding 'How [did she speak] by the accomplishment of the six direct knowledges?', if asked—she spoke of her past conduct in previous lives just before her final extinguishment of the aggregates (khandha-parinibbāna); it should be understood as she spoke it.

To show how Sumedhā spoke of her past lives, the passage beginning with 'In the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana' was said. In that context, 'In the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana' means when the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Koṇāgamana had arisen in the world. 'In a newly established monastery for the Saṅgha' means in a monastery (ārāma) newly built for the sake of the Saṅgha. 'Three women friends, we gave the gift of a monastery' means that we three friends—Dhanañjānī, Khemā, and I—gave the gift of a monastery, an ārāma, to the Saṅgha.

'Ten times, a hundred times' means that by the power of that gift of a monastery, we were reborn ten times among the devas; after being reborn among humans, we were reborn again a hundred times among the devas; after that, being reborn among humans, we were reborn again a thousand times among the devas; after that, being reborn among humans, we were reborn again ten thousand times among the devas. As for being reborn among humans, it goes without saying. Thus, there is no need to even mention the number of times we were reborn among humans; the meaning is that we were reborn many thousands and tens of thousands of times.

'We were of great power among the devas' means that when reborn in the heavens, we were of great power and great majesty among those various groups of devas. 'What need to speak of the human state?' means that when obtaining human birth, there is no need to even mention our great power. Now, wishing to show that extraordinary great power even in that human life, she said: 'I was the chief queen of the one with seven treasures, the woman-treasure.' In that statement, 'one with seven treasures' refers to a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) who possesses the seven treasures such as the wheel-treasure; (the meaning is that she was the chief queen) of that Universal Monarch.
300:
I was once a person who was like a jewel among women, endowed with such qualities as being free from the six faults, possessed of the five beauties, surpassing human beauty but not yet reaching divine beauty.

'So hetu' refers to the donation of a monastery (vihāra-dāna) to the Saṅgha during the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana; that donation is the cause of the aforementioned divine splendor. 'So pabhavo taṃ mūlaṃ' are simply synonyms for that same cause. 'Sāva sāsane khantī' refers to the receptive insight (nijjhānakkhanti) that contemplates the Dhamma in this teaching of the Buddha. 'Taṃ paṭhamasamodhānaṃ' means the first encounter or the first meeting with the Dhamma of the Teacher’s dispensation. Because one will reach Nibbāna at the end of such delight in the dispensation, the cause is metaphorically called 'Nibbāna' by way of its fruit. These four verses are also included in the Apadāna Pāḷi as they serve to clarify the hagiography (apadāna) of the Therī.

In the final verse, 'Evaṃ karonti' means that others practice and follow just as I have practiced in previous lives and in this life. Who are those who practice thus? It is said: 'Ye saddahanti vacanaṃ anomapaññassa'—those individuals who believe the words of the Fully Enlightened One, who is possessed of perfect wisdom reaching the limit of all that should be known, thinking 'It is just so,' they practice and follow in this way. Now, to show their exalted practice, it is said: 'Nibbindanti bhavagate, nibbinditvā virajjanti.' Its meaning is: those who truly believe the words of the Blessed One, while practicing the path of purity, become weary through insight-wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) of all conditioned things (saṅkhāra) existing in the three realms of existence. Having become weary, they become entirely dispassionate through the Noble Path (ariya-magga) and are liberated from all existence. When the dispassionate Noble Path is attained, they are indeed liberated.

Thus, these verses of the Therīs, ending with those of Sumedhā Therī, are collected here together due to their similarity in nature, amounting to seventy-three in number. In terms of recitation sections (bhāṇavāra), there are more than six hundred verses of the Therīs. Just as all these Therīs are of one kind by being female disciples (sāvikā) of the Fully Enlightened One, they are also of one kind by being Asekhas (Perfected Ones), having the bar [of ignorance] lifted, the moat [of saṃsāra] filled, the pillar [of craving] pulled up, being boltless, having laid down the burden, being unfettered, and having lived the ten noble abodes (ariya-vāsa). Indeed, they have abandoned the five factors, are endowed with the six factors, and have a single guard.
301:
(The Community of Bhikkhunīs) is of one kind according to the method (found in Dīgha Nikāya 3, 360) such as: having the four reliances, having individual truths discarded, having searchings properly tranquilized, having unsullied intentions, having tranquilized bodily formations, being well-liberated in mind, and being well-liberated in wisdom.

They are of two kinds by way of being 'in the presence' (sammukhā) or 'away from the presence' (parammukhā). Those such as Mahāpajāpatigotamī, who were born into the Noble birth while the Teacher was still alive, are called direct disciples (sammukhā-sāvikā). Those who attained the distinction after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna are called indirect disciples (parammukhā-sāvikā) because, although the Dhamma-body of the Teacher is present, his physical body is not. Likewise, they are of two kinds by way of liberation both ways (ubhatobhāga-vimutti) and liberation by wisdom (paññā-vimutti). However, those mentioned in this Pāḷi text are all liberated both ways. Likewise, they are of two kinds by way of having an 'Apadāna' (hagiography/past deeds) or not. Those who have performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) under previous Fully Enlightened Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Disciple-Buddhas are called 'Sāpadāna' (with Apadāna). Those who do not have such are called 'Nāpadāna' (without Apadāna). Likewise, there are two kinds: those who received ordination from the Teacher and those who received ordination from the Saṅgha. Mahāpajāpatigotamī, who received ordination by accepting the eight Garudhamma (Heavy Rules), is called one who received ordination from the Teacher (Satthuladdhūpasampadā) because she received it directly from him. All others received ordination from the Saṅgha. They are further divided into two: those ordained by one side (ekatoupasampannā) and those ordained by both sides (ubhatoupasampannā). Among them, the five hundred Sakyan princesses who went forth with Mahāpajāpatigotamī are called 'ordained by one side' because they received ordination only from the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, excluding Mahāpajāpatigotamī. The others are called 'ordained by both sides' because they received ordination from both Saṅghas.

The pair 'Ehi Bhikkhunī' (Come, nun) is not found here like the pair 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, monk). Why? Because such a form of ordination does not exist for Bhikkhunīs. If that is so, what about the words spoken in the verses of Subhaddā Therī and Kuṇဍalakesā Therī: 'Having knelt and paid homage, I performed the añjali in his presence; "Come, Bhaddā," he said to me, and that was my ordination'? And likewise in the Apadāna: 'Then, being requested, the Leader said, "Come, Bhaddā"; then I was ordained, and I saw a little water'?
302:
What does this statement mean? This was not said in reference to the higher ordination (upasampadā) obtained through the status of an 'Ehi Bhikkhunī'. Rather, because it is the cause of the higher ordination, the Blessed One's command is stated as 'The higher ordination occurred for me.'

Thus, it is stated in the Commentary: 'The Teacher said to me, he commanded me: "Come, lady, go to the nunnery and receive the going-forth and higher ordination in the presence of the bhikkhunīs." Because that command of the Teacher was the cause for my higher ordination, it became my higher ordination.' In this way, it should be understood that the meaning of the Apadāna verse is also explained.

This being so, what is the meaning of this phrase 'Ehi Bhikkhunī' in the Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga? It is a statement showing the non-existence of the higher ordination of bhikkhunīs through the status of 'Ehi Bhikkhunī'. This is because such a type of higher ordination does not exist among bhikkhunīs. If that is the case, why is 'Ehi Bhikkhunī' explained in detail in the Vibhaṅga? It is because it falls within the scope of the method of teaching (desanānaya). This 'falling within the scope' means that although it might be obtainable in some places, it is not brought forward here.

For example, in the Abhidhamma, in the explanation of the mind-element (manodhātu), the factors of absorption (jhānaṅga) that could be obtained are not extracted and shown because they fall within the scope of the five-fold consciousness. This is because they are impossible in certain teachings. Just as in that same Abhidhamma, in the explanation of the bases (vatthu), the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is included by way of comprehensive inclusion even though it is not obtainable in some places. The same applies to the explanation of the 'aeon-stayer' (thitakappī). As it is said:

'What kind of person is an aeon-stayer? If a person is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), and it is the time for the world-system to be consumed by fire, that world-system will not burn as long as this person has not realized the fruit of stream-entry.'

Similarly, here too, it should be understood by way of inclusion even though it is not obtainable. This is merely a hypothetical statement: if the Blessed One were to say 'Ehi Bhikkhunī' to any woman worthy of the status of a bhikkhunī, then the status of a bhikkhunī would indeed occur in that way. Why then did the Blessed One not speak thus? It is because there were no individuals who possessed the necessary specific merit (adhikāra). Those who say, 'Because they are not always present nearby,' and give the reason, 'Only monks usually live near the Teacher and are always present; therefore, only those monks deserve to be addressed as "Ehi Bhikkhu," not the bhikkhunīs'—that is merely their opinion. This is because being near or far from the Teacher does not determine whether one is a capable (bhabba) or incapable (abhabba) person. For it was said by the Blessed One:
303:
Monks, even if a monk were to follow closely behind me, holding the corner of my outer robe (saṅghāṭi), stepping in my every footstep, yet if he is covetous, with strong passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind of ill-will, with corrupt thoughts, muddle-minded, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind and uncontrolled faculties, then he is far from me, and I am far from him. What is the reason for that? Monks, that monk does not see the Dhamma; not seeing the Dhamma, he does not see me.

Monks, even if a monk were to live a hundred leagues away, yet if he is not covetous, without strong passion for sensual pleasures, with a mind free from ill-will, with uncorrupt thoughts, with established mindfulness, with clear comprehension, concentrated, with a one-pointed mind and restrained faculties, then he is near to me, and I am near to him. What is the reason for that? Monks, that monk sees the Dhamma; seeing the Dhamma, he sees me. (Thus he said).

Therefore, being near or far from the Teacher in terms of physical location is not the cause. However, because they had not performed the necessary specific merit (adhikāra) in the past, bhikkhunīs are not suitable for that 'Ehi Bhikkhu' status. Thus it is said: 'The Ehi-bhikkhunī-duka (the status of Ehi Bhikkhunī) is not obtainable in this Dispensation.' In this way, there are two kinds (of bhikkhunīs).

There are three kinds: Chief Female Disciples (aggasāvikā), Great Female Disciples (mahāsāvikā), and Ordinary Female Disciples (pakatisāvikā). Among them, these two elders, Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā, are called Chief Female Disciples. In fact, all the elder nuns who are Arahants (khīṇāsava), having perfected virtue and so forth, with minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), having developed the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) as they really are, and having entirely exhausted the defilements through the sequence of the paths, dwell in the highest fruit of Arahantship. However, just as those who have attained vision (diṭṭhippatta) are preferred over those liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), and those liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta) over those liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta) due to the distinction achieved through the preliminary stage of meditation, similarly, because they have produced extraordinary qualities in their own mental continuities through the greatness of their initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) and the greatness of their past practice (pubbayoga), the female disciples who are great in virtue and so forth are called Great Female Disciples. Among those factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), because of having an appropriate initial aspiration which is the cause for the manifestation of the extraordinary function and power of right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) and right concentration (sammā-samādhi)—which are the leaders and heads—and because of the right practice (sammā-paṭipatti) cultivated respectfully, continuously, and for a long time, in due order, both in wisdom and in concentration...
304:
Those two (Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā) are also called Chief Female Disciples (Aggasāvikā) because they stand in the highest position, distinguished by all virtues. The Therīs such as Mahāpajāpatigotamī are called Great Female Disciples (Mahāsāvikā) because of the special virtues they attained through the greatness of their initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) and the greatness of their past exertion (pubbayoga). The remaining Therīs such as Tissā, Vīrā, and Dhīrā are called Ordinary Female Disciples (Pakatisāvikā) because they lack such greatness of aspiration and so forth. Unlike the Chief Female Disciples and Great Female Disciples, these Ordinary Female Disciples are not limited in number; indeed, they should be understood to number in the many hundreds and many thousands. Thus, there are three types according to the classification of Chief Female Disciples and so on. Similarly, there are three types according to the classification of emptiness-liberation (suññatavimokkha) and so on.

There are four types by the classification of the path of practice (paṭipadā) and so on; five types by the classification of the predominance of faculties (indriya); likewise, five types by the classification of practice (paṭipatti) and so on; six types by the power of signless-liberation (animittavimutta) and so on; seven types by the classification of inclination (adhimutti); eight types by the classification of the burden of practice (dhurapaṭipadā) and so on; and nine or ten types by the classification of liberation (vimutti). When these Therīs are classified by the aforementioned types of burdens (dhura), there are twenty; when classified by the path of practice (paṭipadā), there are forty. Again, when classified by both the types of practice and the types of burdens, there are eighty. Alternatively, when classified by emptiness-liberation (suññatavimutta) and so on, there are two hundred and forty. Again, when classified by the predominance of faculties, there are one thousand two hundred. In this way, the state of being divided into many classifications should be understood only by the power of the virtues of those Therīs. This is a summary here; the details should be taken in the same manner as already stated in the commentary on the Theragāthā below.

## The Elucidation of the Verses of Sumedhā Therī is finished.

## The Elucidation of the Great Section (Mahānipāta) is finished.
305:
## Concluding Verses

By this much—

The noble Elders such as the Venerable Subhūti, and the Elder Nuns (Therīs), young and old, who are the heart-born sons and daughters of the Teacher, the King of Dhamma, born from his mouth, heirs created by the Dhamma, endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), who have completed their task and are free from taints (āsavas)—

They uttered those verses by way of declaring their attainment of Arahantship and so forth. Collecting all those verses together, the Great Elders of equal virtue compiled them as the 'Theragāthā' and 'Therīgāthā'.

To clarify the meaning of those verses, I began this commentary (atthasaṃvaṇṇanā) relying on the methods of the ancient commentaries (porāṇāṭṭhakathā). This commentary is named 'Paramatthadīpanī' because it elucidates the ultimate meanings (paramattha) in various places as appropriate. This commentary, complete with clear decisions and amounting to 92 recital units (bhāṇavāra) in the Pali text, has now reached its conclusion.

By the power of the merit I have acquired through composing this commentary, may all beings enter the Dispensation of the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) and, through the pure practice of morality and so forth, partake in the taste of liberation (vimuttirasa).

May the Dispensation of the Fully Enlightened One endure long in the world. May all living beings always have reverence for that Dispensation.

May the rain-god (deva) send down rain properly at the right time. May the King, the lord of the earth, delighting in the True Dhamma, rule the world only with righteousness (dhamma).

## Composed by the Teacher, Elder Dhammapāla, residing at the Badaratittha Monastery.
## The Elucidation of the Meaning of the Therīgāthā is finished.
## The Commentary on the Therīgāthā is finished.
